issue.page_hint: mini-case, paragraph beginning 'The rate comparison hides the memory geometry'
issue.quoted_clause: against 1 rps × 8.6 s ≈ 8.6 requests in flight per host (~32 GB of KV across both hosts against ~17 in flight)
issue.observed: The sentence compares ~32 GB of KV capacity across both hosts with ~17 requests in flight, but each full-context request is stated to require 24.9 GB of KV. At 17 requests in flight, the KV demand is ~423 GB, not ~32 GB. The ~32 GB figure is the remaining capacity, not the demand. The text therefore understates the shortfall by roughly an order of magnitude.
issue.evidence: Per host: 16 GB KV capacity after reserve. Two hosts: 32 GB. One 9,500-token FP16-KV request: 24.9 GB. 32 / 24.9 ≈ 1.29 requests total, or 0.64 per host. At 1 rps per host and 8.6 s service time, Little's law gives 8.6 in flight per host, 17.2 across both hosts. 17.2 × 24.9 GB ≈ 428 GB. The stated ~32 GB is capacity, not demand; the comparison is dimensionally and numerically wrong.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case conflates remaining KV capacity with in-flight KV demand and then compares them as if they were the same quantity.
issue.correction: Rewrite the sentence to separate capacity from demand: '~32 GB of KV capacity remains across both hosts, while ~17 full-context requests in flight would require ~423 GB of KV; the configuration therefore misses the full-context KV budget by roughly 13×.' If the intended comparison is per host, state '~16 GB capacity vs ~8.6 in-flight requests requiring ~214 GB' and make the shortfall explicit.
issue.acceptance_test: The revised sentence must state both the available KV capacity and the KV demand at the stated concurrency, with units, and must show that demand exceeds capacity by the correct factor. A reader must not be able to infer that 32 GB is sufficient for 17 full-context requests.

issue.quoted_clause: The token arithmetic alone therefore does not send this startup to the API; it points to self-hosting. ... The CTO did not buy the servers. ... A team that cannot say that, or that has a second engineer to spare, runs the same numbers and buys the servers.
issue.observed: The mini-case first establishes that the two-server configuration cannot serve the canonical full-context workload at all: ~16 GB of KV per host holds 0.64 of one 9,500-token request. It then concludes that the token arithmetic 'points to self-hosting' and that a team with a second engineer 'runs the same numbers and buys the servers.' That conclusion contradicts the capability gate. A second engineer does not add KV capacity; buying two servers that cannot hold one full-context request per host is not made viable by extra staff.
issue.evidence: The text itself says: '~16 GB of KV holds 0.64 of one 9,500-token request, so this two-host configuration cannot serve the canonical full-context workload at all.' The later verdict treats the opportunity cost of the engineer's time as the only remaining decision lever and says a second engineer makes self-hosting viable. That is false for the stated configuration: the binding constraint is KV capacity, not staff time.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case does not carry the capability-gate failure through to the final decision narrative. It switches from 'this configuration is infeasible' to 'the decision is about opportunity cost' without requiring a feasible configuration.
issue.correction: Make the capability gate the primary verdict. State explicitly: 'Do not buy two servers for this workload; they fail the full-context KV capacity gate. The TCO and opportunity-cost comparison below is illustrative only for a feasible configuration (e.g., more hosts, shorter context, or a different KV precision). A second engineer does not fix the KV shortfall.' Then present the $90K opportunity-cost threshold only as a conditional comparison for a configuration that has already passed the capability gate.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case's final verdict must say that the two-server configuration is infeasible for the canonical full-context workload and must not recommend buying it merely because a second engineer is available. The opportunity-cost threshold must be explicitly conditional on a feasible configuration.

issue.page_hint: mini-case, paragraph beginning 'On Mode 1's ~$10K/mo staff alloc'
issue.quoted_clause: On Mode 1's ~$10K/mo staff alloc the self-host cost is ~$23.9K/mo and the gap ~$80.1K/mo.
issue.observed: The text has just said that Mode 1's ~$10K/mo staff alloc is for 21 hosts and that the mini-case must be re-priced on one staffing basis before comparing. It then applies the entire 21-host staff alloc to a two-host deployment. That is not a like-for-like staffing basis: $10K/mo for 21 hosts is ~$476/host/mo; for two hosts the scaled alloc would be ~$0.95K/mo, not $10K/mo. The resulting $23.9K/mo self-host cost and $80.1K/mo gap are therefore not on the stated basis.
issue.evidence: The text says: 'Mode 1's mature-operator alloc (~$10K/mo for 21 hosts) — re-price on one staffing basis before comparing.' It then uses the full $10K/mo for a two-host case. If the alloc is per fleet, it should be scaled; if it is a fixed minimum staff cost, that must be stated. As written, the comparison mixes a 21-host staff alloc with a 2-host deployment.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case uses an absolute fleet-level staff alloc without scaling it to the two-host deployment, despite having just warned against basis mismatches.
issue.correction: Either scale the Mode 1 alloc to the two-host deployment (e.g., ~$0.95K/mo if linear in hosts) and state that assumption, or explicitly say 'using the full 21-host staff alloc as a conservative upper bound for the two-host case' and explain why that is conservative. Do not present the resulting gap as a like-for-like comparison without that qualification.
issue.acceptance_test: The revised text must state the staffing basis explicitly and must not compare a 21-host staff alloc with a 2-host deployment without either scaling it or labeling it as a deliberate upper bound.

issue.quoted_clause: The break-even graph did not make the answer self-evident; it narrowed the whole decision to one labeled assumption
issue.observed: The break-even graph (Fig 16.1) is the canonical 21-host fleet at $155,816.93/mo with a ~7.5M req/mo crossover. The mini-case is a two-server startup at ~$40K/mo with a ~1.9M req/mo crossover. The graph does not plot the two-server scenario and does not contain the mini-case's break-even. Saying that 'the break-even graph' narrowed the mini-case decision is therefore misleading: the relevant break-even is the mini-case's own division, not the canonical graph.
issue.evidence: The mini-case computes its own break-even as '$40,000 ÷ $0.0208 ≈ 1.9M requests/month.' The figure caption and Note 16.1-1 describe the graph as the frozen 21-host self-host line at $155,816.93/mo crossing at ~7.5M req/mo. These are different scenarios and different crossovers.
issue.root_cause: The narrative refers to the canonical figure as if it were the mini-case's decision chart.
issue.correction: Replace 'The break-even graph did not make the answer self-evident' with 'The mini-case's own break-even division did not make the answer self-evident' or explicitly say that the canonical Fig 16.1 is a different scenario and is not the chart for the two-server case. If the figure is meant to be used, add the two-server line or marker to it.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case must not attribute its decision to a graph that does not plot its scenario. Either the graph must include the two-server case, or the text must refer to the mini-case's own calculation.

issue.page_hint: mini-case, paragraph beginning 'Request volume is not the lever'
issue.quoted_clause: the two hosts are sized for ~4 rps of rate only
issue.observed: Earlier the mini-case says '2 rps average is 1 rps per host, well inside the 40/21 ≈ 1.9 rps per host the canonical 21-host fleet sustains at its 40 rps peak.' If two hosts are sized for ~4 rps total, that is ~2 rps per host, which is slightly above the 1.9 rps/host canonical comparison. The '~4 rps' figure is not derived and is in mild tension with the earlier per-host comparison.
issue.evidence: 2 hosts × 1.9 rps/host ≈ 3.8 rps, which could be rounded to ~4 rps. But the text does not show that derivation, and the earlier sentence uses 1.9 rps/host as the benchmark. The reader cannot tell whether ~4 rps is a measured rate, a derived rate, or a rounded canonical rate.
issue.root_cause: The ~4 rps figure is introduced without derivation or a clear link to the earlier 1.9 rps/host comparison.
issue.correction: Either derive it ('2 hosts × ~1.9 rps/host ≈ 3.8 rps, rounded to ~4 rps') or replace it with the exact basis used. If it is a measured or assumed rate, label it as such.
issue.acceptance_test: The revised text must show where ~4 rps comes from and must be consistent with the earlier 1.9 rps/host comparison.

issue.quoted_clause: so the break-even is a set of crossing points, not a single value — not apples-to-apples
issue.observed: The phrase 'not apples-to-apples' is ambiguous. It is unclear whether it refers to the price points, the crossovers, the three cost modes, or the availability scopes. The caption already says the three modes are not compared on matched availability/SLO/warm-capacity assumptions; repeating 'not apples-to-apples' without an object weakens the caveat.
issue.evidence: The sentence lists a price band, one crossing per price point, and says the break-even is a set of crossing points. 'Not apples-to-apples' could be read as saying the price points are not comparable, which is not the intended point: each price point is a legitimate sensitivity case, but the crossovers are not a confidence interval.
issue.root_cause: The caveat uses a colloquial phrase without specifying what is being compared.
issue.correction: Replace 'not apples-to-apples' with a precise statement, e.g., 'these are alternative price scenarios, not a confidence interval or a single procurement threshold; the three cost modes are also not availability-matched (see below).'
issue.acceptance_test: The revised caveat must name the objects that are not comparable and must not leave 'not apples-to-apples' as an uninterpreted phrase.

issue.quoted_clause: TCO is the final gate in the design loop ... It settles which candidate survives
issue.observed: The same paragraph later says the surviving recommendation is conditional and that the candidate is 'screened, not committed.' 'It settles which candidate survives' overstates the role of TCO in this chapter, especially because the decision state explicitly says the candidate is not committable and four items are outstanding.
issue.evidence: The decision-state box says 'CANDIDATE SCREENED; NOT COMMITTABLE' and lists regional availability, failover, SLO-goodput, and matched-scope costs as pending. TCO cannot 'settle' the candidate while those gates are open.
issue.root_cause: The opening sentence uses a stronger verb than the chapter's own decision state supports.
issue.correction: Change to 'TCO is the final cost gate in the design loop; it screens candidates but does not by itself commit them' or similar. Reserve 'settles' for a candidate that has passed all gates.
issue.acceptance_test: The revised sentence must be consistent with the decision-state box: TCO screens, but does not commit, a candidate with outstanding availability, failover, SLO-goodput, and matched-scope items.

issue.quoted_clause: 68% of requests terminating in T=1, 25% in T=2, 5% in T=3, and 2% exceeding the turn limit (falling back to single-shot). That makes ... the 95th percentile T=3 (cumulative 68+25+5 = 98% by T=3).
issue.observed: The fallback population is counted inconsistently. If the 2% exceeding the turn limit fall back to single-shot, they are T=1, so the distribution becomes 70% T=1, 25% T=2, 5% T=3; cumulative at T=2 is 95%, making p95 T=2, not T=3. If the 2% are excluded, p95=T=3 only for the successful-request subpopulation, not for all requests.
issue.evidence: Fallback T=1: 68+2=70% at T=1; 70+25=95% by T=2; p95=T=2. At T=2, I=9,200+2×865+300=11,230 tokens; KV=11,230×2.62144 MB≈29.43 GB; C=436/29.43≈14.8, floor 14, not the printed 13.8/floor 13. Excluding fallback: p95 of successful requests is T=3, but overall p95 including fallback T=1 is T=2.
issue.root_cause: Population/denominator error: fallback requests are assigned to a separate tail while also being described as single-shot, and the percentile is computed on the wrong population.
issue.correction: Define explicitly whether fallback requests are T=1 or excluded. If T=1, p95=T=2 and update C≈14.8 (floor 14) and all downstream agentic host counts. If excluded, label the percentile as 'among successful requests' and carry the 2% fallback/failure rate separately. Recompute all T=3 stress-point numbers.
issue.acceptance_test: The turn distribution sums to 100% with fallback assigned; p95 is recomputed from that distribution; downstream C, W, and host counts are updated and consistent.

issue.quoted_clause: W_e2e ... ≈ 10 s planning round (Ch 4: retrieval ~0.12 s + prefill 1.08 s + decode 7.5 s, rounded)
issue.observed: The listed components sum to 0.12+1.08+7.5=8.70 s, not ≈10 s. The table and later prose use W_e2e≈10 s, leaving a 1.3 s unexplained gap.
issue.evidence: 0.12+1.08+7.5=8.70. Rounding 8.7 to one significant figure gives 9, not 10. If queue/tool/orchestration time is included, it is not named in the decomposition.
issue.root_cause: Numerical inconsistency / missing component in the W_e2e decomposition.
issue.correction: Change W_e2e to ≈8.7 s, or add and name the missing ~1.3 s (queue/tool/orchestration) and update all references. Keep W_GPU-exec=8.6 s and W_e2e distinct.
issue.acceptance_test: The sum of named components equals the stated W_e2e within rounding; all W_e2e references use the same value.

issue.quoted_clause: If user sessions must maintain conversation state (KV cache, accumulated tool outputs, retrieval context), the load balancer must route subsequent requests from the same user to the same host (sticky sessions).
issue.observed: Conversation state can be externalized (shared KV/prefix cache, session store, state transfer) and rehydrated on any host. Sticky sessions are one implementation choice, not a requirement. The word 'must' overstates and can lead to an unnecessary affinity architecture.
issue.evidence: The text itself later contrasts stateless routing; stateful serving systems can use external caches or disaggregated state. Affinity is not logically necessary.
issue.root_cause: Mechanism/implementation conflation: session state with host affinity.
issue.correction: Replace 'must' with 'may require affinity unless state is externalized or shared'; describe sticky sessions as one option with trade-offs.
issue.acceptance_test: The text no longer asserts affinity is mandatory and names at least one externalized-state alternative.

issue.quoted_clause: The architect must choose between density (sticky sessions, higher per-host utilization) and evenness (stateless routing, lower per-host utilization but better load balance).
issue.observed: Sticky sessions can improve KV/cache locality and effective density, but they can also cause skew: a popular user pins one host to capacity while others are underutilized, lowering system-wide utilization. The phrase 'higher per-host utilization' is ambiguous and can be read as higher system utilization, which is not generally true.
issue.evidence: The preceding sentence says sticky sessions 'limit effective parallelism' because a popular user can pin a single host while others stand underutilized. That is lower system utilization, not higher.
issue.root_cause: Ambiguous/contradictory trade-off label; conflates cache locality with utilization.
issue.correction: Distinguish 'cache locality / KV reuse' from 'load balance.' Say sticky sessions can increase per-host cache hit rate and reduce recomputation, but risk skew and lower fleet utilization; stateless routing improves balance at the cost of lost locality.
issue.acceptance_test: The text no longer claims sticky sessions generally yield higher per-host utilization; the trade-off is stated as locality vs balance with skew risk.

issue.quoted_clause: so 2.0 req/s/host is not simultaneously sustainable with decode. The 21/31/32 host counts derived from that rate are the KV screen's counts, unchanged. Under case(i) the prefill leg leaves ~7% headroom and does not bind against the 21-host KV screen
issue.observed: The prefill check only shows prefill consumes ~93% of the idealized prefill ceiling under case(i); it does not compute decode's compute/bandwidth demand or show that the remaining ~7% is insufficient. The next sentence says case(i) 'does not bind,' which contradicts 'not simultaneously sustainable.' The claim is asserted, not derived.
issue.evidence: A simultaneous feasibility check requires comparing both prefill and decode demand to the same resource budget. The text provides only prefill demand and prefill ceiling; decode demand is not quantified in this check.
issue.root_cause: Incomplete conservation/feasibility check; conclusion outruns evidence.
issue.correction: Either perform the decode resource check at 2 req/s and show the combined demand exceeds capacity, or soften to 'prefill alone leaves little headroom; simultaneous decode feasibility is not established by this screen.' Make the case(i) treatment consistent.
issue.acceptance_test: The text either includes a decode demand calculation that supports non-sustainability, or no longer asserts non-sustainability; the case(i) 'does not bind' and 'not sustainable' statements are reconciled.

issue.quoted_clause: The two readings agree on the base case: moving 5 MB at the fabric's own 1.25 GB/s takes t_transfer = 5 MB ÷ 1.25 GB/s = 4 ms, comfortably inside the 20 ms observed duration
issue.observed: The two readings are 250 MB/s effective goodput and 1.25 GB/s instantaneous link rate — a 5× difference. They do not 'agree'; they both show the base case is benign. The phrase can mislead readers into thinking the effective and instantaneous rates are equal.
issue.evidence: 1.25 GB/s ÷ 250 MB/s = 5. The text itself says the per-request goodput sits ~5× under the link rate.
issue.root_cause: Imprecise wording; conflates 'both pass the check' with 'the values agree.'
issue.correction: Replace 'agree' with 'both show the base case is benign' or 'the transfer fits within the observed duration.'
issue.acceptance_test: The wording no longer implies the two rates are equal and distinguishes effective goodput from instantaneous link rate.

issue.quoted_clause: A host may hold 17.5 KV-resident requests but never serve 17.5 at the quoted service time
issue.observed: 17.5 is a concurrency (requests), not a rate. The sentence likely means 'serve 17.5 requests per second' or 'complete 17.5 requests per service time.' As written, it is dimensionally ambiguous.
issue.evidence: C is in requests; C/W is in requests/s. The sentence mixes them.
issue.root_cause: Unit/quantity ambiguity.
issue.correction: Say 'hold 17.5 KV-resident requests but never sustain 17.5 request completions per second at the quoted service time' or 'never serve 17.5 concurrent requests at the quoted per-request latency.'
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence states units explicitly and matches C vs C/W.

issue.quoted_clause: per decode step the weights are read once (~14 GB) and B tokens are produced, so the per-GPU decode token rate ≈ B × HBM_BW ÷ weight_bytes, capped by compute and KV — at batch 1 that is ~239 tok/s per GPU ... at batch 100 ~23,900 tok/s per GPU
issue.observed: The bandwidth formula counts only weight bytes. At the stated 600-token context and a 7B model, KV traffic is material: κ ≈ 0.524 MB/token, so batch 100 reads ≈31.4 GB of KV per decode step in addition to ≈14 GB of weights.
issue.evidence: With HBM_BW ≈3.35 TB/s, the stated formula gives 3.35e12/14e9 ≈239 steps/s at B=1 and 100×239 ≈23,900 tok/s at B=100. Including KV gives 3.35e12/(14e9+100×600×0.524e6) ≈73.8 steps/s, or ≈7,380 tok/s at B=100, about 3.2× lower.
issue.root_cause: Decode bandwidth model omits KV-cache read traffic; 'capped by compute and KV' is treated as a capacity check rather than a bandwidth term.
issue.correction: Use denominator weight_bytes + B×context×κ (plus other per-step traffic) for the bandwidth-bound decode rate, or explicitly state the context/batch regime where KV traffic is negligible; recompute the 200-rps host count.
issue.acceptance_test: At B=100, context=600, κ≈0.524 MB/token, HBM_BW≈3.35 TB/s, the printed per-GPU token rate is ≤≈7.4k tok/s, and the host-count derivation uses that rate.

issue.quoted_clause: 6.24M requests/month × 9,500 tokens ≈ 5.93×10^10 tokens/month — giving ~$155,817 ÷ 5.93×10^10 ≈ $2.63/1M
issue.observed: The canonical workload is stated as 10 rps average. At 10 rps over 30 days, monthly requests = 10×2,592,000 = 25.92M, not 6.24M. 6.24M/month implies ≈2.41 rps average.
issue.evidence: 25.92M×9,500 = 2.4624×10^11 tokens/month; $155,817/2.4624×10^11 ≈ $0.633/1M, not $2.63/1M. The printed $2.63/1M and the 'close to $2.50' comparison depend on the 6.24M basis.
issue.root_cause: Monthly volume basis is inconsistent with the canonical 10-rps average; the $/1M calculation and its comparison to the $2.50 FP16 row inherit the wrong denominator.
issue.correction: Reconcile the volume basis: either use 25.92M requests/month for 10 rps average and recompute $/1M, or explicitly define 6.24M as a different average-rate scenario and stop calling it the canonical 10-rps workload.
issue.acceptance_test: Monthly requests = average_rps×2.592×10^6; if average_rps=10, the text uses 25.92M and recomputes $/1M; if 6.24M is retained, the implied 2.41 rps is stated and the canonical 10-rps label is removed.

issue.quoted_clause: 70B dense FP16 | 140 GB | — | — | 1 GPU | 1 ... 70B MoE FP16 (2/16 experts) | 140 GB | — | — | 1 GPU | 1
issue.observed: A 140 GB weight footprint cannot fit on one 80 GB H100. The same row says the weights are spread across the 8-GPU pool under TP, so 'GPUs per instance = 1 GPU' contradicts both the VRAM and the parenthetical.
issue.evidence: 140 GB > 80 GB; minimum single-instance placement without KV is ceil(140/80)=2 GPUs, and the canonical 436 GB KV budget requires the full 8-GPU pool. The MoE FP16 row has the same 140 GB footprint and the same error.
issue.root_cause: The 'GPUs per instance' column was filled with the number of instances or a nominal model count rather than the minimum device count required by the stated VRAM.
issue.correction: Change the 70B dense FP16 and 70B MoE FP16 rows to 8 GPUs per instance for the canonical KV profile (or 2 GPUs minimum without KV), and make the 'instances on one 8×H100 pool' column consistent with that placement.
issue.acceptance_test: For every row, GPUs_per_instance×80 GB ≥ weights + KV for the stated profile; the 70B FP16 and MoE FP16 rows no longer claim 1 GPU for 140 GB.

issue.quoted_clause: The canonical case is *one* regime — a mid-context, mid-rate RAG workload where the KV-residency ceiling happens to be the binding constraint. ... Under case (ii) the prefill screen — not the KV screen — sets the 40-rps capacity floor (34 vs 32).
issue.observed: The first sentence says the canonical case is KV-bound; the Table 17-2 note says under case (ii) the prefill screen sets the 40-rps floor (34 vs 32). Both cannot be true for the same canonical case without qualification.
issue.evidence: Table 17-2 gives KV-only 32 total at 40 rps and case (ii) prefill 34 total; the note explicitly says prefill, not KV, sets the floor under case (ii). The counter-scenario lesson also repeats 'canonical regime ... KV-bound'.
issue.root_cause: The canonical case is described as KV-bound without naming the prefill case; the later case (ii) screen contradicts the unqualified claim.
issue.correction: Qualify the canonical claim: KV is the binding term among the KV/bandwidth screens, but the full-square prefill screen can bind under case (ii); state which case is being used whenever 'KV-bound' is asserted.
issue.acceptance_test: Every canonical 'KV-bound' statement names the prefill case or is changed to 'KV-bound under case (iii)/KV-only screen'; the Table 17-2 note and the counter-scenario lesson agree.

issue.quoted_clause: That is ~350 GB of weights, leaving ~290 GB of VRAM after weights — 226 GB of KV once the ~64 GB runtime/workspace reserve is subtracted (640 − 350 − 64; the figure used below, C = floor(226/24.89) = 9)
issue.observed: The calculation treats 8×H100 as one 640 GB pool. The 70B FP16 tier is tensor-parallel across all 8 GPUs; the 8-bit tiers need 2 GPUs each; the 4-bit copies need 1 GPU each. Aggregate free memory does not guarantee per-GPU free memory or a feasible TP placement.
issue.evidence: A plausible placement leaves some GPUs with ≈27.5 GB free and others with ≈62.5 GB free before reserve. The FP16 tier's per-request KV is sharded across all 8 GPUs (≈3.11 GB/GPU per canonical request), so the minimum-free GPU, not the 226 GB sum, bounds C. The stated C=9 may not be achievable.
issue.root_cause: Aggregate VRAM arithmetic ignores per-GPU capacity, TP group boundaries, and placement constraints.
issue.correction: Show a per-GPU memory ledger for the co-resident placement and compute C from the minimum free memory in the TP group (or use a placement solver); if C=9 is not feasible, reduce it and update the fleet arithmetic.
issue.acceptance_test: A per-GPU table lists weights, reserve, and free memory for each of the 8 GPUs; C is derived from the minimum free per-GPU memory times TP size divided by per-request KV, and the co-residency claim is accepted only if every GPU stays within 80 GB.

issue.quoted_clause: 226 GB of KV once the ~64 GB runtime/workspace reserve is subtracted ... — for KV cache and for smaller specialized models (e.g., 22B, 8B) for classification or routing
issue.observed: The same 226 GB is then fully consumed by C = floor(226/24.89) = 9 canonical requests. No capacity remains for the smaller specialized models the sentence says the 226 GB is also for.
issue.evidence: 9×24.89 GB = 224.0 GB, leaving ≈2 GB of the 226 GB, not enough for a 22B or 8B model at any useful precision. The sentence and the C calculation use the same budget for different purposes.
issue.root_cause: The KV budget and the smaller-model budget are not separated; the prose implies both share 226 GB while the arithmetic assigns all of it to KV.
issue.correction: Either state that C=9 is the KV-only capacity before smaller models and reduce C by the smaller-model weights, or allocate a separate VRAM line for the smaller models and recompute C.
issue.acceptance_test: The sum of KV for C requests + smaller-model weights + reserve ≤640 GB, and the text states the same C after the smaller-model allocation.

issue.quoted_clause: which minimizes weighted cost = α·token_cost + β·latency_cost?
issue.observed: token_cost is USD per 1M tokens and latency_cost is USD per ms (or a normalized score). The table's formula adds quantities with different units; the following note says the gate must be evaluated in a per-request additive form or after normalization.
issue.evidence: The note itself states 'different units, so the gate is evaluated in the per-request additive form cost = α·rate_tok·n_tok + β·rate_ms·n_ms ... or equivalently by normalizing both terms to [0,1]'. The table formula is dimensionally invalid as printed.
issue.root_cause: The table was not updated when the units note was added; it still shows the pre-normalization shorthand as if it were the decision formula.
issue.correction: Replace the table formula with the per-request additive form or with normalized scores, and make the table match the note and §18.3.4.
issue.acceptance_test: Table 18-1's formula has consistent units and is identical in form to the units note; a reader can substitute the §18.3.2 rates without an implicit normalization step.

issue.quoted_clause: 70B 4-bit GGUF | — | — | ~35 GB | 1 GPU ... 70B 4-bit GGUF local, no GPU
issue.observed: The hardware table gives the 70B 4-bit GGUF row 1 GPU and counts GPU-resident copies, while the row-hardware note says the same tier is 'local, no GPU'. The $0.15/1M rate is 'energy only' and is not comparable to the GPU-resident copies.
issue.evidence: The table's last column says '~18 by weights alone; ~5 if the 436 GB canonical KV budget is reserved ... worked deployment reserves 2', which is a GPU-memory calculation. The row-hardware note says 'local, no GPU'. These describe different deployments under one row label.
issue.root_cause: The CPU/edge GGUF tier and the GPU-resident 4-bit fallback copies are conflated in one table row and one price row.
issue.correction: Split the 4-bit GGUF row into (a) CPU/edge local, no GPU, energy-only and (b) GPU-resident 4-bit copies with capital+energy; or relabel the table row and price basis to the GPU-resident deployment and move the local tier to a separate row.
issue.acceptance_test: The 4-bit GGUF row's GPU count, instance count, and price basis all describe the same deployment; the 'local, no GPU' tier is not used to justify a GPU-resident copy count.

issue.quoted_clause: derive per-host concurrent capacity C from the *canonical* per-token KV (2 × layers × hidden × bytes)
issue.observed: The formula 2×layers×hidden×bytes is the full-MHA KV size per token. For GQA/MQA, the KV dimension is n_kv_heads×head_dim, not hidden. The same lesson lists GQA/MQA as a capacity lever, so the checklist formula does not transfer to the lever it recommends.
issue.evidence: For full MHA, hidden = n_heads×head_dim and the formula is correct. For GQA/MQA, n_kv_heads < n_heads, so using hidden overstates KV by n_heads/n_kv_heads. The canonical 70B full-MHA reference is a special case, not the general formula.
issue.root_cause: The canonical full-MHA formula is presented as the general per-token KV formula in the architect's checklist.
issue.correction: Write the general form as 2×layers×n_kv_heads×head_dim×bytes, note that full MHA sets n_kv_heads=n_heads, and use the canonical 2×layers×hidden×bytes only for the full-MHA reference.
issue.acceptance_test: The checklist formula reduces to the canonical 2.62 MB/token for the 70B full-MHA reference and to a smaller value for GQA/MQA; the GQA/MQA lever is not evaluated with the full-MHA formula.

issue.quoted_clause: 70 GB weights + 24.9 GB FP16 KV = 94.9 GB > 80 GB per GPU
issue.observed: 94.9 GB is the per-instance total, not a per-GPU quantity. With 2 GPUs per instance, the per-GPU share is ≈47.45 GB, which is below 80 GB. The comparison as written is dimensionally wrong even though the 2-GPU conclusion is correct.
issue.evidence: The row says '2 GPU' and '94.9 GB > 80 GB per GPU'. The correct statement is '94.9 GB > 80 GB single-GPU capacity, so 2 GPUs are required'; the per-GPU load after sharding is 47.45 GB.
issue.root_cause: Total instance memory is compared to per-GPU capacity without dividing by the number of GPUs.
issue.correction: Rewrite as '94.9 GB total > 80 GB single-GPU capacity; with 2 GPUs the per-GPU share is ≈47.45 GB' and apply the same wording to the MoE 8-bit row.
issue.acceptance_test: The row's inequality uses consistent units: total instance bytes vs total capacity of the stated GPU count, or per-GPU bytes vs 80 GB.

issue.quoted_clause: priced on two bases (self-amortized capital+energy, energy-only) ... 70B dense FP16 | $2.50 | 120 | capital + energy
issue.observed: The note says there are two bases: self-amortized capital+energy and energy-only. The FP16 row's basis is 'capital + energy', which is not one of the two named bases. If it is the same as self-amortized, the label should match; if it is a third basis, the note is wrong.
issue.evidence: The table's other capital rows say 'self-amortized capital + energy'; the FP16 row says 'capital + energy'. The basis note's two-basis taxonomy does not include the latter label.

issue.correction: Unify the FP16 row to 'self-amortized capital + energy' if that is the intended basis, or add the third basis to the note and explain how it differs.

issue.page_hint: Ch 19 §8, 'Unconditional fallback-inclusive ledger' table and following paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: Peak KV residency follows the retained-context convention of §4 — 12,095 × 2.62 MB ≈ 31.7 GB at the completed T = 3 class.
issue.observed: The table mixes bases: T=1 26.4 GB = 10,065×2.62 (input only), T=2 28.6 GB = 10,930×2.62 (input only), T=3 31.7 GB = 12,095×2.62 (input+300 output), fallback 30.9 GB = 11,795×2.62 (input only). The note only flags T=1 and fallback, not T=2.
issue.root_cause: Two KV-residency conventions are used in one table; the explanatory note is incomplete.
issue.correction: Choose one convention for all rows. If using final retained context incl terminal answer, print 27.2 / 29.4 / 31.7 / 30.9 GB (fallback no synthesis). If using input-only, print 26.4 / 28.6 / 30.9 / 30.9 GB. Update the note to cover every row.
issue.acceptance_test: Every row's GB value must equal the declared token basis × 2.62 MB; no row may switch basis.

issue.quoted_clause: A bottleneck in the tool backend will manifest as increased λ_tool, which directly inflates the per-turn loop overhead L_agent (§4), and through it the full service time W.
issue.observed: This contradicts the earlier explicit separation: W's tool leg uses Chapter 17's ~133 ms/turn tool/retrieval rate, not L_agent's λ_tool≈100 ms; the text says the two are 'not additive' and 'different quantities.'
issue.evidence: W(T) formula uses T·λ_tool/retr (≈133 ms/turn), while L_agent=λ_step+λ_tool≈220 ms/turn. An increase in λ_tool does not mechanically flow into W as defined.
issue.root_cause: The paragraph collapses two distinct tool-latency quantities that the chapter elsewhere separates.
issue.correction: Say the bottleneck inflates L_agent; if the W evaluator's tool/retrieval rate is also updated, W rises, but the mapping must be stated explicitly. Do not say 'through it' without qualification.
issue.acceptance_test: Trace λ_tool into the W formula; show whether W uses λ_tool or λ_tool/retr, and keep the two rates distinct.

issue.quoted_clause: The **incremental added latency** — the base generation plus the added orchestration overhead — is: L_orch(T) = L_base + T · L_agent
issue.observed: L_orch(0)=L_base, so this is not incremental added latency; it is base-plus-orchestration total. The incremental added latency is T·L_agent.
issue.evidence: At T=0, L_orch=8.6 s, which is the baseline, not an increment. The chapter later calls the same row 'Base + orchestration subtotal.'
issue.root_cause: The label 'incremental added latency' is applied to a total that includes the baseline.
issue.correction: Rename to 'orchestration-view total latency' or 'base + orchestration subtotal'; reserve 'incremental added latency' for T·L_agent. Update the following sentence that says it 'isolates how much the agentic layer's orchestration adds.'
issue.acceptance_test: Check L_orch(0)=L_base; the quantity labeled incremental must be zero at T=0.

issue.quoted_clause: Introducing an agentic layer reshapes the system architecture in seven ways:
issue.observed: The section then presents eight bolded subsections: State-management policy; Two token counts; The durable lesson; Inference scaling; Task economics; Tool backend provisioning; Observability requirements; Fallback & degradation pathways.
issue.evidence: Count the bold headings following the sentence.
issue.root_cause: Count not updated after a subsection was added.
issue.correction: Change 'seven' to 'eight' or merge/remove one subsection so the count matches.
issue.acceptance_test: Count the enumerated bold subsections; the number must equal the stated count.

issue.quoted_clause: a fallback request attempts the full cap (T = 3 — 3 model calls + 3 tool calls) before the guardrail trips
issue.observed: This conflicts with the earlier definition: 'A T-turn trace is T+1 model invocations.' A completed T=3 trace has four model invocations; the fallback has three attempted turns plus a single-shot re-dispatch and no terminal synthesis call.
issue.evidence: Earlier: 'A T-turn trace is T+1 model invocations.' Fallback ledger inputs 9,200+10,065+10,930=30,195 for three attempted turns, then +9,200 single-shot; no 11,795 terminal synthesis call.
issue.root_cause: The fallback's 'T=3' means three attempted agent turns, not a completed T=3 trace; the parenthetical uses the wrong call count.
issue.correction: Write 'three attempted agent turns (3 model calls + 3 tool calls), with no terminal synthesis call' or otherwise distinguish attempted turns from completed T=3.
issue.acceptance_test: Count model calls in the fallback trace; the description must match the ledger's 3 attempted + 1 single-shot calls.

issue.quoted_clause: The guardrail budget caps total input at 13,000 tokens — a safety margin above the append-only worst case (12,660 at T = 4, Table 19-1), so the turn cap binds before the guardrail does.
issue.observed: 'Total input' is ambiguous. If it means cumulative input across calls, T=1 already sums to 19,265 tokens, far above 13,000. The comparison to 12,660 only makes sense for per-call final context length.
issue.evidence: Table 19-1's 12,660 is 'Retained-context input, final call'; the §8 ledger's T=1 Σ per-call input is 19,265.
issue.root_cause: The guardrail is described as a total-input cap but compared to a per-call context length.
issue.correction: Say 'caps per-call input context at 13,000 tokens' or 'caps the final-call context at 13,000 tokens'; if the guardrail is cumulative, recompute the binding point.
issue.acceptance_test: State the guardrail's unit and interval; verify 13,000 against the same quantity (per-call vs cumulative).

issue.quoted_clause: The scheduling unit is the whole request, not the model call: the request holds its KV slot across every tool round-trip, so a T = 3 request occupies capacity for W ≈ 17.70 s even though the GPU is idle for the tool legs — concurrency is set by wall-clock occupancy, not by GPU-busy time.
issue.observed: This is presented as a universal architecture consequence, but it depends on the stated no-reuse/hold-KV policy. Systems that offload, swap, or free KV during tool waits would not have concurrency set by full wall-clock occupancy.
issue.evidence: The chapter's own policy says no prefix cache is reused and the request holds its KV slot; other serving designs can offload KV.
issue.root_cause: A policy-dependent statement is written as a general law.
issue.correction: Qualify: 'Under the stated hold-KV/no-reuse policy...' and note that KV offload/swap changes the occupancy calculation.
issue.acceptance_test: Check whether the sentence is true under alternative KV-offload policies; if not, add the qualifier.

issue.quoted_clause: Under this convention the 2% fallback is a high-tail/failure category that incurs zero added turns (single-shot)
issue.observed: The fallback actually attempts three turns before re-dispatching; it incurs 660 ms of attempted orchestration plus ~200 ms re-dispatch in the unconditional ledger. 'Zero added turns' is only true for the retained-context expectation, not for the fallback's work.
issue.evidence: The same section's ledger gives fallback added orchestration 660 ms + ~200 ms ≈860 ms and 39,395 input tokens.
issue.root_cause: The qualifier 'for retained-context expectation' is dropped in the conditional paragraph.
issue.correction: Say 'incurs zero added retained-context turns for this expectation, though its failed-attempt work is counted in the unconditional ledger.'
issue.acceptance_test: Check that the fallback's 860 ms and 39,395 input are not described as zero work.

issue.page_hint: Ch 20 §5, Common Mistakes, 'Overlooking data movement cost'
issue.quoted_clause: if every host fetches independently, each query moves its full context bytes, repeated for every query and every host
issue.observed: The sentence implies one query is fetched by every host. In a normal serving fleet a query is routed to one host; independent per-host caches cause repeated fetches across queries and cache misses, not one fetch per host per query.
issue.evidence: The surrounding paragraph is about bytes fetched per query and cross-query overlap. The correct accounting is: one serving host fetches the context for the query it serves; independent caches may duplicate that fetch across queries and hosts when the same context is requested again, but not 'every host' for one query.
issue.root_cause: Conflates per-query fetch with per-host cache replication/miss behavior.
issue.correction: Rewrite to distinguish (a) one fetch by the serving host per query, (b) duplicate fetches across queries when caches are cold or not shared, and (c) replication cost when the same index/context is stored on many hosts. Do not say a single query is fetched by every host.
issue.acceptance_test: The revised paragraph contains no claim that one query is fetched by every host; it separately accounts per-query fetch, cross-query cache reuse, and per-host replication.

issue.quoted_clause: decode weight-read per token | ~140 GB | full-weight-read model (70B FP16) [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
issue.observed: The 140 GB per token figure is a batch-1 figure. At the canonical host's ~17 concurrent requests, the weight read is amortized across the batch: per-token weight traffic is ~140/17 ≈ 8.2 GB, while the host still reads ~140 GB per decode step. The table labels the batch-1 figure simply 'per token' without the batch-1 qualifier.
issue.evidence: Ch 25 ADR 0017 explicitly distinguishes batch 1 (140 GB weights against ~24.9 GB KV) from C≈17.5 (435.6 GB KV against 140 GB weights). Ch 22's own mental model says 'low-batch decode is bandwidth-bound', but Table 22-1 and the Architecture Consequence drop that qualifier.
issue.root_cause: Batch-1 weight-read traffic is presented as a per-token canonical quantity without carrying its operating-point scope.
issue.correction: Label the 140 GB row as 'batch-1 decode weight-read per token' and add the amortized per-token figure at the canonical concurrency, or replace the row with 'host weight-read per decode step ~140 GB' and state that per-token traffic is 140/C GB. In §6, qualify the 5.6 TB/s rate as the batch-1/host-step rate and note that at C≈17 the per-token weight traffic is ~8.2 GB and arithmetic intensity rises to ~4.3 FLOP/byte.
issue.acceptance_test: Every occurrence of '140 GB per token' or '5.6 TB/s' in Ch 22 states its batch/concurrency scope; no unqualified per-token claim remains.

issue.quoted_clause: a ~21–32-host fleet at the canonical peak (Ch 17/20/24)
issue.observed: The range omits the governing 23-host ρ-derated case-(ii) screen and the 34-host full-policy case-(ii) screen that Ch 20 and Ch 25 report. Ch 24 also summarizes the screens as '21 hosts KV / 19–22 prefill / 32 policy', omitting 23 and 34.
issue.evidence: Ch 20 states: 23 hosts governs before the full policy under case (ii) with ρ=0.95; 34 hosts under 70%×95%+N−1 for case (ii), versus 32 for KV-only. Ch 25 ADR 0015 R1 repeats 21/32 and 22/34.
issue.root_cause: Host-count summaries use different subsets of the screen set without labeling raw versus ρ-derated versus full-policy cases.
issue.correction: Standardize the summary range and label each endpoint: e.g. '21 hosts KV raw; 22 KV with ρ; 23 case-(ii) prefill with ρ; 32 KV full policy; 34 case-(ii) full policy.' Do not use a 21–32 range that excludes 23 and 34.
issue.acceptance_test: All cross-chapter host-count summaries either include 23 and 34 or explicitly state that they are reporting only the raw KV and KV-policy screens.

issue.quoted_clause: leaves Candidate B as a candidate pending measurement — and on check 4 (peak KV residency) neither candidate survives the full screen set at the canonical peak: A fails prefill and KV, B fails peak KV (8 hosts hold 136 — 8 × 17 whole slots — of the 344 in-flight) until sized to ≥21 hosts and re-run.
issue.observed: The paragraph first says Candidate B remains a candidate, then says B as specified (8 hosts) fails peak KV and must be resized to ≥21 hosts. Candidate B at 8 hosts is therefore eliminated, not a surviving candidate.
issue.evidence: The same paragraph says 'neither candidate survives the full screen set at the canonical peak' and 'B fails peak KV ... until sized to ≥21 hosts and re-run.'
issue.root_cause: The outcome conflates 'Candidate B as specified' with 'a resized B configuration'.
issue.correction: State explicitly: Candidate A is eliminated; Candidate B at 8 hosts is also eliminated at the canonical peak; the only surviving object is a resized B (≥21 hosts, plus the prefill screen) that must be benchmarked. Do not call the 8-host B a candidate.
issue.acceptance_test: The outcome paragraph distinguishes B-as-specified from resized-B and does not describe an 8-host B as a surviving candidate.

issue.quoted_clause: 70B dense FP16 deployment (FP16 label; see ADR 0016)
issue.observed: ADR 0016 in the same chapter decides 'Render the serving model in BF16' and says 'this record sets the canonical deployment's precision label to BF16.' The chapter opening still calls the deployment FP16. Many earlier chapters also use '70B dense FP16' as the canonical label.
issue.evidence: ADR 0016 Decision: 'Render the serving model in BF16.' Consequences: 'Accepted, this record sets the canonical deployment's precision label to BF16.' Ch 25 §4 still says '70B FP16 model footprint'.
issue.root_cause: The canonical weight-precision label was not globally reconciled after ADR 0016 introduced BF16.
issue.correction: Choose one canonical label. Either keep the deployment FP16 and make ADR 0016 an illustrative/hypothetical record that does not change the canonical label, or globally update the canonical label to BF16 and explain that all byte-based figures are unchanged because both formats are 2 B/parameter. Update Ch 25 opening and §4 accordingly.

issue.quoted_clause: its decision body is kept, not rewritten — the status is updated to superseded, with a link to the successor
issue.observed: The record immediately below has Status: HOLD — screened, not committed. The parenthetical says the status is updated to superseded, which contradicts the displayed HOLD status.
issue.evidence: ADR 0015 Status field: 'HOLD — screened, not committed.' The parenthetical describes a supersession event that has not occurred.

issue.quoted_clause: the canonical peak already needs 21 hosts on the KV screen (22 under the case (ii) prefill screen; Ch 16/17/20), so 'adding hosts beyond the 21' misunderstands the scale
issue.observed: The same sentence acknowledges that case (ii) needs 22 hosts. If the governing screen is 22 (or 23 with ρ), then adding a host beyond 21 is exactly what the screen requires; it is not a misunderstanding of scale.
issue.evidence: Ch 20 states 22 raw case-(ii) prefill and 23 with ρ; Ch 25 ADR 0015 R1 also carries 22/34. The alternative rejects 'adding capacity' by treating 21 as the scale, while simultaneously naming 22.
issue.root_cause: The alternative uses the KV-only 21-host screen as if it were the governing screen, then mentions the higher prefill screen without reconciling the argument.
issue.correction: Rewrite the alternative to say: adding hosts beyond the governing screen (21 KV raw, 22 case-(ii) raw, 23 with ρ, 32/34 under full policy) is not the first lever for the KV-capacity problem; FP8 KV relaxes the KV ceiling without commissioning new hardware. Do not dismiss the one host needed to meet case (ii) as a misunderstanding.
issue.acceptance_test: The alternative text uses the governing screen consistently and does not call a required case-(ii) host addition a misunderstanding.

issue.quoted_clause: We measure four things continuously: 1. Gate pass rate ... False-promotion rate ... 2. Canary-to-production time and rollback time ... 3. Model freshness / data staleness ... 4. MTTR for a bad release
issue.observed: The list contains at least six distinct metrics: gate pass rate, false-promotion rate, canary-to-production time, rollback time, model freshness/data staleness, and MTTR. Calling them 'four things' is a counting error.
issue.evidence: The enumerated list itself contains two metrics in item 1 and two in item 2, plus items 3 and 4.
issue.root_cause: Grouped metrics are counted as single 'things' without saying so.
issue.correction: Either say 'we measure four groups of things' and keep the grouping, or say 'we measure six metrics' and enumerate them separately.
issue.acceptance_test: The count word matches the number of enumerated metrics or the text explicitly says it is counting groups.

issue.quoted_clause: Deeper continuous batching on the single host, on top of the baseline sharding, cannot raise throughput here: resident-request capacity is KV-bound at C ≈ 17.5 (Ch 15), so admitting more requests only lengthens the waiting queue and adds prefill interference
issue.observed: The argument treats the KV-resident concurrency ceiling C ≈ 17.5 as if the baseline already operates at that ceiling. A KV ceiling bounds steady-state resident requests; it does not by itself prove that deeper continuous batching cannot raise throughput from a lower baseline batch size up to C.
issue.evidence: Throughput can rise as batch size increases toward the KV-capacity limit even when C is fixed. The claim is only valid once the scheduler is already at C; otherwise deeper batching can improve utilization and throughput before queueing dominates. The text does not state that the baseline is already at C.
issue.root_cause: Capacity ceiling conflated with current operating point.
issue.correction: Qualify the claim: 'once the scheduler is already at the KV-resident ceiling C ≈ 17.5, deeper batching cannot raise steady-state concurrency further; below C it may raise throughput until queueing and prefill interference dominate.' If the capstone assumes the baseline is already at C, state that assumption explicitly.
issue.acceptance_test: The passage distinguishes the KV capacity ceiling from the baseline operating batch/concurrency and states the condition under which deeper batching cannot help.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 26 Table 26-2 cost row and following note
issue.quoted_clause: Cost | $ per query — metered API spend at the canonical 9,200/300 mix, marginal-generation-work share only (DERIVED from FACT inputs, §26.8 — not itself a FACT) | < $0.015 | $0.0076 (API-basis marginal: canonical-mix unit price $0.01164 — a conservative upper bound for this short-prompt leg — × 0.65; self-host all-in is a separate basis, §26.8)
issue.observed: The row mixes two cost bases: 'metered API spend' and 'marginal-generation-work share only.' Multiplying an API unit price by 0.65 produces an API-spend estimate, not a self-hosted marginal-generation-work estimate. The note then calls the modeled cell a marginal-generation-work statement.

The note says the cell is a marginal-generation-work statement, but the cell's inputs are API list prices.
issue.root_cause: Cost-basis labels were carried over from the self-host discussion into an API-priced row.
issue.correction: Either label the row explicitly as 'API-basis marginal spend after cache-hit reduction' and remove 'marginal-generation-work share only,' or compute a separate self-hosted marginal-generation-work figure and keep the API-basis figure in a separate row/column. Do not describe the API-priced cell as a marginal-generation-work estimate.
issue.acceptance_test: The cost row's label, arithmetic, and note all name the same basis; API spend and self-hosted marginal generation work are not conflated.

issue.page_hint: Appendix A post-snapshot notes, multiple paragraphs

issue.observed: Multiple footnote clusters contain stray caret-comma-caret sequences between footnote references, e.g. `[^oct-mt-huginn]^,^[^oct-mt-ouro]`, `[^oct-mt-ouro-code]^,^[^oct-mt-ouro-card]`, and similar patterns in the Intel and video notes.

issue.observed: The phrase 'the table is offloadable' is ambiguous in context: 'table' refers to Qwen's N-gram embedding table, but the sentence sits near references to the book's tables and the Fig A.1 table.

issue.issue: The diagram's token labels and central 'append K/V one step later' box can be read as saying that every token's K/V is appended one step after the token is processed, including the token labelled 'end of prefill'. That conflicts with the caption's statement that prompt-token K/V is written during prefill and with the prose on printed p. 15 that a token's K/V enters the cache on the step in which it is the input, not the step in which it is sampled.
issue.evidence: Figure 1.1 labels the first token 'token1 / end of prefill' and routes it through the box 'append K/V / one step later'. The caption says: 'for a generated token, written when that token is next processed as input, one step after it is sampled; prompt-token K/V is written during prefill.' The diagram does not visually separate prompt-token KV writes (during prefill) from generated-token KV writes (one step later). Printed p. 15 states: 'A token's K/V therefore enters the cache on the step in which it is the input, not on the step in which it is sampled.'
issue.acceptance_test: Redraw or relabel Figure 1.1 so that (a) prompt-token K/V is shown as written during prefill, and (b) generated-token K/V is shown as written when that token is next processed as input. The label 'token1 / end of prefill' must be disambiguated as either the last prompt token or the first sampled token, and the 'one step later' annotation must apply only to the generated-token path.

issue.figure: Figure 2.2 — Prefill and decode split by the roofline ridge
issue.issue: The drawn roofline diagonal is not the H100 roofline implied by the figure's own stated inputs. With 989 TFLOPS peak and 3.35 TB/s HBM3, the memory-bound segment should be performance = 3.35e12 × arithmetic intensity, so at 1 FLOP/byte the roof is ~3.35e12 FLOP/s. The chart instead starts the diagonal at ~1e12 FLOP/s at 1 FLOP/byte, making the slope steeper than 1 on the log-log plot and placing the entire memory-bound roof too low.
issue.evidence: Figure 2.2's bottom annotation states: 'H100 SXM, BF16 dense: 989 TFLOPS peak, 3.35 TB/s HBM3 → ridge at 295 FLOP/byte'. The roofline equation is attainable performance = min(peak, bandwidth × arithmetic intensity). At arithmetic intensity = 1 FLOP/byte, bandwidth × intensity = 3.35e12 FLOP/s. The drawn diagonal visibly starts at the 1e12 gridline at x = 1, not at ~3.35e12. The ridge point is drawn at ~295 FLOP/byte and 989 TFLOPS, so the line from (1, 1e12) to (295, 989e12) has log-log slope ≈ 1.21, not the required slope of 1 for a bandwidth-limited roofline segment.
issue.acceptance_test: Replot the memory-bound roofline segment through (1, 3.35e12) and (295, 989e12) on the same log-log axes, or explicitly state that the drawn diagonal is a schematic not to scale. If the diagonal is retained as a schematic, remove the quantitative '3.35 TB/s HBM3 → ridge at 295 FLOP/byte' claim from the same visual or label the diagonal as 'schematic, not to scale'.

issue.figure: Figure 2.2 — Prefill and decode split by the roofline ridge
issue.issue: The blue 'prefill' marker is not plotted at the canonical prefill arithmetic intensity stated in the caption (~9.2K FLOP/byte). On the log x-axis it sits visibly closer to the middle of the 10^3–10^4 decade, roughly a few thousand FLOP/byte, rather than near the 10^4 edge where ~9.2K would fall.
issue.evidence: The caption states: 'arithmetic intensity places the canonical prefill point ~9.2K FLOP/byte, well to the right of the ~295 ridge'. The x-axis is logarithmic with ticks at 1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000. The blue triangle labelled 'prefill' is drawn well to the left of the 10000 tick, at approximately the middle of the 1000–10000 decade. A value of 9.2K would be at ~0.96 of that decade, very close to the 10000 tick.
issue.acceptance_test: Move the prefill marker to x ≈ 9.2×10^3 FLOP/byte on the log axis, or change the caption to state the value actually plotted. If the marker is intentionally schematic, label it 'schematic position' and remove the precise '~9.2K' claim from the same figure.

issue.issue: Panel B draws a solid bracket under the partially accepted canvas (A ? C ?), visually marking it as finalized prefix state, while the caption says prompt-state reuse is not assumed and accepted IDs alone do not establish reusable K/V.
issue.evidence: Caption: 'Here, accepted IDs stay fixed; prompt-state reuse is not assumed.' and 'Solid brackets identify finalized prefix state; accepted token IDs alone do not establish reusable K/V.' Panel B shows a solid bracket beneath the A ? C ? canvas.

issue.issue: The 'Five selection surfaces' box includes 'retrieve-vs-generate', but the caption calls these 'model-selection dimensions'; retrieve-vs-generate is a system/architecture split, not a model-selection surface.
issue.evidence: Figure box: 'quality · latency · KV cache · $/tok · retrieve-vs-generate'; caption: 'The five surfaces are the model-selection dimensions'; the diagram itself splits into retrieval and generation legs.
issue.acceptance_test: Either rename the box/caption to 'system-selection surfaces' or replace 'retrieve-vs-generate' with a genuine model-selection dimension and move the retrieve-vs-generate decision to the split arrows.

issue.issue: The Serving metrics box includes 'queue depth (scheduler)', but the prose on the facing page explicitly says queue depth is not a serving metric; the box also omits ITL, which the prose lists.
issue.evidence: Page 96: 'Queue depth is not one of them: it is a scheduler state, a leading indicator that helps explain these serving metrics.' Figure 6.1 Serving metrics: 'TTFT · TPOT · goodput · queue depth (scheduler)'.
issue.acceptance_test: Move queue depth outside the Serving metrics box (e.g., a separate scheduler-state annotation) and add ITL to the Serving metrics list; ensure caption and prose agree.

issue.issue: Caption calls the second dimension 'Traffic / concurrency' while the figure labels it 'Request rate & arrival pattern'; the two are related but not identical, creating terminology drift.
issue.evidence: Figure left box: 'Request rate & arrival pattern'; caption: 'Traffic / concurrency → concurrency & batching'.
issue.acceptance_test: Use one label consistently in figure and caption, e.g., 'Request rate & arrival pattern (traffic/concurrency)'.

issue.issue: The diagram's DERIVED box says 'decode bandwidth-bound (low-batch regime)', but the figure is explicitly a TTFT loop (baseline TTFT p99 ~450 ms; validate p99 < 300 ms; target ≤ 800 ms). The caption itself says the TTFT budget is 'prefill- and queue-dominated' and that 'decode bandwidth governs TPOT/ITL, not TTFT'. The drawn causal chain therefore contradicts its own caption and the surrounding prose.
issue.evidence: Box 2 reads 'decode bandwidth-bound (low-batch regime)'. Caption: 'the DERIVED stage (box 2), which for this TTFT budget is prefill- and queue-dominated ... Decode bandwidth governs TPOT/ITL, not TTFT, so it is the relevant term only for the output-side budget, not for the numbers in this diagram.'
issue.acceptance_test: Replace box 2 with the actual TTFT constraint (e.g., 'prefill + queueing dominated (TTFT)') or split the diagram into separate TTFT and TPOT/ITL paths. Re-read the figure without the caption: a reader must not infer that decode bandwidth is the derived constraint for TTFT.

issue.issue: The green forward arrow from DERIVED to PATTERN is labeled 'validate', but validation is a measurement/feedback action, not a forward selection step. The red feedback arrow from PATTERN back to ASSUMPTION is the actual measurement loop. The caption says 'The loop closes by measurement — an assumption that fails validation returns to box 1 for adjustment', which places validation on the feedback path, not on the DERIVED→PATTERN arrow.
issue.evidence: Green arrow label: 'validate p99 < 300 ms (target ≤ 800 ms)'. Red arrow labels: 'feedback' and 'adjust + pick pattern'. Caption: 'The loop closes by measurement — an assumption that fails validation returns to box 1 for adjustment, and only measured FACTs enter the decision.'
issue.acceptance_test: Move the 'validate' label to the feedback arrow or add an explicit measurement/validation box on the return path. The forward arrow should be labeled as a target/selection criterion (e.g., 'select pattern to meet criterion'), not as validation.

issue.figure: Figure 26.1 — Workload fingerprints on the six axes
issue.issue: The critical caveat 'per-axis 0-1 scale; compare within an axis, not across axes' is set in small, light gray type below the legend. At print size it is easy to miss, yet it is the only in-figure warning that prevents a reader from comparing bars across different axes as if they were a single measured scale. The y-axis label 'Authored intensity (0-1)' further invites cross-axis comparison.
issue.evidence: The note appears below the legend in small gray text: 'per-axis 0-1 scale; compare within an axis, not across axes.' The y-axis is labeled 'Authored intensity (0-1)'. The prose on the next page clarifies that the scores are subjective authored values, but the figure itself must carry that warning legibly.
issue.acceptance_test: Increase the caveat to at least the 8 pt figure-annotation floor and darken it, or move it into the caption. A reader viewing only the figure should immediately understand that the six axes are separate 0–1 scales and that bar heights are not comparable across axes.

issue.figure: Figure 25.1 — The Anatomy of an Architecture Decision Record
issue.issue: The top ADR is labeled 'kept, not edited', while the caption says 'only the Status line is updated when a successor supersedes it.' A careful reader can read 'not edited' as contradicting the status update. The intended meaning is that the body is kept unchanged while the status is updated.
issue.evidence: Top box: 'ADR-001 (superseded)' with gray italic label 'kept, not edited'. Caption: 'the body is never rewritten, and only the Status line is updated when a successor supersedes it.'
issue.acceptance_test: Change the label to something unambiguous such as 'body kept; status updated' or 'kept on file (body unchanged)'. The figure and caption should agree without requiring the caption to rescue the label.

issue.figure: Figure A.1 — Extreme sparsity: four selected families (2026)
issue.issue: The chart places four bars on a single 'Active fraction' axis even though the Qwen bar uses a different denominator (125B backbone only, excluding 51B n-gram and 4B MTP) and the caption says the four bars are 'not one like-for-like series'. The asterisk and footnote are present, but the visual encoding still invites direct comparison of bar lengths. The caveat is carried mainly by small gray annotation text.
issue.evidence: Qwen row: '*4.8%' with annotation '125B backbone/6B active (+51B n-gram, 4B MTP)'. Footnote: '* Qwen bar = backbone ratio (125B backbone), excluding the 51B n-gram embedding and 4B MTP.' Caption: 'denominators differ by vendor and the Qwen bar is its 125 B backbone only, so the four bars are not one like-for-like series'.
issue.acceptance_test: Either visually separate the Qwen bar (e.g., a distinct panel or a clear break/annotation) or add an explicit in-figure warning at readable size that bar lengths are not directly comparable across rows. A reader should not have to read the footnote to avoid treating the four bars as a single ranked series.

issue.issue: The scope annotations that carry the figure's central caveat are set in small, low-contrast gray type, while the bold percentages dominate. A reader scanning the table can easily take '~7%', '~10%', '~23%', and '~33%' as comparable cross-model numbers and miss that the DeepSeek rows are single-token whole-model ratios while the GLM rows are per-layer/per-head ratios.
issue.evidence: The table's main numbers are large and bold; the qualifying text ('single-token KV cache', 'single-token inference FLOPs', 'per-layer KV (BF16)', 'attention only per head / layer') is small gray text beneath each row. The red warning box says 'no shared scale', but the scope text that explains why is visually subordinate.
issue.acceptance_test: At print size, the scope text for each row is at least as legible as the footnote and is visually attached to the number it qualifies; a reader can state the scope of each row without reading the caption.

issue.figure: Figure A.3 — A chronology of frontier AI systems
issue.issue: The figure is drawn as a stack of touching horizontal bars, which visually encodes cumulative layering or substrate dependency. The caption explicitly says it is 'not a substrate stack' and 'not a causal lineage', but the visual form contradicts the caption. A reader can reasonably infer that each stage builds on or requires the previous one, which is the opposite of the intended claim.
issue.evidence: The bars are stacked vertically with no gaps, each sitting directly on the one below, and the caption has to negate the visual: 'not a causal lineage and not a substrate stack: a later stage does not require the one before it'. The dates are listed to the right, not positioned on a time axis, so the stack is the dominant visual encoding.
issue.acceptance_test: The figure no longer reads as a stack or dependency chain without the caption; a reader shown only the figure can correctly say that the stages are a chronology of selected milestones, not a cumulative stack.

issue.figure: Figure A.4 — Where Should Intelligence Live?
issue.issue: The band 'Inside post-training (build-time)' is colored blue, which the legend defines as 'system-side', but post-training is a model-building process that shapes the weights and is conceptually model-side. It also has no chapter reference, unlike every other band. The result is a taxonomic inconsistency: the figure places a build-time model process in the system-side group and leaves it unmapped to the book's chapters.
issue.evidence: Legend: 'blue = system-side · green = model-side'. The band 'Inside post-training (build-time)' is blue and sits above the green model-side bands. Every other band has a chapter reference (Ch18, Ch20; Ch17–20, Ch24; Ch19, Ch24; Ch22; Ch10; Ch7, Ch8; Ch3, Ch8); this band has none.
issue.acceptance_test: The post-training band is either recolored/moved to the model-side group with an appropriate chapter reference, or the caption explicitly explains why build-time post-training is classified as system-side and why it has no chapter mapping.

issue.figure: Figure A.5 — Shared weights do not remove executed work
issue.issue: The legend says 'Dashed arrows = weight reuse', but dashed arrows are also used from each pass down to its iteration history cache. Those arrows represent cache/history state, not weight reuse. The same line style therefore carries two different meanings, and the legend does not define the cache-state meaning.
issue.evidence: Top section: dashed arrows run from 'one shared core weight set' to pass 1/pass 2/pass 3 (weight reuse), and dashed arrows also run from each pass down to 'iteration 1 history cache', 'iteration 2 history cache', and 'iteration 3 history cache'. The legend at the bottom defines only 'Dashed arrows = weight reuse'.
issue.acceptance_test: Weight reuse and history-cache state use visually distinct line styles, and the legend defines both; a reader can tell which dashed arrows mean weight reuse and which mean cache state.

issue.figure: Figure A.5 — Shared weights do not remove executed work
issue.issue: In the 'Actual stop' row, the path is drawn as pass 1 → pass 2 → pass 3 (not executed) → exit. This visually puts the non-executed pass on the runtime path, contradicting the caption's claim that 'a true exit omits later work'. The reader cannot tell whether pass 3 is bypassed or merely marked as not executed while still being traversed.
issue.evidence: The 'Actual stop' row shows a solid arrow from pass 2 into the dashed box 'pass 3 (not executed)', then an arrow from that box to 'exit'. The caption says 'A true exit omits later work'; the legend says 'dashed box = not executed'. If pass 3 is not executed, the exit should branch from pass 2 directly, not pass through the non-executed box.
issue.acceptance_test: The 'Actual stop' path shows pass 2 → exit directly, with pass 3 ghosted off the path or omitted; a reader can immediately see that pass 3 is skipped rather than traversed.

issue.figure: Figure A.5 — Shared weights do not remove executed work
issue.issue: The dashed box 'pass 3 (not executed)' and its connecting arrows are low-contrast light gray. At print size, the dashed outline and the text inside are harder to read than the solid boxes, which weakens the figure's ability to communicate the skipped-work distinction.
issue.evidence: The 'pass 3 (not executed)' box is drawn in light gray with a dashed border, while the executed passes are dark-bordered boxes with black text. The dashed arrows around it are also light.
issue.acceptance_test: The non-executed pass remains visually distinct but its label and outline are legible at print size and in grayscale without squinting.

issue.issue: The inline annotation reads '8× savings vs GQA FP16 (2.62 → 0.33 MB/tok)', which names GQA FP16 as the comparison baseline. The arrow and the numbers show the reduction is from full-MHA FP16 (2.62 MB/tok) to GQA FP16 (0.33 MB/tok); GQA is the smaller value, not the baseline being reduced.
issue.evidence: Annotation in Figure 7.5: '8× savings vs GQA FP16 (2.62 → 0.33 MB/tok)'; legend identifies 2.62 MB/tok as full-MHA FP16 and 0.33 MB/tok as GQA FP16; caption says 'GQA with a 64:8 query-to-KV head ratio ~8× smaller.'
issue.acceptance_test: Annotation names the correct baseline and direction, e.g. 'GQA FP16: 8× smaller than full-MHA FP16 (2.62 → 0.33 MB/tok)' or '8× savings vs full-MHA FP16'.

issue.issue: The inline annotations ('9.5K max context ...', '8× savings ...', '~436 GB budget at 166K') are set noticeably smaller than the axis/legend text and are difficult to read at print size; the dense annotation text also competes with the plotted lines.
issue.evidence: At 150 dpi the annotation glyphs are visibly smaller than the axis tick labels and legend; the '8× savings...' line is a long string placed inside the plot area.
issue.acceptance_test: All figure annotations measure at least 8 pt at print size, or the detail is moved into the caption/legend with only short leader labels left in the plot.

issue.issue: The figure states 'No compatible kernel: reject; fallback is not guaranteed.' The caption says 'Unsupported combinations may be rejected; fallback is not guaranteed.' The figure's unqualified 'reject' is stronger than the caption and can be read as a universal guarantee of rejection, whereas some runtimes may fall back to a slower path or fail differently.
issue.evidence: Figure text: 'No compatible kernel: reject; fallback is not guaranteed.' Caption: 'Unsupported combinations may be rejected; fallback is not guaranteed.'
issue.acceptance_test: Figure text matches the caption's modality, e.g. 'No compatible kernel: may reject; fallback is not guaranteed' or 'cannot execute without a compatible kernel'.

issue.issue: The arrows from 'Error-control method' and 'Numerical representation' terminate on the outer 'Container wraps tensors + metadata' box rather than on the 'Packed tensor' box. This blurs the distinction the caption draws between the packed tensor and the checkpoint container.
issue.evidence: In Figure 7.3 the two top boxes' downward arrows enter the top edge of the large container box; the 'Packed tensor: values + scales...' box sits inside that container and receives no arrow.
issue.acceptance_test: Arrows terminate on the packed-tensor box, or the container is clearly drawn as a downstream wrapper after packing.

issue.issue: The 'sample p99' label is placed at the top left of the plot, far from the red dashed 1.33 s line it names, and has no leader. A reader can momentarily associate the label with the nearby p50/p90/p95 cluster instead of the 1.33 s line.
issue.evidence: In Figure 6.2 the red 'sample p99' text sits above the green p50 label near x≈0.8, while the red dashed sample-p99 line is at x≈1.33; the boxed note 'sample p99 (interpolation) = 1.33s' is the only direct tie.
issue.acceptance_test: The 'sample p99' label is adjacent to the 1.33 s line or connected by a leader; no ambiguity remains at print size.

issue.issue: The bar fills use hatching on the inference and QLoRA bars but a solid fill on the full fine-tune bar, with no legend or caption explaining what the pattern encodes. This is a gratuitous visual distinction that can imply a semantic difference where none is stated.
issue.evidence: Figure 7.6: inference bar is blue with diagonal hatching; QLoRA bar is green with diagonal hatching; full fine-tune bar is solid red. The caption and in-figure notes describe only the quantities, not the fill patterns.
issue.acceptance_test: Either the hatching encodes a stated distinction (and is explained in the caption/legend), or all bars use a consistent fill treatment.

issue.issue: The faint vertical rules said to mark 24.9 GB request slots inside the KV band are not visually distinguishable from the orange dotted fill. The figure therefore does not actually communicate the 17-request slot decomposition it claims to show; the reader must rely on the equation below.
issue.evidence: Caption: “the faint vertical rules inside the KV band mark those 24.9 GB request slots.” In the rendered figure, the KV band is filled with a regular white-dot pattern; no separate slot-boundary rules are legible at print size. The equation below the bar carries the entire 436 ÷ 24.9 ≈ 17.5 → ~17 message.
issue.acceptance_test: At 100% print size, a reader can distinguish 17 slot boundaries from the decorative fill pattern without reading the caption or equation. If the slot boundaries are not intended to be countable, remove the claim that they mark request slots and let the equation carry the arithmetic.

issue.issue: The 80 GB rank-boundary lines are unlabeled and visually merge with the ordinary horizontal grid. The caption says they are a visualization guide, but the figure itself gives no key distinguishing rank boundaries from grid lines, so the reader cannot tell which lines carry the per-rank caveat.
issue.evidence: Caption: “(light rules = 80 GB rank boundaries)” and “the 80 GB rank-boundary lines are a visualization guide.” The chart shows several light horizontal rules, but no line is marked or keyed as a rank boundary; the 640 GB dashed line is the only annotated horizontal reference.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can identify which horizontal rules are the 80 GB rank boundaries without reading the caption, e.g. by a distinct line style, a single labeled example, or a small legend entry.

issue.figure: Figure 8.1 — Where inference computation and data movement actually live
issue.issue: The compute box “tensor cores / ALU” is placed inside the vertical memory-hierarchy ladder, and the red gradient arrow “capacity grows / speed drops / distance grows” spans the entire stack including that compute box. This visually implies that tensor cores/ALU are a level of the memory hierarchy, contradicting the caption’s statement that compute, memory, and interconnect are separate groups.
issue.evidence: Caption: “the figure groups the resources three ways: compute units (tensor cores/ALU); the memory hierarchy … and interconnect” and “only the memory hierarchy is a smallest-to-largest ladder.” In the figure, the blue compute box sits between registers and shared memory, and the red gradient arrow runs past it as if it were a rung on the same ladder.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can tell at a glance that tensor cores/ALU are a separate compute group, not a memory level, and that the speed/capacity/distance gradient applies only to the memory hierarchy. This may require offsetting the compute box, breaking the gradient arrow around it, or adding a visual bracket that separates compute from the memory ladder.

issue.figure: Figure 8.1 — Where inference computation and data movement actually live
issue.issue: White labels over dense orange and green crosshatch fills have reduced contrast, especially the smaller secondary lines such as “fastest · smallest,” “on-chip · close,” “on-die,” and “large · slower.” The pattern competes with the text at print size.
issue.evidence: The figure uses a high-frequency crosshatch behind white text in the registers, shared-memory, L2, HBM, GPU-interconnect, and remote-GPU boxes. The primary labels remain readable, but the secondary lines are visibly busier than the same text would be on a solid fill.
issue.acceptance_test: At 100% print size, every label and secondary annotation remains comfortably readable without zooming, and the fill pattern does not create shimmer or legibility loss in grayscale.

issue.figure: Figure 8.2 — Per-GPU roofline: dense FP16, one H100 vs one H200
issue.issue: The annotation “decode batch B=8 (intensity ≈ B FLOP/byte)” uses a long arrow that crosses the H100 roofline and points to a small marker. The reading order is not immediate: the eye must trace a long connector across the plot to associate the label with the correct point.
issue.evidence: The label sits in the left-middle region of the chart, while the B=8 point is near x ≈ 8 on the H100 line. The arrow crosses the blue H100 line and passes near other annotations, making the association less direct than the other point labels.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can associate the B=8 label with its point within a few seconds without tracing a connector across unrelated lines, e.g. by placing the label closer to the point or using a short leader line.

issue.issue: The feedback loop on the right side of the Wan2.2 box is drawn with the same solid line style that the legend defines as “data/state flow,” but the loop represents denoising/scheduler iteration — a control/iteration loop, not a data/state flow. The figure therefore does not visually distinguish control flow from data flow, even though the caption explicitly says the loop is “denoising/scheduler iteration, not architectural recurrence.”
issue.evidence: Legend: “Solid: data/state flow. Dashed: denoiser conditioning.” The loop arrow from the right side of the Wan2.2 box back into the same box is solid. Caption: “The feedback loop is denoising/scheduler iteration, not architectural recurrence.”
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can tell from the figure alone, without the caption, that the loop is a control/iteration loop rather than a data/state dependency. This requires a distinct line style, a loop-specific label, or an explicit control-flow legend entry.

issue.figure: Figure 9.1 — Ring traffic and directional bandwidth
issue.issue: The annotation says “140 GB tensor” while the x-axis and surrounding prose define the quantity as logical input tensor per rank. A reader can misread the annotation as a 140 GB total tensor rather than 140 GB per rank.
issue.evidence: The x-axis label is “Logical input tensor per rank (GB)”; the annotation reads “140 GB tensor (245 GB sent at 1.75×)”; the caption says “At 140 GB the ideal times are about 0.54 s, 6.1 s and 98 s.” The prose on printed p. 162 says the eight-rank ring “sends 245 GB per rank.”
issue.acceptance_test: Change the annotation to “140 GB per rank” or “140 GB logical tensor per rank,” and verify the caption uses the same per-rank qualifier at least once.
