issue.issue: The parenthetical “(8 B/rank)” is ambiguous: it can be read as the amount each rank sends, but the figure later states each rank sends 12 B across both phases. The 8 B is the input size per rank, not the communication volume.
issue.evidence: The figure header says “Four ranks; four FP16 elements per input (8 B/rank).” The reduce-scatter and all-gather annotations each say “6 B sent + 6 B received/rank,” and the bottom box says “Per rank: 12 B sent + 12 B received = 24 B endpoint total.”
issue.acceptance_test: Replace “(8 B/rank)” with “(8 B input per rank)” or “(8 B payload per rank before communication),” and confirm the caption still states the 12 B sent / 12 B received total.

issue.figure: Figure 9.3 — The payload path is not the bootstrap path
issue.issue: The dashed red setup arrows are thin and low-contrast relative to the solid black payload arrows. In grayscale they become mid-gray dashed lines, and at print size the connection from the setup box to ProcessGroupNCCL/ProcessGroupXCCL is easy to miss.
issue.evidence: The legend distinguishes “Payload / execution” as a solid black arrow and “Control / setup” as a dashed red arrow. The dashed red lines run from the top setup box down the outside of the framework-backend boxes; they are visibly lighter and thinner than the solid arrows.
issue.acceptance_test: Increase the dashed setup-line weight or contrast, or add a short direct label on each dashed connector (“setup only”), and inspect a grayscale print proof to confirm the dashed path remains immediately visible.

issue.figure: Figure 10.1 — Three parallelism patterns, one per panel
issue.issue: Panel A labels the all-reduce communication step in a floating red dashed box below the GPUs, but no arrows connect the GPUs to that box or the box to “full output.” The communication step is therefore visually detached from the computation it summarizes.
issue.evidence: Panel A shows GPU 0 and GPU 1 with weight shards W0 and W1, then a red dashed box reading “all-reduce partial sums → full output” beneath them. There are no connector arrows from the GPU boxes into or out of the all-reduce box.
issue.acceptance_test: Add arrows from GPU 0 and GPU 1 into the all-reduce box and from the all-reduce box to a “full output” label, or redraw the all-reduce as a connected stage in the panel-A flow.

issue.figure: Figure 10.1 — Three parallelism patterns, one per panel
issue.issue: Panel B says “idle (bubble) at fill/drain — pipeline-wide” but the diagram does not visually encode the bubble. The panel shows only three sequential stage boxes and arrows; the key pipeline-parallel cost is asserted in text rather than shown.
issue.evidence: Panel B draws GPU 0 (layers 1–8), GPU 1 (layers 9–16), and GPU 2 (layers 17–24) with P2P arrows. The only representation of the fill/drain bubble is the text line “idle (bubble) at fill/drain — pipeline-wide.”
issue.acceptance_test: Add a small schedule strip or shaded idle intervals at the start and end of the pipeline, or explicitly state in the caption that the bubble is not drawn and is only named; then verify the panel still reads correctly in grayscale.

issue.issue: The green admission events are drawn as finite-width blocks, and the annotation arrow 'a finishing sequence frees its slot immediately' points at one of those green blocks. This conflates the freeing event (end of a blue sequence) with the admission event (start of the next sequence) and visually implies that admission consumes decode-step time.
issue.evidence: Legend: 'admission event (backfill)' is a green rectangle; caption calls it an 'admission tick'; the arrow from 'a finishing sequence frees its slot immediately' terminates on a green bar, not on the end of the preceding blue block or the freed slot. The green bars have visible width along the time axis.
issue.acceptance_test: Redraw admission as a zero-width vertical tick at the slot boundary (or explicitly label it as instantaneous), and point the 'frees its slot' arrow to the end of the blue sequence / the freed slot, not to the admission tick. Verify that a reader cannot infer that admission takes a decode step.

issue.issue: The legend distinguishes 'sequence in flight' (blue) from 'admission event' (green) by hue alone. In grayscale the two colors have nearly identical luminance, so the narrow green admission bars become visually indistinguishable from blue sequence blocks.
issue.evidence: Legend uses solid blue for sequence and solid green for admission; no pattern or shape difference. Approximate luminance of the blue and green fills is very close, and the green bars are small, making the distinction fragile in grayscale or for color-vision differences.
issue.acceptance_test: Add a non-color distinction (hatching, outline, or a clearly different luminance) to the admission event, and verify the figure in grayscale at print size. The reader must still distinguish sequence blocks from admission events without color.

issue.figure: Figure 11.3 — P/D disaggregation: two cases, two different KV links
issue.issue: The prefill boxes are labeled 'PREFFILL' (double F) in both panels. This is a visible spelling error in a key figure label.
issue.evidence: Panel A red box reads 'PREFFILL 4 GPUs'; panel B red box reads 'PREFFILL 8 GPUs'. The correct term used throughout the prose is 'prefill'.
issue.acceptance_test: Correct both labels to 'PREFILL' and re-render the figure.

issue.figure: Figure 11.3 — P/D disaggregation: two cases, two different KV links
issue.issue: Panel A draws a single thick KV arrow between the 4-GPU prefill group and the 4-GPU decode group, labeled '450 GB/s per GPU per direction'. The single-arrow visual suggests one shared 450 GB/s link, while the prose and caveat treat the case as four per-GPU links whose aggregate is 1.8 TB/s. The figure's caveat then says '1.4 TB/s exceeds any single link above', which is true per link but can be misread as saying the panel-A configuration cannot absorb the aggregate load.
issue.evidence: Panel A: one arrow labeled '450 GB/s per GPU per direction'; note 'square = one GPU'. Prose Note 11.3-1: 'the panel's 4-way shard would be 35 ÷ (4 × 450) ≈ 0.02 s' and '4 decode GPUs × 450 GB/s = 1.8 TB/s aggregate ingress absorbs the 1.4 TB/s'. Figure caveat: '1.4 TB/s exceeds any single link above.'
issue.acceptance_test: Either draw four per-GPU KV links (or a labeled aggregate '4 × 450 GB/s = 1.8 TB/s') in panel A, or revise the arrow label and caveat to distinguish single-link capacity from aggregate capacity. Verify that a reader cannot conclude panel A is infeasible at 40 req/s when the prose says the aggregate is feasible but tight.

issue.figure: Figure 11.4 — Device visibility is not a validated serving path
issue.issue: The figure is text-dense, and the smallest text — especially the multi-line 'Kernels / runtime' descriptions and the qualification-gate requirements — appears below the book's 8 pt figure-annotation floor at print size.
issue.evidence: The box text is visibly smaller than the caption and body text; the qualification-gate box packs three lines of small text, and the 'Kernels / runtime' boxes contain 3–4 lines each. At 150 dpi the glyphs are legible on screen but are at the lower limit for print.
issue.acceptance_test: Measure the actual font size in the figure source. If any in-figure annotation is below 8 pt, enlarge the figure or simplify the text so every label meets the 8 pt floor at final trim size.

issue.issue: The outcome box says “CAPACITY SCREEN: (a) · (b) pass … ~5 avg / ~19 peak hosts” without saying these are prefill hosts only. For candidate (b), P/D-disaggregated, Table 12-2 on PDF 238 / printed 218 adds a separate decode pool sized to 3K tok/s avg / 12K tok/s peak. A reader can therefore infer that (b) needs only ~19 hosts total, which contradicts the table and understates the fleet.
issue.evidence: Figure 12.1 outcome box: “CAPACITY SCREEN: (a) · (b) pass … ~5 avg / ~19 peak hosts”. Table 12-2: (b) has “prefill pool ~19 hosts before headroom” and “decode pool sized to 3K tok/s avg / 12K tok/s peak”. The figure does not label the host count as prefill-only and does not show the decode pool.
issue.acceptance_test: The figure either labels the count “prefill hosts” and adds a decode-pool annotation for (b), or explicitly states “prefill capacity screen only; total fleet includes decode pool (Table 12-2)”.

issue.issue: The blue de-escalation label lists “privacy · sovereignty · cost” but omits “on-device requirements”, which the caption explicitly names as a de-escalation trigger. The figure and caption therefore disagree on the trigger set.
issue.evidence: Figure blue label: “DE-ESCALATE: privacy · sovereignty · cost”. Caption: “de-escalation (blue) fires on data-residency/sovereignty, on-device requirements, and cost”.
issue.acceptance_test: The blue label includes “on-device” (or the caption removes it), so the figure and caption name the same de-escalation triggers.

issue.issue: The repeated phrase “no binding constraint → STOP” under every tier is ambiguous. “STOP” can be read as “stop serving” or “stop the architecture”, whereas the intended meaning is “stop escalating”. The bottom note clarifies, but the repeated label itself is not self-explanatory.
issue.evidence: Each tier box has “no binding constraint → STOP”; bottom note says “escalate only when a constraint binds — else STOP”.
issue.acceptance_test: Replace “STOP” with “stop escalating” or “stay at this tier” in the repeated labels, or remove the repeated labels and rely on the bottom note.

issue.figure: Figure 15.1 — FlashAttention: the same math, far less HBM traffic
issue.issue: The BEFORE panel’s HBM box is labeled only “Q/K/V HBM”, but the panel’s text and caption say the L×L intermediate attention matrix is written to HBM. The visual does not show the intermediate matrix as a distinct HBM-resident object, so the diagram’s central mechanism — materializing and re-reading the L×L intermediate — is not visually encoded. A reader can infer that the only HBM traffic is Q/K/V reads/writes, which is the misconception the figure is meant to correct.
issue.evidence: BEFORE panel: HBM box label “Q/K/V HBM”; subtitle “intermediate written to HBM”; bottom text “O(L²) HBM traffic: L×L intermediate written + every query re-reads the K/V rows”. Caption: “the intermediate attention matrix is materialized to HBM and re-read … down = the L×L intermediate write”. The HBM box itself does not show or label the intermediate.
issue.acceptance_test: The BEFORE panel visually distinguishes the L×L intermediate in HBM — e.g., a separate “L×L intermediate” block, or an HBM box labeled “Q/K/V + L×L intermediate” with the write arrow landing on that block — so the diagram alone shows what is materialized and re-read.

issue.figure: Figure 15.1 — FlashAttention: the same math, far less HBM traffic
issue.issue: The caption’s reduction-factor calculation is dimensionally ambiguous. It gives “M/d² (≈6× at d = 128, M ≈ 192 KB of fp16)”, but M in the formula is an element count, while “192 KB of fp16” is a byte capacity. If a reader substitutes 192 KB directly, M/d² ≈ 12, not 6. The printed 6× is correct only if M is read as ~96K fp16 elements.
issue.evidence: Caption: “a reduction factor of M/d² (≈6× at d = 128, M ≈ 192 KB of fp16)”. 192 KB of fp16 = 98,304 elements; 98,304 / 128² ≈ 6. But 192,000 / 128² ≈ 11.7. The caption does not state that M is in elements.
issue.acceptance_test: The caption states M in the same units as d², e.g. “M ≈ 96K fp16 elements (192 KB)” or “M/d² ≈ 6× at d = 128, M ≈ 96K elements”, so the arithmetic is unambiguous.

issue.figure: Figure 15.1 — FlashAttention: the same math, far less HBM traffic
issue.issue: The AFTER panel’s phrase “no single global K/V pass” is ambiguous. It can be read as “there is no global K/V pass at all”, whereas the intended meaning is “there is no single global pass over all K/V for all queries; K/V is re-read per tile”. The caption clarifies, but the diagram label itself is misleading.
issue.evidence: AFTER panel: “K/V reused per tile — no single global K/V pass; no L×L intermediate at HBM”. Caption: “it is not a guarantee that every K/V element is read exactly once globally across all query blocks”.
issue.acceptance_test: Rephrase to “K/V re-read per tile; not a single global pass” or “no single global K/V pass over all queries”, so the label cannot be read as denying all global K/V reads.

issue.issue: The Cost/SLO gate is semantically under-specified. A single 'yes' arrow splits to both Frontier and Small gen, with the label 'yes → SLO: frontier cost: small'. The diagram does not show the decision rule that distinguishes Frontier from Small gen, so the reader cannot tell whether the gate is choosing by SLO, cost, or both.
issue.evidence: Diagram label: 'yes → SLO: frontier cost: small' with one arrow splitting to 'Frontier' and 'Small gen'. Caption: 'cost/SLO gate (route = f(cost, SLO))'. The caption defers thresholds to §18.3.1–§18.3.4, but the figure itself does not encode the branch condition.
issue.acceptance_test: Replace the single 'yes' branch with two explicit branches (e.g., 'SLO requires frontier → Frontier' and 'cost-sensitive → Small gen'), or add a decision diamond with the actual criteria. A reader should be able to explain the Frontier-vs-Small-gen choice from the figure alone.

issue.figure: Figure 19.1 — The agent loop: a four-state machine
issue.issue: The diagram contradicts the caption on what terminates the loop at the limit. The caption says 'a turn/token budget check — not the model's judgment — ends the loop at the limit', but the 'limit hit' arrow originates from the 'Decide' state, which is labeled 'check' and 'resolved?'. This visually implies the model's Decide state determines the limit hit.
issue.evidence: Diagram: 'Decide' box contains 'check' and 'resolved?'; solid arrow labeled 'limit hit' runs from Decide to 'Stopped'. Caption: 'a turn/token budget check — not the model's judgment — ends the loop at the limit.'
issue.acceptance_test: Add a separate budget/turn-limit check (decision diamond or explicit gate) on the loop/exit path, or split the Decide state into 'resolved?' and 'budget exhausted?' with the limit-hit arrow originating from the budget check. The figure must not imply that the model's judgment enforces the hard limit.

issue.figure: Figure 19.2 — Token growth vs resulting KV growth across agent turns
issue.issue: The figure caption/note conflates two different token metrics. The bars show retained context/KV growing from 9,500 to 12,960 tokens (~1.36x), but the note says 'tokens per submitted request grow ~2.5x under no prefix reuse (mix 68/25/5/2%, Table 19-1: 2.52x)'. The 2.52x is not the retained-context growth shown in the chart; it is a different (billed/processed) metric. A reader can reasonably infer that the bars grow 2.5x, which they do not.
issue.evidence: Panel (a) bars: 9,500 → 10,365 → 11,230 → 12,095 → 12,960. Panel (b): 24.9 → 27.2 → 29.4 → 31.7 → 34.0 GB. Caption: 'Per-request tokens and FP16 KV cache climb linearly with agent turns, from 24.9 GB single-shot to 34.0 GB at four turns.' Note: 'Bars are RETAINED context/KV, not summed per-call processed or billed tokens; tokens per submitted request grow ~2.5x under no prefix reuse (mix 68/25/5/2%, Table 19-1: 2.52x).'
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite the note to say explicitly that the ~2.52x figure is average billed/processed tokens (sum over calls) under the 68/25/5/2 mix, not the retained-context bars; or remove the 2.52x sentence from this figure. The caption must not juxtapose a 1.36x retained-context chart with a 2.52x token-growth claim without labeling the metric change.

issue.figure: Figure 19.2 — Token growth vs resulting KV growth across agent turns
issue.issue: The caption's final sentence groups prefix caching with fleet sizing and FP8 KV as a response to KV footprint growth, but the same caption correctly says prefix caching 'does not by itself reduce the request's own KV-resident context'. This is an internal contradiction about what prefix caching solves.
issue.evidence: Caption: '...which is exactly why a fleet (Ch 17), prefix caching, or FP8 KV pay for themselves on agentic workloads.' Earlier in the same caption: 'prefix caching reduces recomputation and shares prefix KV but does not by itself reduce the request's own KV-resident context (§6).'
issue.acceptance_test: Revise the final sentence to separate the levers: fleet/FP8 KV address KV capacity; prefix caching addresses recomputation and billed tokens, not the request's own KV footprint. The caption should not imply that prefix caching reduces the KV growth shown in panel (b).

issue.figure: Figure 19.2 — Token growth vs resulting KV growth across agent turns
issue.issue: The caption's arithmetic wording is ambiguous for turn 0. It says '9,200 input + 300 output + 800 + 65 per turn', which can be read as including 800 + 65 at turn 0, but the chart's turn-0 bar is 9,500 (9,200 + 300), not 10,365.
issue.evidence: Caption: 'each column is a counterfactual completion (9,200 input + 300 output + 800 + 65 per turn)'. Panel (a) turn 0 bar is ~9,500; turn 1 bar is ~10,365.
issue.acceptance_test: Reword to '9,200 input + 300 output, plus 800 retrieved + 65 generated per additional turn' or equivalent, so the turn-0 value is unambiguous.

issue.figure: Figure 19.2 — Token growth vs resulting KV growth across agent turns
issue.issue: The legend labels 'generated (γ=65)' and 'output (O=300)' as separate categories without clarifying that both are generated tokens. This can confuse readers about what is being counted, especially because the text distinguishes per-turn reasoning tokens from the final answer.
issue.evidence: Legend: 'generated (γ=65)' and 'output (O=300)'. Caption: '9,200 input + 300 output + 800 + 65 per turn'. Text on p. 342 distinguishes 'per-turn reasoning tokens' from the final answer.
issue.acceptance_test: Rename the legend entries to 'per-turn generated/reasoning (γ=65)' and 'final output (O=300)' (or similar) so the distinction is explicit.

issue.issue: The six gates are drawn as a parallel row of boxes below the pipeline, not as gates on the transition seams. The top-row arrows run directly from stage to stage, and no PASS arrow connects a gate to the next stage. This contradicts the caption's claim that 'PASS permits the next stage' and can mislead readers into thinking the gates are optional side checks.
issue.evidence: Caption: 'Six gates align with the transition seams: PASS permits the next stage'; diagram: Data→Train→Eval→Canary→Observe→Promote→Serve arrows are unbroken, while gate boxes sit below with dotted vertical connectors and only FAIL arrows to the rollback bar.
issue.acceptance_test: Redraw with gate diamonds/boxes inline between stages, or add explicit PASS arrows from each gate to the next stage and remove/redirect the direct stage-to-stage arrows; keep FAIL branches to the rollback bar.

issue.issue: The green feedback loop visually returns only to Data, while the caption and label say 'data/evaluation'.
issue.evidence: Caption: 'Production feedback returns evidence to data/evaluation'; green loop enters at Data; label: 'production feedback → data / evaluation'.
issue.acceptance_test: Branch the feedback loop to both Data and Eval, or change the label/caption to Data only.

issue.issue: The causal-triangle crossover at ~106.8K is outside the plotted x-axis range (10^0–10^2 K tokens = 1–100K), so the figure claims a crossover that is not visible; the annotation arrow points to the blue line near the right edge rather than to the crossing.
issue.evidence: Caption: 'the quadratic attention term overtakes the parameterized-linear term at ~53.4K context tokens under full-square counting and ~106.8K under causal-triangle counting'; left panel x-axis ends at 10^2 K tokens; annotation: 'causal-triangle quad term overtakes linear ~106.8K'.
issue.acceptance_test: Extend the x-axis to at least 200K (e.g., 10^0–10^3 K tokens) so both crossovers are visible, or add an explicit off-chart arrow/label indicating the ~106.8K crossing is beyond the plotted range.

issue.issue: The left-panel legend text is visibly smaller than the axis labels and caption; at 150 dpi it is ~13–14 px high, below the 8 pt print floor (~16.7 px at 150 dpi). The legend is essential to distinguish the five lines.
issue.evidence: Legend entries 'linear 2·N·L', 'quadratic 4·n_layers·L^2·d', etc. are set in a smaller size than the axis labels; the legend is dense and contains equations.
issue.acceptance_test: Increase legend font to at least 8 pt (preferably 9 pt) and/or move the legend outside the plot area; verify all five entries remain legible at print size.

issue.issue: The legend calls C_analytic 'analytical host capacity', but the plotted quantity is fleet rate (req/s) and the caption calls it 'Fleet capacity vs host count'. This is a terminology mismatch that can be misread as per-host capacity.
issue.evidence: Legend: 'analytical host capacity C_analytic = N × 17/8.6 (req/s)'; y-axis: 'Fleet rate (req/s)'; caption: 'Fleet capacity vs host count'.
issue.acceptance_test: Change legend to 'analytical fleet capacity C_analytic = N × 17/8.6 (req/s)'.

issue.issue: The red 'UNUSED capacity' region starts at N=22, but S = min(40, C_eff) reaches the 40 rps cap at N≈21.3; the small unused-capacity region between 21.3 and 22 is unshaded. The label 'N ≥ 22' is explicit, but the visual boundary does not match the arithmetic crossing.
issue.evidence: Red region label: 'UNUSED capacity (N ≥ 22)'; C_eff = 0.95 × N × 17/8.6; setting C_eff = 40 gives N ≈ 21.3.
issue.acceptance_test: Start the shading at the exact crossing (N≈21.3) or add a note that integer provisioning rounds up to 22; ensure the shaded boundary matches the stated arithmetic.

issue.issue: The annotation '21 hosts (ideal) / 22 at 95%: served demand plateaus at 40 rps' can be misread as saying 21 hosts at 95% achieve 40 rps; at N=21, C_eff≈39.4 rps, so the plateau begins only at N≈21.3 (integer 22).
issue.evidence: Annotation: 'KV screen only: 21 hosts (ideal) / 22 at 95%: served demand plateaus at 40 rps'; at N=21, C_eff = 0.95×21×17/8.6 ≈ 39.4.
issue.acceptance_test: Revise to '21 ideal / 22 at 95% (40 rps plateau begins at ~21.3; integer provisioning requires 22)' or equivalent.

issue.issue: The prefix-cache eviction bar is labeled '34.0 GB unchanged', while the caption says the policy frees cached prefix memory; the annotation 'moves cache/re-prefill' is grammatically unclear. A reader can misread 'unchanged' as total memory unchanged.
issue.evidence: Bar label: '34.0 GB unchanged'; caption: 'leaves the request's own context and KV unchanged (still 34.0 GB) while freeing cached prefix memory'; annotation: 'evicts the reusable prefix — moves cache/re-prefill'.
issue.acceptance_test: Relabel the bar to '34.0 GB request KV (prefix cache freed)' and rewrite the annotation to 'evicts reusable prefix — frees cache but forces re-prefill'.

issue.issue: The final green box is shifted right relative to the orange stack, the arrow from box 5 enters left of center, and the second line 'decisions enabled: KV FP16→FP8 + prefix cache + routing' runs to the right border with almost no padding. The first line is centered while the second is left-aligned.
issue.evidence: Green box text touches the right border; box center is offset from the orange boxes; arrow from box 5 enters off-center.
issue.acceptance_test: Center the green box under the orange stack, align the arrow to its center, widen/reflow the second line with adequate padding, and use consistent alignment for both lines.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 2, §6 Architecture Consequence, prefill levers bullet
issue.quoted_clause: Changing format at the same byte width (BF16 in place of FP16) changes neither the bytes stored nor the H100 dense tensor-core peak: it trades mantissa bits (10 → 8) for exponent range, a numerical-stability choice rather than a throughput one.
issue.observed: FP16 has 10 explicit mantissa bits (11 including the implicit bit); BF16 has 7 explicit mantissa bits (8 including the implicit bit). The parenthetical 10 → 8 mixes explicit and total precision and is not correct as written.
issue.evidence: IEEE 754 half precision: 1 sign, 5 exponent, 10 mantissa; bfloat16: 1 sign, 8 exponent, 7 mantissa. If counting the implicit leading bit, precision is 11 vs 8, not 10 vs 8.
issue.root_cause: Imprecise bit-field description.
issue.correction: Change to 'it trades mantissa precision (10 explicit bits, or 11 including the implicit bit, for 7 explicit, or 8 including the implicit bit) for exponent range' or simply 'it trades precision for exponent range'.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can state FP16 and BF16 explicit mantissa widths correctly from the sentence.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 2, §2 Mental Model, decode bandwidth-bound paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: It is like pushing the water of that same 140 GB reservoir through a standard garden hose: the whole volume must flow every 25 milliseconds just to deliver one glass of water — one generated token. The reservoir is not drained — the same 140 GB is re-read every step. The pump (compute) is more than powerful enough, but the diameter of the hose (HBM bandwidth) physically cannot move that volume of water in that time frame.
issue.observed: This describes a single-device 140 GB weight stream requiring 5.6 TB/s, but the canonical host is 8×H100 with the weight sharded to 17.5 GB/GPU, requiring 700 GB/s per GPU and taking ~5.2 ms, which the later canonical host verdict says is inside the 25 ms TPOT budget and not HBM-saturating. The analogy's 'physically cannot move' is a capacity claim that conflicts with the canonical host feasibility.
issue.evidence: Ch2 §3: 'decode shard 70B/8 = 8.75B params = 17.5 GB/GPU per step → 17.5 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 5.2 ms, inside the 25 ms TPOT budget'; 'At the canonical operating point the 5.2 ms weight read is not HBM-saturating'.
issue.root_cause: Conflating logical aggregate weight footprint with per-GPU HBM traffic in the mental-model analogy.
issue.correction: Reword to distinguish the batch-1-equivalent single-device illustration from the canonical 8×H100 host: e.g. 'In the single-device illustration, the 140 GB logical weight footprint would need 5.6 TB/s through one H100's hose; on the canonical 8×H100 host the same step is sharded to 17.5 GB/GPU (700 GB/s), so the step is memory-dominated but not HBM-saturating.'
issue.acceptance_test: The analogy no longer implies the canonical 8×H100 host cannot meet the 25 ms TPOT due to HBM saturation, and it matches the later 17.5 GB/GPU arithmetic.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 3, §4 Measurement, bullet 3; also §5 Common Mistakes first bullet
issue.quoted_clause: For MoE models, the number of experts × parameters-per-expert gives the total; the routing hyperparameter (top-k) × parameters-per-expert gives the active per token.
issue.observed: This formula omits always-on attention/shared/embedding parameters. The chapter's own Mixtral example uses active = 2×5.7B routed experts + 1.4B always-on = 12.8B, not 11.4B.
issue.evidence: Table 3-2: 'Active parameters per token (top-2 routing) | ~12.8B | 2 × 5.7B routed experts + ~1.4B always-on attention/shared = 12.8B'.
issue.root_cause: Shortcut formula stated without the always-on term.
issue.correction: Change to 'top-k × parameters-per-expert gives the routed-expert active parameters; add always-on attention/shared/embedding parameters to get total active per token.' Also adjust Common Mistakes phrase 'only the routed experts are read' to include always-on parameters.
issue.acceptance_test: Applying the corrected formula to the Mixtral example yields ~12.8B active, matching Table 3-2.

issue.quoted_clause: The token-counting habits of Ch 1 §1.4 apply unchanged
issue.observed: Chapter 1's measurement material is in section 4 ('## 4. Measurement'), not §1.4. The reference is stale or uses a different numbering scheme.
issue.evidence: Chunk shows Chapter 1 headings: '## 4. Measurement' and no '§1.4'.
issue.root_cause: Incorrect cross-reference after section numbering.
issue.correction: Change to 'Ch 1 §4' or 'Chapter 1, Measurement'.
issue.acceptance_test: The cross-reference resolves to the token-counting measurement section in Chapter 1.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 2, §3 Worked Example, Table 2-1 and prefill FLOPs paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: The required rate against the ~1.08 s prefill budget is
issue.observed: Chapter 4 later defines 1.08 s as a two-term-only upper cap (TTFT 1.2 s minus retrieval 0.12 s) that leaves zero for admission/queue and tokenization/transfer, and explicitly says it is not a feasible deployed prefill target. Chapter 2 uses it as 'the prefill budget' without that qualification, which can make the analytical infeasibility argument look like a deployed deadline.
issue.evidence: Ch4 Table 4-2: 'Prefill compute budget — two-term-only upper cap, NOT a feasible deployed prefill target ... budget_prefill ≤ 1.08 s − B_other'.
issue.root_cause: Cross-chapter scope drift for the 1.08 s residual.
issue.correction: In Ch2, label it 'the two-term residual after retrieval (an upper cap, not a deployed prefill target)' or add a forward note that Ch4 subtracts B_other for queue/tokenization.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader sees that the 1.08 s in Ch2 is the same two-term-only upper cap used in Ch4, not a guaranteed deployed prefill budget.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 2 Fig 2.1 caption; Chapter 4 Latency from SLO TPOT bullet
issue.quoted_clause: DECODE (bottom) is the single-token autoregressive loop, measured by TPOT (time per output token; equivalently the mean ITL, inter-token latency)
issue.observed: The book's timing convention assigns the first sampled token to prefill, so a 300-token output has 299 inter-token intervals after the first token. Later text uses '300 × 25 ms = 7.5 s' as total decode time. The 'equivalently' and 300×25 can imply TPOT is computed over 300 ITLs, which is inconsistent with the first-token convention.
issue.evidence: Ch2 timing convention: 'prefill = processing the prompt + sampling token 1, and decode = the per-token loop that begins with token 1 as its first input and produces token 2 onward.' Ch4: 'A 300-token answer therefore takes ~7.5 s of total decode time' from 300 × 25 ms.
issue.root_cause: Ambiguous TPOT denominator (output tokens vs output tokens minus one) relative to the first-token convention.
issue.correction: Define TPOT as a planning per-generated-token rate and state that the 300×25 ms figure is a rounded planning approximation; if using mean ITL strictly, use (N−1) intervals or say the first token is included in the planning count.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can reconcile the first-token convention with the 7.5 s decode estimate without assuming 300 inter-token intervals.

issue.quoted_clause: ≈24–27% for top-2-from-8
issue.observed: Top-2-from-8 is exactly 25% of the expert mass; adding always-on parameters raises the total active fraction to ~27% in the Mixtral example. The lower bound '~24%' is not derived from the stated numbers.
issue.root_cause: Unexplained range lower bound.
issue.correction: Change to '~25% of expert mass, ~27% of total in the Mixtral example' or explain the 24% case (e.g. different always-on mass).
issue.acceptance_test: Every number in the range is traceable to the stated expert/always-on split.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 3, §6 Architecture Consequence, Weight residency budget
issue.quoted_clause: Offloading inactives is a further option, priced in bandwidth.
issue.observed: 'inactives' is not a standard noun here; likely intended 'inactive experts' or 'inactive parameters'.
issue.evidence: Context discusses expert offloading/swapping.
issue.root_cause: Typo/word choice.
issue.correction: Change to 'Offloading inactive experts is a further option, priced in bandwidth.'
issue.acceptance_test: Sentence reads as standard technical prose.

issue.observed: The right-hand side omits the FLOP unit; '25.6B' and '140B' can be read as parameters rather than FLOPs, although the intended values are 25.6 GFLOP and 140 GFLOP.
issue.evidence: Earlier text: '25.6 GFLOP ÷ 140 GFLOP'.
issue.root_cause: Unit abbreviation ambiguity in table derivation.
issue.correction: Write '25.6 GFLOP ÷ 140 GFLOP' or '25.6B FLOP ÷ 140B FLOP'.
issue.acceptance_test: The table derivation is dimensionally clear as FLOPs, not parameters.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 4, §7 What We Still Don't Know, KV cache scaling bullet
issue.quoted_clause: at 128 K a single request alone needs ~335 GB of KV, leaving little for any concurrency
issue.observed: After 140 GB weights and ~64 GB runtime, a 335 GB KV request leaves ~100 GB, which can support a few shorter-context requests even though it cannot support additional 128K requests. 'any concurrency' is too broad.
issue.evidence: 640 − 140 − 64 − 335.5 ≈ 100.5 GB; canonical 9.5K resident request is ~24.9 GB, so ~4 such requests could fit in the residual.
issue.root_cause: Overgeneralization from no additional 128K concurrency to no concurrency of any kind.
issue.correction: Change to 'leaving little room for additional 128K requests (and only a few shorter-context requests)' or specify the concurrency class.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence does not imply zero residual capacity for all possible request sizes.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 4, §5 Common Mistakes, Ignoring the input–output asymmetry
issue.quoted_clause: Raising aggregate decode throughput (output tokens/s across the fleet, e.g. via more batching) on an input-heavy workload moves the needle negligibly — the binding constraints are KV residency and prefill, not output rate; but per-request decode rate and TPOT are reciprocals, so reducing TPOT does shorten service time and host count
issue.observed: The sentence can be read as saying reducing TPOT has negligible effect, then immediately says it does shorten service time and host count. The distinction between aggregate output-token capacity and per-request TPOT is not explicit enough.
issue.evidence: In the canonical workload, decode is ~7.5 s of ~8.58 s service time; reducing TPOT materially changes W_exec and Little's-law occupancy.
issue.root_cause: Dense sentence conflates two different levers.
issue.correction: Split into two sentences: 'Increasing aggregate output-token capacity without improving per-request TPOT may not reduce host count when KV/prefill are binding. Reducing per-request TPOT does reduce W_exec and can materially reduce host count, though prefill/KV may remain the binding screens.'
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can distinguish aggregate decode capacity from per-request TPOT and see that TPOT reduction can affect host count.

issue.quoted_clause: sparse/linear attention and retrieval cut the quadratic prefill term
issue.observed: Retrieval (RAG) reduces the context length L and therefore the value of the quadratic term, but it does not change the quadratic dependence of full attention. Sparse/linear attention changes the algorithmic complexity. Grouping them as 'cut the quadratic prefill term' is imprecise.
issue.evidence: The same paragraph defines the quadratic term as growing as L²; retrieval changes L, not the L² law.
issue.root_cause: Conflating reducing L with changing attention complexity.
issue.correction: Change to 'sparse/linear attention can reduce the quadratic dependence, while retrieval reduces L and therefore the size of the quadratic prefill term'.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence distinguishes complexity change from context-length reduction.

issue.quoted_clause: time-to-first-token (TTFT), which encompasses retrieval and prefill
issue.observed: Later in the same chapter, TTFT_e2e is defined as retrieval + admission/queue + tokenization/transfer + prefill. The early definition omits queue/tokenization and can be read as exhaustive.
issue.evidence: Ch4 Latency from SLO: 'TTFT_e2e = retrieval + admission/queue + tokenization/transfer + prefill'.
issue.root_cause: Early shorthand not marked as two-term model.
issue.correction: Change to 'which in the canonical two-term model comprises retrieval and prefill (with queue/tokenization added in the full TTFT_e2e definition below)' or 'typically includes retrieval and prefill, plus queueing/transfer in the full e2e definition'.
issue.acceptance_test: The early definition does not contradict the later TTFT_e2e decomposition.

issue.quoted_clause: MXFP4 weights realize ~3.57× at 0.53125 B/value, §7.3
issue.observed: The stated reduction factor does not match the stated bytes-per-value for MXFP4.
issue.evidence: 2 bytes / 0.53125 B/value = 3.7647. The chapter's own 4096×4096 example gives BF16 33,554,432 bytes and MXFP4 8,912,896 bytes, a ratio of 3.7647. The ~3.57 value corresponds to 2 / 0.56 (or close to NVFP4's 2 / 0.5625 = 3.5556), not MXFP4 at 0.53125 B/value.
issue.root_cause: Likely transposition of the NVFP4 byte/value result into the MXFP4 sentence.
issue.correction: Change to 'MXFP4 weights realize ~3.76× at 0.53125 B/value', or if the intended format is common 1D NVFP4, say 'common 1D NVFP4 weights realize ~3.56× at 0.5625 B/value'.
issue.acceptance_test: Recompute 2/0.53125 and 2/0.5625; the named format, bytes-per-value, and reduction factor all agree.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 8, §3 Worked Example, 'The 1.08 s budget versus the 35% planning rate'
issue.quoted_clause: 1.08 s is the *end-to-end prefill budget* inside the 1.2 s TTFT (it absorbs queueing, scheduling, tokenization and admission overhead)
issue.observed: This conflicts with Chapters 5 and 6, where 1.08 s is the prefill component after retrieval and queueing/tokenization/admission are explicitly scoped out.
issue.evidence: Chapter 5 says the retrieval+prefill budget estimate has 'queueing, tokenization, network transit, scheduling and first-token sampling scoped out' and totals ~1.20 s. Chapter 6 says 'We budget TTFT ≤ 1.2 s (retrieval ~120 ms + prefill ~1.08 s)'. If 1.08 s included those overheads, the derived 15% MFU would not be a pure prefill-compute rate.
issue.root_cause: The phrase 'end-to-end prefill budget' plus the parenthetical incorrectly imports non-prefill overhead into the 1.08 s number.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: '1.08 s is the prefill compute budget inside the 1.2 s TTFT after the ~120 ms retrieval allocation; queueing, tokenization, admission, and first-token sampling are scoped out in the canonical budget (Ch 5/6). If a deployment includes those in the 1.08 s, the implied MFU must be recomputed after subtracting them.'
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can state unambiguously whether 1.08 s includes queueing/tokenization/admission, and Ch 5, Ch 6, and Ch 8 agree.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 6, §1 Concept, Metric Hierarchy, serving-metrics bullet
issue.quoted_clause: the canonical SLO targets are TTFT 1.2 s / TPOT ~25 ms
issue.observed: 1.2 s and ~25 ms are design budgets, not the p95 SLOs used elsewhere in the canonical scenario.
issue.evidence: Chapter 5 states 'TTFT budget 1.2 s ... p95 TTFT ≤ 2 s, p95 TPOT ≤ 35 ms'. Chapter 6 later says 'Under the canonical p95 TTFT SLO of ≤ 2 s' and 'p95 TTFT at 2.4 s against a 2 s SLO'.
issue.root_cause: The word 'SLO targets' is applied to internal budgets rather than the percentile SLOs.
issue.correction: Change to: 'the canonical design budgets are TTFT 1.2 s / TPOT ~25 ms; the p95 SLOs are TTFT ≤ 2 s / TPOT ≤ 35 ms.'
issue.acceptance_test: Search Ch 5 and Ch 6 for 'SLO'; 1.2 s and 25 ms are labeled budgets, while 2 s and 35 ms are labeled p95 SLOs.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 5, §3(b), 'tokens/s per dollar with prefill included'
issue.quoted_clause: The per‑dollar economics therefore favor models that reduce the *prefill compute* burden (smaller context, larger batch, lower per‑token FLOP) more than models that optimize decode throughput alone
issue.observed: The conclusion is stronger than the immediately preceding reasoning supports.
issue.evidence: The same paragraph says prefill is ~97% of tokens/linear FLOPs but only ~15% of single-stream wall-clock, and that 'GPU-hour cost follows occupancy, batching and scheduling — it is not proportional to either share without a stated utilization assumption.' If decode wall-clock dominates and sets the latency SLO, improving decode throughput can also reduce GPU-hours per request; prefill FLOP share alone does not establish that prefill reduction is economically more important than decode optimization.
issue.root_cause: Inferring a cost priority from FLOP share after explicitly disclaiming proportionality between FLOP share and GPU-hour cost.
issue.correction: Qualify the sentence: 'For this input-heavy workload, prefill compute is the dominant FLOP term, so prefill efficiency is a first-order cost lever when the host is FLOP/occupancy-limited; decode throughput remains the primary latency SLO lever. The relative economic priority must be measured under the target batching and utilization.'
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence no longer asserts a universal economic preference from FLOP share alone; it conditions the priority on measured occupancy, batching, and SLO behavior.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 5, Table 5-2, row 'Total tokens per dollar (prefill + decode, stated concurrency)'
issue.quoted_clause: Total tokens per dollar (prefill + decode, stated concurrency) | ~285,000 tokens per dollar at 300 output tokens/request
issue.observed: The label 'stated concurrency' does not match the derivation, which uses a continuous-batching overlap assumption rather than an explicit concurrency count.
issue.evidence: The text derives the value as 'under continuous batching (prefill of one request overlapping decode of another), on a combined prefill+decode basis the same host moves 50 × (1 + 9,200/300) ≈ 1,583 tok/s'. No concurrency number is stated.
issue.root_cause: The table label names a quantity that is not actually stated in the derivation.
issue.correction: Change the label to 'Total tokens per dollar (prefill + decode, continuous-batching overlap assumption)' or 'one prefill overlapping one decode'.
issue.acceptance_test: The table label matches the assumption used in the derivation.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 5, §1 Concept, 'Inference mode is a candidate, not a selection verdict'
issue.quoted_clause: For workloads that might use non‑AR generation (editing, infilling, image-to-text), the mode itself becomes an additional selection dimension.
issue.observed: Image-to-text is normally an autoregressive task, so it is a misleading example of non-AR generation.
issue.evidence: Most image-to-text models generate text token-by-token with an AR decoder. Non-AR text-generation examples are diffusion-style/parallel decoding or non-AR infilling, not image-to-text per se.
issue.root_cause: Conflating multimodal input with non-AR output generation.
issue.correction: Replace 'image-to-text' with 'image generation' or 'non-AR text generation (e.g. diffusion-style or parallel decoding)'. If image-to-text is intended, remove it from the non-AR list or qualify that many image-to-text decoders are AR and the mode must be checked per model.
issue.acceptance_test: The examples listed are actually non-AR generation modes, or the sentence explicitly qualifies the exception.

issue.quoted_clause: the RAG pipeline's ~1.08 s prefill dominates any plausible TTFT delta
issue.observed: This suggests fine-tuning's TTFT change is negligible, but fine-tuning may remove or shorten the retrieved context, which can materially change prefill time.
issue.evidence: Earlier in the same section: 'Inference uses the fine-tuned weights without a retrieval step, or with a much shorter retrieved context.' If the 8K retrieved block is removed, prefill FLOPs and time can drop by a large fraction of the 1.08 s RAG baseline.
issue.root_cause: Using the RAG baseline prefill as a de minimis bound on the TTFT delta.
issue.correction: Change to: 'The RAG pipeline's ~1.08 s prefill is the baseline TTFT component; any TTFT change from a shorter or absent retrieved context must be measured and can be material.'
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence no longer implies that the TTFT delta from fine-tuning is small or negligible.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 5, §7 What We Still Don't Know, first bullet
issue.quoted_clause: no public study quantifies this domain-dependence
issue.observed: This is a strong negative universal claim about the literature without a source or scope.
issue.evidence: The chunk does not cite a survey or search. Many embedding benchmark papers evaluate domain-specific retrieval, so the absolute 'no public study' claim is hard to support as written.
issue.root_cause: Overstatement of a literature gap.
issue.correction: Soften to 'we are not aware of a public study that quantifies this specific 768-vs-1024 domain dependence for enterprise legal/engineering/creative corpora', or cite a relevant survey if one exists.
issue.acceptance_test: The claim is scoped to the author's knowledge or supported by a citation.

issue.quoted_clause: adding the quadratic attention term raises it to ~10.6K
issue.observed: Using the book's own full-square prefill FLOPs gives ~10.8K FLOP/byte, not ~10.6K.
issue.evidence: Full-square prefill FLOPs = 1.5099 PFLOP. 1.5099e15 / 140e9 = 10,785 FLOP/byte, i.e. ~10.8K. The linear term is 9,200; the attention term adds ~1,585.
issue.root_cause: Rounding or use of a slightly different attention term.
issue.correction: Change to '~10.8K', or state the exact convention if 10.6K is intended.
issue.acceptance_test: Recompute full-square prefill FLOPs / 140 GB; the table value matches the stated convention.

issue.quoted_clause: QLoRA's 4-bit base + adapters + optimizer floor is ~36 GB (no inference KV cache sits in a training step), so it fits on a single GPU.
issue.observed: 'Single GPU' is not specified; 36 GB fits an 80 GB H100 but not the 24 GB or 32 GB devices discussed earlier in the chapter.
issue.evidence: The same chapter uses 24 GB and 32 GB devices as counterexamples; 36 GB > 24 GB and 36 GB > 32 GB.
issue.root_cause: Omitted device capacity.
issue.correction: Change to 'fits on a single 80 GB GPU (e.g. H100), but not on a 24 GB or 32 GB device.'
issue.acceptance_test: The caption names the GPU capacity or class for which the fit claim is true.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 7, §7 What We Still Don't Know, second bullet
issue.quoted_clause: The primary sources anchor FP8 KV ≈50% of FP16 (raw byte-halving) with only a small loss in the cited benchmarks
issue.observed: 'Cited benchmarks' and 'small loss' are empirical claims not identified in this chunk.
issue.evidence: The sentence does not name the benchmark, paper, or source that supports 'small loss' for FP8 KV. The byte-halving part is arithmetic, but the quality-loss part is empirical.
issue.root_cause: Missing source attribution for an empirical quality claim.
issue.correction: Name the source/benchmark and scope the claim, e.g. 'in the cited KIVI/FP8-KV benchmarks, quality loss is small under those settings', or label it as a secondary empirical observation if no primary source is available.
issue.acceptance_test: The quality-loss claim has an identifiable source and scope, or is explicitly labeled as an unverified observation.

issue.quoted_clause: actual per-token FLOPs vary with layer depth, activation choice (SiLU vs. ReLU), and whether kernel fusion combines matmuls
issue.observed: Kernel fusion changes the execution path and profiler-reported operation mix, but does not by itself change the mathematical per-token FLOP count; 'layer depth' is already captured by N.
issue.evidence: The 2N rule is a model-operation count. Fusion can add/remove auxiliary operations or change how a profiler attributes work, but the ideal transformer FLOPs are set by architecture and sequence length.
issue.root_cause: Conflating mathematical FLOP count with measured/profiler FLOPs.
issue.correction: Change to: 'actual per-token FLOPs vary with architecture (including layer depth and activation functions) and with profiler conventions; kernel fusion changes the execution path and measured operation mix, not the ideal 2N baseline by itself.'
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence distinguishes model FLOPs from measured/profiler FLOPs.

issue.quoted_clause: If prefill is FLOP-bound (as it is for 70B+ models with long contexts)
issue.observed: The claim ties compute-bound prefill to model size and 'long contexts' without stating the roofline condition.
issue.evidence: Earlier in Ch 8, prefill weight-only intensity is approximately L FLOP/byte; it is compute-bound only when L (and kernel efficiency) puts intensity above the ridge (~295 for H100 dense FP16). A 70B model with short prefill or a different hardware ridge may not be FLOP-bound.
issue.root_cause: Using model class as a proxy for an operating-point roofline regime.
issue.correction: Change to: 'If prefill is FLOP-bound (as it is for the canonical 70B model at 9.2K, where weight-only intensity ~9,200 FLOP/byte is far above the H100 ridge; for other models/hardware check L and the ridge)'
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence no longer implies all 70B+ long-context prefills are compute-bound without checking intensity and hardware ridge.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 8, §8 Mini-Case, paragraph after the four prefill bottleneck candidates
issue.quoted_clause: If the prefill kernel is running at 12% MFU, the problem is occupancy or launch — grow the batch or fuse kernels.
issue.observed: Low MFU can also be caused by exposed communication, memory stalls, or inefficient kernels; mapping 12% MFU directly to occupancy/launch is too strong.
issue.evidence: The preceding list includes communication-bound and attention-term constrained cases. A 12% MFU prefill kernel could be waiting on NVLink, HBM, or collective synchronization rather than simply underfilling SMs.
issue.root_cause: Using a single scalar (MFU) to select among multiple bottleneck classes.
issue.correction: Change to: 'If MFU is low, use the trace to distinguish occupancy/launch limits from exposed communication or memory stalls; grow batch or fuse kernels only when the trace shows occupancy/launch limits.'
issue.acceptance_test: The text does not infer a single cause from MFU alone.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 11, §3 When to Disaggregate and Fig 11.3 note
issue.quoted_clause: at batch size 1 and 25 ms TPOT — 40 tokens/s — the whole-model weight-read rate of ~5.6 TB/s if served by one device vs 3.35 TB/s per GPU, sharded to ~0.70 TB/s per GPU under the canonical 8×H100 host, Ch 6; batching divides the rate proportionally
issue.observed: The decode-bandwidth wording conflates required per-step HBM traffic with available HBM bandwidth, and it says batching divides the whole-model weight-read rate. In autoregressive decode, the weights are read once per step for the whole batch, so at fixed TPOT the per-step whole-model weight-read requirement is approximately independent of batch size; batching increases total token rate and reduces per-token weight-read cost, not the per-step whole-model read rate. The same issue appears in §3, where 3.35 TB/s is listed as if it were a weight-read rate rather than the H100 HBM ceiling.
issue.evidence: 140 GB / 0.025 s = 5.6 TB/s per step if unsharded. With 8-way TP, 140/8 = 17.5 GB per GPU, and 17.5 GB / 0.025 s = 0.70 TB/s per GPU per step. H100 HBM bandwidth is 3.35 TB/s per GPU (Table 9-1), not a required weight-read rate. Increasing batch from 1 to 17.5 changes token rate from 40 tok/s to about 700 tok/s while the per-step weight-read requirement remains about 5.6 TB/s unsharded or 0.70 TB/s per GPU sharded.
issue.root_cause: Per-step HBM traffic, available HBM bandwidth, and per-token amortized cost are not kept distinct.
issue.correction: In both locations, rewrite to distinguish required versus available bandwidth and per-step versus per-token cost. For example: 'the required whole-model weight-read rate is ~5.6 TB/s if unsharded, against 3.35 TB/s per GPU of HBM bandwidth, and ~0.70 TB/s per GPU when sharded across the canonical 8×H100 host; batching divides the per-token weight-read cost, not the per-step whole-model weight-read rate at fixed TPOT.'
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in Chapter 11 lists 3.35 TB/s as a required weight-read rate, and no sentence implies that the per-step whole-model HBM weight-read bandwidth decreases as batch size increases at fixed TPOT.

issue.quoted_clause: If the architecture calls for data-parallel training of a 70B FP16 model across 8 nodes (an eight-rank DP group, e.g. one rank per node), the all-reduce bandwidth dictates whether the nodes are connected by InfiniBand, 200 GbE, or even 100 GbE.
issue.observed: The sentence can be read as assuming a feasible plain data-parallel training deployment of a 70B FP16 model with one rank per node/GPU. Plain DP requires each rank to hold the full 140 GB model plus training state, which does not fit an 80 GB H100. The chapter and Chapter 10 explicitly say the 140 GB weight tensor does not fit one 80 GB GPU and that plain DP is infeasible for the canonical 70B on H100.
issue.evidence: Chapter 9 §3: 'Neither a 140 GB weight tensor nor this gradient buffer fits on one 80 GB GPU.' Chapter 10 §3: 'Plain data parallelism is infeasible here: it would replicate the 140 GB model on every GPU, and at 80 GB HBM per H100 the replica does not fit on one device.'
issue.root_cause: Missing qualification that the DP all-reduce example is communication-only or that each DP rank is backed by a multi-GPU node / sharded DP layout.
issue.correction: Reword to make the feasibility assumption explicit, e.g. 'If the architecture models an eight-rank DP all-reduce for a 70B FP16 training job (communication-only, or with each rank backed by an 8-GPU node / sharded DP), the inter-node all-reduce bandwidth dictates ...' or 'one rank per 8-GPU node' instead of 'one rank per node' if rank means GPU.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence does not imply that a single H100 rank can hold a full 70B FP16 training replica.

issue.quoted_clause: MoE models (if chosen per Ch3) push toward EP, because the full expert set must be resident (the active count sets compute per token, not residency) and EP shards the experts across GPUs.
issue.observed: The clause states that the full expert set must be resident as a general reason for using EP. Expert offloading, caching, or non-resident expert storage can change the residency requirement. The same chapter later qualifies this point in §7, so the unqualified statement in the architecture-consequence section is inconsistent with the more careful later treatment.
issue.evidence: Chapter 10 §7 says: 'the total expert residency that must be sharded if the deployment keeps all experts resident in HBM (expert offloading or caching otherwise changes the capacity calculus).'
issue.root_cause: The summary bullet omits the residency assumption that is present in the uncertainty section.
issue.correction: Add scope: 'when the deployment keeps the full expert set resident in HBM; expert offloading or caching changes the residency calculus (see §7).'
issue.acceptance_test: The MoE bullet does not assert full expert residency as unconditional.

issue.quoted_clause: each per-layer all-reduce operates on a ~256 KiB logical tensor — batch × hidden × bytes — so an 8-rank ring sends 1.75 × that ≈ 0.45 MB per rank; across all 80 layers the per-step total is ~36 MB of per-rank send traffic, against ~20 MB of logical volume, sub-MB to tens of MB and not GBs at the canonical batch and hidden size
issue.observed: This mini-case uses one 256 KiB all-reduce per layer and calls the result canonical. Chapter 10's TP decode budget uses two 256 KiB all-reduces per transformer block (attention output and MLP), giving 70 MiB per rank per step, roughly double the Chapter 9 figure. Also, 256 KiB corresponds to 16 sequences, while the canonical decode concurrency used elsewhere is about 17.5.
issue.evidence: Chapter 10 §3: 'Assume two output all-reduces per transformer block — attention output and MLP — 80 blocks ... Across 160 calls ... each rank sends 70 MiB and receives 70 MiB in that one decode step.' Chapter 11 §3: 'canonical ~17.5-concurrent operating point.'
issue.root_cause: A simplified one-collective-per-layer, 16-sequence example is presented as canonical without aligning it to Chapter 10's two-collective assumption or the canonical concurrency.
issue.correction: Either label the Chapter 9 example as 'simplified one-collective-per-layer, 16-sequence illustrative' or update it to two collectives per block and/or 17.5 sequences, with a cross-reference to Chapter 10's TP decode budget.
issue.acceptance_test: Chapter 9 mini-case and Chapter 10 TP decode example either match or explicitly state different assumptions.

issue.quoted_clause: model fits one GPU; need throughput
issue.observed: The 'Fits when' cell for data parallelism can be read as requiring the full model to fit one GPU for any DP use. Plain DP does require that, but DP is commonly composed with TP/PP when the model does not fit one device. The chapter's own canonical 70B uses TP=8 within each DP replica, so the table cell is too narrow if read as a general DP condition.
issue.evidence: Chapter 10 §6: 'The canonical 70B fits across an 8×H100 node through intra-host model parallelism; additional replicas address fleet capacity.' The table footnote says the canonical 70B exceeds one H100, so DP is not its baseline, but the cell still says 'model fits one GPU.'
issue.root_cause: The table compresses plain-DP feasibility into a general DP condition without noting composition with TP/PP.
issue.correction: Change the cell to 'plain DP (without TP/PP): full model fits one device; DP can be composed with TP/PP for larger models' or add a table note.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader does not conclude that DP is unavailable for a 70B simply because the model does not fit one H100.

issue.quoted_clause: the decode pool runs bandwidth-saturated on the 300 output tokens
issue.observed: 'Bandwidth-saturated' can mean HBM bandwidth is near its maximum. At the canonical 8×H100 TP=8 decode operating point, the sharded weight-read requirement is about 0.70 TB/s per GPU, well below the 3.35 TB/s HBM ceiling. Decode is bandwidth-bound in the roofline sense, not necessarily saturated.
issue.evidence: Chapter 11 §3 gives the sharded decode weight-read rate as ~0.70 TB/s per GPU, and Table 9-1 gives H100 HBM bandwidth as 3.35 TB/s per GPU.
issue.root_cause: Use of 'saturated' where 'bound' is intended.
issue.correction: Reword to 'the decode pool runs bandwidth-bound (not necessarily HBM-saturated) on the 300 output tokens.'
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence claims the canonical decode pool uses near-100% HBM bandwidth.

issue.quoted_clause: SLO
issue.observed: The table column headed 'SLO' contains memory checks, phase-split capability, and quality status, not only SLO/latency compliance. This blurs the three gates (memory fit, throughput at the SLO, quality) and can make readers think memory and quality are SLO items.
issue.evidence: Row (a) SLO cell: '✓ memory 164 < 640 GB · ? TTFT SLO unmeasured'; row (b): '✓ memory per host · ✓ phase-split enables independent scaling'; row (c): '✗ quality — provisional.'
issue.root_cause: Column label is too narrow for mixed gate status.
issue.correction: Rename the column to 'Gate status' or split it into 'Memory', 'Throughput/SLO', and 'Quality' columns consistent with the table title.
issue.acceptance_test: Table 12-1 column headers accurately describe the content; the SLO column contains only latency/SLO compliance or is renamed.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 10, §7 What We Still Don't Know, EP bullet
issue.quoted_clause: as in DeepSeek's DeepEP/TileLang infra
issue.observed: The phrase can be read as attributing TileLang to DeepSeek. DeepEP is a DeepSeek project, but TileLang is commonly treated as a separate tile-based kernel language/ecosystem. If the cited arXiv source does not present TileLang as DeepSeek's infrastructure, the attribution is misleading.
issue.evidence: The chunk cites [1P: arXiv 2606.19348] but does not show that TileLang is DeepSeek-owned. The wording 'DeepSeek's DeepEP/TileLang infra' implies joint ownership.
issue.root_cause: Possibly imprecise source attribution in a time-sensitive implementation note.
issue.correction: Verify the primary source. If TileLang is not DeepSeek's, reword to 'DeepEP and related tile-based kernels (e.g., TileLang)' or cite the appropriate primary source for TileLang.
issue.acceptance_test: The text does not imply TileLang is a DeepSeek product unless the cited primary source says so.

issue.quoted_clause: Fast Inference from Transformers via Radix Attention
issue.observed: The cited SGLang/RadixAttention primary source title appears to be a descriptive paraphrase. The known primary paper is 'Fast Inference from Transformers with Decoupled Attention' (Zheng et al., 2023), which introduces RadixAttention. If [S3] is intended as the primary source, the title should match the publication.
issue.evidence: The chunk gives no arXiv/DOI for [S3]; the title 'via Radix Attention' is not the standard primary title verifiable from the chunk alone, so this is a verification flag rather than a confirmed error.
issue.root_cause: Possible inaccurate primary-source title.
issue.correction: Verify against the official SGLang/RadixAttention paper and correct [S3] to the exact title, authors, venue, and identifier.
issue.acceptance_test: [S3] matches the primary publication's exact title or is replaced by the correct primary source.

issue.quoted_clause: Server — one host with 1-8 GPUs, typically H100/H200 — multi-GPU servers joined by NVLink/NVSwitch (a 1-GPU host uses PCIe; no intra-host fabric is needed). Serves dense models up to ~70B-180B with real concurrency.
issue.observed: The server tier spans 1-8 GPUs, but the model range ~70B-180B is only feasible at the multi-GPU end (e.g., 8×H100). As written, a 1-GPU server could be misread as serving 70B-180B.
issue.evidence: 70B FP16 = 140 GB, exceeding one 80 GB H100; 180B FP16 = 360 GB, requiring multiple GPUs. Chapter 10 states 140 GB does not fit one H100.
issue.root_cause: The tier row combines a GPU-count range with a model range without qualifying the model range to the 8-GPU end.
issue.correction: Reword to 'Serves dense models up to ~70B-180B at the 8-GPU end of the tier (with real concurrency)' or split 1-GPU and multi-GPU server rows.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader does not infer that a single-GPU server can serve 70B-180B FP16.

issue.quoted_clause: so the self-host totals do not scale purely per-host ($155,816.93, ≈$24.97/1K on the 6.24M‑req/mo business‑hours basis, Ch 16 — the cloud legs are $87,600 ≈ $14.04/1K at the default paid-occupancy input and $306,600 ≈ $49.13/1K at 21 hosts always-on)
issue.observed: The parenthetical mixes self-host 21-host cost, cloud default paid-occupancy cost, and 21-host always-on cloud cost in one clause, making it hard to see which number supports which fleet size. The sentence's main point (self-host has fixed staff cost, so totals are not purely per-host) is obscured.
issue.evidence: The same paragraph already states 32-host self-host ~$232.2K and 32-host cloud-equivalent ~$467.2K; the parenthetical then introduces $155,816.93, $87,600, and $306,600 without clear mapping to those fleet sizes.
issue.root_cause: Overloaded parenthetical with multiple cost bases.
issue.correction: Split into separate sentences or a small table: 21-host self-host $155.8K; 32-host self-host $232.2K; 21-host always-on cloud $306.6K; default paid-occupancy cloud $87.6K. State which is used for the 10.4×/15.5×/31× comparisons.
issue.acceptance_test: Each cost figure is explicitly tied to a fleet size and cost basis before being used in a ratio.

issue.quoted_clause: not because traffic splits across links; each link of a ring carries a large fraction of the tensor
issue.observed: The phrase 'not because traffic splits across links' is potentially confusing because a ring all-reduce does distribute the tensor across links over the course of the algorithm. The intended point is that per-link load remains high, not that the logical tensor is fragmented across parallel links in a way that reduces per-link bytes.
issue.evidence: The same bullet later says for N=2 each link carries 2(N−1)/N = one full tensor over the full all-reduce; for N=8 each link carries 1.75× the tensor total, so per-link load is large.
issue.root_cause: Ambiguous negation about traffic splitting.
issue.correction: Reword to: 'not because the logical tensor is spread so thinly across many links that each link sees only a small fraction; in a ring, each link still carries a large fraction of the tensor per phase.'
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence does not imply ring traffic is not distributed across links.

issue.quoted_clause: TPOT median ≤ 25 ms, p95 ≤ 35 ms (Ch 4, Table 4-2)
issue.observed: Ch15 states that the canonical SLO includes a TPOT p95 bound, while Ch14 explicitly says TPOT p95 is recorded for tail diagnosis and is not SLO-bound.
issue.evidence: Ch14: 'TPOT p50/p95 (SLO: p50 ≤ ~25 ms/token; record p95 for tail diagnosis, not SLO-bound)'. Ch15: 'The canonical SLO this chapter measures against: TTFT median ≤ 1.2 s, p95 ≤ 2 s, TPOT median ≤ 25 ms, p95 ≤ 35 ms (Ch 4, Table 4-2).'
issue.root_cause: The canonical SLO set was not synchronized across the benchmarking and performance-engineering chapters; one chapter treats p95 TPOT as diagnostic, the other as an SLO.
issue.correction: Align both chapters with Ch4 Table 4-2. If p95 TPOT ≤ 35 ms is an SLO, update Ch14 so the deployment benchmark enforces it in acceptance and goodput. If it is only a diagnostic target, remove 'p95 ≤ 35 ms' from Ch15's canonical SLO or label it as a non-SLO diagnostic bound.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can state one canonical TPOT SLO set, and Ch14's benchmark acceptance criteria and Ch15's measured SLO use the same percentiles and thresholds.

issue.quoted_clause: ~32 GB of KV across both hosts against ~17 in flight
issue.observed: The clause can be read as saying the in-flight KV demand is ~32 GB for ~17 in-flight requests. In fact, ~32 GB is the available KV after weights/runtime (16 GB per host), while ~17 in-flight full-context requests would need ~17 × 24.9 GB ≈ 423 GB.
issue.evidence: Same paragraph: '4 replicas per host × 140 GB = 560 GB of the 640 GB per-host pool. After the ~64 GB runtime reserve, ~16 GB of KV remains per host ... against 1 rps × 8.6 s ≈ 8.6 requests in flight per host (~32 GB of KV across both hosts against ~17 in flight).'
issue.root_cause: Ambiguous noun phrase: '32 GB of KV' is available KV, not in-flight KV demand.
issue.correction: Change to '32 GB of available KV across both hosts, against ~17 in-flight requests that would need ~423 GB of KV' or similar.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence cannot be interpreted as 32 GB being the KV requirement for 17 in-flight requests.

issue.quoted_clause: M/d² (≈6× at d = 128, M ≈ 192 KB of fp16)
issue.observed: The reduction factor is dimensionally inconsistent if M is bytes: 192 KB / 128² ≈ 12, not 6. The ≈6× result requires M to be the number of fp16 elements that fit in on-chip memory (192 KB / 2 B ≈ 96k elements; 96k / 128² ≈ 5.9).
issue.evidence: Caption says 'in matched units' but then gives M in bytes ('192 KB of fp16') while d is a head dimension in elements.
issue.root_cause: M is not explicitly defined as elements vs bytes in the I/O formula.
issue.correction: State 'M is the number of fp16 elements that fit in on-chip memory (≈96k for 192 KB)' or rewrite the factor as (M_bytes / 2) / d².
issue.acceptance_test: The formula and the ≈6× numeric example use the same unit for M and d².

issue.quoted_clause: Operating (opex) — the recurring cost of running it: electricity and cooling, staff, software/licenses, cloud instance rental, and replacement/amortization of hardware.
issue.observed: Amortization is an allocation of capex over time, not a recurring cash operating cost. Including it in opex can double-count or blur the capex/opex separation used later.
issue.evidence: The same chapter later prices capex as '$350,000 ÷ 60 mo' and lists energy/staff separately; the concept section's opex list includes 'replacement/amortization'.
issue.root_cause: Loose cost-family definition.
issue.correction: Reword to 'replacement (or amortized capex, if using accounting cost)' or move amortization explicitly to capex allocation and keep opex as cash/recurring costs.
issue.acceptance_test: The capex and opex definitions do not both include the same hardware amortization term.

issue.quoted_clause: at 12,000 decode tokens/s the demand is ≈ 12,000 × 33.1 GB ≈ 398 TB/s against the host's 8 × 3.35 = 26.8 TB/s HBM peak
issue.observed: 12,000 decode tokens/s is the fleet-wide peak output rate (40 rps × 300), not a per-host rate. Comparing it directly to one host's HBM peak without saying it is a hypothetical one-host assignment can mislead readers into thinking a single host is expected to deliver 12,000 tok/s.
issue.evidence: Earlier: 'decode demand = 40 rps × 300 = 12,000 output tokens/s'. Later: 'per-host decode ceiling ... 809 tok/s/host, i.e. ⌈12,000/809⌉ ≈ 15 hosts'.
issue.root_cause: Missing scope marker on the 398 TB/s demand calculation.
issue.correction: Add 'if the full 12,000 tok/s were assigned to one host at B=17' before the 398 TB/s comparison, or present it as 'fleet demand 398 TB/s vs one host 26.8 TB/s, hence ~15 hosts'.

issue.quoted_clause: Retrieved 2026-10-28. Timing results are vendor-reported, not measurements made for this book.

issue.quoted_clause: FlashAttention‑2 for the attention computation

issue.quoted_clause: 17/8.6 ≈ 1.98 req/s is a single-host residency ceiling
issue.observed: A quantity in req/s is a rate ceiling, not a residency ceiling. The residency ceiling is 17 slots; the derived admitted completion-rate ceiling is 17/8.6 req/s. Ch16 later calls it 'KV-slot-based analytical UPPER bound on admitted request completion rate'.
issue.evidence: Same paragraph: 'C ≈ 17.5 ... gives at most 17 whole-context slots'; Ch16: 'C_KV / E[W_KV-resident] ≈ 17 / 8.6 ≈ 2.0 req/s is a KV-slot-based analytical UPPER bound on admitted request completion rate'.
issue.root_cause: Terminology drift between residency and rate.
issue.correction: Change to 'a single-host admitted-completion-rate ceiling derived from the 17-slot residency bound' or similar.
issue.acceptance_test: The req/s figure is not labeled as a residency ceiling.

issue.quoted_clause: 70B dense FP16 | 140 GB | — | — | 1 GPU | 1 (140 GB weights across the 8-GPU pool, ~17.5 GB/GPU under TP
issue.observed: The table cell says GPUs per instance is 1 for a 140 GB FP16 70B model, but the parenthetical says the 140 GB weights are spread across the 8-GPU pool at ~17.5 GB/GPU.
issue.evidence: An H100 has 80 GB HBM; 140 GB cannot reside on one GPU. 140/8 = 17.5 GB/GPU, matching the parenthetical. The 70B MoE FP16 row has the same 140 GB / 1 GPU pattern.
issue.root_cause: The cell likely records '1 instance' in the 'GPUs per instance' column, or the canonical 8-GPU placement was not transcribed.
issue.correction: Set GPUs per instance to 8 for the canonical 70B dense FP16 and 70B MoE FP16 rows, or explicitly state the minimum 2-GPU placement and the canonical 8-GPU placement used for the 436 GB KV budget.
issue.acceptance_test: Every row's weights plus per-instance KV fit within the stated per-GPU HBM, and the table matches the 8xH100 canonical host used in Ch 17.

issue.page_hint: Ch 19, §19.8, Unconditional fallback-inclusive ledger and note
issue.quoted_clause: Completed T = 1 (68%) | 220 ms | 19,265 | 365 | 19,630 | ≈26.4 GB ... The T = 1 and fallback rows quote the last retained context without a separate terminal answer on top
issue.observed: The completed T = 1 row has a terminal 300-token answer, but its peak KV is printed as ≈26.4 GB, which corresponds to 10,065 tokens before the final answer. Table 19-1 and §4 use the incl.-output peak, 10,365 tokens ≈ 27.2 GB. The completed T = 2 row has the same issue: ≈28.6 GB corresponds to 10,930 tokens, while Table 19-1 prints ≈29.4 GB for 11,230 tokens.
issue.evidence: 10,065 × 2.62144 MB ≈ 26.38 GB; 10,365 × 2.62144 MB ≈ 27.17 GB. 10,930 × 2.62144 MB ≈ 28.65 GB; 11,230 × 2.62144 MB ≈ 29.44 GB. §4 states peak residency follows the incl.-output convention for T = 3 (12,095 → 31.7 GB).
issue.root_cause: The ledger mixes two peak-KV conventions: pre-synthesis retained context for T = 1/T = 2/fallback and incl.-output retained context for completed T = 3.
issue.correction: Use one convention for all completed rows. If peak means end-of-decode, print 27.2 GB for T = 1 and 29.4 GB for T = 2. If peak means pre-synthesis, apply that to T = 3 as well and reconcile with Table 19-1 and Ch 17.
issue.acceptance_test: The ledger's peak KV column matches the §4 incl.-output convention and Table 19-1 for every completed row, or the alternative convention is stated and applied consistently.

issue.page_hint: Ch 17, Table 17-1 paragraph, recomputed canonical peak screens

issue.quoted_clause: Consolidate when: workload profile overlap ≥70%, latency tolerance ≥300 ms, and cost differential >30%.

issue.quoted_clause: against 21/31 single-model under the canonical C = 17 — 31 (no spare) / 32 (with the N−1 spare, the Ch 17 provisioned fleet)

issue.quoted_clause: they drive β, the p50/p90/p95 headline (220 / 440 / 660 ms), the W tool leg, and the §8 SLA scoping

issue.quoted_clause: 12,095 tokens at T = 3 (Table 19-1), whereas Σ per-call input across the task is 23,927 tokens/request — §8 ledger — and that is the token count the cost model uses

issue.evidence: Single-model tail: ⌈34.4/11.305⌉ = 4. Shared mixed tail: ⌈34.4/5.985⌉ = 6.
