issue.page_hint: Chapter 22, §8 End-of-Chapter Mini-Case, “The decision the team must make”
issue.quoted_clause: a homogeneous cluster sized at ~17–19 hosts clears both budgets (prefill- or KV-bound depending on the KV budget, with a 21-host build carrying the margin)
issue.observed: The 17–19 host range mixes two non-canonical sensitivities: 17 is the 40%-MFU linear-only prefill floor, and 19 comes from the 24.1 GB/request input-only KV calculation. The canonical whole-slot KV screen is 21 hosts, and the case-(ii) prefill screen is 22 raw / 23 with the ρ derate. As written, the sentence can make a reader think 17–19 hosts may clear the canonical peak.
issue.evidence: Ch 22 mini-case: 40 × 1.288 = 51.5 PFLOP/s; 51.5 / (7.91 × 0.40) ≈ 16.3 → 17 hosts. The same section’s KV calculation using 24.1 GB gives ~19 hosts. Ch 20 canonical screens: KV 21, case-(ii) prefill 22 raw / 23 with ρ, full policy 34.
issue.root_cause: Local sensitivity values are presented alongside the canonical screen without enough separation.
issue.correction: Reword to: “A 17–19 host range appears only under the 40%-MFU linear-only prefill sensitivity and the 9.2K-input-only KV sensitivity; the canonical whole-slot KV screen is 21 hosts, and the case-(ii) prefill screen is 22 raw / 23 with the ρ derate. A 21-host build is therefore the canonical KV margin, not a small add-on to a 17–19 host design.”
issue.acceptance_test: The text no longer implies that 17–19 hosts can clear the canonical peak; it distinguishes sensitivities from the canonical 21/22/23 screens.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 25, Architect’s Question and ADR 0016 Consequences
issue.quoted_clause: Accepted, this record sets the canonical deployment's precision label to BF16; because FP16 and BF16 are both 2 B/parameter, every footprint, KV and cost figure in this handbook is unchanged.
issue.observed: The chapter opening calls the canonical system “a 70B dense FP16 deployment (FP16 label; see ADR 0016),” but ADR 0016 says the accepted record sets the canonical deployment’s precision label to BF16. This leaves the reader unsure whether the canonical label is FP16, BF16, or a generic 16-bit label.
issue.evidence: Both clauses are in Chapter 25. If ADR 0016 is accepted, the runtime precision is BF16. If the book continues to use “FP16” as a shorthand for 16-bit footprint arithmetic, that convention should be stated explicitly rather than contradicted by “sets the canonical deployment's precision label to BF16.”
issue.root_cause: Ambiguity between “FP16 as a 16-bit footprint label” and “BF16 as the chosen runtime precision.”
issue.correction: Align the two statements. For example: opening: “a 70B dense 16-bit deployment (BF16 per ADR 0016; FP16/BF16 footprints are identical, so the book’s 16-bit arithmetic is unchanged)”; or ADR 0016: “sets the canonical runtime precision to BF16; the book’s 16-bit footprint label remains FP16/BF16-equivalent.” Ensure all “FP16 deployment” references are either qualified or changed to “16-bit (BF16).”
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can state unambiguously whether the canonical deployment is labeled FP16, BF16, or 16-bit, and why the arithmetic is unchanged.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 25, §3 Worked Example: Model-Shape ADR, ADR 0016 Context
issue.quoted_clause: each serving host is an 8×H100 node (640 GB), and the canonical fleet is 21 hosts at peak.
issue.observed: 21 hosts is the KV-screen host count. Ch 20’s governing pre-full-policy screen is 23 hosts (case (ii) with the ρ derate), and the full policy is 34 hosts. Calling 21 “the canonical fleet” without qualification can contradict the more complete screen set in ADR 0015 R1.
issue.evidence: Ch 20: “governing 23-host sizing … 34 at the 70% × 95% + N−1 policy.” Ch 25 ADR 0015 R1: “21 hosts (KV, case-independent); prefill screen 19 case (i) / 22 case (ii); 70% × 95% + N−1 policy: 32 (KV screen) / 34 (case (ii) prefill screen).”
issue.root_cause: Using the KV-screen headline as if it were the full canonical fleet size.
issue.correction: Change to: “the canonical single-region KV-screen fleet is 21 hosts at peak (23 under the case-(ii) ρ-derated prefill screen, 32/34 under the full policy; see ADR 0015 R1),” or “a 21-host KV-screen baseline.”
issue.acceptance_test: The ADR 0016 context does not imply that 21 is the only or final canonical fleet size.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 20, §3 Worked Example, after KV-residency bound and in Simultaneous feasibility check
issue.quoted_clause: The binding per-host rate is the minimum of the two — here the KV/latency bound under cases (i) and (iii); a third, phase-resolved prefill-compute screen is evaluated below and binds under case (ii)
issue.observed: The text first says the KV/latency bound is binding under cases (i) and (iii), but later shows that at the displayed 2.0 req/s stress screen, case (iii) prefill demand exceeds the ceiling by about 1%. Without qualification, this looks contradictory.
issue.evidence: Case (iii) ceiling is ≈18,210 input tokens/s. At the displayed 2.0 req/s, demand is 2.0 × 9,200 = 18,400 tokens/s, so 18,400 / 18,210 ≈ 101%. At the unrounded KV rate 17/8.6 = 1.9767 req/s, demand is 1.9767 × 9,200 ≈ 18,186 tokens/s, which is below 18,210. Thus case (iii) is non-binding at the exact KV rate but not at the rounded 2.0 stress screen.
issue.root_cause: Conflating the displayed ~2.0 req/s stress screen with the unrounded 1.977 req/s used for the binding-screen statement.
issue.correction: Add: “At the unrounded 1.977 req/s, case (iii) prefill demand is ≈18,190 tokens/s, just below the ≈18,210 ceiling; the 101% figure applies only to the deliberately rounded 2.0 req/s stress screen.” Or change the earlier sentence to “under cases (i) and (iii) at the unrounded 1.977 req/s.”
issue.acceptance_test: A careful reader can see why case (iii) is called non-binding despite the later 101% at 2.0 req/s.

issue.quoted_clause: The **average** cost per query declines only along the canonical 10 → 40 rps ramp, where fixed overhead (model loading, infrastructure, staff) is spread across 4× the requests and across more SLO-compliant completions per observation window (Ch 14's goodput definition), cost per request may decline until additional capacity steps dominate; adding idle hosts at fixed demand increases unit cost.
issue.observed: The sentence is syntactically broken. The clause after the comma, “cost per request may decline,” is not grammatically connected to the preceding “where” clause, and the idea is repeated awkwardly.
issue.evidence: The main clause begins “The average cost per query declines only along …,” but the later “cost per request may decline” creates a second predicate without a clear subject or conjunction.
issue.root_cause: Editing artifact / overlong sentence.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: “The average cost per query may decline only along the canonical 10 → 40 rps ramp, where fixed overhead (model loading, infrastructure, staff) is spread across 4× the requests and across more SLO-compliant completions per observation window (Ch 14's goodput definition). Even then, cost per request may decline only until additional capacity steps dominate; adding idle hosts at fixed demand increases unit cost.”
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence parses without a dangling comma and states the condition and limitation clearly.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 23, §8 Mini-Case, “The burst buffer, spelled out”
issue.quoted_clause: with the ~500-token prefill included the total request rate is ~71 rps at 100% MFU (~21–28 rps at 30–40% MFU), so r = 50 in the worked example below is an optimistic decode-only illustration
issue.observed: r = 50 is a total request-rate assumption (requests per second), not a decode-only rate. It is below the 100%-MFU total ceiling of ~71 rps and above the 30–40% MFU total range, so calling it “decode-only” is misleading.
issue.evidence: The preceding sentence defines the total request rate including prefill as ~71 rps at 100% MFU. The worked example then uses r = 50 as the service rate for total requests during the burst: 200 arrivals in 1 s, 50 served during the burst, 150 queued.
issue.root_cause: Imprecise label.
issue.correction: Change to: “so r = 50 in the worked example below is an optimistic total-rate illustration (below the 100%-MFU total ceiling of ~71 rps but above the 30–40% MFU total range); the measured per-host total rate must replace it before the burst budget is trusted.”
issue.acceptance_test: The text no longer implies that r = 50 is a decode-only token or request rate.

issue.quoted_clause: At batch 1 the weight read dominates a decode step: 140 GB of weights against ~24.9 GB of KV, so the KV read is a secondary ~15% term (~15% of batch-1 decode reads; halving it cuts total read traffic ≈7.5% at batch 1) and intensity is ~1 FLOP/byte.
issue.observed: The intensity figure’s denominator is ambiguous. If the 24.9 GB KV read is included in the byte count, batch-1 intensity is 140 GB / (140 GB + 24.9 GB) ≈ 0.85 FLOP/byte, not ~1. If the intended intensity is weight-only, that should be stated.
issue.evidence: Decode parameter FLOPs per token are 2N = 140 GFLOP. Weight-only bytes are 140 GB, giving 1.0 FLOP/byte. Including the 24.9 GB KV read gives 140 / 164.9 ≈ 0.849 FLOP/byte.
issue.root_cause: Mixing weight-only arithmetic intensity with a sentence that explicitly includes the KV read.
issue.correction: Reword to: “weight-only intensity is 1.0 FLOP/byte; including the 24.9 GB KV read, total batch-1 intensity is ≈0.85 FLOP/byte.”
issue.acceptance_test: The intensity figure’s denominator is explicit, and the reader can distinguish weight-only from total decode intensity.

issue.quoted_clause: so the monthly denominator averages ~2.4 rps, while the 21-host capacity screen is peak-sized at 40 rps
issue.observed: The phrase “the 21-host capacity screen” can be read as the single canonical capacity screen, but Ch 20 and ADR 0015 R1 distinguish the 21-host KV screen from the 22/23-host prefill screens and the 32/34-host full-policy screens.
issue.evidence: ADR 0015 R1 in the same chapter says: “KV-residency screen … 21 hosts (KV, case-independent); prefill screen 19 case (i) / 22 case (ii); 70% × 95% + N−1 policy: 32 (KV screen) / 34 (case (ii) prefill screen).” Ch 20 says the governing pre-full-policy screen is 23 hosts.
issue.root_cause: Using the KV-screen headline without the “KV” qualifier in a sentence that could be read as the full capacity screen.
issue.correction: Change to: “while the 21-host KV capacity screen is peak-sized at 40 rps (with higher prefill/policy screens in ADR 0015 R1).”
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence no longer implies that 21 hosts is the only or final peak capacity screen.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 26, §8, Table 26-2 cost row and footnote
issue.quoted_clause: $ per query — metered API spend at the canonical 9,200/300 mix, marginal-generation-work share only (DERIVED from FACT inputs, §26.8 — not itself a FACT) | < $0.015 | $0.0076 (API-basis marginal: canonical-mix unit price $0.01164 — a conservative upper bound for this short-prompt leg — × 0.65; self-host all-in is a separate basis, §26.8)
issue.observed: The same cost cell is labeled both as metered API spend and as a marginal-generation-work statement, and the footnote computes the dollar figure from an API price while calling it marginal generation work.
issue.evidence: R-01 in §2 says marginal generation work, metered API spend, and all-in TCO are separate units, never collapsed. 0.01164 × 0.65 = 0.007566, which is an average variable API-spend figure if 35% of API calls are skipped; it is not a direct marginal-generation-work measure unless the API price is explicitly a proxy.
issue.root_cause: The table tries to express a marginal-work saving in dollars using an API price without choosing one R-01 basis.
issue.correction: Choose one basis. If the cell is variable metered API spend, label it as such and state the API-price upper bound. If it is marginal generation work, state 65% of uncached marginal work and put the API-price proxy in a separate note, not as the same cost basis.
issue.acceptance_test: No cost cell combines metered API spend and marginal-generation-work as the same basis; the table and footnote use the same R-01 category for the $0.0076 figure.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 26, §1 Concept; Fig 26.1 provenance note; §8 Step 0
issue.quoted_clause: with the §2.1 workload matrix and Table 26-1's FACT set serving as the checklists; three representative families of the §26.2.1 matrix; applies the §26.2.1 method
issue.observed: The same workload-to-strategy matrix is referenced as §2.1 in one place and §26.2.1 in others.
issue.evidence: The heading is '2.1 Workload-to-Strategy decision matrix', but the body uses both '§2.1' and '§26.2.1' for the same object.
issue.root_cause: Inconsistent section-numbering convention, likely chapter-local versus chapter-prefixed cross-referencing.

issue.issue: The text drawn in box 2 (DERIVED) — 'decode bandwidth-bound (low-batch regime)' — contradicts the figure's own caption and the chapter's reasoning. Per the figure-causality standard, the diagram currently requires the caption to be read correctly.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 161: seven same-width boxes stacked with uniform spacing; the red double-headed arrow labeled 'capacity grows / speed drops / distance grows' runs down the right side across the middle of the column; the blue 'tensor cores / ALU' box sits between 'registers' and 'shared mem (SRAM)'. issue.page_hint: Ch 2 §3 'Worked Example' — 'Occupancy thresholds' paragraph (after the 'Canonical host verdict' bullet)
issue.quoted_clause: At the canonical operating point the 5.2 ms weight read is not HBM-saturating; it saturates HBM above ~5 concurrent sequences per GPU (~40 per host) only in the batch-1-equivalent case where each sequence streams its own full 17.5 GB shard, with no weight-read amortization.
issue.observed: As written, the first clause is false for the canonical host. The 5.2 ms figure IS the time to stream the 17.5 GB shard at peak HBM bandwidth: 17.5 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 5.22 ms, i.e. 100% of peak. The sentence appears to intend 'the weight read does not saturate HBM for the whole 25 ms step', but the literal reading tells the reader that a single sequence leaves the memory system idle — the opposite of the truth, and the opposite of the decode-bandwidth-bound verdict the same chapter establishes.
issue.evidence: Recomputed: 17.5e9 B / 3.35e12 B/s = 5.224 ms (matches the book's 5.2 ms). The ~5-seq/GPU threshold is separately correct under a 25 ms-budget reading: B x 17.5 GB / 0.025 s = 3.35 TB/s at B = 4.79 ~ 5; and 5 x 8 = 40 per host. So the numbers are right; the sentence that frames them is wrong.
issue.root_cause: Two different framings (bandwidth saturation vs. latency-budget occupancy) are compressed into one clause, and 'batch-1-equivalent' is reused for a second, incompatible meaning (single-request whole-model streaming in §3 vs. a hypothetical multi-sequence no-amortization case here).
issue.correction: Rewrite as two explicit statements: (a) 'At batch 1 the 17.5 GB shard read takes 5.2 ms at peak HBM bandwidth — i.e. the weight read alone saturates HBM for 5.2 ms of the 25 ms step, so the step is bandwidth-bound, not idle.' (b) 'Under a no-amortization model in which each of B sequences independently streams the full shard, the aggregate demand reaches the 3.35 TB/s ceiling at B ~ 4.8 sequences per GPU (~40 per host) within the 25 ms budget; no production engine behaves this way (a real engine reads the shard once per step for the whole batch), so this is an upper bound, not an operating point.' Rename the second case (e.g. 'no-amortization upper bound') so it does not collide with 'batch-1-equivalent'.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader who computes 17.5 GB / 3.35 TB/s from the text reaches 5.2 ms and finds the sentence consistent with their own arithmetic; the two batching models are named distinctly and each threshold is traceable to one of them.

issue.page_hint: Ch 2 §3 — Table 2-1, row 'Decode: bandwidth verdict'; and the 'Decode bandwidth' bullet of 'Worked example arithmetic details'
issue.quoted_clause: | Decode: bandwidth verdict | bandwidth-bound | 5.6 > 3.35 → under the batch-1-equivalent model, a single H100 cannot meet the demand; batching/amortization change this (see later chapters) [canonical scenario][DERIVED] |

[...] At 9.2K tokens the raw byte-halving figure gives ~12.06 GB (not ~13.4 GB ...)
issue.observed: The canonical scenario declares KV precision = FP16 (Ch 4 box: 'KV precision | FP16 (2.62 MB/token -> ~24.1 GB @ 9.2K input-only; ~24.9 GB @ 9.5K input+output'), and every capacity number in the book (24.1/24.9 GB per request, 436 GB KV budget, 17 slots, 6/21/9/32 hosts) is built on the FP16 figure. But the headline per-token KV number the reader meets first (Ch 1) is the 8-bit figure, and Ch 3's Table 3-3 states the canonical request's KV as '~12 GB' (8-bit) with no FP16 row. Two different per-request KV figures for the same canonical request (12.06 GB and 24.1 GB) circulate across three chapters, distinguished only by a precision tag the reader must carry. A reader who lifts '1.31 MB/token' from Ch 1 into a capacity calculation halves the canonical KV budget and doubles the concurrency ceiling.
issue.evidence: Ch 1: 1.31 MB/token (8-bit) headline, with 2.62 MB/token (FP16) mentioned in the same paragraph. Ch 3 Table 3-3: 'KV cache per request (9.2K ctx, 8-bit) | ~12 GB | ~0.6 GB' (FP16 values appear only in the prose: '~24 GB' and '~1.2 GB'). Ch 4: canonical KV precision FP16; all fleet arithmetic on 24.9 GB/request. Recomputed: 9,200 x 1.31072 MB = 12.06 GB; 9,200 x 2.62144 MB = 24.12 GB; 9,500 x 2.62144 MB = 24.90 GB.
issue.root_cause: Ch 1 introduces the quantization variant as the illustrative headline because it is the more interesting number, while the canonical scenario's declared precision is FP16; the two were never reconciled at the point of first use.
issue.correction: In Ch 1, lead with the canonical precision: 'at the canonical FP16 KV precision, ~2.62 MB/token for the 70B reference (2 x 80 x 8,192 x 2 B), i.e. ~24.1 GB for a 9.2K request; at 8-bit this halves to ~1.31 MB/token and ~12.06 GB'. In Ch 3 Table 3-3, add the FP16 row (dense ~24.1 GB, challenger ~1.2 GB) alongside the 8-bit row, or relabel the row 'at 8-bit KV (canonical FP16 values in the prose)'. Add one sentence in Ch 1 pointing forward: 'the canonical scenario's KV precision is FP16 (Ch 4); the 8-bit figures here are the quantization variant, not the canonical budget'.
issue.acceptance_test: Every canonical per-request KV figure quoted anywhere in the book states its precision in the same line; the canonical request's KV budget (24.1/24.9 GB) is the first figure a reader meets, and the 8-bit variant is explicitly marked as a variant.

issue.page_hint: Book-wide — figure captions for Fig 1.1, Fig 1.2, Fig 2.1, Fig 2.2, Fig 3.1, Fig 3.2, Fig 3.3, Fig 3.4, Fig 4.1
issue.quoted_clause: Fig 2.1 — The canonical end-to-end inference pipeline, in two process bands plus the persistent KV cache. PREFILL (top) is the one-shot parallel pass over the whole prompt; it populates the persistent KV cache and is the dominant contributor to TTFT (time to first token — though TTFT also includes queueing, preprocessing, and transport, so model prefill latency is a component of, not identical to, user-observed TTFT). [...] Color is figure-local decoration — each box is titled. [...] [ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual]
issue.observed: Every figure caption in the chunk runs roughly 80–160 words and mixes four distinct jobs: (a) what the figure shows, (b) scope/caveat qualifications, (c) label and colour conventions, (d) cross-references to other figures and chapters. The result is that the caption — the only text a reader sees next to a figure — is longer and harder to parse than the figure it describes, and the reader's first line of orientation ('what should I learn from this?') is buried in the middle of a defensive paragraph. The 'Color is figure-local decoration — each box is titled; do not carry a color meaning from Fig 1.1 into this figure' disclaimer is repeated verbatim in at least two captions and belongs in a single front-matter note.
issue.evidence: Caption lengths in the chunk: Fig 1.1 ~95 words; Fig 1.2 ~130 words; Fig 2.1 ~150 words; Fig 2.2 ~75 words; Fig 3.1 ~65 words; Fig 3.2 ~85 words; Fig 3.3 ~70 words; Fig 3.4 ~110 words; Fig 4.1 ~70 words. Each caption ends with a bracketed evidence label and several carry a second italic 'what to learn' line beneath the figure, so the reader encounters two prose blocks per figure.
issue.root_cause: Captions were written as self-contained defence documents (each figure must survive being read out of context) rather than as reader-facing orientation, with no house rule separating 'what to learn' from 'scope caveats'.
issue.correction: Adopt a two-tier caption convention and state it once in the front matter: (1) a bold one-sentence 'what to learn' line immediately under the figure (this is the line the reader should be able to quote); (2) a smaller 'Scope / caveats' line for qualifications, colour/label conventions, and cross-references. Move the repeated colour disclaimer into the front-matter figure-conventions note. Where the italic line under the figure already says what to learn, merge it into tier (1) rather than duplicating it.
issue.acceptance_test: No figure caption exceeds ~45 words before any scope line; every figure has exactly one 'what to learn' sentence; the colour-convention disclaimer appears once in the book, not once per figure.

issue.quoted_clause: Prefill FLOPs scale with input length; in decode, the weight-read bytes per token are fixed, so at a given HBM bandwidth the decode rate is roughly constant per token.
issue.observed: The clause is about the weight-read component but is phrased as a statement about the decode rate, which contradicts the chapter's own §4 Measurement item 2 ('An increasing TPOT as the sequence lengthens reveals growing KV-attention cost' and 'TPOT does not have to stay constant'). A reader could carry away 'decode time per token is constant regardless of context length', which is the misconception the book elsewhere warns against.
issue.evidence: Ch 2 §4 item 2 states the opposite emphasis; Ch 1 §1 'Attention' states 'the per-token step is a linear cost in context length'; Ch 2 §1 'Decode' states 'the attention term grows with context and is the one that eventually binds at long context'.
issue.root_cause: A component-level statement was generalized to the whole step.
issue.correction: Rewrite: 'in decode, the weight-read bytes per token are fixed, so the weight-streaming component of the step is constant per token; the attention component grows linearly with the cached sequence, so the observed TPOT can rise with context length — measure the curve rather than assuming either shape.'
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 2 asserts that decode time per token is constant in context length without naming the component it refers to.

issue.quoted_clause: The full-attention component is *not* captured by $2NL$ — it grows ~quadratically with sequence length (Ch 22), so for a 9.2K-token prefill $2NL$ is a lower bound on total compute, not the whole story.
issue.observed: The caveat is correct but unquantified, and at the canonical context length the omitted term is negligible. A reader who has just been told 'the lower bound already exceeds the H100 peak' may reasonably suspect the omitted attention term could change the verdict, and the book gives no basis for judging. Quantifying it removes a needless worry and strengthens the argument.
issue.evidence: Recomputed for the canonical geometry (L = 9,200, d_model = 8,192, causal): attention FLOPs = 2 x L^2 x d_model = 2 x 8.464e7 x 8,192 = 1.39e12 FLOPs (1.39 TFLOP), i.e. ~0.11% of the 1.288 PFLOP 2NL figure (0.22% if the causal halving is not applied). The lower bound is therefore tight to within ~0.2% at 9.2K.
issue.root_cause: The caveat was carried over from the general L^2 discussion without a canonical-scale check.
issue.correction: Add one clause: 'at the canonical 9.2K context the omitted attention term is ~1.4 TFLOP, about 0.1% of 2NL, so the lower bound is tight here; the gap widens with context (Ch 22).'
issue.acceptance_test: The reader can tell from the text whether the omitted attention term could change the canonical prefill verdict, and the answer is given numerically.

issue.page_hint: Ch 2 §3 — Table 2-1 row 'Prefill: regime verdict'; Fig 2.2 caption; 'Worked example arithmetic details' prefill bullet
issue.quoted_clause: | Prefill: regime verdict | compute-bound regime | arithmetic intensity ~9.2K FLOP/byte > ridge ~295 -> on the compute-bound side of the roofline [canonical scenario][DERIVED] |
issue.observed: The ~9.2K FLOP/byte figure is the single-request prefill intensity (one request's 9,200 tokens against one pass over the 140 GB of weights). At the canonical fleet operating point several prefills share a weight pass, so the intensity is B x 9.2K FLOP/byte — strictly further from the ridge. The book never says this, so the reader may take ~9.2K as the fleet's operating intensity and infer the compute-bound verdict is marginal (9.2K vs 295 is ~31x, so it is not marginal, but the margin is understated).
issue.evidence: Recomputed: prefill weight-matmul FLOPs per GPU per step = 2 x 8.75e9 x (B x 9,200); weight bytes = 17.5 GB; AI = B x 9,200 FLOP/byte. At B = 2.1 (the canonical 17 slots / 8 GPUs) AI = ~19.3K FLOP/byte, i.e. ~65x the ridge.
issue.root_cause: The intensity was computed for the single-request illustration and reused as the regime statement without noting the batching dependence.
issue.correction: Add to the regime row or the prefill bullet: 'the ~9.2K FLOP/byte figure is the single-request intensity; with B concurrent prefills sharing the weight pass the intensity is B x 9.2K, so the compute-bound verdict strengthens with batching, not weakens.'
issue.acceptance_test: The reader can state the prefill arithmetic intensity at the canonical concurrency and confirm it is further from the ridge than the single-request value.

issue.quoted_clause: the attention portion reads KV cache at an intensity of only ~1–8 FLOP/byte and stays bandwidth-bound at every realistic batch size
issue.observed: The '~1–8' range is unexplained. For the canonical full-MHA FP16 model the attention intensity is exactly 1 FLOP/byte; 8 FLOP/byte corresponds to an 8:1 GQA geometry (attention FLOPs are unchanged by head sharing while KV bytes fall by the sharing factor). The reader cannot tell which end applies to the canonical model, and the range reads as measurement scatter rather than as an architectural dependence.
issue.evidence: Recomputed per decode step per GPU: attention FLOPs = 4 x L x d_model / 8 (TP=8) = 4 x 9,500 x 8,192 / 8 = 38.9 MFLOP; KV bytes = 2 x L x (n_kv x d_head) x 2 / 8. Full MHA (n_kv x d_head = 8,192): 38.9 MB -> AI = 1.0 FLOP/byte. GQA 8 x 128 (width 1,024): 4.87 MB -> AI = 8.0 FLOP/byte.
issue.root_cause: The range was carried from a general note without tying each end to a geometry.
issue.correction: Write it as: 'the attention portion reads KV cache at ~1 FLOP/byte for the canonical full-MHA FP16 geometry (and ~8 FLOP/byte for an 8:1 GQA geometry, since head sharing cuts KV bytes without cutting attention FLOPs) — in either case far below the ~295 ridge, so it stays bandwidth-bound at every realistic batch size.'
issue.acceptance_test: Each end of the quoted intensity range is tied to a named geometry, and the canonical model's value is stated unambiguously.

issue.quoted_clause: the real saturation threshold, which includes KV traffic (~3.01 GB/seq at canonical context per GPU), must be measured rather than read off either subset.
issue.observed: The 3.01 GB/seq figure is the input-only basis (24.1 GB / 8 GPUs), while the slot-counting basis used everywhere else in the book (and in the same chapter's host verdict) is the 9.5K resident basis of 24.9 GB, i.e. 3.11 GB/seq. Mixing the two bases inside one paragraph on KV traffic is exactly the kind of slip the book elsewhere polices.
issue.evidence: Recomputed: 24.1 GB / 8 = 3.0125 GB/seq (input-only); 24.9 GB / 8 = 3.1125 GB/seq (resident). Ch 2's own host verdict uses 24.1 GB and 24.9 GB side by side.
issue.root_cause: The input-only figure was carried over from the KV-total arithmetic without switching to the resident basis used for per-sequence traffic.
issue.correction: State the basis explicitly: '~3.01 GB/seq per GPU at the 9.2K input-only basis (~3.11 GB/seq on the 9.5K resident basis used for slot counting)'.
issue.acceptance_test: Every per-sequence KV figure in the book names its basis (input-only vs resident) at the point of use.

issue.page_hint: Ch 3 §3 — subsection heading 'MoE model representative (Mixtral 8x7B class, [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION])' and its preamble; Table 3-2 caption
issue.quoted_clause: We contrast with a representative MoE model in the Mixtral lineage. The exact parameter split is not always published in vendor model cards; the numbers below are plausibility-checked and flagged.
issue.observed: Two problems. (a) The claim that the parameter split 'is not always published in vendor model cards' is misleading for the model actually being used: Mixtral 8x7B's total and active parameter counts are published by the model author (46.7B total, 12.9B active), and the book's numbers (47B / 12.8B) are within rounding of them. (b) The chapter labels the model [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] while simultaneously using a real named family's published geometry (32 layers, hidden 4096, GQA 8 x 128) for the KV comparison. A reader who knows Mixtral will read the numbers as Mixtral's actuals despite the label; a reader who does not will think the geometry is invented.
issue.evidence: The book's own numbers: 5.7B x 8 + 1.4B = 47B total; 2 x 5.7B + 1.4B = 12.8B active. Published Mixtral 8x7B: 46.7B total, 12.9B active, 32 layers, hidden 4096, 32 attention heads, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128 — the same geometry the chapter uses for the KV arithmetic.
issue.root_cause: The chapter wanted a worked example that is not the canonical model, and used [ILLUSTRATIVE] to signal that, without noticing that the numbers and geometry are first-party published facts.
issue.correction: Pick one of two honest framings. (i) Cite the model card: relabel the subsection '[1P][FACT] geometry, [canonical scenario][DERIVED] arithmetic' with the Mixtral model card as the source, and state the published 46.7B/12.9B figures alongside the book's rounded 47B/12.8B so the rounding is visible. (ii) Rename the model to a generic '8-expert MoE, 32L/4096H, GQA 8 x 128' and keep [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION], deleting the Mixtral attribution and the claim about unpublished splits. Do not keep the current mixture.
issue.acceptance_test: The provenance label on the MoE geometry matches whether the geometry is a published fact or an invented variant; no sentence claims a parameter split is unpublished for a model whose split is published.

issue.page_hint: Ch 3 §6 — 'One verified 2026 transfer: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next', KV cache bullet
issue.quoted_clause: So per-token KV no longer follows the dense formula, and no KV metric for this model is stated anywhere in this book. Chapter 7 works a configuration-backed version of exactly this two-term budget — Qwen3.8-27B's 16 full-attention layers priced separately from its 48 Gated DeltaNet layers — into its own history-state arithmetic, so we do not re-derive it here.
issue.observed: The sentence 'no KV metric for this model is stated anywhere in this book' is immediately followed by a pointer to a KV metric for a sibling model (Qwen3.8-27B) in Ch 7. The two statements sit in adjacent sentences and read as contradictory. The intended distinction (Flash-Next vs 27B) is not signalled.
issue.evidence: Both sentences are in the same bullet of the same subsection.
issue.root_cause: Two different models with similar names are being distinguished in a way the prose does not make explicit.
issue.correction: Rewrite: 'so per-token KV for Flash-Next no longer follows the dense formula, and this book states no KV metric for Flash-Next itself. Chapter 7 does price the equivalent two-term budget for the sibling Qwen3.8-27B (16 full-attention layers priced separately from its 48 Gated DeltaNet layers); that is a different model and its numbers do not transfer.'
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can tell, from the sentence alone, which model any KV figure in Ch 7 belongs to.

issue.page_hint: Ch 3 §3 — Table 3-3, row 'KV cache per request (9.2K ctx, 8-bit)'
issue.quoted_clause: | KV cache per request (9.2K ctx, 8-bit) | ~12 GB | ~0.6 GB | set by attention shape, not routing: dense 80L/8192H full-MHA = 1.31 MB/token x 9,200 ~ 12.06 GB; the challenger's own 32L/4096H GQA (8 KV-heads x 128) = 0.0655 MB/token x 9,200 ~ 0.60 GB — a dense model with the challenger's shape holds the same ~0.6 GB [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] |
issue.observed: The table's KV row is stated only at 8-bit, while the canonical scenario's declared KV precision is FP16 and every fleet number in the book uses the FP16 figures (24.1/24.9 GB). The FP16 values exist only in the prose ('~24 GB', '~1.2 GB'), so a reader comparing Table 3-3's '~12 GB' with Ch 4's '24.1 GB' for the same canonical request sees an unexplained factor of two. This is the same precision-basis issue as FT-08, seen from the table side.
issue.evidence: Recomputed: dense 9,200 x 2.62144 MB = 24.12 GB (FP16); challenger 9,200 x 0.131072 MB = 1.206 GB (FP16). Table 3-3 shows only 12.06 GB and 0.60 GB (8-bit).
issue.root_cause: The table was built around the quantization variant for the comparison's sake and the canonical precision was left to the prose.
issue.correction: Add a second row 'KV cache per request (9.2K ctx, FP16 — canonical precision) | ~24.1 GB | ~1.2 GB', or convert the existing row to FP16 and move the 8-bit figures to a parenthetical. Whichever is chosen, the row label must state the precision and the canonical precision must be the one the fleet arithmetic uses.
issue.acceptance_test: Every KV figure in Ch 3's tables carries its precision, and the canonical-precision row matches the 24.1/24.9 GB used in Ch 4.

issue.page_hint: Ch 3 §6 — 'One verified 2026 transfer: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next', first bullet
issue.quoted_clause: **125B total / 6B active** (plus a separate 51B of offloadable N-gram embedding parameters), **512 MoE experts** (10 routed + 1 shared per token), and **hybrid attention** — Gated DeltaNet (GDN) on three of every four layers plus Qwen Sparse Attention (QSA) on the fourth.
issue.observed: The chapter's central discipline is total-vs-active, and it asks the reader to apply it to this model, but it never shows how the stated 6B active follows from the stated geometry (512 experts, 10 routed + 1 shared, 125B total, 51B offloadable N-gram). The reader is given two numbers (125B, 6B) and a routing configuration and asked to take the ratio on trust — the exact move the chapter warns against elsewhere ('pause and ask: is this total or active?').
issue.evidence: Arithmetic available to the reader: 125B - 51B N-gram = ~74B of expert + attention mass; 10/512 routed experts is ~1.9% of expert mass, so the ~6B active figure implies a large always-on attention/shared component (~4.5B) that the text does not state. The book does not show this reconciliation, so the 6B cannot be checked against the geometry.
issue.root_cause: The frontier-model figures were imported as first-party constants without the derivation the chapter itself demands of the reader.
issue.correction: Add one line of reconciliation: 'the 6B active is the routed expert mass (10 of 512) plus the always-on attention/shared parameters; the 51B N-gram embedding table is offloadable and is not part of the per-token working set.' If the always-on component is not first-party published, say so and mark the 6B as a first-party figure whose composition the book does not decompose.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can reconstruct the 6B active figure from the stated geometry, or is told explicitly which part of it the book cannot decompose.

issue.quoted_clause: but the 140 GB footprint means KV cache for 9.2 K context adds ~20–30 GB of GPU memory per request at peak, leaving headroom but not abundance.
issue.observed: The book computes this quantity precisely everywhere else (24.1 GB at 9.2K input-only, 24.9 GB at 9.5K resident) and uses the precise figure for the 17-slot screen, the 436 GB budget and the host counts. Here it degrades to a '~20–30 GB' range, and 'at peak' is undefined (peak of what — context length, concurrency, or traffic?). The reader cannot tell whether the range is a context-length sensitivity band or a rounding of 24.1 GB.
issue.evidence: Ch 4 §6 'Memory planning' in the same chapter: 'giving ~9,200 x 2.62 MB ~ 24.1 GB of initial KV per request; a resident request also holds its 300 output tokens, so the slot-counting basis is 9,500 x 2.62 MB ~ 24.9 GB'.
issue.root_cause: An early draft's approximate figure survived in prose after the chapter's arithmetic was tightened.
issue.correction: Replace with the precise figure and name the basis: 'the 140 GB footprint means KV cache for 9.2K context adds ~24.1 GB of GPU memory per request (~24.9 GB on the resident slot-counting basis), leaving headroom but not abundance.' If a sensitivity band is intended, state the context range it corresponds to (e.g. '~24 GB at 9.2K, ~84 GB at 32K').
issue.acceptance_test: Every per-request KV figure in Ch 4 is a single precise number with a named basis, or an explicitly parameterised range.

issue.quoted_clause: On each host, continuous batching (e.g. vLLM) is nearly mandatory under this load to hold the 1.2 s TTFT budget: it reduces queueing and improves utilization under concurrency (it does not shorten a single request's 9.2 K prefill); without admission scheduling, queued prefills can push p95 TTFT past the 2 s ceiling
issue.observed: 'Nearly mandatory' is a strong architectural claim presented without the mechanism that would make it true, in a chapter whose own standard is that every optimization is a hypothesis about which resource it shifts. The text does not show what happens without it: at the canonical 17 resident slots per host, a static batch would prefill 17 x 9,200 = 156K tokens in one pass, which at the host's ~19,800 tok/s planning rate is ~7.9 s — roughly 6.6x the 1.2 s TTFT budget. That single calculation turns the assertion into a demonstrated consequence and shows exactly which resource (prefill compute, serialized behind the batch) is being protected.
issue.evidence: Recomputed: 17 x 9,200 = 156,400 tokens; 156,400 / 19,800 tok/s = 7.90 s vs the 1.2 s TTFT budget and the 2 s p95 ceiling. The book's own host planning rate (~19,800 tok/s at 35% MFU) is the right denominator.
issue.root_cause: The claim was stated as a design conclusion rather than derived from the canonical concurrency, which is the derivation the chapter has available.
issue.correction: Replace 'is nearly mandatory' with the demonstrated version: 'continuous batching (e.g. vLLM) is effectively required at this concurrency: with 17 resident slots per host, a static batch would prefill ~156K tokens in one pass, ~7.9 s at the host's ~19,800 tok/s planning rate — far past the 1.2 s TTFT budget and the 2 s p95 ceiling. Continuous batching (or chunked prefill) is what keeps the prefill burst from serialising behind the whole batch.'
issue.acceptance_test: Every 'required / mandatory / necessary' claim about a serving mechanism in the book is accompanied by the arithmetic that makes it necessary at the canonical operating point.

issue.quoted_clause: | **Quality** | Factual accuracy >85% on enterprise Q&A; reasoning via retrieval; no tool use beyond search API | [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] author-chosen target, set with reference to enterprise retrieval-Q&A benchmark suites (e.g. HotpotQA-style) |
issue.observed: The reference adds a false flavour of grounding. HotpotQA is a multi-hop Wikipedia question-answering benchmark; it does not measure 'factual accuracy on enterprise Q&A', and no enterprise RAG accuracy suite is named. The row is correctly labelled 'author-chosen target', but the parenthetical citation invites the reader to treat >85% as benchmark-anchored. The book's own §6 'Model selection' bullet already concedes that 'factual accuracy still depends on retrieval quality, context, and evaluation' — which is the honest framing.
issue.evidence: The row's own status label says 'author-chosen target'; the cited suite does not measure the stated metric on the stated domain.
issue.root_cause: A familiar benchmark name was used as a gesture toward grounding rather than as a measurement anchor.
issue.correction: Either drop the benchmark reference and keep 'author-chosen target; to be validated on an internal eval set (retrieval recall@k plus answer faithfulness)', or name a real measurement protocol: '>85% answer faithfulness on an internal eval set of ~200 graded questions; retrieval recall@5 >= 90%'. The point is that the target must be paired with the instrument that will test it.
issue.acceptance_test: Every quality target in the canonical scenario names the measurement that will validate it, and no benchmark is cited that does not measure the stated metric.

issue.quoted_clause: | **Traffic** | ~10 rps average; peaks ~40 rps | [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] declared traffic inputs (~2,000 registered users x one request ~every 200 s ~ 10 rps; peak scaled) — declared, not derived from the user population (walk-through in §4.3); $L_{\mathrm{exec}}$ = λ x $W_{\mathrm{exec}}$ ~ 86 (~344 at 40 rps) is a separate derived quantity. |
issue.observed: The row carries a single [ASSUMPTION] label but contains a derived quantity (the ~86 / ~344 occupancy) inside the same cell. The book's own table-level convention says a derived value carries [canonical scenario][DERIVED], and the row's own text calls the occupancy 'a separate derived quantity'. The label scope therefore contradicts the prose in the same cell.
issue.evidence: Table 4-1's table-level provenance note: 'a value arithmetically derived from those assumed inputs (an occupancy, a tokens-per-second rate, a cost-per-request, a tokens-per-dollar figure) is [canonical scenario][DERIVED]'. The Traffic row's occupancy is exactly the listed example of a derived value.
issue.root_cause: The row was compressed to fit the table and the derived figure was appended to the assumption cell without a second label.
issue.correction: Label the two quantities separately inside the cell: '~10 rps average; peaks ~40 rps [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] ... ; execution occupancy ~86 (~344 at 40 rps) [canonical scenario][DERIVED]'. Apply the same treatment to any other row that mixes an input with a derived figure (the Economic row mixes several).
issue.acceptance_test: Every cell in Table 4-1 that contains a derived figure carries a [DERIVED] label on that figure, distinct from the [ASSUMPTION] label on the inputs.

issue.quoted_clause: [1P][FACT] A high-frequency English word is often one token (verifiable on most vendor tokenizer demos — e.g. common words like *the*, *we*, *run* render as single tokens); a rare technical term, a long digit string, or dense code is frequently several.
issue.observed: [1P] means first-party — a vendor's own specification or artifact for that vendor's product. The clause generalises across vendors ('most vendor tokenizer demos') and the supporting evidence is a demo page, not a specification. The claim is true but its provenance label overstates it: the first-party artifact supports the claim for one vendor's tokenizer, not for 'most' tokenizers.
issue.evidence: The book's own axis definition (Ch 4 Note 1): '[1P] first-party (vendor spec, method paper)'; '[2°] reputable second-hand (textbook, survey, independent benchmark)'.
issue.root_cause: A verifiable-in-practice claim was labelled with the strongest available provenance rather than the accurate one.
issue.correction: Either relabel as [2°] (a cross-vendor generalisation supported by vendor demos and tokenizer documentation), or make it first-party and specific: '[1P][FACT] In the canonical model's tokenizer, common English words such as *the*, *we* and *run* are single tokens (verifiable on the model card's tokenizer demo); the pattern is typical of byte-level BPE vocabularies [2°].'
issue.acceptance_test: Every [1P] label in the book is attached to a claim about one identified first-party artifact, and cross-vendor generalisations carry [2°].

issue.page_hint: Ch 1 §1 'Concept' — 'KV cache as a concept' subsection, the vLLM FP8-KV sentence
issue.quoted_clause: the vLLM FP8-KV blog post's often-quoted '54%' — from its Llama-3.1-8B Table 3 (vLLM blog, post dated 2026-04-22; retrieved 2026-11-15) [S6] — is, on this book's reading, a decode inter-token-latency (ITL) slope, not a memory ratio or footprint coefficient.
issue.observed: Two issues. (a) The citation key '[S6]' does not match the book's citation style: every other source in the chunk is an inline markdown link with a title and URL (e.g. '[Wan2.2 sampling loop](https://github.com/...)', '[Expert Parallel Deployment](https://docs.vllm.ai/...)'). A bare '[S6]' is unresolvable from the page and forces a trip to the sources section for a claim the reader is being asked to accept against the vendor's own framing. (b) The claim is a strong reinterpretation of a vendor's published number, and the text gives the reader no basis for it beyond 'on this book's reading'. A reader who has seen the blog quoted elsewhere will want to know what the vendor actually plotted.
issue.evidence: Citation style survey across the chunk: inline links at Ch 2 (Wan2.2 x2), Ch 3 (Wan2.2, vLLM expert-parallel docs), Ch 3 ('source: HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B', 'source: Meta via vLLM-Recipes'). '[S6]' is the only bracketed numeric key.
issue.root_cause: The citation was drafted against a numbered source list that the manuscript does not use, and the interpretive claim was written without its supporting evidence.
issue.correction: Convert to the book's inline-link style with the URL and the specific table reference, and state the evidence for the reading: e.g. 'the vLLM FP8-KV post's Table 3 reports ITL against batch size for FP16 vs FP8 KV on Llama-3.1-8B; the '54%' is the slope of that ITL curve, not a memory ratio — on this book's reading [1P][FACT] ([vLLM FP8 KV cache blog](url), Table 3, post dated 2026-04-22, retrieved 2026-11-15)'. If the reading cannot be evidenced from the post itself, downgrade the claim to an explicitly labelled [HYPOTHESIS].
issue.acceptance_test: Every citation in the book is resolvable from the page (inline link with title and URL) or is a key that is defined in a numbered list the reader can find; the reinterpretation of the '54%' figure states what the vendor actually measured.

issue.page_hint: Ch 3 §6 — 'Why the trend signal should not be read as "dense is dead"' and 'One verified 2026 transfer: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next'
issue.quoted_clause: **Qwen3.8-27B** ([1P][FACT], source: HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B) is a dense 27.8B model whose 4-bit weights fit on a single 24 GB consumer GPU, and **Muse Glimmer 30B** ([2°][FACT], source: Meta via vLLM-Recipes) is a dense 29.6B local-agentic model that runs in ~18 GB at ~5-bit weights.
issue.observed: Two citation-hygiene problems in the same sentence. (a) 'source: HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B' is a bare model-card reference with no URL, unlike the inline links used elsewhere in the book; a reader cannot verify it from the page. (b) 'Muse Glimmer 30B' is attributed to 'Meta via vLLM-Recipes' and labelled [2°], but the underlying artifact is a first-party model card from the model's author; the house convention prefers primary sources where a primary source is readily available, and a recipe repository is a secondary restatement of a first-party claim. The [2°] label is honest but the sourcing choice is not the best available.
issue.evidence: The book's own convention (Ch 4 Note 1): '[1P] first-party (vendor spec, method paper)'; '[2°] reputable second-hand'. Elsewhere the book links primary sources inline (Wan2.2 repository at a pinned revision, vLLM expert-parallel docs).
issue.root_cause: Frontier-model citations were added from working notes rather than from the book's citation standard.
issue.correction: Give both models inline links to their first-party model cards and label them [1P][FACT]; if a figure (e.g. the ~18 GB at ~5-bit figure) comes only from the recipe, split the claim: the parameter count and architecture from the model card [1P][FACT], the memory footprint from the recipe [2°][FACT], each labelled separately.
issue.acceptance_test: Every model-specific factual claim in Ch 3 carries an inline link to a first-party artifact, and any figure that exists only in a secondary source is labelled [2°] on its own.

issue.page_hint: Ch 2 §5 'Common Mistakes' — second bullet; compare Ch 4 §5 ('Ch 1 §5's') and Ch 4 §6 ('Ch 2 §1')
issue.quoted_clause: **Assuming one H100 suffices for 70B inference.** The arithmetic in §2.3 shows that a single H100 cannot hold or stream the whole 140 GB model
issue.observed: The book uses two incompatible styles for internal references: '§2.3' (Ch 2) and '§2.2' (Ch 2 Architect's Question) versus 'Ch 1 §5's', 'Ch 1 §4', 'Ch 2 §1', 'Ch 3 §6, Ch. 18'. Under the 'Ch.S' reading, '§2.3' resolves to Ch 2 §3 (Worked Example) and is correct; under the ordinary 'section 2.3' reading it resolves to nothing, because Ch 2 has no §2.3. A reader who reads it the ordinary way is sent to a nonexistent location.
issue.evidence: Reference inventory in the chunk: '§2.2 and Ch 8' (Ch 2 Architect's Question), '§2.3' (Ch 2 §5), '§4.3' (Ch 4 §6), '§6' (Ch 4 §3), '§4.3' (Ch 4 §3), 'Ch 1 §4', 'Ch 1 §5', 'Ch 2 §1', 'Ch 3 §6', 'Ch 4 Table 4-2'.
issue.root_cause: Two reference conventions were used in drafting and neither was declared.
issue.correction: Standardise on 'Ch N §M' everywhere (the form already used for cross-chapter references) and change '§2.3' to 'Ch 2 §3' and '§2.2' to 'Ch 2 §2'. Within-chapter references may keep the bare '§M' form only if the chapter is unambiguous from the page.
issue.acceptance_test: Every internal reference resolves under the book's single declared convention, and no reference uses a dotted '§C.S' form that could be misread as a subsection number.

issue.quoted_clause: the measured per-phase utilization and goodput (throughput that meets the SLO; Ch 7, Ch 8, Ch 14) are what confirm it.
issue.observed: Goodput is defined in the metrics chapter (Ch 6), which is where the book introduces the metric vocabulary and the resource table's 'throughput / goodput' row points ('metrics (Ch. 6)'). The parenthetical definition here points to Ch 7, Ch 8 and Ch 14 — the chapters that use goodput, not the one that defines it. A reader who wants the definition is sent to three chapters that assume it.
issue.evidence: Ch 2 §1 resource table: '| throughput / goodput | useful tokens/s under SLO | completed work, not just tokens/s | metrics (Ch. 6) |'. Ch 2's Fig 2.1 roadmap paragraph also assigns 'Chapter 6 (metrics) measures which phase is the bottleneck'.
issue.root_cause: The cross-reference list was assembled from where goodput is used rather than where it is defined.
issue.correction: Change to '(throughput that meets the SLO; defined in Ch 6, applied in Ch 7, Ch 8 and Ch 14)'.
issue.acceptance_test: Every metric a chapter uses for the first time points to the chapter that defines it, not only to the chapters that apply it.

issue.quoted_clause: At the canonical instance rate (~$20/hr per 8xH100 host), the canonical 6–21-host fleet on the owned/self-host basis is roughly **$87.6K–$306.6K/month** (6 hosts at ~$87.6K/month — $87,600 = 6 x 730 h default paid-occupancy input ~ $14.04/1K — up to 21 hosts always-on at peak, $306,600 ~ $49.13/1K (full-util 6/21; the provisioning-policy fleet is 9/32 — see the §8 parenthetical; and the 21-host rows are peak-provisioned capacity divided by the average 10 rps volume — a peak-capacity-cost-per-1K-average-volume figure, not a per-request cost at either traffic level: at the 40 rps peak volume of 24.96M/month (40 rps over the same active-hours window: 40 x 3,600 x 8 h x 260 workdays / 12), $306,600 / 24,960K ~ $12.28/1K)
issue.observed: This paragraph re-derives, in parenthetical prose, the entire sidebar table that appears a few pages earlier in the same chapter: $87,600 / $14.04 per 1K, $306,600 / $49.13 per 1K, the 9/32 policy fleet, the 24.96M peak volume and the $12.28 per 1K figure. The mini-case's own contribution — the 50 rps growth scenario and its 26/37/39/40-host sizing — is buried between two blocks of repeated cost arithmetic. This is redundant repetition (class C): the second occurrence adds no new reasoning.
issue.evidence: The sidebar table in §3 already contains: 'Cloud, 6 hosts — default paid-occupancy input | $87,600 | ~ $14.04', 'Cloud, 21 hosts always-on at peak | $306,600 | ~ $49.13', and the note 'at the 40 rps peak volume (24.96M/month) $306,600 / 24,960K ~ $12.28/1K'. All three appear again in the mini-case.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case was written to be self-contained and re-derived the cost basis instead of citing the sidebar.
issue.correction: Replace the parenthetical block with a one-line pointer: 'the canonical 6–21-host fleet costs $87.6K–$306.6K/month on the owned/self-host basis (~$14.04–$49.13 per 1K requests; see the §3 sidebar for the basis and the active-hours variant)'. Keep the mini-case's own new content — the 50 rps sizing, the prefill cross-check, and the distinction from the canonical 40 rps case.
issue.acceptance_test: No number appears twice in Ch 4 unless the second occurrence adds a new derivation or a new basis; the mini-case's length is dominated by its own scenario, not by restated canonical costs.

issue.page_hint: Ch 1 §8 'End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: The Internal Q&A Tool, From First Principles'
issue.quoted_clause: From the token-level work alone (which we worked through in this chapter), the architect can already establish: the unit is tokens; the request shape will be prompt + retrieved context + output; the working hypothesis is input-heavy (Ch 4 quantifies it); and the first number to lock down is tokens-per-request, because every downstream decision (which model fits, how much memory, what latency is possible) is priced against it.
issue.observed: The mini-case resolves no decision, computes nothing, and uses none of the chapter's specific content (tokenization, the 4-chars-per-token heuristic, input/output asymmetry, context-window reservation). It restates the chapter's conclusions in the architect's voice. By the book's own standard for mini-cases — a decision, evidence, competing interpretations, a calculation that resolves it, and an architectural consequence — this one does not exercise the reasoning it is meant to consolidate. The chapter's own §4 Measurement section supplies the obvious missing exercise: run the model's tokenizer on representative prompts.
issue.evidence: Compare Ch 3's mini-case (computes the residency delta, separates the two accounting lines, refuses the challenger with reasons) and Ch 4's mini-case (new scenario, Little's-law sizing, prefill cross-check, explicit non-contradiction with the canonical case). Ch 1's mini-case has no calculation.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case was written as a scene-setting bridge to Ch 4 rather than as an exercise of Ch 1's content.
issue.correction: Give the architect a concrete token-counting task with a finding that changes a number: e.g. 'the architect runs the candidate model's tokenizer over 200 sample queries and finds the mean prompt is 1,340 tokens, not the 1,200 assumed — and that 12% of queries contain a 20K-token pasted document, so the context distribution has a tail the mean hides. The canonical 9.2K input assumption is replaced by a measured distribution, and the KV budget must be sized against the tail, not the mean.' That single exercise exercises tokenization, the input/output split, the peak-vs-average measurement habit, and the KV consequence, and it hands Ch 4 a measured input rather than a declared one.
issue.acceptance_test: Each chapter's mini-case contains at least one calculation or measurement the reader must perform, and the outcome changes a number the chapter established.

issue.page_hint: Ch 2 §8 'End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: TTFT and the Prefill/Decode Split'
issue.quoted_clause: From the unit-and-token work of Ch 1 alone, the architect can already state the hard numbers: each request carries ~9.2K input tokens and ~300 output tokens. At 10 rps average, the system must sustain ~92,000 input tokens/s in prefill and ~3,000 output tokens/s in decode. [...] The architect can also state the two opposite bottlenecks: prefill will be compute-bound (~1.29 PFLOP per request at 9.2K input), and decode will be bandwidth-bound (a ~140 GB/token weight-read requiring ~5.6 TB/s sustained over each ~25 ms decode step
issue.observed: The sentence attributes the whole set of numbers to 'the unit-and-token work of Ch 1 alone', but the numbers that follow include 1.29 PFLOP and 5.6 TB/s, which are Ch 2's own derivations, not Ch 1's. The misattribution is small but it obscures the chapter's actual teaching move — that the token counts from Ch 1 become FLOP and bandwidth demands only after Ch 2's model is applied.
issue.evidence: Ch 1 contains no FLOP or bandwidth arithmetic; Ch 2 §3 derives both.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case's opening sentence was written to bridge Ch 1 to Ch 2 and then the paragraph was expanded with Ch 2 content without updating the attribution.
issue.correction: Rewrite the opening: 'From Ch 1's token counts and Ch 2's cost model, the architect can state the hard numbers: ...' and, better, make the bridge explicit by showing the two-step derivation (tokens -> FLOPs/bytes -> regime) rather than presenting the results as a single block.
issue.acceptance_test: Every mini-case's attribution of a number to a chapter matches where that number is actually derived.

issue.page_hint: Ch 2 §1 'Concept' — 'Figure convention (used throughout the book)' paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: Arrows in the diagrams carry different meanings by context, and the reader should not assume one universal reading: a **data-flow** arrow (Fig 2.1, 11.3) shows tokens or activations moving; a **dependency** arrow shows "must be decided before"; an **influence** arrow (Fig 4.1) shows "constrains/informs"; a **causation** arrow (Fig 6.1) shows "drives / causes"; and a **conceptual-association** arrow (App. A.4) shows "relates to." Where a figure's arrows are ambiguous, the caption states the intended reading.
issue.observed: The convention list has no category for control flow, yet Fig 2.1's caption distinguishes exactly that: 'The initialize path (labelled initialize) seeds the loop with the first sampled token', and the surrounding prose calls it 'the green initialize path'. A reader applying the stated convention will read the initialize arrow as data flow (tokens moving) when it is sequencing/control (the loop's initialisation). The list also omits the 'append'/'write' arrow used in Fig 1.2 ('written (append) and read (read past K,V, the backward read arrow from the KV cache back to attention)').
issue.evidence: Fig 2.1 caption and Ch 2 §1 prose both name the initialize path as a distinct arrow type; Fig 1.2's caption names a backward read arrow and an append operation; neither maps to the five listed categories.
issue.root_cause: The convention list was written from the figures that existed when it was drafted and was not extended when the KV-cache and pipeline figures were added.
issue.correction: Extend the list: 'a **control/sequencing** arrow (Fig 2.1's initialize path) shows ordering or loop initialisation, not data movement; a **state-write** arrow (Fig 1.2's append) shows persistent state being updated; a **state-read** arrow (Fig 1.2's backward read) shows persistent state being consumed.' Then state the convention once in the front matter rather than inside Ch 2 §1, where it currently competes with the concept material.
issue.acceptance_test: Every arrow type used in any figure maps to a named category in the book's figure convention, and the convention is stated once in the front matter.

issue.page_hint: Ch 4 §3 — Table 4-1 table-level provenance note; canonical box 'Assumption-change log'; Table 4-2 'Note 1'; Table 4-2 table-level provenance note
issue.quoted_clause: *(Table-level provenance — applies to every row unless a row overrides inline. The convention: an input or parameter assumption (traffic, latency target, price, token count) is [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]; a value arithmetically derived from those assumed inputs (an occupancy, a tokens-per-second rate, a cost-per-request, a tokens-per-dollar figure) is [canonical scenario][DERIVED]; ...)* [...] **Note 1 (Table 4-2) — the three label axes, and why the change log does not mix them.** Axis 1 **provenance** ... Axis 2 **epistemic status** ... Axis 3 **measurement status** ... *(Table-level provenance for Table 4-2 — the one convention this chapter and the book uses: one label from the provenance axis and one from the epistemic axis per value, with the measurement status riding along. ...)*
issue.observed: The label taxonomy is restated four times within a single chapter section (Table 4-1 note, the canonical box's change log, Note 1, Table 4-2's note), and the book says it is also defined in the Preface and in 'Sources, Method, and Reproducibility'. Five statements of one convention inside the first chapter the reader meets it is a cognitive tax and a contradiction risk: the four statements are not worded identically (the Table 4-1 note omits Axis 3; Note 1 adds the 'a hypothesis is tagged [HYPOTHESIS], never [ILLUSTRATIVE]' rule; the change log adds the four-state given -> derived -> hypothesized -> validated narrative).
issue.evidence: Four distinct statements of the same convention in Ch 4 §3, plus two external locations cited by the chapter itself.
issue.root_cause: Each artifact was made self-contained, at the cost of repeating the taxonomy; no single canonical statement was designated.
issue.correction: Designate one canonical statement (Note 1 is the natural home, or the Preface) and have every other location point to it with only the delta: e.g. in Table 4-1's note, 'Provenance and status labels follow Note 1 below; this table's rows are all canonical-scenario inputs and derived values, with the inline overrides marked.' Keep the change-log narrative in the canonical box but strip its re-definition of the axes.
issue.acceptance_test: The label taxonomy is defined once in the book; every other mention is a pointer plus a local delta, and no two statements of it differ in wording or content.

issue.page_hint: Ch 4 §3 — 'Economic Constraints' subsection (from '**Infrastructure**' bullet through the cost-basis table)
issue.quoted_clause: **Cost per request**: At 10 rps, each request carries ~9,500 tokens (9,200 input + 300 output). At the per-million rates, cost per request ~ ($1.20 x 9.2 + $2.00 x 0.3) / 1,000 ~ $0.01164 ~ **$0.012 per request** per inference cycle. [...] **Basis note — two different cost bases, not interchangeable.** [...] So the owned per-request cost **on the active service-hour basis** [...] is (N_hosts x $20/hr) / (rps x 3600) ~ (6 x $20) / (10 x 3600) ~ **~$0.0033 per request** at average, and (21 x $20) / (40 x 3600) ~ **~$0.0029 per request** at peak
issue.observed: The Economic Constraints subsection runs to roughly 1,100 words and asks the reader to hold four cost bases simultaneously (mid-tier API list price; frontier-class API list price; owned-fleet active-hours; owned-fleet wall-clock paid-occupancy), each with its own denominator, plus a blended rate, plus a per-1K-request normalisation, plus the 6.24M vs 24.96M volume bases. The distinctions are all correct and all necessary, but they are delivered as a single unbroken block of prose with nested parentheticals, which is the hardest possible form for a reader who must later reuse the numbers. The subsection also duplicates the sidebar table's content.
issue.evidence: The subsection contains: the API price basis, the frontier-tier basis, the whole-fleet tokens-per-dollar basis, the always-on basis, the single-host prefill-rate basis, the API cost-per-request, the owned-fleet cost-per-request at two rates, the 9/32-host policy variant, the one-host unit-error warning, and a two-row cost-basis table — all within one subsection, with the sidebar table repeating several of the same figures.
issue.root_cause: The subsection accumulated successive corrections (each new basis added as a paragraph rather than as a row in a single comparison), and the sidebar was added later without folding the prose into it.
issue.correction: Restructure into (a) a short statement of the two bases (hosted-API price vs owned-fleet cost) with the rule for which to use, (b) one table with a row per basis and columns for derivation, denominator, and value — absorbing the current cost-basis table and the sidebar's overlapping rows, and (c) a short 'common errors' paragraph for the two unit errors the text currently handles in prose (dividing the offered rate by one host's price; dividing one host's price by the whole workload's rps). Move the sidebar's four delivery-mode rows into the same table with an explicit 'volume basis' column so the 6.24M vs 24.96M distinction is visible in the table rather than in a footnote.
issue.acceptance_test: Every cost figure in Ch 4 appears in exactly one table with an explicit denominator and volume basis; the prose around it explains which basis to use rather than re-deriving each one.

issue.quoted_clause: **Canonical host verdict.** On the canonical 8xH100 host (TP = 8): prefill 1.29 PFLOP / (8 x 0.989 PFLOPS) = 0.16 s at peak, ~0.47 s at 35% MFU, inside the 1.08 s budget; decode shard 70B/8 = 8.75B params = 17.5 GB/GPU per step -> 17.5 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 5.2 ms, inside the 25 ms TPOT budget
issue.observed: Two gaps. (a) The prefill verdict is stated as 'inside the 1.08 s budget' without the qualification Ch 4 attaches to that number: Table 4-2 labels 1.08 s a 'two-term-only upper cap, NOT a feasible deployed prefill target' that 'leaves zero allowance for admission/queue and tokenization/transfer', so the correct statement is 'inside the 1.08 s upper cap, with no allowance left for queueing or tokenization'. (b) The decode verdict quotes only the weight-shard read (5.2 ms) as the step time; the step also reads the KV cache (~3.01 GB/seq per GPU at the canonical context) and pays TP communication, so 5.2 ms is a component, not the step. The reader could take 5.2 ms as the achievable TPOT.
issue.evidence: Ch 4 Table 4-2 row: 'Prefill compute budget — two-term-only upper cap, NOT a feasible deployed prefill target | 1.08 s | ... it leaves zero allowance for admission/queue and tokenization/transfer, so budget_prefill <= 1.08 s - B_other where B_other is positive and must be measured.' Ch 2's own occupancy paragraph adds the KV traffic term (3.01 GB/seq per GPU) that the host verdict omits.
issue.root_cause: The host verdict was written before Ch 4 tightened the prefill-budget caveat and before the KV-traffic term was introduced in the same section.
issue.correction: Rewrite the verdict: 'prefill 1.29 PFLOP / (8 x 0.989 PFLOPS) = 0.16 s at peak, ~0.47 s at 35% MFU — inside the 1.08 s upper cap, but that cap carries no allowance for admission/queue or tokenization (Ch 4), so the real prefill budget is smaller; decode shard 70B/8 = 8.75B params = 17.5 GB/GPU per step -> 5.2 ms of weight streaming at peak HBM bandwidth, plus the KV read (~3.01 GB/seq per GPU at the canonical context) and TP communication — comfortably inside the 25 ms TPOT budget, but 5.2 ms is the weight component, not the step.'
issue.acceptance_test: Every 'inside the budget' verdict in the book names the budget's own caveats, and every quoted step time is labelled as a component or as the whole step.

issue.quoted_clause: A token is often a *word fragment*, not a whole word: a high-frequency English word is frequently one token, but a longer or rarer word is usually split into several subword tokens, and code, numerics, and non-Latin scripts can run 2–5x (rule of thumb; the multiplier is tokenizer- and language-specific) the naive word-count estimate.
issue.observed: The sentence is grammatically broken: 'can run 2–5x ... the naive word-count estimate' has no verb complement ('can run 2–5x the naive word-count estimate' is missing 'times' or 'of'). The intended meaning — tokens per word can be 2–5x the naive one-token-per-word assumption — is recoverable but the sentence as printed is not grammatical.
issue.evidence: The same chapter states the counterpart rule correctly: 'The "one token ~ 4 characters" rule of thumb is for rough estimation of general-English prose, never a law'.
issue.root_cause: An inserted qualifier ('rule of thumb; the multiplier is tokenizer- and language-specific') was spliced into the middle of a sentence without re-flowing it.
issue.correction: Rewrite: 'and code, numerics, and non-Latin scripts can run 2–5x the naive one-token-per-word estimate (rule of thumb; the multiplier is tokenizer- and language-specific).'
issue.acceptance_test: Every sentence in Ch 1 §5 parses without a missing complement, and the qualifier sits at the end of the clause it qualifies.

issue.page_hint: Ch 6 §8 (mini-case, 'The Post-Lunch Slowdown'); Ch 8 §3 (Scope note; 'n_hosts' derivation); Ch 5 §8 (mini-case, 'served on 8×H100 with vLLM continuous batching')
issue.quoted_clause: Ch 6 §8: "The architecture is memory- and compute-sane at the 10 rps design point but was never sized for the lunch peak." | Ch 8 §3: "n_hosts = 92,000/19,800 ≈ 4.6 → ~5 hosts" | Ch 8 §8: "at ~10 rps the prefill leg alone demands ~12.9 PFLOP/s, so the fleet spans several nodes — Ch 24's prefill screen: 1.63 nodes at 100% MFU, ~5 at 35% MFU"
issue.observed: Ch 6's mini-case asserts the canonical design point is compute-sane on one 8×H100 host. The book's own compute screen (Ch 8 §3) says the opposite: at 10 rps the prefill demand is 92,000 tokens/s (12.9 PFLOP/s) against a per-host sustained prefill rate of ~19,800 tokens/s (2.7692 PFLOP/s at 35% MFU), i.e. ~4.66× oversubscribed, requiring ~5 hosts. Ch 8 §8 states the same ('the fleet spans several nodes ... ~5 at 35% MFU'). Ch 8's Scope note disclaims only the 40 rps peak ('It is not a claim that one host absorbs the 40 rps peak arrival rate'), leaving the 10 rps average implication unstated, and Ch 5's mini-case presents a single 8×H100 host as the architecture for the 10 rps workload.
issue.evidence: Independent rederivation: 10 rps × 9,200 tokens = 92,000 tokens/s; 92,000 ÷ 19,768 tokens/s per host = 4.66 → 5 hosts. Equivalently 12.9 PFLOP/s ÷ 2.7692 PFLOP/s = 4.66×. Ch 6 §3 itself computes 40 × 1.29 ≈ 51.6 PFLOP/s vs 2.77 PFLOP/s = 18.6× at the peak, so the same host is 4.66× oversubscribed at the *average*, not merely at the peak.
issue.root_cause: The per-host 'feasibility container' framing (Ch 8 §3 Scope note) was applied to the peak only, and Ch 6's mini-case was written against the memory-fit conclusion (one host holds the model) rather than the compute screen. The two screens were never reconciled in prose.
issue.correction: In Ch 6 §8, replace the design-point claim with the compute screen: 'The architecture is memory-sane at the 10 rps design point but compute-oversubscribed on a single host: 12.9 PFLOP/s of prefill demand against ~2.77 PFLOP/s of sustained per-host capacity (~4.7×), so the canonical fleet is ~5 hosts at 35% MFU (Ch 8 §3).' Extend Ch 8 §3's Scope note to disclaim the 10 rps average as well as the 40 rps peak, and add a one-line qualifier in Ch 5 §8's mini-case that the 8×H100 host is the per-request/per-host container, not the whole fleet.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader who reads Ch 5 §8, Ch 6 §8 and Ch 8 §3 in sequence can state, without contradiction, how many 8×H100 hosts the canonical 10 rps workload needs and why; no sentence in Ch 5/6/8 asserts that one host is compute-sane at 10 rps.

issue.page_hint: Ch 5 §3, Table 5-2 (row 'Total tokens per dollar'); Ch 5 §3(b) 'tokens/s per dollar with prefill included'
issue.quoted_clause: Table 5-2: "| Total tokens per dollar (prefill + decode, stated concurrency) | ~285,000 tokens per dollar at 300 output tokens/request | 50 × (1 + 9,200/300) ≈ 1,583 tok/s × 3600 ÷ $20 [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] |"
issue.observed: The row label says 'stated concurrency', but the derivation contains no concurrency: 50 tok/s is the single-stream decode rate and 9,200/300 is a per-request token ratio, so the figure describes one stream with prefill overlapped (the §3(b) 'continuous batching' case). The row immediately above it is explicitly labelled 'single-stream decode', so the table juxtaposes a single-stream output-token metric with a batched total-token metric without saying so. The prose in §3(b) supplies the missing scope ('the 9,000 tokens-per-dollar figure should be read as a floor set by the single-stream assumption'), but the table — the artifact a reader copies from — loses it.
issue.evidence: Re-derivation: 50 × (1 + 9,200/300) = 1,583.3 tok/s; × 3600 ÷ $20 = 285,000 tokens/$. The strictly serial single-stream figure is 9,500/7.08 = 1,341.8 tok/s → 241,530 ≈ 242,000 tokens/$ (also in §3(b)). The canonical workload's 10 rps concurrency would imply 95,000 tokens/s, which is neither figure.
issue.root_cause: Table rows were written as self-contained derivations without carrying the operating-point qualifier that the surrounding prose had established.
issue.correction: Relabel the row: 'Total tokens per dollar (single-stream decode + overlapped prefill; not the 10 rps fleet point) | ~285,000 tokens per dollar at 300 output tokens/request' and add a second row for the strictly serial single-stream floor (~242,000 tokens/$) so the two operating points are visible in the table rather than only in prose.
issue.acceptance_test: Every row of Table 5-2 states its operating point (single-stream / overlapped / batched) and its concurrency basis; no reader can take 285,000 tokens/$ as the canonical 10 rps fleet figure.

issue.page_hint: Ch 5 §3(a), paragraph beginning 'On that basis the incremental cost stays well within…'
issue.quoted_clause: "On that basis the incremental cost stays well within the ~120 ms retrieval budget; single-core encoding fits only above ≈92.8 GFLOP/s sustained per core (11.14 GFLOP ÷ 0.12 s), beyond the typical sustained range (371 ms at 30 GFLOP/s vs 186 ms at 60 GFLOP/s) — conditional on measured single-core throughput."
issue.observed: The conclusion sentence is stated before its qualification and reads as applying to both bases presented in the preceding paragraph. On the CPU basis the incremental cost is 186–371 ms, which is 1.6–3.1× the 120 ms retrieval budget — i.e. it does NOT fit. Only the GPU basis (~1.1 ms) fits. The semicolon then supplies the correct CPU verdict, so the paragraph contains a flat 'stays well within the budget' immediately followed by the arithmetic showing it does not.
issue.evidence: 11.14 GFLOP ÷ 30 GFLOP/s = 0.371 s; ÷ 60 GFLOP/s = 0.186 s; both > 0.12 s. 11.14 ÷ 0.12 = 92.8 GFLOP/s required. GPU: 11.14 GFLOP ÷ 10,000 GFLOP/s = 1.1 ms.
issue.root_cause: The GPU and CPU bases were presented in one paragraph and the summary sentence was written for the GPU case without naming it.
issue.correction: Split the sentence: 'On the GPU basis the incremental cost (~1.1 ms) stays well within the ~120 ms retrieval budget. On a single CPU core it does not: 186–371 ms at 30–60 GFLOP/s sustained exceeds the budget, and single-core encoding would require ≈92.8 GFLOP/s sustained per core — conditional on measured single-core throughput.'
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in §3(a) asserts that the incremental embedding cost fits the 120 ms budget without naming the execution basis (GPU vs single CPU core).

issue.page_hint: Ch 5 §3(a), Table 5-1 footnote; §3(a) 'The decision hinges on…'; §3(a) Takeaway; §8 mini-case bullet 1
issue.quoted_clause: Footnote: "the proxy ratio (4.8×) is a lower bound on the true body-only compute ratio (≈7.7×), not an upper bound." | Decision text: "justify the ~4.8×FLOP cost (14.08 vs 2.94 GFLOP per 64-token query, Table 5-1)" | Takeaway: "the ~4.8× FLOP cost is paid"
issue.observed: The chapter establishes that the 2×params×L proxy understates the true cross-model compute ratio (4.8× total-params vs ≈7.7× body-only), then uses the understated 4.8× figure as the decision threshold in three places (the decision paragraph, the Takeaway, and the mini-case). The bar the reader is told to apply is therefore the one the chapter has just shown to be the wrong one for a cross-model comparison.
issue.evidence: Total-params ratio 110/23 = 4.78. Body-only: mpnet 109.5M − 23.4M embedding = 86.1M; MiniLM 22.7M − 11.7M embedding = 11.0M; 86.1/11.0 = 7.8. The proxy overstates each model's compute most for the smallest model, so the proxy ratio is the lower bound — as the footnote itself states.
issue.root_cause: The footnote correction was added without propagating the corrected constant into the decision rule that depends on it.
issue.correction: Use one stated bar everywhere: 'the cross-model compute ratio is ≈4.8× on total parameters and ≈7.7× on body parameters (the proxy understates it); the quality gain must clear the body-parameter ratio, ≈7.7×, to justify the larger encoder.' Alternatively, state explicitly that the decision is taken on the Table 5-1 proxy rows and that the true ratio is higher, so the bar is conservative in the wrong direction and must be re-derived before use.
issue.acceptance_test: Every occurrence of the cross-model FLOP-cost ratio in Ch 5 states which parameter basis it uses, and no occurrence uses 4.8× as the decision threshold after the chapter has established 7.7× as the true body-only ratio.

issue.page_hint: Ch 5 §3(a) Takeaway; §3(a) 'The decision hinges on…'; §8 mini-case bullet 1
issue.quoted_clause: Takeaway: "768-dim (all-mpnet-base-v2) is the recommended embedding model. It balances compute, storage, and expected quality as a mid-range candidate — compute and storage alone favour the 384-dim option — and the quality claim itself is the §5.3(a)/§7 item still to validate on the target corpus"
issue.observed: The chapter's own analysis says compute and storage both favour the 384-dim option, and the only evidence for the 768-dim option is a quality uplift the chapter explicitly labels an unverified scenario input that 'cannot be assumed to transfer across model families' — yet the decision being made is cross-model (mpnet vs MiniLM). The recommendation therefore rests on no admissible evidence, and no decision rule is given that would let the reader reach the same conclusion from the same inputs. The mini-case then presents the choice as settled ('the team has agreed on the retrieval architecture: … 768-dim all-mpnet-base-v2'), so the reader is never asked to make the decision the chapter is named for.
issue.evidence: The chapter's own text: 'an unquantified gain would have to clear a ~3× FLOP bar … validate the gain on the target corpus before paying it' (bge-large) and 'the mpnet-vs-MiniLM quality gap must be measured on the target corpus before the ~4.8× FLOP cost is paid'. The ~15% MAP figure is explicitly 'not quantified for this model pair'.
