issue.root_cause: The worked example was written to demonstrate the method, but the method's output (a conditional recommendation) was replaced by an unconditional recommendation to make the mini-case read cleanly.
issue.correction: Replace the unconditional recommendation with the decision rule the chapter's own analysis implies: 'Choose 768-dim if the measured MAP/answer-quality uplift over MiniLM on the target corpus exceeds the threshold at which the ≈7.7× body-parameter compute cost is repaid; otherwise choose 384-dim, which compute and storage both favour. Until that measurement exists, the defensible default is the 384-dim option and the 768-dim option is a pending-quality-gate candidate.' In the mini-case, give the architect the measurement task rather than the answer.
issue.acceptance_test: The §3(a) takeaway and the mini-case both state a conditional rule with a measurable threshold; a reader who assumes the quality uplift is zero reaches the 384-dim option from the text alone.

issue.page_hint: Ch 5 §3(a) (index-storage paragraph); Ch 5 §6 Architecture Consequence, bullet 2
issue.quoted_clause: §6: "The embedding model is chosen at ingestion time (compute-light, storage-bound) but also carries query-time embedding cost and latency"
issue.observed: The chapter compares embedding models on query-time compute and index storage but never prices ingestion-time embedding compute, and then characterizes the ingestion leg as 'compute-light'. For the chapter's own 1 M-chunk corpus, ingestion at 14.08 GFLOP/chunk is 1.41×10¹⁶ FLOP (14 PFLOP) for mpnet versus 2.94×10¹⁵ FLOP (2.9 PFLOP) for MiniLM — the same ≈4.8× ratio as the query-time cost, and roughly 5 host-hours of the canonical host's sustained prefill capacity (2.77 PFLOP/s) for mpnet versus ~1 host-hour for MiniLM. Calling the ingestion leg 'compute-light' is not supported by the chapter's own workload.
issue.evidence: 1×10⁶ chunks × 14.08 GFLOP = 1.408×10¹⁶ FLOP; ÷ 2.7692 PFLOP/s = 5,085 s ≈ 1.41 h. MiniLM: 1×10⁶ × 2.94 GFLOP = 2.94×10¹⁵ FLOP; ÷ 2.7692 = 1,062 s ≈ 0.30 h. At 10 M chunks the mpnet figure is ~14.1 host-hours.
issue.root_cause: The selection surfaces were applied only to the query path; the ingestion path was treated as a storage-only concern.
issue.correction: Add the ingestion leg to the comparison: one sentence giving ingestion FLOPs per corpus size for the two candidates, and either drop 'compute-light' or replace it with 'one-time, corpus-scaled, and amortized over the corpus lifetime — but not negligible: ~1.4 host-hours per 1 M chunks at 14.08 GFLOP/chunk on the canonical host.'
issue.acceptance_test: The §3(a) comparison and the §6 bullet both account for ingestion-time compute, and the word 'compute-light' no longer appears without a quantified basis.

issue.page_hint: Ch 5 §2 Mental Model; compare Ch 5 §6 bullet 3 and Ch 8 §3 ('Whether prefill compute or KV residency is the binding fleet constraint depends on the FLOP-counting case')
issue.quoted_clause: "the system is first-order memory-capacity-bound (the KV cache's HBM footprint limits how many concurrent requests fit — KV HBM capacity limits concurrency, not bandwidth — at the Ch 17 concurrency screen) and prefill-dominated in FLOPs"
issue.observed: The label 'first-order memory-capacity-bound' is applied to the canonical workload without qualification, while the book's own analysis elsewhere concludes that the binding constraint is case-dependent (Ch 8 §3: 'KV residency binds under case (i); case (iii) is a 21/21 tie; compute binds under case (ii)'), and Ch 5's own §6 says 'prefill often compute-bound and decode often memory-bandwidth-bound'. Ch 8 §1 explicitly warns that 'Input-heavy does not by itself mean memory-bound'. The parenthetical does the qualifying work, but the sentence's leading label is the part a reader remembers.
issue.evidence: Ch 8 §3 host screens: compute 19/21/22 hosts vs KV-residency 21 hosts; Ch 8 §3 'the screens are within one host for cases (ii) and (iii); case (i) is two hosts apart'. Ch 5 §3(b) shows a single request's 24.1 GB KV is only ~5.5% of the ~436 GB KV budget.
issue.root_cause: The mental-model paragraph was written before the case-dependent fleet screens existed, and was not revised when they did.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: 'the system is first-order KV-capacity-constrained for concurrency (the KV cache's HBM footprint caps resident requests per host) and prefill-dominated in FLOPs; which of the two binds the fleet is case-dependent (Ch 8 §3) and must be computed, not assumed.'
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 5 labels the canonical workload 'memory-bound' or 'memory-capacity-bound' without naming which constraint and which screen it refers to.

issue.page_hint: Ch 5 §3(b), 'tokens/s per dollar with prefill included', final sentence
issue.quoted_clause: "GPU-hour cost follows occupancy, batching and scheduling — it is not proportional to either share without a stated utilization assumption. The per-dollar economics therefore favor models that reduce the *prefill compute* burden (smaller context, larger batch, lower per-token FLOP) more than models that optimize decode throughput alone — but a deployment must balance both, since decode still sets the latency SLO."
issue.observed: The paragraph correctly disclaims any directional conclusion ('not proportional to either share without a stated utilization assumption') and then immediately draws one ('therefore favor models that reduce the prefill compute burden … more than models that optimize decode throughput alone'). Worse, the conclusion is backwards for the operating point the paragraph just computed: at the single-stream point, cost per token is set by decode wall-clock (300 output tokens at 50 tok/s = 6 s per request), so halving the context from 9.2K to 4.6K leaves the request time unchanged while halving the tokens delivered — cost per token roughly doubles. 'Larger batch' is also listed under 'reduce the prefill compute burden', but batching amortizes prefill rather than reducing it.
issue.evidence: Single-stream: 6 s/request → 600 requests/h × 9,500 tokens = 5.7M tokens/h → $20/5.7M = $3.51 per M tokens. Halving context: 600 × 4,800 = 2.88M tokens/h → $6.94 per M tokens. The prefill is hidden under the decode time at this operating point (1.08 s of prefill against 6 s of decode), so it is not the cost driver here.
issue.root_cause: A regime-dependent conclusion was written without naming the regime, immediately after a sentence that says a regime must be named.
issue.correction: Name the regimes: 'In the batched regime, where prefill FLOPs set host capacity, reducing the prefill burden (smaller context, lower per-token FLOP) lowers cost per token more than decode tuning does. In the single-stream regime used above, cost per token is set by decode wall-clock, so the same context reduction raises cost per token. Which regime applies is a scheduling decision, not a property of the model.'
issue.acceptance_test: Every directional economic claim in §3(b) names the operating regime (single-stream vs batched) it holds in, and no sentence follows a 'not proportional without a stated utilization assumption' disclaimer with an unqualified 'therefore'.

issue.page_hint: Ch 5 §1 (five selection surfaces); Ch 5 §3(b) opening ('The architect must decide whether a base 70B-class dense model, a smaller dense model, or a fine-tuned variant…'); Ch 5 §8 mini-case
issue.quoted_clause: §1 surface 2: "This surface determines whether we need a dense 70B, a distilled 13B, or a MoE variant." | §3(b): "The architect must decide whether a base 70B-class dense model, a smaller dense model, or a fine-tuned variant best satisfies the latency, quality, and economic constraints."
issue.observed: The chapter promises a five-surface framework and a three-way generation-model comparison, but the worked example prices only the 70B candidate. No smaller dense model is costed or latency-checked, and the MoE challenger appears only as a parenthetical in the mini-case ('was not rejected on residency'). Surface 5 (retrieve-then-generate vs end-to-end) is asserted as a decision but never examined — the chapter assumes the two-leg split throughout. The framework's most useful behaviour (narrowing the model space across sizes on latency and cost) is therefore never demonstrated.
issue.evidence: §3(b) contains only 'Derived arithmetic for the 70B candidate'; the mini-case's shortlist is '768-dim all-mpnet-base-v2 for the retrieval leg, and the 70B FP16 base model for the generation leg' with the MoE challenger mentioned only in parentheses.
issue.root_cause: The worked example was scoped to the canonical 70B geometry for numerical consistency with Ch 7/8, and the cross-size comparison was dropped rather than carried as a labelled sensitivity.
issue.correction: Add a short comparison table in §3(b) pricing at least one smaller dense candidate and the MoE challenger on the same surfaces (weights, KV/token, per-request residency, decode rate, tokens/$, and the quality gate), with the quality gate marked as the deciding surface. Alternatively, state explicitly that the cross-size comparison is deferred to Ch 14/17 and cross-reference it.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can name at least two generation-model candidates that were compared on the five surfaces, and can say which surface decided between them.

issue.page_hint: Ch 6 §1 (Serving metrics bullet); compare Ch 6 §4 habit 2 and Ch 5 §3 opening
issue.quoted_clause: §1: "These are the dependent variables; they are what the SLO is written against — the canonical SLO targets are TTFT 1.2 s / TPOT ~25 ms." | §4: "State the SLO window (p95 ≤ 2 s TTFT) before quoting any rate" | Ch 5: "TTFT budget 1.2 s (retrieval ~120 ms + prefill), TPOT ~25 ms/token; p95 TTFT ≤ 2 s, p95 TPOT ≤ 35 ms."
issue.observed: Ch 6 §1 labels the internal design budget (1.2 s TTFT / 25 ms TPOT) as 'the canonical SLO targets'. Ch 5, Ch 6 §3, Ch 6 §4 and Ch 8 §8 all distinguish the design budget (1.2 s / 25 ms) from the SLO (p95 ≤ 2 s / p95 ≤ 35 ms). Ch 6 therefore contradicts itself between §1 and §4, and mislabels the budget in a chapter whose entire thesis is that the metric you SLO against is the one that matters.
issue.evidence: Ch 8 §8: 'p95 TTFT is 2.8 s, exceeding the 2 s p95 TTFT SLO (the 1.2 s figure is the internal design budget)'. Ch 6 §3: 'We budget TTFT ≤ 1.2 s … with a p95 ≤ 2 s.'
issue.root_cause: Terminology drift between 'budget' and 'SLO' introduced when the canonical scenario's two numbers were first written down.
issue.correction: In Ch 6 §1, replace with: 'the canonical design budgets are TTFT 1.2 s / TPOT ~25 ms; the SLOs written against them are p95 TTFT ≤ 2 s and p95 TPOT ≤ 35 ms (Ch 4, Table 4-2).'
issue.acceptance_test: Every occurrence of '1.2 s' and '25 ms' in Ch 5–8 is labelled either 'design budget' or 'SLO', and the two labels are never interchanged.

issue.quoted_clause: "Deploying a higher-throughput configuration can *reduce* goodput: goodput = raw_rate × compliant_fraction, so a throughput increase helps goodput only if the compliant fraction holds." | Scenario A: "goodput … is effectively unchanged *in this case*" | Scenario B: "goodput is 50×0.96 = 48 vs 70×0.94 = 65.8 — it *rises* despite the p95 breach."
issue.observed: The section's headline claim is that a higher-throughput configuration can reduce goodput, but neither scenario demonstrates a reduction: Scenario A shows goodput unchanged (compliant fraction falls proportionally, 96% → 68.6%) and Scenario B shows it rising (96% → 94%). The case that would support the claim — compliant fraction falling faster than the raw rate rises, e.g. 50 → 70 tok/s with compliant fraction 96% → 60%, giving 48 → 42 — is never shown. The reader is asked to accept the most consequential claim in the section without a worked instance of it.
issue.evidence: goodput = raw_rate × compliant_fraction. Scenario A: 70 × (0.96 × 50/70) = 48 = 50 × 0.96 (unchanged). Scenario B: 70 × 0.94 = 65.8 > 48 (rises). A decreasing case requires compliant_fraction < 48/70 = 68.6%.
issue.root_cause: The two scenarios were written to explore the compliant-fraction sensitivity but neither was chosen to instantiate the section's own claim.
issue.correction: Add Scenario C with a compliant fraction that falls faster than the rate rises (e.g. 50 → 70 tok/s, compliant 96% → 60% → goodput 48 → 42, a 12.5% goodput loss on a 40% raw-throughput gain), and reorder so the section's claim is demonstrated first and the two existing scenarios are presented as the boundary cases.
issue.acceptance_test: At least one worked scenario in the section shows goodput decreasing as raw throughput increases, and the reader can state the compliant-fraction threshold at which the sign flips (48/70 ≈ 68.6% for the 50→70 case).

issue.page_hint: Ch 6 §3, 'Apply this to the canonical workload'; compare Ch 6 §3 'Reading Telemetry Into a Decision' and Ch 6 §8
issue.quoted_clause: "Suppose a flash crowd (the ~40 rps peak) causes prefill requests to queue. If on average the batch is well-behaved, p50 TTFT might sit at ~1.0 s. But the jobs that arrive behind ~1–2 same-time prefill requests each pay the full 1.08 s prefill of the job(s) ahead of them, so p95 TTFT drifts to ~2.5 s."
issue.observed: The queueing model assumes only one or two prefill jobs ahead of an arriving request. The same chapter, two paragraphs later, computes that at the 40 rps peak the host is ~18.6× oversubscribed on prefill (51.6 PFLOP/s demand vs 2.77 PFLOP/s sustained), which means the queue is unbounded, not one-to-two deep, and that p95 TTFT would drift far past 2.5 s. The two passages describe incompatible operating regimes for the same event (the 40 rps peak).
issue.evidence: 51.6 ÷ 2.77 = 18.63×. At 18.6× oversubscription, the arrival-to-service ratio means the queue grows at ~17.6 jobs per second of wall-clock; a p95 TTFT of 2.5 s (≈1.4 jobs of queue) is not a stable operating point. Ch 6 §8 itself says 'the prefill queue grows until backpressure or prefix caching intervenes'.
issue.root_cause: The illustrative queueing example was written before the oversubscription arithmetic existed and was not revisited; the two use different implicit fleet sizes (one host vs the fleet).
issue.correction: State the fleet assumption explicitly in the example and reconcile it: either (a) note that the 1–2-jobs-ahead model describes a fleet sized for the peak (≈19–22 hosts, Ch 8 §3) rather than one host, or (b) replace the example with the single-host behaviour the chapter actually derives (queue growth at 18.6× oversubscription, p95 TTFT unbounded until admission control), and keep the 2.5 s figure only as the multi-host case.
issue.acceptance_test: Every queueing illustration in Ch 6 states the fleet size it assumes, and the single-host and fleet-wide behaviours are not conflated.

issue.page_hint: Ch 7 §1 ('Practical host requirement' bullet); Ch 7 §3 Table 7-1 note and Fig 7.7 technical note; Ch 8 §3 host-count screens
issue.quoted_clause: Ch 7 §1: "[ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] The ~64 GB is a planning reserve, not a measured constant … The exact value must come from a deployment benchmark on the target stack (Chapter 14); the 436 GB KV budget (640 − 140 − 64) shifts by the same amount if the measured reserve differs."
issue.observed: The 64 GB runtime/workspace reserve is the single most load-bearing unmeasured assumption in the memory→concurrency→fleet→cost chain: it produces the ~436 GB KV budget, the ~17.5 (floor 17) concurrency, the ⌈344/17⌉ = 21-host KV screen, and (via Ch 16) the ~$155,816.93/mo fleet cost. The chapter flags it as an assumption but never quantifies its effect, and neither Ch 7's concurrency screen nor Ch 8's host-count screens restate it as a sensitivity. A reader cannot see how much of the fleet sizing is assumption rather than arithmetic.
issue.evidence: KV budget = 640 − 140 − R. R = 48 → 452 GB → 452/24.9037 = 18.15 → 18 concurrent → ⌈344/18⌉ = 20 hosts. R = 64 → 436 GB → 17.51 → 17 → ⌈344/17⌉ = 21 hosts. R = 80 → 420 GB → 16.87 → 16 → ⌈344/16⌉ = 22 hosts. A ±16 GB reserve swings the fleet screen by ±1 host and the per-rank occupancy from 99.97% to ~93%/~107% (the latter infeasible).
issue.root_cause: The reserve was introduced as a labelled assumption and then consumed silently as a constant by three downstream chapters.
issue.correction: Add a one-line sensitivity wherever the 436 GB budget or the 17-request concurrency is quoted: 'KV budget = 640 − 140 − R; at R = 48/64/80 GB the budget is 452/436/420 GB, concurrency is 18/17/16, and the Ch 17 fleet screen is 20/21/22 hosts.' Carry the same three-value range into Ch 8's host-count table and Ch 16's cost screen.
issue.acceptance_test: Every downstream figure derived from the 436 GB budget is accompanied by the reserve's stated range, and a reader can state the fleet-size swing attributable to the reserve alone.

issue.page_hint: Ch 8 §3, 'The 1.08 s budget versus the 35% planning rate'; compare Ch 6 §3 and Table 6-1, Ch 5 §3(b), Ch 5 economics unit note
issue.quoted_clause: Ch 8 §3: "1.08 s is the *end-to-end prefill budget* inside the 1.2 s TTFT (it absorbs queueing, scheduling, tokenization and admission overhead), while ~19,800 tokens/s/host is the *sustained planning rate* for capacity arithmetic." | Ch 6 §3: "against the ~1.08 s prefill budget implies a required rate of ≈ 1.19 PFLOPS"
issue.observed: The 1.08 s figure carries two incompatible meanings. Ch 5, Ch 6 and Ch 8's own Table 8-1 treat 1.08 s as the prefill compute window (9,200 tokens ÷ 1.08 s = 8,519 tokens/s is called 'the prefill-side rate' in Ch 5's economics note; Ch 6 divides 1.29 PFLOP by 1.08 s to get the required prefill rate). Ch 8's parenthetical says 1.08 s absorbs queueing, scheduling, tokenization and admission overhead, which would make the pure prefill compute window shorter and the required rate higher than 1.19 PFLOPS. The two readings give different required rates, different implied MFU (15% vs lower), and different host counts (44 vs more).
issue.evidence: Ch 6/Table 6-1: 1.288 PFLOP ÷ 1.08 s = 1.19 PFLOPS required; Ch 8: 1.288 ÷ 1.08 ÷ 8 = 149 TFLOPS/GPU = 15% MFU. If 1.08 s includes non-prefill overhead, the prefill kernel's own rate is higher than 149 TFLOPS/GPU and the 44-host figure is a lower bound.
issue.root_cause: The canonical 1.08 s was derived once as a prefill-compute time and later annotated with a broader meaning in one parenthetical, without propagating the change to the arithmetic that consumes it.
issue.correction: Pick one meaning and state it once in Ch 4 (Table 4-2) and reference it thereafter. If 1.08 s is the prefill compute window, delete the 'absorbs queueing, scheduling, tokenization and admission overhead' clause and instead say that those overheads are what the 1.2 s TTFT budget leaves room for (0.12 s, shared with retrieval). If 1.08 s is an end-to-end leg time, relabel it and restate the required prefill rate as a lower bound.
issue.acceptance_test: The 1.08 s figure has one definition stated in Ch 4 and referenced identically in Ch 5, Ch 6 and Ch 8; the 1.19 PFLOPS, 15% MFU and 44-host figures are all derived from that same definition.

issue.quoted_clause: "Their labeled 70% × 95% + N−1 policy totals: case (i) 19 → 29 compute, fleet 21 → 32; case (iii) 21 → 32; case (ii) 22 → 34; KV-only 21 → 32. The ρ = 1 u-only screen reads 30 / 32 (ceil(N ÷ 0.7) for KV-only 21 and case (ii) 22)."
issue.observed: The policy that produces these totals is never stated, so the reader cannot reproduce them; the '+ N−1' descriptor does not match either candidate formula; 'ρ = 1 u-only' is undefined jargon; and the paragraph mixes 'N → M' totals with Ch 17's '31 working / 32 total' pair without saying which of the two numbers is working and which is total. The totals are consistent with total = ⌈N/(0.7×0.95)⌉ (19→29, 21→32, 22→34) and with working = total − 1, but neither reading is stated, and the '+ N−1' wording suggests a redundancy term that would give 47, 52 and 55 rather than 29, 32 and 34.
issue.evidence: ⌈19/0.665⌉ = 29; ⌈21/0.665⌉ = 32; ⌈22/0.665⌉ = 34; ⌈21/0.7⌉ = 30; ⌈22/0.7⌉ = 32. Ch 17's '31 working / 32 total' is consistent with working = ⌈N/0.665⌉ − 1 and total = ⌈N/0.665⌉, but is inconsistent with a '+ N−1' spare-host policy.
issue.root_cause: A summary line was added to Ch 8 to avoid a cross-chapter page-flip, but the policy it summarizes lives in Ch 16/17 and was not restated with its formula.
issue.correction: Restate the policy inline in one line, e.g. 'Policy: working hosts = ⌈N/(0.7×0.95)⌉ − 1, total = ⌈N/(0.7×0.95)⌉ (Ch 16/17); the ρ=1 utilization-only variant is ⌈N/0.7⌉.' Then give the table as working/total pairs rather than 'N → M' arrows, and delete or define '+ N−1' and 'u-only'.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader with only Ch 8 in hand can recompute all six host-count numbers from a stated formula and can tell which numbers are working hosts and which are total hosts.

issue.quoted_clause: "(adding the quadratic attention term raises it to ~10.6K, activation traffic lowers it — either way ≫ 295)"
issue.observed: The full-square attention intensity at 9.2K is ~10.8K FLOP/byte, not ~10.6K. The value is not used in any downstream decision, but it is a derived number in a table footnote that a reader can check, and it disagrees with the book's own case-(ii) total (1.5099 PFLOP, Table 8-1).
issue.evidence: 1.5099e15 FLOP ÷ 140e9 B = 10,785 FLOP/byte ≈ 10.8K. (Case (iii) would give 1.3989e15 ÷ 140e9 = 9,992 ≈ 10.0K; neither equals 10.6K.)
issue.root_cause: The footnote was written from a rounded intermediate rather than from the case-(ii) total the chapter elsewhere fixes.
issue.correction: Change '~10.6K' to '~10.8K' (or state '≈10.8K under case (ii)').
issue.acceptance_test: The Table 6-1 footnote's intensity figure equals 1.5099 PFLOP ÷ 140 GB to the displayed precision.

issue.page_hint: Ch 8 §3 ('This rough sizing illustrates that prefill is FLOP-bound at this scale'); Ch 8 §5 Common Mistakes bullet 2
issue.quoted_clause: "This rough sizing illustrates that prefill is FLOP-bound at this scale" | "prefill reads the full context once and is FLOP-bound (weight-only intensity ~9,200 FLOP/byte …)"
issue.observed: The book defines a three-way distinction between compute-bound, memory-bandwidth-bound and memory-capacity-constrained in §8.1 and uses 'compute-bound' consistently in Ch 6 and Ch 8 §6. Here the term 'FLOP-bound' is used, which is not one of the three defined labels and reads as a fourth regime. The §5 bullet is the more consequential instance because it is a Common Mistake entry that will be quoted.
issue.evidence: Ch 8 §1: '**Compute-bound** means performance is limited primarily by arithmetic throughput'. Ch 6 §3: 'Prefill is compute-bound at the canonical long-prompt operating point.' Ch 8 §6: '**If prefill is FLOP-bound** (as it is for 70B+ models with long contexts)'.
issue.root_cause: Terminology drift between the roofline vocabulary introduced in §8.1 and the older shorthand used in the worked example and mistakes list.
issue.correction: Replace 'FLOP-bound' with 'compute-bound' in all three places (Ch 8 §3, Ch 8 §5, Ch 8 §6), keeping 'FLOP' only for the quantity itself.
issue.acceptance_test: The strings 'FLOP-bound' and 'memory-bound' (unqualified) do not appear anywhere in the book; only the three defined labels are used.

issue.page_hint: Ch 8 §4, measurement habit 2; compare Ch 8 §3 'The 1.08 s budget versus the 35% planning rate'
issue.quoted_clause: "A well-tuned transformer on H100 FP16 typically lands in the 30–40% range; below 20% suggests a memory or communication bottleneck that should be diagnosed before scaling."
issue.observed: The 20% diagnostic threshold is stated without distinguishing the kernel's achieved MFU from a latency-budget-implied rate. The chapter's own canonical prefill point implies ~15% MFU (1.288 PFLOP ÷ 1.08 s ÷ 8 GPUs = 149 TFLOPS/GPU), which would trip the rule and be diagnosed as 'memory or communication bound' even though the chapter has just argued prefill is compute-bound. The two numbers measure different things, as §3 says, but §4's rule does not carry the distinction.
issue.evidence: 149.07 TFLOPS ÷ 989 TFLOPS = 15.1% MFU (Ch 8 §3).
issue.root_cause: The measurement habit was written as a standalone rule and did not inherit the scope qualifier that §3 attaches to the same quantity.
issue.correction: Qualify the rule: 'below 20% *kernel* MFU (measured on the prefill kernel itself, not inferred from an end-to-end latency budget) suggests a memory or communication bottleneck.' Add a parenthetical noting that the canonical 1.08 s-implied 15% is a budget-implied figure, not a kernel MFU.
issue.acceptance_test: The 20% rule names the measurement it applies to, and a reader who computes 15% from the canonical budget does not conclude the canonical prefill kernel is memory-bound.

issue.quoted_clause: "**If prefill is FLOP-bound** (as it is for 70B+ models with long contexts), the primary optimization is batching"
issue.observed: The parenthetical generalizes the regime to a model class ('70B+ models with long contexts'), which the chapter's own §5 and §8.1 explicitly refuse to do ('both are operating-point properties: decode's intensity rises with batch, and prefill's falls as context shortens'). The generalization is also not needed for the bullet's argument, which is conditional on the regime.
issue.evidence: Ch 8 §5: 'both are operating-point properties'. Ch 8 §1: 'These regime labels are operating-point properties: they shift with batch size and precision.'
issue.root_cause: A conditional bullet was given a parenthetical generalization to sound decisive, contradicting the chapter's stated discipline.
issue.correction: Delete the parenthetical, or replace it with the scoped form: '(as it is at the canonical 9.2K operating point on this model geometry — an operating-point property, not a property of the model class; see §8.1).'
issue.acceptance_test: No regime label in Ch 8 is asserted for a model class rather than for a named operating point.

issue.page_hint: Ch 8 §1, subsection 'Fewer sequential evaluations can mean more total work' (with footnote [^ch8-2n-example]); compare Ch 5 §1 'Inference mode is a candidate, not a selection verdict'
issue.quoted_clause: "For an iterative language generator, the approximately 2N projection-cost rule applies to processed positions, not just final output tokens. … a diffusion-style generator that evaluates 8× positions per step has 8× the projection work even with ¼ the sequential steps — fewer rounds ≠ less total work."
issue.observed: This subsection carries its own worked example (in a footnote), its own vendor citation, a MoE expert-pool digression and a fleet-decision conclusion, all inside the Concept section, before the chapter's core arithmetic is introduced. It duplicates the inference-mode material in Ch 5 §1 and the MoE material in Ch 3, and it breaks the Concept → Mental Model → Worked Example progression the chapter otherwise follows. The content is good; its placement is not.
issue.evidence: The subsection's own worked example (7B active, 256 tokens, 32-token blocks, 8 evaluations per block → 2,048 positions, 28.672 TFLOP vs 3.584 TFLOP) is arithmetically self-contained and does not depend on anything introduced later in Ch 8.
issue.root_cause: A late addition was placed in §1 for topical convenience rather than in §3 (Worked Example) or cross-referenced to Ch 5.
issue.correction: Move the subsection to §3 as a labelled worked example ('A counterexample: fewer sequential evaluations ≠ less total work'), or move it to Ch 5 §1 next to 'Inference mode is a candidate' and cross-reference it from Ch 8 §3. Keep the MoE expert-pool paragraph with it.
issue.acceptance_test: Ch 8 §1 contains no worked example with its own footnote; the diffusion/MoE material appears once in the book, in a section whose job is to host it.

issue.quoted_clause: "### Decode: bandwidth-bound"
issue.observed: The heading asserts a regime as a flat fact while the body immediately qualifies it ('This is an operating-point property, not an identity, and it is a weight-only statement: at high batch decode climbs the intensity slope and can become compute-bound'), and §8.1 has just established that regime labels are operating-point properties. A heading is the most quoted element of a section and currently carries the strongest form of the claim.
issue.evidence: Ch 8 §1: 'These regime labels are operating-point properties: they shift with batch size and precision'. Ch 8 §3 body: 'at high batch decode climbs the intensity slope and can become compute-bound'.
issue.root_cause: Headings were written as topic labels rather than as claims, and the topic chosen was the unqualified regime.
issue.correction: Retitle to 'Decode: the low-batch bandwidth-bound regime' or 'Decode: bandwidth-bound at low batch (and why the label is conditional)'.
issue.acceptance_test: Every regime-named heading in Ch 6–8 carries its operating-point qualifier in the heading itself.

issue.page_hint: Ch 7 §3, Table 7-1 row 'fits 3×H100 at 9.2K?' and the note beneath it
issue.quoted_clause: "a canonical hidden-dim of 8192 does not split evenly into 3 shards (8192/3 not integral); viable TP=3 requires a supported sharding/head-partition plan, per-rank allocation and a working engine benchmark"
issue.observed: The stated divisibility constraint is the wrong one. Tensor parallelism does not shard the hidden dimension; it shards attention heads (and MLP intermediate channels). The quantities that must divide by 3 are n_heads (64 for the canonical full-MHA geometry), n_kv_heads, and the MLP intermediate size — not d_hidden. The chapter's conclusion (TP=3 placement not established) is defensible, but the reason given is technically inaccurate and would mislead a reader who checks it.
issue.evidence: For the canonical geometry, 64 query heads / 3 = 21.33 and 8 KV heads / 3 = 2.67 are the actual non-divisibilities; 8192/3 = 2730.67 is not a quantity any TP scheme partitions. Modern engines can also shard unevenly, so the correct statement is 'requires a supported head-partition plan', which the chapter does add.
issue.root_cause: The divisibility argument was written from the hidden dimension because that is the number quoted most often in the chapter's tables, rather than from the sharding dimensions.
issue.correction: Replace the hidden-dim argument with the head-count argument: 'a canonical 64-head / 8-KV-head geometry does not partition evenly into 3 ranks (64/3, 8/3), and the MLP intermediate size must also divide; viable TP=3 requires a supported head-partition plan, per-rank allocation and a working engine benchmark.'
issue.acceptance_test: The TP=3 row names the sharding dimensions that must divide, and a reader who checks them finds the same non-divisibility the chapter claims.

issue.quoted_clause: "On the vendor-binary basis the aggregate test still reads 164.1 < 171.0 GB, but per rank 70 + 12.05 + ~8 GB reserve = 90.05 GB > 85.5 GB, so the ≥3-GPU conclusion is unchanged."
issue.observed: The word 'still' is wrong: on the decimal basis the aggregate test reads 164.1 > 160 GB (fails); on the vendor-binary basis it reads 164.1 < 171.0 GB (passes). The aggregate verdict changes between the two bases — it is the per-rank test that preserves the ≥3-GPU conclusion. As written, the sentence can be read as claiming the aggregate test was already passing.
issue.evidence: Decimal: 140 + 24.1 = 164.1 GB vs 2 × 80 = 160 GB → fails. Vendor-binary: 2 × 85.5 = 171.0 GB → passes. Per-rank: 70 + 12.05 + 8 = 90.05 GB > 85.5 GB → fails, which is what preserves the conclusion.
issue.root_cause: The sentence was compressed from a longer explanation and the transition word was not updated when the aggregate comparison was added.
issue.correction: Rewrite: 'On the vendor-binary basis the aggregate test flips to passing (164.1 < 171.0 GB), but the per-rank test still fails (70 + 12.05 + ~8 GB reserve = 90.05 GB > 85.5 GB), so the ≥3-GPU conclusion is unchanged.'
issue.acceptance_test: The unit-basis paragraph states explicitly which of the two gates (aggregate vs per-rank) changes between the decimal and vendor-binary bases.

issue.page_hint: Ch 7 §1 ('Count state by lifetime…', closing sentence); Ch 7 §2 ('Persistent state is architecture-specific', closing sentence)
issue.quoted_clause: §1: "A block-causal boundary can make an earlier prefix immutable. Approximate cache policies instead trade refresh work against quality. Memory capacity and cache validity are separate checks. [1P][FACT]" | §2: "Static prompt embeddings can remain reusable, but that is not the growing autoregressive cache. [1P][FACT]"
issue.observed: Both passages attach [1P][FACT] to general architectural statements that carry no citation and are not first-party facts about a named artifact. The book's own taxonomy reserves [1P] for first-party specifications and primary sources; these are analytical statements about mechanism. The labels are in the allowed set, so this is a span/scope problem rather than an undefined-label problem.
issue.evidence: Neither passage cites a source; the surrounding paragraphs in the same subsections carry explicit citations (Qwen3.8-27B config, KIVI, AWQ, GPTQ) where first-party facts are asserted.
issue.root_cause: The [1P][FACT] label was applied as a general 'this is true' marker rather than as a provenance marker.
issue.correction: Relabel both as [DERIVED] (or [LAB][DERIVED] where they are architectural readings), and reserve [1P][FACT] for statements with an attached first-party citation.
issue.acceptance_test: Every [1P][FACT] label in Ch 7 is adjacent to a citation or a named first-party specification.

issue.page_hint: Ch 7 §1 ('Count state by lifetime, not by the model label', closing paragraph) and Ch 7 §2 ('Persistent state is architecture-specific', closing paragraph)
issue.quoted_clause: §1: "None of this changes the canonical autoregressive budget above — it changes what must be inventoried before that budget's arithmetic is reused for a different generation mechanism." | §2: "The canonical KV table below is untouched: it prices the autoregressive text path this chapter sizes. The boundary changes which state function we plug into 'does it fit?' for a different generator — the same decision, a different inventory."
issue.observed: The two closing paragraphs make the same point in the same words — the canonical budget is unchanged, only the inventory changes — and §2's paragraph adds no new content beyond §1's. This is Class C redundant repetition: the second occurrence does not deepen, quantify or operationalize the first.
issue.evidence: Both paragraphs are the terminal sentences of adjacent subsections and assert the identical proposition with the identical framing ('the same decision, a different inventory' / 'what must be inventoried before that budget's arithmetic is reused').
issue.root_cause: The §2 subsection was added later as a short bridge and repeated the §1 conclusion rather than advancing it.
issue.correction: Delete §2's closing paragraph and let §2's video-denoiser example stand on its own, or replace it with content that advances the model: e.g. the specific state-inventory differences for a video denoiser (latent video tensors, scheduler-step state, per-branch CFG state) priced against the AR weights+KV inventory.
issue.acceptance_test: Reading §1 and §2 consecutively, the second adds a fact the first did not contain; no sentence in §2 restates §1's conclusion.

issue.quoted_clause: "We see: p95 TTFT climbing (serving), KV cache hit ratio low (resource: memory), and prefill queue depth growing (serving)."
issue.observed: The prefix-cache hit ratio is classified as a resource metric ('resource: memory'), but within the chapter's own hierarchy it is a cache-policy/scheduler state, exactly like queue depth, which the same sentence correctly labels '(serving)' and which §1 explicitly places outside the three layers ('Queue depth is not one of them: it is a scheduler state'). The misclassification matters because the chapter's diagnostic chain is the thing it teaches.
issue.evidence: Ch 6 §1: 'Admitted concurrency is a serving/scheduler state (Little's law), not a workload input' and 'Queue depth is not one of them: it is a scheduler state, a leading indicator that helps explain these serving metrics.' A prefix-cache hit ratio is a cache-policy state of the same kind.
issue.root_cause: The trace was written by symptom type rather than by the chapter's own layer definitions.
issue.correction: Relabel: 'p95 TTFT climbing (serving), prefix-cache hit ratio low (scheduler/cache-policy state, a leading indicator of prefill work), and prefill queue depth growing (scheduler state)'. Then note that the resource layer is reached via the prefill FLOP demand these two states imply.
issue.acceptance_test: Every telemetry item in the Ch 6 trace is assigned to one of the chapter's three layers or explicitly to the scheduler-state category, consistently with §1.

issue.page_hint: Ch 6 §3 ('Reading Telemetry Into a Decision', final sentence) and Ch 6 §8 mini-case
issue.quoted_clause: "The decision: enable prefix / RadixAttention-style caching (SGLang) or Automatic Prefix Caching (vLLM) so the byte-identical shared prefix is reused instead of re-prefilled … prefix caching is therefore a partial mitigation, not the fix for the 40 rps prefill queue"
issue.observed: The paragraph names prefix caching as 'the decision' and then, in the same paragraph, establishes that it addresses only ~13% of prefill FLOPs and cannot close an ~18.6× oversubscription. The mini-case then reaches a different decision (capacity/scheduling, admission control, chunked prefill, P/D disaggregation). The reader is therefore shown a decision that the chapter's own analysis rejects, and the chapter never states the decision the evidence supports.
issue.evidence: 1,200/9,200 = 13.0% of prefill FLOPs; 51.6 × 0.87 = 44.9 PFLOP/s vs 2.77 PFLOP/s = 16.2× remaining oversubscription (Ch 6 §8).
issue.root_cause: The trace was written to illustrate prefix caching (the mechanism under discussion) rather than to follow the diagnosis to the decision the evidence supports.
issue.correction: Restate the decision as the diagnosis implies: 'The decision is capacity and scheduling first (admission control, chunked prefill, additional prefill capacity, or P/D disaggregation); prefix caching is enabled as a secondary, partial mitigation worth ~13% of prefill FLOPs in this workload, not as the fix.'
issue.acceptance_test: The decision named in §3 is the same decision the mini-case reaches, and the mitigation is labelled with its measured share of the problem.

issue.quoted_clause: Table 5-1 header: "| Embedding model | Dim | Params | GFLOPs per embedding (64-token query) | Typical use case |"
issue.observed: Table 5-1 carries no provenance note and no evidence label, unlike the book's other tables (Table 7-1, Table 7-2, Table 7-3, Table 8-1 all carry explicit [1P]/[DERIVED]/[ILLUSTRATIVE] notes). The Dim and Params columns are first-party model-card facts and the GFLOPs column is a derivation from them; the reader cannot tell which is which, and the 'Typical use case' column is an unsourced qualitative claim.
issue.evidence: Compare Table 8-1's note: '*(Per-token FLOP and prefill PFLOP computations are [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] … hardware peaks [1P: vendor datasheet] …)*' and Table 7-3's '*(first-party reported, not independently reprofiled)*'.
issue.root_cause: Table 5-1 was written early, before the book's table-provenance convention was adopted.
issue.correction: Add a note under Table 5-1: 'Dim and Params are first-party model-card values [1P][FACT]; GFLOPs per embedding is [DERIVED] from 2 × params × L at L = 64 (see footnote); the use-case column is a qualitative summary, not a measured ranking.'
issue.acceptance_test: Every table in Ch 5–8 carries a provenance note identifying which columns are first-party, which are derived, and which are qualitative.

issue.quoted_clause: "(see the caveat in §5.3(a); section references §N.M read as chapter N, section M)"
issue.observed: A production/editorial note about the book's own cross-reference convention is embedded in a Common Mistakes bullet addressed to the reader. It is not a mistake the reader can make, and it interrupts the bullet's argument.
issue.evidence: The same convention is used correctly elsewhere in the chunk (Ch 5 §3(a) '§5.3(a)', Ch 7 §3 '§7.4', Ch 8 §3 '§8.6') without any explanatory aside.
issue.root_cause: An editorial instruction to the author was left in the body text.
issue.correction: Delete the parenthetical 'section references §N.M read as chapter N, section M'. If the convention needs stating, put it once in the front matter or the glossary.
issue.acceptance_test: No editorial or production note appears in the body text of Ch 5–8.

issue.quoted_clause: "The team has agreed on the retrieval architecture: vector search with embeddings, 768-dim all-mpnet-base-v2, single-vector (cosine/dot-product ANN) retrieval over a 1 M-chunk corpus."
issue.observed: The mini-case is titled 'Choosing the Model for the Enterprise Q&A', but the embedding-model half of the chapter's decision is supplied as an agreed premise. The reader is therefore never asked to make the decision the chapter's worked example was built to teach, and the mini-case's first bullet re-derives the cost of a choice already made rather than testing one.
issue.evidence: The mini-case's first bullet: '**768-dim embeddings** are the agreed candidate; their retrieval quality is the gate still to validate on the target corpus (§5.3(a), §7)'.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case was written to be a summary of the chapter's conclusions rather than a decision exercise.
issue.correction: Either (a) make the embedding dimension the decision the architect must make, giving the three Table 5-1 candidates and the measured-quality gate as the evidence, or (b) retitle the mini-case to reflect that it is a consolidation exercise ('Consolidating the Model Choice') and move the decision-rule exercise into §3(a).
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case states a decision the reader must make with the evidence provided, and at least one candidate is not pre-selected.

issue.page_hint: Ch 10, section 'Data Parallelism: Replicating, Then Syncing Gradients', paragraph 1 (final sentence)
issue.quoted_clause: The sync cost, not compute, often caps DP at small scale unless the interconnect is fast.
issue.observed: The sentence asserts that gradient-sync cost limits DP to *small* scale. The chapter's own ring model shows the opposite relationship: per-rank send volume is 2(N-1)/N x S, which is monotonically increasing but asymptotically flat in N. Sync time therefore does not grow materially with replica count; it is a fixed per-step tax. The binding fact is that the tax is large in absolute terms relative to a ~1 s step, at *any* N.
issue.evidence: Recomputation from the section's own formula: per-rank send = 2(N-1)/N x 280 GB. N=2 -> 280 GB; N=8 -> 490 GB; N=16 -> 525 GB; N=64 -> 547 GB. At 25 GB/s: N=2 -> 11.2 s, N=8 -> 19.6 s, N=64 -> 21.9 s. At 450 GB/s: N=2 -> 0.62 s, N=8 -> 1.09 s, N=64 -> 1.22 s. So the sync cost is essentially N-independent; it does not 'cap DP at small scale', it caps DP *entirely* unless the interconnect is fast. The section's own numbers (19.6 s vs a ~1 s step at 25 GB/s; 1.09 s vs a ~1 s step even at 450 GB/s) support the 'absolute tax' reading, not the 'scale' reading.
issue.root_cause: The ring normalization was applied to the byte count but not carried through to the scaling conclusion; 'scale' was used as a synonym for 'absolute overhead'.
issue.correction: Replace with something like: 'Because ring all-reduce moves 2(N-1)/N x S per rank, the sync time is nearly independent of the replica count: adding DP replicas buys throughput at a fixed per-step tax rather than reducing the tax. DP is viable only when the interconnect is fast enough that this tax is a small fraction of the step (here 1.09 s at 450 GB/s against a ~1 s step - still marginal).'
issue.acceptance_test: A reader who has read the section can state, without consulting the text, whether adding DP replicas increases or decreases per-step synchronization time, and can cite 2(N-1)/N as the reason. The phrase 'caps DP at small scale' no longer appears anywhere in the chapter.

issue.page_hint: Ch 10, section 'Data Parallelism: Replicating, Then Syncing Gradients', paragraph 1 (the sentence 'this remains a communication model, not proof of training-state fit')
issue.quoted_clause: this remains a communication model, not proof of training-state fit
issue.observed: The section asserts DP is infeasible on weights alone (140 GB > 80 GB) and then hedges that its arithmetic says nothing about training-state fit - but never quantifies the training state. The decisive number for the canonical 70B model is missing, and the hedge is left as an unfulfilled promissory note. This is also the number that explains *why* FSDP exists, which the next paragraph asserts without support.
issue.evidence: Independent rederivation for the canonical 70B model (70e9 params): BF16 weights 70e9 x 2 B = 140 GB; FP32 gradients 70e9 x 4 B = 280 GB; FP32 master weights = 280 GB; Adam m = 280 GB; Adam v = 280 GB. Total = 1,260 GB (~1.12 TB without master weights). Over 8 GPUs that is ~158 GB/GPU, still above the 80 GB HBM of an H100. So even FSDP across a full 8-GPU node does not hold Adam state in HBM; ZeRO-Offload / CPU Adam or >=16 shards is required. The training-state footprint is ~9x the weight footprint the section uses to justify its headline claim.
issue.root_cause: The section models only the communication object and treats the memory object as settled by the 140 GB figure, when the training-state footprint is an order of magnitude larger and is the actual reason sharded DP exists.
issue.correction: Add a short paragraph giving the training-state budget (weights + gradients + optimizer states) for the canonical model and the resulting shard count, then tie it directly to the FSDP paragraph that follows. This also lets the section retire its own hedge with a number instead of a caveat.
issue.acceptance_test: The section states a training-state byte total for the canonical 70B model and the resulting per-GPU requirement, and a reader can reconcile that figure with the FSDP discussion in the following paragraph.

issue.page_hint: Ch 10, section 'Data Parallelism: Replicating, Then Syncing Gradients', paragraph 1
issue.quoted_clause: a ring all-reduce moves $2\frac{N-1}{N}$ times the per-rank gradient through each rank
issue.observed: 'Through' is ambiguous between send volume (490 GB) and send-plus-receive (980 GB). The next sentence resolves it to send, but the phrase as written can be read the other way - and the book elsewhere insists on distinguishing these two quantities precisely (it devotes a sentence to it).
issue.evidence: The section's own numbers: 'the per-rank send volume is 2 x 245 ~ 490 GB (490 GB received as well, so 980 GB of send-plus-receive traffic)'. The phrase 'moves ... through each rank' therefore equals 490 GB under the send reading and 980 GB under the total-traffic reading.
issue.root_cause: Loose verb chosen for a quantity the book elsewhere defines strictly.
issue.correction: '...moves 2(N-1)/N x S = 490 GB through each rank's send path, and the same again on its receive path.'
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in the chapter uses 'through' to describe a collective volume without naming send or receive explicitly.

issue.page_hint: Ch 10, section 'Data Parallelism: Replicating, Then Syncing Gradients', paragraph 1
issue.quoted_clause: here and in Chapter 9, *per-rank traffic* means send volume unless stated otherwise
issue.observed: This is a book-wide accounting convention, not a local one: it governs every collective time estimate in Ch 9, in this section, and in the inference-side TP/PP communication budgets that follow. It is stated inside a training-gradient paragraph, which an inference-only reader (the book's stated audience) is unlikely to reach or to notice.
issue.evidence: The convention is load-bearing in at least three places visible here: the 490 GB / 19.6 s figure, the 980 GB / 900 GB/s equivalence, and the FSDP 56 MiB figures. Each depends on the reader knowing that 'per-rank traffic' means send.
issue.root_cause: A global convention was introduced at the point of first incidental use rather than at the point where the collective model is established.
issue.correction: Promote the convention to a single prominent statement where the collective model is introduced (Ch 9's collective section, or a boxed 'collective accounting conventions' note), and have Ch 10 and the inference chapters cross-reference it rather than re-deriving it.
issue.acceptance_test: The convention is stated once, at a location an inference-only reader reaches, and Ch 10 refers to it rather than restating it.

issue.quoted_clause: The same byte term is larger at 25 GB/s than at 450 GB/s
issue.observed: The byte term is identical at both bandwidths; only the time differs. As written, the sentence asserts that the number of bytes changes with link speed, which is a category error in a section whose whole point is byte accounting.
issue.evidence: The section's own figures: 490 GB at both 25 GB/s and 450 GB/s; the times differ (490/25 = 19.6 s vs 490/450 = 1.09 s). The ratio is ~18x.
issue.root_cause: Slipped noun: 'time' was replaced by 'byte term' when the sentence was written.
issue.correction: 'The same byte term takes ~18x longer at 25 GB/s than at 450 GB/s (490/25 = 19.6 s vs 490/450 = 1.09 s).'
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in the book attributes a change in a byte count to a change in bandwidth.

issue.quoted_clause: **Splitting with DP when the model doesn't fit.** DP replicates weights; if 140 GB > 80 GB, one DP replica doesn't even fit one GPU. Reach for TP/PP first.
issue.observed: The chapter introduces FSDP two paragraphs earlier as precisely the sharded-DP answer to this problem ('which is why sharded variants such as FSDP exist'), then the Common Mistakes bullet tells the reader to reach for TP/PP and never mentions FSDP or ZeRO. A reader can legitimately conclude that FSDP is not an option. The bullet also delivers training-scoped advice inside an inference chapter without marking the scope, while the Architecture Consequence states 'Gradient synchronization applies only to training or fine-tuning.'
issue.evidence: The chapter's own text: DP section paragraph 1 introduces 'sharded variants such as FSDP exist'; the FSDP paragraph then develops FSDP's all-gather/reduce-scatter object in detail. The Common Mistakes bullet, which is the section a reader consults for a decision, omits it entirely.
issue.root_cause: The Common Mistakes list was written from the inference-only frame (TP/PP/replicas) and not reconciled with the training-family material the same chapter had just introduced.
issue.correction: Rewrite the bullet to (a) scope it explicitly - for inference, 'DP' means independent replicas, not gradient sync - and (b) name the training-family alternative (FSDP / ZeRO-3) for the case where a replica does not fit, pointing to the FSDP paragraph.
issue.acceptance_test: The Common Mistakes section names FSDP or ZeRO at least once, and every bullet in that section is either inference-scoped or explicitly labelled as training/fine-tuning advice.

issue.page_hint: Ch 10, section '6. Architecture Consequence', opening sentence; contradicted by section 8 mini-case
issue.quoted_clause: The parallelism strategy is forced by the binding constraint, and that constraint is usually **memory** for large models
issue.observed: The chapter's own mini-case contradicts this framing. In the mini-case the binding constraint was communication (45 ms of an 80 ms TPOT attributed to cross-node per-layer all-reduce), and the fix was a communication-side decomposition change (TP -> PP), not a memory change. Memory determined *feasibility* (which decompositions were legal); communication determined *performance* (which legal decomposition was fastest). The Architecture Consequence collapses the two into a single 'binding constraint', which is the chapter's headline architectural claim.
issue.evidence: Mini-case text: 'profiling the inherited configuration attributes 45 ms of the 80 ms TPOT to its cross-node per-layer all-reduce'; 'Moving the cross-node decomposition from TP to PP cuts TPOT from 80 ms to 38 ms'. The memory constraint was satisfied in the inherited configuration (the model fit, just not on one node) and was not what changed.
issue.root_cause: The section was written as a memory-first heuristic before the mini-case was designed, and the mini-case was not used to test the heuristic.
issue.correction: Split the claim explicitly: 'Memory determines feasibility - which decompositions are legal at all. Communication determines performance - which legal decomposition is fastest. The two rarely bind at the same time; the mini-case below is an instance where memory was satisfied and communication was not.' Then make the mini-case's diagnosis visibly an instance of that distinction.
issue.acceptance_test: The Architecture Consequence section distinguishes feasibility constraints from performance constraints, and the mini-case's diagnosis is consistent with that distinction rather than contradicting it.

issue.quoted_clause: or PP (across nodes, low comm)
issue.observed: 'Low comm' glosses over the two costs the chapter's own mini-case quantifies - the pipeline bubble (u = m/(m+P-1)) and per-stage activation memory ('per-stage memory cost bounds P from below'). As written, PP looks free on the communication axis, which is the opposite of the mini-case's careful treatment and could lead a reader to pick PP without budgeting the bubble.
issue.evidence: Mini-case: 'they choose the stage count P and micro-batch count m jointly to shrink the bubble (utilization u = m/(m+P-1); each stage also carries its own activation memory, so per-stage memory cost bounds P from below)'. The Architecture Consequence bullet contains neither cost.
issue.root_cause: The bullet compresses a two-axis trade-off into a single adjective.
issue.correction: 'PP (across nodes, low communication volume, but a pipeline bubble and per-stage activation memory that bound the stage count)'.
issue.acceptance_test: The Architecture Consequence bullet and the mini-case use compatible descriptions of PP's costs; a reader does not have to learn PP's bubble cost only from the mini-case.

issue.page_hint: Ch 10, section '6. Architecture Consequence', closing paragraph (Table 10-1 reference)
issue.quoted_clause: Table 10-1 above consolidates the five parallelization strategies; ... the table adds the specialist EP and CP rows.
issue.observed: CP (context parallelism) appears as a Table 10-1 row, and the chapter flags 'long-context models' as an open question, but the Architecture Consequence decision framework (memory -> TP/PP; throughput -> independent replicas; MoE -> EP) never mentions context parallelism. A reader with a long-context problem gets no guidance from the chapter's decision section, and the table promises a row the prose never uses.
issue.evidence: Section 6 bullets cover: model exceeds one GPU's memory (TP/PP); high throughput demand (replicas); MoE (EP); canonical answer (TP=8). No CP. Section 7 bullet 1 names 'long-context models' as an open question without pointing to CP.
issue.root_cause: The decision framework was written before the specialist rows (EP, CP) were added to the table, and was not updated.
issue.correction: Add a CP bullet (long-context workloads where the KV/activation working set, not the weights, forces a decomposition), or explicitly scope the framework to the strategies it covers and point to where CP is treated.
issue.acceptance_test: Every strategy row in Table 10-1 appears in the Architecture Consequence decision framework or is explicitly excluded with a stated reason.

issue.quoted_clause: they verify the DP gradient-sync (if fine-tuning) stays under ~20% [ILLUSTRATIVE heuristic] of step time
issue.observed: The chapter's own ring model makes this check unsatisfiable for the mini-case's 400B model. The check is stated as a routine verification step without noting that the configuration it describes cannot meet it, so a reader either performs an impossible check or silently ignores the chapter's own arithmetic.
issue.evidence: Recomputation with the chapter's formulas: 400e9 params x 4 B = 1,600 GB of FP32 gradients. Ring per-rank send = 2(N-1)/N x 1,600 GB ~ 3,200 GB for large N. At the H100 NVLink directional peak of 450 GB/s: 3,200/450 = 7.1 s per step. At 25 GB/s: 3,200/25 = 128 s per step. A 20% budget therefore requires a step time of >= 35.6 s (NVLink) or >= 640 s (25 GB/s). The mini-case's own TPOT figures (80 ms -> 38 ms) imply a step time on the order of tens of milliseconds.

issue.correction: Either state that the fine-tuning path uses sharded DP (FSDP/ZeRO) so the synchronized object is a per-shard gradient rather than a full-replica gradient, or replace the check with the sharded-DP accounting and its own numbers. If the check is retained as-is, add the sentence that it is unsatisfiable at 400B without sharding.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can compute the gradient-sync time for the mini-case's model from the chapter's own formulas and can state what configuration would bring it under 20% of step time.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, section '3. Worked Example', subsection 'Discrete Batching Wastes the GPU', bullet 2
issue.quoted_clause: The batch is locked until its *slowest* member finishes (the batch runs to completion), so a short 100-token output tails behind the longest while the GPU finishes the whole batch - idle bubbles at the end of every batch.
issue.observed: The bullet names two effects - head-of-line blocking on response delivery, and the drain bubble between batches - but omits the primary GPU-efficiency loss in discrete batching: sequences that finish early keep consuming compute slots (padding to the batch's longest member) until the batch completes. That is the effect continuous batching removes, and it is the one the subsection's own title ('Wastes the GPU') points at.
issue.evidence: The canonical output is ~300 tokens and the bullet's example is a 100-token output - a 3x spread within one batch, which is exactly the regime where padding waste dominates. The bullet's 'idle bubbles at the end of every batch' describes the inter-batch drain, not the intra-batch waste.

issue.correction: Add the padding-waste effect explicitly and distinguish it from the drain bubble: finished sequences occupy slots and consume compute until the batch's longest member completes, and separately the GPU drains between batches.
issue.acceptance_test: The discrete-batching subsection names at least three distinct costs and identifies which one continuous batching removes and which it does not.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, Note 11.3-1 (Fig 11.3) (anchor by note heading; PDF/printed page not determinable from chunk)
issue.quoted_clause: The 1.4 TB/s caveat is the *aggregate* check (35 GB/request x 40 req/s against the shared fabric), not a per-request time; the per-request times above assume the link is not shared. Per case: (A) 4 decode GPUs x 450 GB/s = 1.8 TB/s aggregate ingress absorbs the 1.4 TB/s (~78% - feasible but tight); (B) the 40 GB/s NIC cannot (~35x over) - so the transfer link, not topology alone, decides whether P/D disaggregation pays. The two quantities live at different population levels, and the two admissible readings give opposite verdicts: (i) 40 rps is the fleet peak, so per-pool ingress is ~1/17 of that and case (A) is ~4-5% utilised, not 78%; (ii) 40 rps is a single pool's load, in which case the pool is 17x larger than the canonical host the chapter has been sizing. The chapter never says which. The same ambiguity applies to the 0.96 TB/s figure. Recomputation at the canonical per-pool rate: 2.3 rps x 35 GB = ~80 GB/s, which is 4.5% of the 1.8 TB/s NVLink aggregate (case A) and ~2x the 40 GB/s NIC (case B) - not 78% and 35x. The printed arithmetic (35 x 40 = 1,400 GB/s; 1.4/1.8 = 78%; 1,400/40 = 35x) is internally consistent, so the defect is in the population, not the arithmetic.
issue.root_cause: A fleet-scale demand figure was reused inside a pool-scale capacity check without re-deriving the per-pool population; the note's own parenthetical ('the aggregate check') signals that a different scope was intended but never states it.
issue.correction: State the population for every aggregate figure in Note 11.3-1. Give both readings explicitly: (a) stress case - a single P/D pair carrying the entire canonical fleet peak of 40 rps needs 1.4 TB/s of fabric ingress, which is 78% of the 4-way NVLink aggregate and 35x a 40 GB/s NIC; (b) canonical deployment - per-pool ingress at the stated ~1.3-2 req/s per host is ~80 GB/s, i.e. ~4.5% of the NVLink aggregate and ~2x a 40 GB/s NIC. Then state which case the 'feasible but tight' and 'cannot' verdicts refer to. Also replace '40 req/s' with 'the canonical 40 rps fleet peak' so it cannot be confused with the 40 tokens/s decode rate quoted in the Fig 11.3 caption.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, §3 'When to Disaggregate: Prefill and Decode Want Different Pools' and §6 'Architecture Consequence' (anchor by heading)
issue.quoted_clause: Serving both from one pool forces a compromise: batch for prefill and it slows decode; optimize for decode and prefill starves. **P/D disaggregation (Splitwise/DistServe/Mooncake [S4][1P])** runs prefill nodes at high FLOP-utilization and decode nodes at high bandwidth-utilization
issue.observed: The chapter diagnoses prefill/decode interference on a shared pool and then jumps directly to splitting the pools. The intermediate remedy - subdividing a large prefill into chunks and interleaving those chunks with latency-sensitive decode steps (chunked prefill / prefill-decode interleaving) - is never introduced, even though it is the cheaper and more commonly deployed response to exactly the conflict the chapter names, and it is the mechanism that determines whether pool splitting is needed at all. If chunked prefill is covered in another chapter, this chapter gives no cross-reference, so the reader is left with a false dichotomy.
issue.evidence: Structural: the chunk contains no occurrence of chunked prefill, prefill chunking, or interleaving. The chapter's own diagnosis ('prefill starves decode') is the textbook trigger condition for chunked prefill; the chapter's own §4 measurement item 3 ('Measure prefill-vs-decode utilization separately ... tells us when to disaggregate') presupposes a scheduler that can interleave the two phases, which is the chunked-prefill mechanism.
issue.root_cause: The chapter was organised around the mechanisms that map onto named papers (Orca, vLLM, SGLang, Mooncake) rather than around the causal chain 'conflict -> cheapest remedy -> costlier remedy', so the middle step was skipped.
issue.correction: Insert a subsection between 'Prefix Caching' and 'When to Disaggregate' that establishes chunked prefill mechanistically: large prefill -> substantial resource occupancy -> interference with decode -> subdivision of the prefill into chunks -> interleaving with decode steps -> scheduler policy (chunk size, priority, budget) -> latency/throughput trade-off (TTFT rises, ITL jitter appears, throughput may fall slightly) -> conditions under which it helps (moderate prefill, latency-sensitive decode) and where it does not (prefill is itself the SLO-critical path; very long prefills where chunk overhead dominates; prefill already short enough not to interfere). Then make the P/D decision explicitly conditional on chunked prefill having been tried and measured. If the mechanism is already taught in Ch 6/7/12, add an explicit cross-reference in this section rather than leaving the reader with a two-way choice.
issue.acceptance_test: The chapter contains either (a) a mechanism description of chunked prefill with its trade-off and its failure conditions, or (b) an explicit cross-reference to the section that provides it, and the P/D recommendation is stated as conditional on measured phase conflict after that remedy.

issue.quoted_clause: each request's KV cache for 9.2K input is ~24.1 GB (FP16, ~2.62 MB/token x 9,200, initial KV) ... the canonical ~17.5-concurrent operating point (Ch 4 §6 / Ch 7 / Ch 17; 436 GB / 24.9 GB = KV budget / per-request KV)
