issue.correction: Label both figures at first use ('24.1 GB initial KV at 9,200 tokens; 24.9 GB including the 300 generated tokens'), use one basis consistently for concurrency arithmetic, and state explicitly whether 17.5 is the KV-capacity ceiling or the demand-driven concurrency. If the roofline argument is meant to describe the running host, recompute AI at the demand-driven concurrency (~10-15) and present 17.5 as the saturation point.
issue.acceptance_test: Every per-request KV figure in the chapter carries its token basis, and the concurrency used in the roofline argument is labelled as ceiling or demand-driven and is consistent with the chapter's own per-host request rate.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, §3 'When to Disaggregate' and Fig 11.3 caption (anchor by heading/caption)
issue.quoted_clause: the whole-model weight-read rate is ~5.6 TB/s if served by one device, 3.35 TB/s per GPU, and ~0.70 TB/s per GPU when sharded across the canonical 8xH100 host (Ch 6)
issue.observed: A single series of three numbers is introduced as 'the whole-model weight-read rate', but the three are of two different kinds: 5.6 TB/s and 0.70 TB/s are demand rates (bytes that must be read per second to sustain 25 ms/token), while 3.35 TB/s is the supply (one H100's HBM3 bandwidth). A reader can easily take 3.35 TB/s as a third weight-read rate, or as a third sharding case. The Fig 11.3 caption compounds this by writing '~5.6 TB/s if served by one device vs 3.35 TB/s per GPU', which reads as a comparison between two rates of the same kind.
issue.evidence: Demand: 140 GB / 25 ms = 5.6 TB/s; sharded over 8 GPUs: 17.5 GB / 25 ms = 0.70 TB/s per GPU. Supply: H100 SXM HBM3 = 3.35 TB/s per GPU. The feasibility conclusion (5.6 > 3.35, so one device cannot sustain 25 ms/token; 0.70 << 3.35, so the 8-GPU host can) is correct but is never stated, and the caption's 'vs' hides it.
issue.root_cause: Demand and supply were merged into one enumeration to save a sentence, at the cost of the comparison the sentence exists to make.
issue.correction: Rewrite as an explicit demand-versus-supply comparison: 'At 25 ms/token the whole model's 140 GB of FP16 weights must be read every step - 5.6 TB/s of demand. One H100 supplies 3.35 TB/s, so a single device cannot sustain 25 ms/token (it would need 5.6 TB/s). Sharded across the canonical 8xH100 host each GPU reads 17.5 GB per step, i.e. 0.70 TB/s against its 3.35 TB/s of HBM.' Apply the same rewrite to the Fig 11.3 caption. (Note also that this demand figure excludes KV traffic - see FT-01.)
issue.acceptance_test: Every number in the sentence is either explicitly labelled demand or supply, and the caption states the feasibility conclusion rather than leaving the reader to compare two differently-typed quantities.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, §3 'Prefix Caching' and §3 'When to Disaggregate' (anchor by headings)
issue.quoted_clause: 2 x 70 x 10^9 x 8,000 ~ 1.12 PFLOP ... the full 9.2K canonical input is ~1.29 PFLOP ... Prefill needs ~1.29 PFLOP, or ~1.19 PFLOPS over the ~1.08 s prefill budget
issue.observed: The prefill FLOP model is the dense-parameter approximation 2NL, which omits the attention term. The chapter uses this model to size the prefill budget, to price the prefix-cache saving, and to argue the P/D economics, and the book elsewhere reasons about long-context scenarios (13.3K, 128K-class RAG), where the approximation degrades badly. The omission is not stated as an assumption anywhere.
issue.evidence: Causal prefill attention FLOPs per token = 2 x L x d_model x n_layers = 2 x 9,200 x 8,192 x 80 = 1.21e10, versus the dense term 2N = 1.4e11 per token - so attention is ~8.6% of the total at the canonical 9.2K (total ~1.40 PFLOP, not 1.29). The ratio grows linearly with context: attention equals dense at L = N / (d_model x n_layers) = 70e9 / (8,192 x 80) ~ 107K tokens, and dominates beyond that. Decode attention (4 x L x d_model x n_layers per token) is ~18% of decode FLOPs at 9.5K.
issue.root_cause: The 2NL approximation was adopted as a shorthand and then used in budget arithmetic, where it is an assumption rather than an identity; the book never states the crossover at which it stops being safe.
issue.correction: State the approximation and its scope: 'prefill FLOPs ~ 2NL, which ignores the causal-attention term 2 x L x d_model x n_layers per token; at the canonical 9.2K that term is ~9% of the total and becomes dominant beyond ~100K tokens.' Where the chapter reasons about long-context scenarios, either add the attention term or flag that the 2NL figure understates them by the stated factor.
issue.acceptance_test: The prefill FLOP figure is accompanied by an explicit statement of the omitted term and its crossover context length, and any long-context prefill figure in the chapter is either corrected or flagged.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, §6 'Architecture Consequence' (second bullet, 'Scaling up') (anchor by heading)
issue.quoted_clause: FP8 KV (raw tensor byte-halving = 1.31 MB/token, exactly 50% of FP16) [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] and KV offloading are memory levers available without restructuring.
issue.observed: The two levers are grouped as equally 'restructuring-free', but they are not. FP8 KV is a representation change with a bounded accuracy cost. KV offloading changes the decode path: KV state must be fetched from host memory over PCIe/NVLink, and in a decode step the engine reads the whole per-request KV, so offloaded state is fetched on the request's critical path (per step or per block, depending on the design). The chapter itself derives exactly this class of cost for P/D transfer a page earlier, then applies the opposite framing here.
issue.evidence: Internal inconsistency: Note 11.3-1 prices KV movement at 35 GB / 40 GB/s = 0.9 s per request over a fabric link; the same arithmetic applied to an offload path (host DRAM/PCIe at ~25-50 GB/s per GPU) puts a 24.9 GB per-request KV fetch at ~0.5-1.0 s, i.e. comparable to the entire 1.08 s prefill budget. Calling offloading 'available without restructuring' therefore understates its cost by an order of magnitude relative to the chapter's own numbers.
issue.root_cause: The bullet was written as a list of 'cheap memory levers' and the offload path's per-step transfer cost was not carried across from the transfer analysis in the same chapter.
issue.correction: Separate the two levers and give offloading its trade-off: 'FP8 KV halves KV bytes with a bounded accuracy cost and no change to the decode path. KV offloading trades HBM capacity for a per-step (or per-block) fetch of KV state over the host link, which lands on the decode critical path; at the canonical 24.9 GB per request and a ~25-50 GB/s host link that is ~0.5-1.0 s of transfer per request, so it is viable only for cold or rarely-touched prefixes, not for the live decode working set.'
issue.acceptance_test: The 'Scaling up' bullet distinguishes the two levers and states the offload transfer cost using the chapter's own per-request KV figure and a stated link bandwidth.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, §6 'Architecture Consequence' (third bullet, 'Beyond a node') (anchor by heading)
issue.quoted_clause: **Beyond a node:** when prefill FLOPs and decode bandwidth fight on one pool, P/D disaggregation (Splitwise/Disterve/Mooncake) is the architecture of choice, with Mooncake's KV-transfer engine moving caches between pools. [S4][1P]
issue.observed: A major architectural choice is asserted without showing why competing alternatives were rejected. The chapter's own §3 argues that disaggregation is premature at the canonical scale and that the decision should be made against measured phase conflict, but §6 then names it 'the architecture of choice' with no comparison against the alternatives a reader would actually consider: chunked prefill with priority scheduling, a larger single pool, separate pools without KV transfer (recompute instead of transfer), or simply accepting a higher TTFT. The bullet also names a product ('Mooncake's KV-transfer engine') in a chapter whose stated principle is 'mechanisms, not the product catalog'.
issue.evidence: Structural: §3 and §6 use different decision criteria (see FT-11), and no alternative is named anywhere in the chapter. The chapter's own Note 11.3-1 concludes that 'the transfer link, not topology alone, decides whether P/D disaggregation pays', which is a conditional conclusion that §6's unconditional phrasing contradicts.
issue.root_cause: The architecture-consequence section was written as a summary of the mechanisms rather than as a decision, so it restates the mechanism's verdict instead of deriving one from requirements, evidence, and alternatives.
issue.correction: Rewrite the bullet as a decision with a visible chain: requirement (measured prefill/decode conflict at the target load) -> alternatives considered (chunked prefill + priority scheduling; larger single pool; separate pools with recompute instead of KV transfer; P/D with KV transfer) -> trade-offs (transfer cost, orchestration, failure modes, operational complexity) -> decision (P/D with KV transfer, conditional on the measured conflict and on the transfer link budget from Note 11.3-1) -> validation criteria (prefill/decode utilisation measured separately; KV transfer time as a fraction of the TTFT budget). Replace the product name with the mechanism ('a dedicated KV-transfer path').
issue.acceptance_test: The bullet names at least two rejected alternatives with the reason for rejection, states the condition under which P/D is chosen, and contains no product name.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, §3 'When to Disaggregate', Table 11-1, and §6 'Architecture Consequence' (anchor by heading/table)
issue.quoted_clause: it pays off when measured prefill/decode interference binds - evaluate it against measured phase conflict, not topology alone ... | P/D disaggregation | Split prefill/decode pools + KV transfer | compute on prefill, bandwidth on decode (both, at scale) | workload outgrows a node | [S4][1P] ... **Beyond a node:** when prefill FLOPs and decode bandwidth fight on one pool
issue.observed: Three different criteria for the same decision appear in one chapter: 'measured prefill/decode interference binds' (§3), 'workload outgrows a node' (Table 11-1), and 'prefill FLOPs and decode bandwidth fight on one pool' (§6). 'Workload outgrows a node' is a capacity condition, not a conflict condition, and it would recommend disaggregation for a workload that has no phase conflict at all. A reader consulting Table 11-1 as a decision aid would reach a different answer from the prose.
issue.evidence: Internal: the three statements are not equivalent. The chapter's own §3 says the decision must be made 'against measured phase conflict, not topology alone', which directly contradicts the Table 11-1 cell.
issue.root_cause: The summary table was written independently of the prose and compressed the prose's conditional into a memorable but different phrase.
issue.correction: Adopt one criterion - measured prefill/decode phase conflict at the target load, with the transfer-link budget as the second gate - and use it verbatim in §3, in the Table 11-1 'When it matters' cell, and in §6. If 'outgrows a node' is retained as a necessary-but-not-sufficient precondition, say so explicitly.
issue.acceptance_test: The criterion wording in §3, Table 11-1, and §6 is identical or explicitly nested, and no table cell states a condition the prose rejects.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, §6 'Architecture Consequence' -> '### The Mechanisms, Not the Product Catalog' -> '#### What the capability table does not promise' (anchor by heading)
issue.quoted_clause: ### The Mechanisms, Not the Product Catalog ... #### Table 11-2 - Serving engines by architectural capability (observed 2026-10-28; time-sensitive)
issue.observed: The engine comparison - two tables plus roughly a page and a half of prose on backend paths, diffusion schedulers, OpenVINO fallback behaviour and graph capture - is nested as a subsection (and sub-subsection) of 'Architecture Consequence'. Three consequences: (a) the chapter's intellectual payoff, the architecture consequence, is separated from the mechanism section by time-sensitive product material; (b) the chapter ends on implementation trivia rather than on the architectural decision it promised; (c) the cross-reference 'see the serving qualification in §6' becomes ambiguous, because §6's title is 'Architecture Consequence' while the qualification actually lives two levels deeper.
issue.evidence: Heading structure in the chunk: '## 6. Architecture Consequence' is followed by '### The Mechanisms, Not the Product Catalog' and '#### What the capability table does not promise'. The engine material is ~1.5 pages of the chapter's tail and is explicitly dated 2026-10-28, i.e. the most perishable content in the chapter.
issue.root_cause: The chapter was extended at the end rather than reorganised, so the newest material was appended under whatever heading was last.
issue.correction: Promote 'The Mechanisms, Not the Product Catalog' to its own numbered section (or move it to an appendix with a dated 'as of' note and a pointer from §6). Either way, end the chapter with the architecture consequence and the mini-case, so the chapter closes on the decision it exists to enable. Keep the qualification material adjacent to Table 11-2, where it is used.
issue.acceptance_test: The chapter's final section is the architecture consequence (or mini-case), and the engine comparison is either a top-level section with its own date stamp or an appendix.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, §5 'Common Mistakes' (last bullet) and §3 'Prefix Caching' (state-preservation sentence) (anchor by heading)
issue.quoted_clause: **Believing speculative decoding (DFlash reports >6x lossless acceleration, up to 2.5x faster than EAGLE-3 [S5][1P]) is a serving baseline.** These are paper-reported results under the paper's evaluation setup, not portable serving-speed figures. Speculative decoding is an optimization for bandwidth-bound decode, not a requirement, and must be validated on the workload.
issue.observed: Speculative decoding appears in this chapter only as a number in a Common Mistakes bullet and as a passing mention in the state-preservation caveat ('speculative rollback'). The mechanism is never given: draft proposal -> candidate sequence -> target verification -> accept/reject -> continuation. The reader is therefore asked to reject a technology whose mechanism they have not been taught, and the bullet's own parenthetical (>6x, 2.5x vs EAGLE-3) reads as evidence in favour of the mistake it is correcting. The chapter also asserts 'an optimization for bandwidth-bound decode' without explaining why - the mechanism-level reason is that speculative decoding reduces the number of weight reads per emitted token, which is precisely the dominant decode bandwidth cost.
issue.evidence: Structural: no occurrence of 'draft', 'acceptance rate', 'verification', or 'rejection' in the chunk. The bullet's logic is inverted: the correction ('not portable serving-speed figures') is weaker than the parenthetical it is attached to, and the reader is given no criterion for when the speedup would transfer (acceptance rate, draft-model cost, batch size, target/draft pairing).
issue.root_cause: The chapter's mechanism coverage was scoped to the four techniques that map onto the cited papers, and speculative decoding was added later as a cautionary bullet rather than as a mechanism.
issue.correction: Either add a short mechanism subsection (draft -> verify -> accept/reject -> continue; the quantity that changes is weight reads per emitted token, so the speedup is bounded by the acceptance rate and by the draft model's own cost; verification adds FLOPs that are cheap only while decode is bandwidth-bound; the gain shrinks as the batch grows because the weight read is already amortised across the batch, and the paper numbers are typically measured at batch 1) or add an explicit cross-reference to the chapter that teaches it. Rewrite the Common Mistakes bullet so the parenthetical is the thing being discounted, and state the transfer criterion: 'a paper's speedup is measured at its own batch size, draft model and acceptance rate; it transfers only if your workload reproduces those.'
issue.acceptance_test: A reader who has read this chapter can state what speculative decoding changes (weight reads per emitted token), what bounds its benefit (acceptance rate, draft cost, batch size), and why the cited paper numbers do not transfer to the canonical 17.5-concurrency operating point.

issue.quoted_clause: continuous batching (vLLM/Orca) is near-mandatory to hold TTFT under the SLO (1.2 s, p95 <= 2 s) at the replica's admitted load (~1.3-2 req/s per Ch 14 Step 3)
issue.observed: The chapter's strongest architectural claim ('near-mandatory') is asserted without the calculation that would establish it. The chapter has all the inputs needed: with discrete batching at the canonical 300-token output length, a batch is locked until its slowest member finishes, so a request arriving at the start of a batch waits ~7.5 s before its own prefill even begins - roughly 6x the 1.2 s TTFT SLO. Without that bound, 'near-mandatory' reads as a preference rather than a consequence, and the reader cannot check it.
issue.evidence: Chapter-internal: 300 tokens x 25 ms/token = 7.5 s (stated in §3); TTFT SLO 1.2 s (stated in §6). Discrete-batching TTFT bound = batch completion time + prefill ~ 7.5 s + 0.47 s (8-GPU prefill at 35% MFU, stated in §3) ~ 8 s, versus a 1.2 s SLO.
issue.root_cause: The claim was carried over from the mechanism discussion as a conclusion rather than derived from the chapter's own timing numbers.
issue.correction: Add the two-line bound: 'Under discrete batching at the canonical 300-token output length, a request waits for the current batch to complete (~7.5 s) before its prefill begins, so TTFT is ~8 s against a 1.2 s SLO; continuous batching is what removes that wait.' This converts 'near-mandatory' into a derived statement and gives the reader a reusable test for any workload shape.
issue.acceptance_test: The 'near-mandatory' claim is immediately preceded by the discrete-batching TTFT bound computed from the chapter's own 300-token / 25 ms / 1.2 s figures.

issue.quoted_clause: Prefix reuse is also only one of the state-preservation requirements a serving system must meet: preemption, speculative rollback, and adaptive-depth execution all constrain what a cache may evict or reuse - see the serving qualification in §6.
issue.observed: The cross-reference points to §6, whose heading is 'Architecture Consequence'. The qualification the sentence refers to (what a cache may evict or reuse, and what a deployment record must contain) is in the sub-subsection 'What the capability table does not promise', nested two levels below §6. A reader following '§6' lands on a section about deployment choices, not on the qualification, and the reference is therefore technically resolvable but conceptually wrong.
issue.evidence: Heading structure in the chunk: '## 6. Architecture Consequence' -> '### The Mechanisms, Not the Product Catalog' -> '#### What the capability table does not promise'. The qualification content (state preservation, deployment record, fallback logs) is in the last of these.
issue.root_cause: The reference was written before the engine-comparison material was nested under §6, and was not updated when the heading hierarchy changed.
issue.correction: Point to the specific subsection by name and number (e.g. 'see the serving qualification in §6.x, "What the capability table does not promise"'), or move the qualification to a numbered subsection of its own so it can be referenced directly.
issue.acceptance_test: The cross-reference resolves to a heading whose title matches the concept the sentence invokes, and the target contains the eviction/reuse constraints the sentence promises.

issue.quoted_clause: | prefix caching | auto prefix | Radix prefix tree | some cache | limited | how much re-prefill is avoided | ... | quantization support | broad (GPTQ/AWQ/FP8) | broad | tight NVIDIA-precision (FP8/INT8/INT4) | GGUF (K-quants) | what precision the kernels are tuned for |
issue.observed: Several cells state a vendor's marketing shorthand or a qualitative impression rather than the mechanism the table's own 'architectural note' column promises ('how much re-prefill is avoided', 'what precision the kernels are tuned for'). 'auto prefix' is not a mechanism; 'some cache' and 'limited' are not comparable quantities; 'tight NVIDIA-precision' is not a precision description. The table's stated purpose - 'a map of which mechanism to look for' - is undercut by cells that cannot be looked up.
issue.evidence: The table's own framing: 'This comparison is organized by *architectural capability* so it transfers across specific products and versions' and the 'architectural note' column defines what each row is supposed to answer. Cells like 'some cache' and 'limited' cannot be checked against that definition.
issue.root_cause: The table was drafted as a quick vendor matrix and the mechanism-level framing was applied to the column headers without rewriting the cell contents.
issue.correction: Rewrite the vague cells as mechanism statements with a checkable criterion: prefix caching -> 'automatic prefix caching (hash-keyed block reuse)', 'radix-tree prefix reuse', 'block-hash prefix reuse (engine-level)', 'slot-level prompt reuse'; quantization -> name the formats and the granularity (e.g. 'weight-only GPTQ/AWQ; FP8 weight+KV paths'), 'weight-only and FP8 KV paths', 'FP8/INT8/INT4 weight and KV paths', 'GGUF weight quantisation (Q4_K/Q5_K/Q8_0); KV quantisation limited'. Keep the table's time-sensitivity flag and the 'not a ranking' framing.
issue.acceptance_test: Every cell in Table 11-2 states a mechanism or a checkable capability, and no cell contains a bare adjective ('some', 'limited', 'broad') without the object it qualifies.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, §3 'Prefix Caching' (first paragraph) and §6 (first bullet) (anchor by heading)
issue.quoted_clause: The RAG request's 8K retrieved-context tokens are largely shared across queries (same documents; the book's K = 1,000). ... prefix caching is the highest-leverage optimization because the workload is repeated-context RAG.
issue.observed: The entire prefix-cache benefit rests on an unstated workload parameter: what fraction of the 8,000-token retrieved span is actually shared between consecutive queries. 'Largely shared' is asserted, not quantified, and the chapter's strongest optimisation claim ('highest-leverage') is derived from it. With top-K = 1,000 retrieval, the overlap between two queries' retrieved sets is a property of the corpus and the query distribution, not of the mechanism, and it can range from near-total (a fixed document set) to near-zero (a diverse query stream).
issue.evidence: The chapter quantifies the saving (1.12-1.29 PFLOP per request) but never the fraction of the prefix that is actually reusable; the saving scales linearly with the shared fraction. The 'highest-leverage' claim in §6 is therefore unfalsifiable as written.
issue.root_cause: The workload assumption was inherited from the canonical-workload chapter without being restated as a number, so the mechanism section cannot be checked against it.
issue.correction: State the assumed overlap explicitly (e.g. 'the canonical workload assumes that X% of the 8,000-token retrieved span is shared between consecutive queries') and show the saving scaling with it: 'at a shared fraction f, the avoidable prefill is f x 1.29 PFLOP per request'. Then qualify the 'highest-leverage' claim with the same number, or replace it with a metric the reader can compute for their own workload ('prefix caching is the highest-leverage optimization when the shared fraction of the retrieved span exceeds Y').
issue.acceptance_test: The prefix-cache saving is expressed as a function of a stated shared-prefix fraction, and the 'highest-leverage' claim in §6 carries the same qualifier.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, Table 11-2 caption (anchor by table caption)
issue.quoted_clause: #### Table 11-2 - Serving engines by architectural capability (observed 2026-10-28; time-sensitive)
issue.observed: The paragraphs immediately below this table carry the explicit qualifier '(observed 2026-10-28, outside the 2026-08-30 snapshot)', but the table caption does not. The table is the most perishable object in the chapter and is the one a reader is most likely to act on directly, so it should carry the same snapshot qualifier as the prose.
issue.evidence: Internal: three paragraphs in the same subsection carry the 'outside the 2026-08-30 snapshot' note; the table caption carries only 'observed 2026-10-28; time-sensitive'.
issue.root_cause: The qualifier was added to prose paragraphs during the evidence-snapshot pass but not to the table caption.
issue.correction: Extend the caption to '(observed 2026-10-28; outside this edition's 2026-08-30 evidence snapshot; time-sensitive)'.
issue.acceptance_test: Every dated observation in the section carries the same snapshot qualifier, in both prose and captions.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, throughout (§3, §5, §6, engine section) (global within chapter)
issue.quoted_clause: Recall from Ch2/Ch6 ... (Ch 4 §6 / Ch 7 / Ch 17) ... (Ch 12) ... (Ch 12/17) ... per Ch 14 Step 3 ... (Ch 6) ... benchmark it against the alternative (Ch. 14) ... §9.8 ... §9.2 ... see "When to Disaggregate", §11.3
issue.observed: Cross-reference style drifts within a single chapter: 'Ch2/Ch6' (no space), 'Ch 4 §6', 'Ch 12/17', 'Ch 14 Step 3', 'Ch. 14' (with a period), and bare '§9.8'/'§9.2' for another chapter's sections. The reader cannot tell whether '§9.8' means Chapter 9 section 8 or Chapter 11 section 8, and 'Ch. 14' is inconsistent with 'Ch 14' two paragraphs earlier.
issue.evidence: All forms occur in the chunk; '§9.8' and '§9.2' are used for Chapter 9 while '§11.3' is used for a section of this chapter, so the same symbol denotes two different things.
issue.root_cause: Cross-references were written at different times by different passes without a house style being applied.
issue.correction: Adopt one form for the whole book - e.g. 'Ch 4 §6', 'Ch 9 §8', 'Ch 11 §3' - and use it consistently; never use a bare '§n' for another chapter's section when the same notation is used for this chapter's own sections.
issue.acceptance_test: A single grep of the chapter yields one cross-reference pattern, and no bare '§n' is ambiguous between chapters.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, §3 'When to Disaggregate' (first paragraph) (anchor by heading)
issue.quoted_clause: at the canonical operating point (9.2K/300, FP16, the stated batch on 8xH100), the two phases sit in different regimes
issue.observed: 'the stated batch' is a back-reference to a number stated elsewhere in the book, in a sentence that is otherwise fully self-contained (9.2K/300, FP16, 8xH100). The reader of this chapter has to find that number to know which operating point is being analysed - and the chapter then derives a different concurrency figure (17.5) two paragraphs later, so the ambiguity is material.
issue.evidence: The chapter's own numbers: 17.5 concurrent (KV-capacity derived) and 1.3-2 req/s per host (admitted load). 'The stated batch' is not resolvable within the chapter.
issue.root_cause: The sentence was drafted as a reminder to readers of an earlier chapter rather than as a self-contained statement of the operating point.
issue.correction: Name the batch size in the sentence (e.g. '9.2K/300, FP16, batch 17.5 on 8xH100') and reconcile it with the concurrency discussion that follows (see FT-06).

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, §3 'Continuous Batching Fills the Bubbles' (anchor by heading)
issue.quoted_clause: while a long decode runs, the freed decode slots and memory-bandwidth capacity are continuously refilled by new short requests, amortizing the per-step weight reads
issue.observed: 'memory-bandwidth capacity ... refilled' is a misuse: admitting more requests consumes bandwidth rather than refilling it. The intended point - that the bandwidth which would otherwise be idle is put to work, and that one weight read now serves more sequences - is correct but is obscured by the metaphor. 'Amortizing the per-step weight reads' is also loose: the amortisation is across the sequences in a step, not across time.
issue.evidence: Internal: the same paragraph's own framing ('idle can still occur from insufficient arrivals, KV capacity, prefill, or scheduling policy') treats bandwidth as a resource that can be idle, not as something that is refilled.
issue.root_cause: The 'filling bubbles' metaphor was extended past the point where it is physically accurate.
issue.correction: Reword: 'while a long decode runs, freed decode slots are refilled every step, so the per-step weight read is amortised across more sequences and the bandwidth that would otherwise be idle is put to work.'
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in the chapter describes bandwidth as being refilled or filled; the amortisation is stated as being across sequences within a step.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, §3 'PagedAttention: Killing the Fragmentation Tax' (anchor by heading)
issue.quoted_clause: **PagedAttention/vLLM [S2][1P]** allocates KV in fixed-size blocks mapped through a per-request block table and evicted like page frames; blocks are shared across requests only when the engine implements copy-on-write or prefix reuse, so the ~24.1 GB per request is packed densely and more concurrent requests fit in the same 640 GB node
issue.observed: Three imprecisions in one sentence. (a) Blocks are freed back to the pool, not 'evicted' - eviction implies a replacement policy that PagedAttention does not have. (b) 'Blocks are shared across requests only when the engine implements copy-on-write or prefix reuse' conflates two different things: copy-on-write is a branching/beam-search concern, while cross-request sharing of identical blocks is what prefix caching does; the sentence risks the reader concluding that PagedAttention itself shares blocks. (c) The label [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] is attached to a sentence whose first half is a mechanism statement from the vLLM paper ([1P]) and whose second half is a derived capacity consequence; the label scope is wrong for the mechanism clause.
issue.evidence: The chapter's own §3 'Prefix Caching' section treats prefix reuse as a separate mechanism layered on the block table, and the Fig 11.2 caption separates 'state management' (PagedAttention) from 'reuse' (prefix caching) as distinct concerns - so the prose in the PagedAttention paragraph contradicts the chapter's own taxonomy.
issue.root_cause: The OS analogy (pages, frames, eviction, copy-on-write) was carried further than the mechanism supports, and the label was applied to the whole sentence rather than to its derived clause.
issue.correction: Rewrite: 'PagedAttention/vLLM [S2][1P] allocates KV in fixed-size blocks and maps them to a request through a per-request block table; blocks are returned to the pool when a request finishes, so the allocator never has to find a contiguous region. PagedAttention alone does not deduplicate identical content across requests - that is prefix caching, a separate mechanism built on the same block table (see below).' Label the mechanism clause [1P] and the capacity consequence [DERIVED].
issue.acceptance_test: The PagedAttention paragraph does not attribute cross-request sharing to PagedAttention, and its labels match the chapter's own four-concern taxonomy in Fig 11.2.

issue.quoted_clause: **Measure KV utilization** - live/allocated KV blocks / total KV block capacity (weights, activations, and workspace reported separately).
issue.observed: The ratio is written with a slash between two quantities and then divided by a third, so it is ambiguous whether the metric is (live / allocated) / capacity, (live + allocated) / capacity, or live / (allocated / capacity). The paragraph then distinguishes two different metrics - 'block utilization' for PagedAttention and 'prefix-hit rate' for prefix caching - which require different numerators and denominators, so the ambiguity is not harmless.
issue.evidence: Internal: the same item names two distinct metrics ('block utilization' and 'prefix-hit rate') but supplies only one ambiguous formula.
issue.root_cause: Two metrics were compressed into one notation.
issue.correction: Write the two metrics separately: 'allocated blocks / total block capacity (how full the KV pool is)' and 'live blocks / allocated blocks (how much of the allocated pool is actually in use - the fragmentation indicator PagedAttention improves)'; report prefix-hit rate separately as 'requests served from a cached prefix / requests eligible for prefix reuse'.
issue.acceptance_test: Each named metric has an unambiguous numerator and denominator, and the two metrics are not written as one ratio.

issue.quoted_clause: **Measure goodput, not raw throughput** - tokens/s that arrive before their SLO deadline (Ch6).
issue.observed: The definition given is a token-weighted goodput, which is a legitimate variant but is not the usual definition (requests meeting an SLO per unit time), and the sentence does not say which it is. It also does not say which SLO: the chapter's own SLO has two components (TTFT 1.2 s / p95 <= 2 s, and a 25 ms TPOT), and a token can satisfy one and violate the other. A reader who implements the metric from this sentence will get a different number from one who implements request-level goodput.
issue.evidence: Internal: §6 states the SLO as '(1.2 s, p95 <= 2 s)' for TTFT, and §3 uses a 25 ms TPOT; the chapter's own §5 mistake bullet says larger batches 'zero goodput', which is a request-level notion.
issue.root_cause: The metric was defined in one clause without specifying the weighting or the SLO components.
issue.correction: State the definition precisely and give both forms: 'goodput = requests per second that satisfy the full SLO (TTFT <= 1.2 s and TPOT <= 25 ms); a token-weighted variant (tokens/s whose request met its SLO) is useful for capacity planning but is not interchangeable with request-level goodput - report both.'
issue.acceptance_test: The definition names the unit (requests/s vs tokens/s), the SLO components, and states whether the two forms are interchangeable.

issue.quoted_clause: 1. **Measure goodput, not raw throughput** ... 2. **Measure KV utilization** ... 3. **Measure prefill-vs-decode utilization separately** ... 4. **Measure the scheduler's real occupancy** ... 5. **Record the model revision and the execution path in use**
issue.observed: The measurement list is well chosen for the mechanisms the chapter covers, but it omits the telemetry for two of the chapter's own subjects. There is no metric for KV-transfer time or fabric utilisation (the quantity Note 11.3-1 identifies as the deciding term for P/D), and no metric for speculative-decoding acceptance rate (the quantity that bounds the mechanism the chapter discusses in §5). There is also no per-phase HBM bandwidth utilisation metric, which is the measurement that would actually show whether decode is bandwidth-bound - the chapter's central regime claim.
issue.evidence: Internal: Note 11.3-1 concludes 'the transfer link, not topology alone, decides whether P/D disaggregation pays', but §4 provides no way to measure that link; §5 discusses speculative decoding without any acceptance-rate metric.
issue.root_cause: The measurement list was written before the transfer analysis and the speculative-decoding caveat were added, and was not extended to cover them.
issue.correction: Add: '6. Measure KV-transfer time and fabric utilisation per request when disaggregation is in use - it is the term that decides whether the split pays. 7. Measure per-phase HBM bandwidth utilisation (bytes read per step / step time / peak bandwidth) for prefill and decode separately; this is the direct test of the compute-bound vs bandwidth-bound claim. 8. If speculative decoding is enabled, measure acceptance rate and the draft model's share of total step time.'
issue.acceptance_test: Every mechanism named in the chapter has at least one corresponding metric in §4, and the metrics map one-to-one onto the mechanisms in Table 11-1.

issue.quoted_clause: - **Assuming bigger batches always help.** ... - **Serving KV contiguous and watching fragmentation.** ... - **Re-prefilling shared context.** ... - **Choosing P/D disaggregation too early.** ... - **Believing speculative decoding ... is a serving baseline.**
issue.observed: The list omits the misconception the chapter's own prose most directly warns against and that a competent reader is most likely to hold after reading §3: that continuous batching eliminates idle time. The section's first paragraph says 'idle can still occur from insufficient arrivals, KV capacity, prefill, or scheduling policy' - a precise, non-obvious statement that belongs in the mistakes list, where it would have to be defended. Its absence leaves the chapter's most valuable qualification in a subordinate clause.
issue.evidence: Internal: §3's first paragraph contains the four idle causes; §5 contains no corresponding mistake. The other four mistakes each correspond to a mechanism discussed in §3, so the list's coverage rule is broken by the omission.
issue.root_cause: The mistakes list was assembled from the mechanisms rather than from the chapter's own stated qualifications.
issue.correction: Add a bullet: '**Assuming continuous batching removes idle time.** It removes the batch boundary, not the idle: a slot stays empty when arrivals are insufficient, when KV capacity is exhausted, when a prefill occupies the device, or when the scheduler's policy defers admission. Measure slot occupancy and queue wait rather than inferring utilisation from the scheduler's existence.'
issue.acceptance_test: Every qualification stated in §3 that constrains a mechanism's benefit appears either as a Common Mistake or is explicitly cross-referenced from one.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, §3 'PagedAttention: Killing the Fragmentation Tax' (anchor by heading)
issue.quoted_clause: so the ~24.1 GB per request is packed densely and more concurrent requests fit in the same 640 GB node [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
issue.observed: The chapter's central claim for PagedAttention - 'more concurrency under the same SLO' - is asserted without a number, in a chapter that quantifies everything else. The reader is left without the magnitude of the win, which is the quantity an architect needs to decide whether the mechanism is worth adopting.
issue.evidence: The chapter has all the inputs: 640 GB node, 140 GB of FP16 weights, ~436 GB KV budget, 24.1-24.9 GB per request. A fragmentation figure (e.g. the fraction of a contiguous allocator wasted at the canonical request length) is not stated anywhere in the chunk.
issue.root_cause: The mechanism was described qualitatively because the fragmentation measurement was never taken.
issue.correction: Quantify: state the assumed fragmentation waste for a contiguous allocator at the canonical request length (e.g. 'a contiguous allocator at 9.2K-token requests wastes on the order of X% of the KV pool to internal fragmentation, because the last block of each request is only partly filled'), and give the resulting concurrency (e.g. '17.5 -> N concurrent requests on the same 640 GB node'). If the figure is workload-dependent, say so and give the range.
issue.acceptance_test: The PagedAttention paragraph states a concurrency figure before and after the mechanism, computed from the chapter's own memory numbers.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, §3 'Continuous Batching Fills the Bubbles' (anchor by heading)
issue.quoted_clause: The utilization gain is the difference between spiky discrete batches and a continuously-fed pipeline. Rather than stipulate a single percent, the mechanism shifts the bottleneck from batch-boundary idle time toward GPU resources when arrivals and KV capacity permit
issue.observed: The refusal to stipulate a percentage is intellectually defensible, but it is a refusal to derive rather than a refusal to generalise. The chapter has the inputs for a derivation that is robust to workload shape: under discrete batching with a fixed slot count and roughly uniform output lengths, average occupancy within a batch decays linearly as members finish, so mean occupancy is about half the slot count; continuous batching holds occupancy near the arrival-limited level. That is a defensible, assumption-stated result that transfers, and it is more useful to the reader than either a bare percentage or a bare refusal.
issue.evidence: The chapter states the canonical output length (300 tokens) and the per-token time (25 ms), which is exactly what the occupancy-decay derivation needs; the derivation is not performed.
issue.root_cause: The author chose not to quantify rather than choosing to quantify under stated assumptions, and the section lost the most transferable part of its argument.
issue.correction: Replace the refusal with the derivation and its assumptions: 'Under discrete batching with S slots and roughly uniform output lengths, members finish at a near-uniform rate, so mean occupancy is about S/2 while the batch is live; continuous batching holds occupancy at the arrival-limited level. The gain therefore depends on the ratio of arrival rate to service rate, not on a fixed percentage - which is why the mechanism is stated as a shift in the binding constraint rather than a number.'
issue.acceptance_test: The section either contains an assumption-stated derivation of the occupancy gain or explicitly says why no such derivation is possible; the reader is left with a transferable method rather than a refusal.

issue.quoted_clause: with Mooncake's KV-transfer engine moving caches between pools. [S4][1P]
issue.observed: The chapter's own stated principle - 'The mechanisms above are what matter; the engines are just implementations of them' - is violated in the architecture-consequence bullet, which names a product's component as the mechanism. A reader who later meets a different KV-transfer implementation should be able to map it onto the mechanism, which the product name prevents.
issue.evidence: Internal: the section heading is 'The Mechanisms, Not the Product Catalog' and the text states 'Never conclude "X is the go-to engine"'.
issue.root_cause: The bullet was written with a specific implementation in mind and the product name was not generalised.
issue.correction: Replace with the mechanism: 'with a dedicated KV-transfer path (RDMA/NVLink-based block transfer) moving the KV state between pools'. Keep the product attribution in the source citation, which already carries [S4][1P].
issue.acceptance_test: No product name appears in the architecture-consequence bullets; product names appear only in source citations and in the explicitly dated engine table.

issue.page_hint: Ch 12, §1 'Concept', para. 4 (page not determinable from chunk)
issue.quoted_clause: as a single host falls against the canonical ~92K input tokens/s
issue.observed: The figure is used as a canonical threshold, but the chunk never states whether it is a per-host capacity or a fleet-level demand, nor the model, precision, host count, or MFU behind it. Under the capacity reading it is arithmetically impossible on the substrate this same chunk fixes; under the demand reading it contradicts the canonical workload's peak input-token rate established in Ch 11's mini-case.
issue.evidence: Canonical model is pinned by this chunk: 70B full-MHA FP16 (KV 2.62 MB/token; 9.2K tokens -> 24.1 GB, 9.5K -> 24.9 GB). Canonical host is pinned by this chunk: 8xH100. Prefill FLOPs/token for a 70B model at 9.2K context ~ 2x70e9 + attention (~4x80x8192x9200 = 2.4e10) ~ 1.64e11. 8xH100 FP16 dense = 8 x 989 TFLOPS = 7.91e15 FLOP/s => <=48.2K tok/s at 100% MFU, and 19-24K tok/s at a realistic 40-50% MFU. FP8 dense (1,979 TFLOPS/H100) => 96.5K tok/s at 100% MFU, so 92K would require ~95% MFU. Demand reading: Ch 11 mini-case fixes the canonical service peak at 40 rps and the canonical request at 9.2K input tokens => 40 x 9,200 = 368K input tokens/s at peak, 4x the 92K figure.
issue.root_cause: A canonical throughput value was carried across chapters without a stated scope (capacity vs. demand), model, precision, or MFU, and without reconciliation against the canonical workload's own token-rate arithmetic.
issue.correction: State explicitly what 92K is. If it is a per-host prefill capacity, re-derive it from the canonical model, precision, host count, and an explicit MFU and correct the number (for 70B on 8xH100 FP16 the ceiling is ~48K tok/s at 100% MFU). If it is a demand, state the request rate and input length that produce it and reconcile it with 40 rps x 9.2K = 368K input tokens/s from Ch 11's mini-case. Add the derivation, or a cross-reference to the chapter that holds it, at first use.
issue.acceptance_test: From the text alone a reader can state (a) whether 92K input tokens/s is a per-host capacity or a fleet demand, (b) the model, precision, host count, and MFU that produce it, and (c) the arithmetic reconciling it with 40 rps x 9.2K input tokens/s. If any of the three is unavailable, the figure is not publication-ready.

issue.page_hint: Ch 12, §1 'Concept', para. 4 (page not determinable from chunk)
issue.quoted_clause: Any architecture that violates any one of these is eliminated before evaluation — candidates that fail a gate are not finalists (a *finalist* is a candidate advanced to evaluation; a *conditional finalist* is one advanced with its gate still open): they return to synthesis or are carried forward only as labeled sensitivity cases.

(a) 'eliminated before evaluation' cannot apply to the quality gate, since quality is only knowable by evaluation — and the same paragraph says 'a smaller-model candidate whose quality is unmeasured is gated, not promoted'. (b) 'carried forward only as labeled sensitivity cases' contradicts 'eliminated before evaluation' if sensitivity cases are evaluated. (c) 'gated, not promoted' conflicts with the definition of a conditional finalist as 'one advanced with its gate still open': the text both advances and does not advance candidates with an open gate.

Change 'eliminated before evaluation' to 'eliminated from the finalist set', and reconcile the quality-gate case explicitly (quality is evaluated, not screened).
issue.acceptance_test: The four candidate statuses are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, and applying them to the three example cases in §1 (single host failing throughput, smaller model with unmeasured quality, memory-fitting but slow layout) yields one unambiguous status each.

issue.correction: Lead with the taxonomy — 'the design problem is a constrained synthesis: one capacity constraint (memory fit), one rate-and-latency constraint (throughput at the SLO), and one empirical constraint (quality)' — and then note that the capacity constraint is the one that behaves like a packing problem. Keep 'packing' for the memory-fit gate only.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can state which of the three gates is a packing constraint and which are not, without re-reading.

issue.page_hint: Ch 12, §2 'Mental Model', resource list (page not determinable from chunk)

issue.evidence: All six forms appear within this chunk: 'Ch 14 keeps the video measurement protocol'; 'Chapter 17 applies joint residency'; '(Ch. 4)'; 'in Chs. 14–16'; 'presented in Ch. 22'; 'prefill is compute-bound, Ch 11'.

issue.quoted_clause: Tokens-per-second that a single device can sustain for prefill and decode, measured on the target hardware. This is the number that, multiplied by the number of devices in the candidate layout, must exceed the workload's tokens-per-second demand (92K input tokens/s average, 3K output tokens/s average, 368K input tokens/s peak, 12K output tokens/s peak).
issue.observed: §4 instructs the reader to multiply a single device's token rate by the number of devices in the layout. §3 of the same chapter spends four sentences correcting exactly this error for the canonical layout: under TP=8 the host aggregate equals the per-GPU rate (~19,800 tok/s), not 8x it, because each GPU carries 1/8 of the FLOPs for the same shared token stream. The chapter therefore states the rule and its negation within ~1,500 words, and the §4 statement is the wrong one.
issue.evidence: Re-derivation: 70B x 2 FLOP/param = 140 GFLOP/token full model. TP=8 -> 17.5 GFLOP/token/GPU. 989 TFLOP/s x 0.35 = 346.15 TFLOP/s effective per GPU. 346.15e12 / 17.5e9 = 19,780 tok/s per GPU; all 8 GPUs advance the same token stream, so the group rate is also 19,780 tok/s. Multiplying 19,780 by 8 (as §4 instructs) yields 158,240 tok/s, which is 8x the true host ceiling and would make the single host appear to pass the throughput gate by a factor of 8. The correct rule is: multiply by the number of independent replicas (data-parallel), not by the number of devices inside a tensor-parallel group.
issue.root_cause: The device-multiplication rule was written for the data-parallel case and never qualified for the tensor-parallel case, even though §3 establishes the distinction explicitly and the whole chapter's host-count screens depend on it.
issue.correction: Rewrite §4 item 3 to state the rule with its scope: 'A device rate may be multiplied by the number of devices only when those devices are independent replicas (data parallel). Inside a tensor-parallel group every device advances the same token stream with a fraction of the FLOPs, so the group's aggregate rate equals the per-device rate, not N times it. The screen is therefore: per-replica rate x number of replicas.' Add a one-line worked cross-check (17.5 GFLOP/token/GPU -> 19,780 tok/s -> host aggregate 19,780) so the rule and §3 cannot drift apart again.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader who applies §4's rule to the canonical 8xH100 layout obtains 19,780 tok/s (not 158,240) and reproduces the ~5-host average prefill screen and the ~21-host peak KV screen. No sentence in Ch 12 or Ch 13 multiplies a per-device rate by a tensor-parallel group size.

issue.page_hint: Ch 12 §3 (Worked Example), all three candidates; §4 item 3; Table 12-2 'Decode pool sizing' row
issue.quoted_clause: 3. **Throughput per device** [ASSUMPTION] canonical (Ch 4, Table 4-2). Tokens-per-second that a single device can sustain for prefill and decode, measured on the target hardware.
issue.observed: The chapter's own method requires a prefill AND a decode throughput number per device. The worked example derives only the prefill number (~19,780 tok/s for the 70B under TP=8; ~24,725 tok/s for the 7B on one H100). No decode rate is computed for any candidate. Table 12-2 has a 'Decode pool sizing' row that is filled with demand only for (b) ('decode pool sized to 3K tok/s avg / 12K tok/s peak'), with 'not sized separately' for (a), and 'not sized in this screen' for (c). Table 12-1's throughput cell for (a) says only 'decode BW-bound' with no number. The reader therefore cannot verify that decode is not the binding constraint, and the chapter's headline gate ('throughput at the SLO') is evaluated on half of the throughput it names.
issue.evidence: Independent re-derivation of the missing decode screen (H100 SXM HBM3 = 3.35 TB/s): 70B FP16 decode reads 140 GB of weights per token step; under TP=8 each GPU reads 17.5 GB per step, so 3.35e12/17.5e9 = 191.4 tok/s per GPU and 191.4 tok/s per host at batch 1, multiplied by the batch (17 concurrent slots) = ~3,250 output tok/s per host at the canonical 17-slot occupancy. Demand is 3K avg / 12K peak, so decode is not binding for (a) at 21 hosts (~68K tok/s) or for (c) at 15 cards (7B: 14 GB weights -> 239 tok/s per card per step x ~46 KV slots x 15 cards = ~165K tok/s). The conclusion survives, but only because the reader performs an arithmetic the chapter never shows and never labels.
issue.root_cause: The worked example was built around the prefill/compute screen (the harder and more novel number) and the decode half of the stated method was dropped rather than deferred with a pointer.
issue.correction: Add the decode screen to §3 and to Table 12-2: state the per-host decode rate at the canonical concurrency (weights-read-amortized over the batch), compare it to 3K/12K tok/s, and fill the 'Decode pool sizing' row for (b) with a host count (decode-phase occupancy is 300 x 25 ms = 7.5 s of the 8.6 s service time, so the decode pool's in-flight population is 40 x 7.5 = 300 requests at peak -> ~18 hosts at 17 slots/host). If the decode screen is deliberately out of scope for this chapter, say so explicitly and cross-reference the chapter that owns it, rather than leaving a half-filled table row.
issue.acceptance_test: Every candidate in Table 12-1 and Table 12-2 has a numeric decode capacity alongside its prefill capacity, and the reader can confirm from the table alone that decode does not bind at either the average or the peak.

issue.quoted_clause: §3: 'the screen below is run at the average — at peak it reads ⌈400 × 8.6 / 17⌉ = 203 hosts at full utilization.'  §8: 'The architect's decision: escalate to the **cluster** tier but keep it on-prem — run a fleet of 8×H100 replicas behind a load balancer. With the canonical whole-slot KV/service-time screen (Ch 16/17), the fleet is ⌈100 × 8.6 / 17⌉ = **51 hosts at full utilization** — 73 working + 1 spare = **74 hosts** at Ch17's 70% target and N−1 rule on the u-only screen (ρ = 1), or 77 working + 1 spare = **78 hosts** at the Table 17-1 policy (u × ρ = 0.70 × 0.95 = 0.665) ... The result, with the 74-host headroom fleet (78 hosts at the Table 17-1 policy): p95 TTFT back under 1.8 s at 100 rps [ILLUSTRATIVE SCENARIO RESULT]
issue.observed: The chapter's own escalation analysis computes the peak screen for the escalated workload (400 rps -> 203 hosts at full utilization) and then the mini-case, which is the chapter's capstone, presents 51/74/78 hosts as 'the fleet' and asserts a recovered SLO, without ever mentioning the 400 rps peak. The mini-case's stated result is therefore true only at average load and false at the peak the chapter itself derived. A reader who takes 78 hosts as the answer will re-saturate the service the moment the daily peak arrives.
issue.evidence: Re-derivation: 78 hosts x (17 slots / 8.6 s) = 78 x 1.977 = 154 rps of capacity against the canonical 4x peak/average shape at 100 rps average = 400 rps peak. Oversubscription = 400/154 = 2.6x. The chapter's own §3 states the peak screen is 203 hosts at full utilization (400 x 8.6 / 17 = 202.35 -> 203), i.e. 203/78 = 2.6x the fleet the mini-case recommends. The mini-case's 'p95 TTFT back under 1.8 s at 100 rps' is a statement about average load only.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case was written around the average-load screen and the peak screen computed in §3 was not carried into it; the mini-case therefore does not integrate the chapter's own reasoning, which is the specific failure mode the mini-case format exists to prevent.
issue.correction: Add the peak to the mini-case: state that the 4x peak/average shape persists, that the peak screen reads 203 hosts at full utilization (and ~300+ under the Table 17-1 policy), and that the architect must either provision for the peak, shape it, or accept a peak SLO breach. Then qualify the 'p95 TTFT back under 1.8 s' result as an average-load result and add the peak-load SLO outcome. Alternatively, if the mini-case is deliberately an average-load scenario, say so and state the peak consequence explicitly.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case states a fleet size, the load (average and peak) it serves, and the SLO outcome at both. A reader cannot leave the mini-case believing 78 hosts satisfies the escalated workload's peak.

issue.page_hint: Ch 12 §8 (mini-case) vs Table 12-2 'Monthly fully loaded cost' row
issue.quoted_clause: §8: 'The decision between Candidates (a) and (b) hinges on whether the doubled hardware cost of Candidate (b) is justified by its operational flexibility (e.g., independent scaling of prefill and decode pools, fault isolation).'  Table 12-2: 'not costed / not comparable — the ~21-host figure is the Ch 16 monolithic fleet screen; a two-pool deployment needs the ~19-host prefill pool + a decode pool + KV-transfer fabric, priced in a follow-up screen'
issue.observed: The mini-case's central decision criterion is a cost ratio ('the doubled hardware cost of Candidate (b)') that the chapter explicitly declines to compute and defers to 'a follow-up screen' that the book does not provide. The chapter's headline architectural decision therefore rests on an unevidenced number, and the two statements contradict each other within the same chapter.
issue.evidence: Independent re-derivation of the two-pool host count at the canonical peak, which the chapter could have done: prefill pool is compute-bound -> 368,000 / 19,780 = 18.6 -> 19 hosts. Decode pool is KV-resident for the decode phase only: decode duration = 300 tokens x 25 ms TPOT = 7.5 s, so in-flight decode population at 40 rps = 40 x 7.5 = 300 requests; at 17 slots/host -> 300/17 = 17.6 -> 18 hosts. Total ~37 hosts vs the monolithic 21 -> ~1.76x, not 2x, and the ratio is workload-shape dependent (it approaches 1x when decode is a small fraction of service time and 2x when decode dominates). The chapter's own framing (decode is 7.5 s of the 8.6 s service time) makes the ratio close to 2x, so the mini-case's claim is directionally right but is asserted rather than derived, and the true figure is not exactly 2x.
issue.root_cause: The chapter treats the two-pool host count as a Ch 16 economics matter, but the host count is a capacity result that belongs to this chapter's own screens; only the dollar conversion belongs to Ch 16.
issue.correction: Compute the two-pool host count in §3 (prefill pool from the compute screen, decode pool from the decode-phase KV occupancy screen) and state the resulting host ratio (approximately 1.8x at the canonical peak, with the reason it is not exactly 2x). Then the mini-case's 'doubled hardware cost' becomes a derived figure with a stated derivation, and Table 12-2's 'not costed' cell can be replaced by '~37 hosts (19 prefill + 18 decode) vs 21 monolithic; dollar conversion in Ch 16'.
issue.acceptance_test: The 'doubled hardware cost' claim in the mini-case is traceable to a host-count derivation in §3 or Table 12-2, and the derivation states the workload-shape dependence of the ratio.

issue.quoted_clause: the architect's first return-to-synthesis move is to renegotiate the budget, shape peak demand, or revisit the model class. ... Its memory and economics are trivially favorable; its fate turns on that measured gate. Because candidate (c)'s quality gate is still open **[HYPOTHESIS]**, it is not a finalist — and it stays in the gate evaluation (Ch 14) rather than being excluded pre-measurement; the finalists are Candidates (a) and (b), and the near-term decision falls between them.
issue.observed: The mini-case identifies the binding constraint (the $15,000 monthly budget, which the 21-host fleet exceeds by ~10.4x) and names 'revisit the model class' as one of the three return-to-synthesis moves. Candidate (c) IS the model-class revisit. Yet the mini-case then excludes (c) from the finalist set on the strength of an open quality gate, asserts that (c)'s economics are 'trivially favorable' without a number, and declares that the decision falls between (a) and (b) — two candidates whose own economics fail the budget by 10.4x and 15.5x. The chapter's conclusion therefore excludes the only candidate that could plausibly satisfy the binding constraint, on a gate that is not the binding constraint.
issue.evidence: Independent re-derivation from the chapter's own totals: the self-host per-host monthly cost is recoverable from the two stated totals (21 x X + $10,000 staff = $155,816.93 -> X = $6,943.66/host/mo; cross-check 32 x $6,943.66 + $10,000 = $232,197, matching the stated $232.2K). At $6,943.66/host/mo, candidate (c)'s own screen (~4 H100 cards at average, ~15 at peak) is roughly 15 x (single-card monthly cost) and is plausibly inside the $15,000 budget, whereas (a) at 21 hosts is $155.8K and (b) at ~37 hosts is ~$267K. The chapter never performs this comparison, so the reader cannot see that the budget constraint may be satisfiable only by (c).
issue.root_cause: The mini-case applies the three gates in the order they were defined (memory, throughput, quality) and stops at the first open gate, instead of ranking the gates by which one is actually binding for this stakeholder.
issue.correction: In the mini-case, compute candidate (c)'s monthly cost against the $15,000 budget using the same per-host cost basis the chapter already uses for (a) and (b), and state the result. Then state the conclusion that follows: the binding constraint is economic, not quality, so the quality gate on (c) is worth running first because it is the only candidate whose economics could clear the budget. If (c) is still excluded, the chapter must say why the budget cannot be met by any candidate and what the architect presents to the stakeholder.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case states a monthly cost for each of (a), (b), and (c) on a common basis and identifies which candidates clear the $15,000 budget. The stated finalist set is consistent with that comparison.

issue.page_hint: Ch 13 §6 (Architecture Consequence), Fig 13.1 caption; vs Ch 13 §2 (Mental Model)
issue.quoted_clause: Fig 13.1 caption: 'de-escalation (blue) fires on data-residency/sovereignty, on-device requirements, and cost — but scale-down decisions should also reference **utilization** (sustained low load on a tier), **failure domain** (a smaller tier has a smaller blast radius), **operations burden** (fewer hosts to run), and **SLO margin** (headroom to absorb a burst without breaching the SLO). Make these measurable: thresholds are examples to calibrate to your SLO headroom policy, e.g. de-escalate when 30-day p95 utilization < 40% AND SLO headroom ≥ 2× (30-day p95 TTFT ≤ half the SLO) AND the smaller tier's failure domain is acceptable.'  §2: '**Distance / geography**: SLO can't be met because the users are too far from the serving site → move the serving edge closer or add regional replicas (a *placement* move, not a climb — it belongs with the de-escalation moves in Fig 13.1).'
issue.observed: The figure caption carries roughly 150 words of de-escalation policy, including four named criteria and a concrete numeric threshold rule (30-day p95 utilization < 40% AND SLO headroom >= 2x AND acceptable failure domain), none of which appears anywhere in the chapter's body. Simultaneously, the body's §2 explicitly assigns the geography trigger to 'the de-escalation moves in Fig 13.1', but the caption's de-escalation list does not include geography; and the caption's escalation list ('demand, KV residency, or goodput') omits the body's Memory trigger ('model + KV no longer fits one node -> cluster'). The caption and the body describe different figures.
issue.evidence: Text comparison: §2's escalation triggers are Memory, KV residency per GPU, Traffic, Contention/phase interference, Distance/geography. The caption's escalation triggers are demand, KV residency, goodput. §2's de-escalation content is geography only; the caption's is data-residency, on-device, cost, utilization, failure domain, operations burden, SLO margin. Cost appears only in the caption; geography appears only in the body. The caption also asserts a threshold policy with no derivation and no label beyond the figure's [ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual] tag, which covers the diagram but not a policy rule.
issue.root_cause: The caption was used as a convenient place to park policy prose that had no home in the body, and the figure was then drawn from a trigger list that drifted from the chapter's own §2 list.
issue.correction: Move the de-escalation criteria and the threshold example into §2 (or a short §2 subsection) as body prose with their own evidence label, and reduce the caption to what a caption should do: name the diagram, state the reading order, and say what the reader should learn. Reconcile the trigger lists so that the caption's escalation and de-escalation sets match §2 exactly, including geography and the memory trigger. If the numeric threshold rule is retained, label it [ILLUSTRATIVE heuristic] in the body where it can be argued with, not only inside a caption.
issue.acceptance_test: Every trigger named in the Fig 13.1 caption appears in §2, and every trigger in §2 appears in the caption; the caption is under ~60 words; the threshold policy appears in the body with an explicit evidence label.

issue.quoted_clause: Candidate (a): single 8×H100 host with prefix caching (Ch. 11). This is the per-request-latency baseline — the single 8×H100 host that the early book (Ch 2, 4, 7, 8) establishes as meeting one request's latency SLO. It is *not* a capacity baseline: a lone host cannot carry the arrival rate ... so its throughput-gate failure below is expected
issue.observed: The candidate is defined as 'a single 8×H100 host', but the throughput gate is then evaluated against a replicated fleet ('the gate closes only when the host class is replicated to ~5 hosts ... ~6 ... and ~21 at peak'). A candidate defined as one host can never pass a throughput gate that is evaluated on 21 hosts. The chapter's own verdict for (a) is therefore 'conditional finalist' with 'throughput open' — a candidate that fails a gate by construction, with the gate's verdict computed on a different object than the candidate.
issue.evidence: Structural: §3's verdict for (a) is '✗ single-host capacity: needs ~5 hosts at average load ... ~19 at the 368K peak prefill screen' (Table 12-1) and 'throughput open' (Table 12-1 second table). §6 then advances (a) as a 'conditional finalist'. The object being gated (one host) and the object being scored (a replicated host class) are never reconciled.
issue.root_cause: The chapter conflates two different design objects — a single-host latency baseline and a replicated host class — under one candidate label, then scores the gate on the second while describing the candidate as the first.
issue.correction: Define candidate (a) explicitly as 'the 8xH100 host class, replicated to meet demand; a single instance is the per-request-latency baseline', and state that the throughput gate is evaluated at fleet level for all three candidates (a), (b), and (c) — with the per-instance latency gate evaluated on one host. Then the verdict language ('conditional finalist, throughput open') becomes meaningful: the open gate is the fleet-level throughput and SLO measurement, not a structural failure of the candidate.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can state, for each candidate, what object the memory gate, the throughput gate, and the quality gate are applied to, and no candidate is described as a single host while being scored as a fleet.

issue.page_hint: Ch 12 §3, Candidate (b); §3 'Memory/residency arithmetic summary'; Table 12-1 (b) memory cell; §8
issue.quoted_clause: Each pool therefore needs its own 8×H100 host (residency = 140 GB weights plus the pool's in-flight KV population — at the canonical per-host KV budget (640 − 140 weights − ~64 runtime ≈ 436 GB, Ch 7/17), 140 GB weights + 436 GB KV + ~64 GB runtime = 640 GB — exactly the pool, zero headroom; co-residency beyond the canonical KV budget requires reducing the KV allocation or adding memory; one request's 24 GB is not the pool's population).
issue.observed: The same 436 GB KV population is applied to both pools, and 'zero headroom' is asserted for both. That is true only for the decode pool, which must hold the KV of every in-flight decode. The prefill pool holds KV only transiently for requests currently being prefilled (and hands it off), so its KV population is far smaller and it has substantial headroom. The chapter's own parenthetical ('one request's 24 GB is not the pool's population') shows the author is aware that pool populations differ, but the arithmetic then treats them as identical.
issue.evidence: Independent re-derivation at the canonical peak: decode phase duration = 300 tokens x 25 ms TPOT = 7.5 s, so the decode pool's in-flight population = 40 rps x 7.5 s = 300 requests x 24.9 GB = 7.47 TB of KV, i.e. ~18 hosts at 17 slots/host. The prefill pool's in-flight population = 40 rps x (8.6 - 7.5) s = 44 requests x 24.9 GB = 1.1 TB, i.e. ~3 hosts of KV (and 19 hosts of compute). The two pools' KV populations differ by ~7x, so 'exactly the pool, zero headroom' is correct for the decode pool and wrong for the prefill pool.
issue.root_cause: The canonical per-host KV budget (a capacity figure) was reused as a requirement figure for both pools, without distinguishing the phase in which KV is resident.
issue.correction: Split the statement: the decode pool's requirement is 140 GB weights + up to 436 GB of resident decode KV + ~64 GB runtime = 640 GB (zero headroom at the canonical budget); the prefill pool's requirement is 140 GB weights + a transient KV working set (bounded by the number of concurrent prefills, not by the decode population) + ~64 GB runtime, leaving the balance of the 436 GB as headroom. Update Table 12-1's (b) memory cell and the §3 summary accordingly.
issue.acceptance_test: Table 12-1's (b) memory cell distinguishes the two pools' KV populations, and the 'zero headroom' claim is attached to the decode pool only.

issue.quoted_clause: its throughput is a genuine strength (24,725 prefill tok/s per H100 vs the 70B's ~19,780 per GPU under TP=8 — ~1.25× per GPU, ~10× per host-equivalent; ~4 cards at average load, ~15 at peak, Table 12-2)
issue.observed: The '~10x per host-equivalent' figure compares an 8-card 7B node (8 x 24,725 = 197,800 tok/s) against an 8-card 70B node (19,780 tok/s), but candidate (c)'s declared layout is one H100, not eight. Table 12-2 explicitly warns about exactly this ('the ~197K figure is the 8-GPU node, 8 x 24,725 ≈ 197,800, not this layout'), so the chapter knows the hazard and then states the unqualified 10x in the prose that a reader is most likely to remember.
issue.evidence: Re-derivation: 24,725 / 19,780 = 1.25x (per GPU, correct). 8 x 24,725 / 19,780 = 10.0x (per 8-card node, but candidate (c) declares 1 card). A reader who takes '~10x per host-equivalent' as candidate (c)'s advantage over candidate (a) will believe a single H100 is 10x an 8xH100 host, which is false by a factor of 80.
issue.root_cause: A comparison made for a hypothetical 8-card 7B node was carried into the candidate's own description without the layout qualifier that the table supplies.
issue.correction: Either drop the '~10x per host-equivalent' clause from §3 (the 1.25x per-GPU figure plus the card counts in Table 12-2 carry the argument), or restate it as: '~1.25x per GPU; an 8-card 7B node would be ~10x an 8-card 70B node, but candidate (c) is declared as a single card, so its advantage is 1.25x per card and 4 cards at average load.'
issue.acceptance_test: Every throughput ratio quoted for candidate (c) names the layout it applies to, and no ratio in §3 compares a 1-card layout against an 8-card layout without saying so.

issue.quoted_clause: The 4-bit KV cache is a *memory* optimization, not a quality one; aggressive KV quantization can add its own quality penalty that must also be validated on the target workload.
issue.observed: The two clauses joined by the semicolon contradict each other. 'Not a quality one' read literally means the change has no quality effect, which the second clause denies. The intended meaning is that the change is introduced for memory reasons and is not expected to improve quality — but as written the sentence licenses the inference that 4-bit KV is quality-neutral, which is exactly the inference the chapter's own §7 open question and §5 common mistake ('Using KV-quantization as a free lunch') exist to prevent.
issue.evidence: Internal contradiction within one sentence; the same chapter's §5 states 'Quantizing the KV cache reduces memory footprint but introduces quality degradation that may be unacceptable for the target workload' and §7 lists 8-bit KV quality as an open [HYPOTHESIS].
issue.root_cause: The clause was compressed to make the point that KV quantization is not a quality optimization, and the compression dropped the 'improvement' qualifier that distinguishes 'not introduced for quality reasons' from 'has no quality effect'.
issue.correction: Rewrite: 'The 4-bit KV cache is introduced as a *memory* optimization, not as a quality improvement; it can nonetheless add its own quality penalty, which must be validated on the target workload.'
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in the book asserts or implies that KV quantization is quality-neutral; a reader who reads §3's sentence cannot conclude that 4-bit KV is free.

issue.page_hint: Ch 12 §3 (Candidate (a) prose) vs Table 12-1 (a) verdict cell
issue.quoted_clause: §3: 'a lone host cannot carry the arrival rate (~6 hosts are needed for the canonical average, and ~21 at peak ...) ... the gate closes only when the host class is replicated to ~5 hosts on the average prefill screen (92K ÷ 19.8K ≈ 4.65 → 5), ~6 on the average KV/service-time screen (10 × 8.6 ÷ 17 ≈ 5.06 → 6), and ~21 at peak (40 × 8.6 ÷ 17 ≈ 20.2 → 21)'.  Table 12-1: '✗ single-host capacity: needs ~5 hosts at average load (92K tok/s); ~19 at the 368K peak prefill screen, before headroom'
issue.observed: Two different peak host counts (21 and 19) appear for the same candidate in the same chapter, derived from two different screens, with no statement of which one binds. The prose gives the KV/service-time screen at peak (21) and omits the prefill screen at peak (19); the table gives the prefill screen at peak (19) and omits the KV screen (21). At the average the prose gives both (5 and 6) but does not say that 6 is the binding one. A reader comparing prose to table sees an unexplained 21-vs-19 discrepancy.
issue.evidence: Re-derivation: prefill screen = demand / 19,780 tok/s per host -> 92,000/19,780 = 4.65 -> 5 (avg), 368,000/19,780 = 18.60 -> 19 (peak). KV/service-time screen = rps x 8.6 s / 17 slots -> 10 x 8.6/17 = 5.06 -> 6 (avg), 40 x 8.6/17 = 20.24 -> 21 (peak). The KV screen binds in both cases (6 > 5, 21 > 19). The chapter's own numbers therefore imply a single answer (6 at average, 21 at peak) that the prose and the table each present only partially.
issue.root_cause: Two capacity screens were introduced without a stated combination rule (take the max), and each surface (prose, table) happened to show a different one.
issue.correction: State the combination rule once in §3: 'the fleet size is the maximum of the compute screen and the KV/service-time screen; at the canonical load the KV screen binds (6 hosts at average, 21 at peak, versus 5 and 19 on the compute screen).' Then show both screens in Table 12-1's verdict cell for (a) and (b), and use the binding figure in the prose.
issue.acceptance_test: Every host count quoted for the canonical workload names its screen, and the chapter states which screen binds at average and at peak; no two surfaces quote different peak host counts without labeling the screen.

issue.quoted_clause: the three gates ... **memory fit** (weight memory plus KV cache must fit within the on-premise GPU inventory), **throughput at the SLO** (total tokens-per-second across the installed devices, delivered within the TTFT/TPOT budget, must exceed the traffic demand), and **quality**
issue.observed: The gate is named and defined as SLO-conditioned throughput, but it is evaluated with an idealized, SLO-independent prefill rate (35% MFU, no batching efficiency, no queueing, no TPOT check, no TTFT check). The chapter's own Table 12-1 records the SLO as '? TTFT SLO unmeasured' for (a) and (b), so the gate that is being scored is not the gate that is named. A reader could conclude that a candidate passing the prefill screen has passed 'throughput at the SLO'.
issue.evidence: The computed quantity is 989 TFLOP/s x 35% / 17.5 GFLOP/token = 19,780 tok/s, a raw compute-bound prefill ceiling at an assumed MFU. Nothing in the derivation involves TTFT, TPOT, batching, or admission control. The chapter's §4 item 3 says the number should be 'measured on the target hardware', which the worked example does not do either.
issue.root_cause: The chapter needed a screen computable from the canonical inputs and used a compute ceiling, then attached the SLO-conditioned gate name to it; the distinction between 'capacity screen' and 'goodput at the SLO' was never made explicit.
issue.correction: Rename the computed quantity throughout §3 and Table 12-1 as what it is — 'the idealized prefill capacity screen' — and state explicitly that the throughput-at-the-SLO gate is not closed by this screen and is closed only by the Ch 14 measurement. Add a one-line note that a capacity screen can only ever be an upper bound on goodput, since goodput is capacity minus the requests that miss the SLO.
issue.acceptance_test: No table cell or prose sentence presents the 19,780 tok/s figure as a throughput-at-the-SLO result; the word 'goodput' appears with a definition in this chapter or the reader is pointed to where it is defined.

issue.quoted_clause: §3: 'The KV cache for 9.2K context at FP16 precision ... is approximately 24 GB (2 × num_layers × hidden_dim × 9,200 × 2 bytes per FP16 element)'.  §4: 'where L is the context length (full-MHA assumption: n_KV-heads × d_kv = d_hidden; for GQA/MQA use the reduced KV-head count)'
issue.observed: §4 states the full-MHA caveat explicitly; §3's inline formula uses hidden_dim with no caveat. A reader who reuses §3's formula for a GQA or MQA model — the case the book elsewhere insists on distinguishing — will overstate the KV footprint by the GQA factor (e.g. 8x for an 8-way GQA model). The chapter's own §3 candidate (c) paragraph makes the point that 'the per-token KV depends on the model's own attention shape ... NOT the 70B's constant', which directly contradicts the unqualified hidden_dim formula two paragraphs earlier.
issue.evidence: Formula comparison: §3's form 2 x L x d_hidden x L_ctx x bytes is valid only when n_KV-heads x d_kv = d_hidden. §4's form 2 x L x n_KV-heads x d_kv x L_ctx x bytes is general. For the canonical 70B (80 layers, 8192 hidden, full MHA) both give 2 x 80 x 8192 x 9,200 x 2 = 24.12 GB, so the canonical numbers are unaffected; the risk is in reuse.
issue.root_cause: The opening paragraph uses a shorthand form for the canonical model without marking it as model-specific, while the chapter's own method section gives the general form.
issue.correction: Use the general form in §3 as well, with the canonical substitution shown: '2 x n_layers x n_KV-heads x d_kv x 9,200 x bytes = 2 x 80 x 8192 x 9,200 x 2 = 24.1 GB (full MHA, so n_KV-heads x d_kv = d_hidden = 8,192)'. Add a parenthetical that GQA/MQA reduce this by the KV-head ratio.
issue.acceptance_test: Every KV formula in Ch 12 is the general n_KV-heads x d_kv form, or is explicitly marked '(full MHA)'; a reader applying the chapter's formula to a GQA model gets the correct footprint.

issue.quoted_clause: §3: 'Quality: the 70B is the workload's quality reference, so candidate (a) inherits the reference quality by definition rather than by measurement — the gate is satisfied relative to the reference, and the absolute requirement still needs the Ch 14 capability screen on the true evaluation set.'  §8: '**quality** (answer quality on the evaluation set must meet the ~70B requirement)'
issue.observed: The quality gate is defined as 'must meet the ~70B requirement', but candidates (a) and (b) ARE the 70B.
