A gate defined relative to the model that the candidate is built from is satisfied by construction and cannot discriminate between candidates. The chapter half-acknowledges this ('satisfied relative to the reference') but never states what the absolute bar is, so the quality gate has no operational content for (a) and (b) and the reader cannot tell what Ch 14 will measure against.
issue.evidence: Logical: gate(candidate) = quality(candidate) >= quality(70B); for candidates (a) and (b), quality(candidate) = quality(70B) by construction, so the gate is vacuous for exactly the two candidates that advance. The chapter's own §7 lists 'Whether 8-bit KV caching is sufficient for 9.2K context at FP16-equivalent quality' as an open question, which is the only place where a non-vacuous quality question about (a)/(b) appears.
issue.root_cause: The chapter uses 'quality' for two different things — a relative comparison against a reference model and an absolute capability bar — without separating them, and the gate definition inherits the relative sense.
issue.correction: Split the quality gate into two named checks in §8: (i) a relative check (candidate quality vs the 70B reference on the evaluation set), which is vacuous for (a) and (b) and decisive for (c); and (ii) an absolute capability check (the workload's task-level accuracy bar, e.g. a retrieval-Q&A correctness threshold), which applies to all candidates including (a) and (b). State that (a) and (b) pass (i) by construction and still owe (ii).
issue.acceptance_test: The quality gate has a stated absolute threshold or an explicit pointer to where it is defined, and the chapter says plainly that (a) and (b) satisfy the relative check trivially.

issue.page_hint: Ch 12 §7 (What We Still Don't Know), third bullet
issue.quoted_clause: **P/D-disaggregation communication overhead in multi-host settings.** The KV-transfer volume and latency between prefill and decode pools — as a function of context length, request rate, and fabric bandwidth — is relatively unexplored at the 70B scale; the actual communication volume and its latency impact depend on the routing library and network topology **[HYPOTHESIS]**.
issue.observed: This is listed as an open empirical question, but the KV-transfer volume is fully determined by the canonical workload's own inputs and can be computed analytically. Leaving it as 'relatively unexplored' withholds the single most decision-relevant number for candidate (b), and it is the number that determines whether the two-pool design is even fabric-feasible at the canonical peak.
issue.evidence: Independent re-derivation from the canonical inputs: each request transfers its KV once from the prefill pool to the decode pool. KV per request at the 9.5K context = 24.9 GB. At 10 rps average: 24.9 x 10 = 249 GB/s. At 40 rps peak: 24.9 x 40 = 996 GB/s (~1 TB/s) of sustained KV traffic, one-directional. Against fabric: a single 400 Gb/s InfiniBand NDR port is 50 GB/s, so the peak needs ~20 NDR ports or ~10 XDR (800 Gb/s) ports; a single H100 NVLink 4.0 link is 450 GB/s per direction, so ~3 links sustained at peak. The chapter's own §3 already flags the KV-transfer fabric as a cost item for candidate (b) ('plus the KV-transfer fabric'), so the number belongs in the chapter.
issue.root_cause: The open-questions list was populated from what the author had not measured, without first checking which of the listed unknowns are already determined by the canonical inputs the chapter has adopted.
issue.correction: Convert this bullet into a derived constraint in §3 (candidate (b)): state the KV-transfer rate (249 GB/s average, ~996 GB/s peak), compare it to the fabric the architecture would need, and note that the transfer must complete inside the TTFT budget (a 24.9 GB transfer at, say, 200 GB/s effective adds ~125 ms to TTFT). Then narrow the §7 bullet to what genuinely remains unknown: the achieved efficiency of the routing library, the overlap achieved between transfer and decode, and the behaviour under burst.
issue.acceptance_test: The chapter states a KV-transfer bandwidth figure for the canonical workload and compares it to a named fabric; the §7 bullet no longer lists as 'unknown' anything the chapter's own inputs determine.

issue.quoted_clause: the self-host totals do not scale purely per-host ($155,816.93, ≈$24.97/1K on the 6.24M‑req/mo business‑hours basis, Ch 16 — the cloud legs are $87,600 ≈ $14.04/1K at the default paid-occupancy input and $306,600 ≈ $49.13/1K at 21 hosts always-on)
issue.observed: Two problems. (1) The 6.24M-req/mo basis is not reproducible from anything stated in the chapter: the canonical workload is ~10 rps average, which over a full month is 25.92M requests, and the chapter never states the business-hours assumption (hours per month, or effective rate) that yields 6.24M. The reader cannot check any of the three per-1K figures. (2) The $87,600 cloud leg equals exactly 6 hosts x 730 h x $20/h = $87,600 — that is, it prices the average-load host count (6 hosts, from the KV/service-time screen), not a discount or partial occupancy of the 21-host peak fleet. The label 'default paid-occupancy input' is undefined, and the two cloud legs in the same parenthetical price different fleets while appearing to price the same one.
issue.evidence: Re-derivation: 6.24M requests at 10 rps implies 624,000 s = 173.3 h/month of serving, which the chapter never states (173.3 h is not a recognizable business-hours figure: 8 h x 22 days = 176 h would give 6.336M). Per-1K checks: 155,816.93/6,240 = $24.97; 87,600/6,240 = $14.04; 306,600/6,240 = $49.13 — all three are arithmetically correct against 6.24M, so the defect is the unstated denominator, not the division. 87,600/(730 x 20) = 6.0 hosts exactly.
issue.root_cause: The economics were imported from Ch 16 with a pointer rather than restated with their assumptions, and the mini-case is expected to be self-contained enough for the reader to audit its headline numbers.
issue.correction: State the volume basis in the mini-case: 'the canonical workload serves 6.24M requests/month on a business-hours basis (10 rps average x 173.3 serving hours/month; 25.92M on a 24x7 basis)'. State the paid-occupancy basis explicitly: '$87,600 = 6 hosts x 730 h x $20/h, i.e. the average-load fleet priced always-on, versus $306,600 = 21 hosts x 730 h x $20/h for the peak fleet'. If the 6.24M figure is Ch 16's, keep the cross-reference but add the one-line derivation so the reader can reproduce it.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can reproduce 6.24M, $24.97/1K, $14.04/1K, and $49.13/1K from the mini-case text alone, and can tell which fleet each cloud leg prices.

issue.quoted_clause: Total fleet cost $155.8K/mo (21 hosts) ÷ $15K = ~10.4× the total budget — the economic constraint fails at fleet scale (Ch 16). ... the 21-host full-utilization screen fleet (Ch 16 case (i)/KV-screen line) costs ~$155.8K/mo
issue.observed: The fleet is sized for the 40 rps peak (21 hosts) while the per-1K figures amortize that peak-capacity fleet over the average-volume basis (6.24M requests/month). That is a legitimate planning choice, but the chapter never states it, so the reader sees a peak-sized fleet divided by an average-volume denominator with no indication that the two are on different operating points. This is exactly the kind of denominator/operating-point mismatch that makes a cost figure look better than it is.
issue.evidence: Structural: 21 hosts is derived from 40 rps peak x 8.6 s / 17 slots (Ch 13); 6.24M requests/month corresponds to ~10 rps average over 173.3 h. The fleet therefore carries peak capacity while the unit cost is computed on average volume. The chapter's own Table 12-2 flags 'Peak headroom (N−1): not demonstrated' for all candidates, so the fleet is not even sized for the peak with headroom.
issue.root_cause: Capacity sizing and cost amortization were taken from two different screens without a sentence reconciling the operating points.
issue.correction: Add one sentence: 'The fleet is sized for the 40 rps peak while the unit economics amortize that capacity over the average-volume month; the resulting $/1K is therefore a peak-capacity cost, not a steady-state cost, and it improves only if the peak is shaped or the fleet is scaled down.' Then show the steady-state alternative (6 hosts at average load) alongside the peak fleet so the reader sees both.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case states which operating point each cost figure corresponds to, and a reader cannot mistake the peak-amortized $/1K for a steady-state cost.

issue.quoted_clause: The stakeholder's $15,000 is a total monthly system budget — the chapter notes it equals one host's cloud-equivalent (one 8×H100 at ~$20/hr × 730 hr ≈ $14.6K/mo; an on-premise host has no $/hr, so this is a budget cap, not a metered cost, and the cloud-equivalent is a proxy at those assumptions). ... The operational constraint is that the system must run on existing on-premise GPU infrastructure (no cloud add-ons).
issue.observed: The chapter compares the $15,000 budget only against a cloud proxy that the architect is explicitly forbidden from buying, and never against the on-premise cost it already computes elsewhere in the same paragraph. The on-premise per-host monthly cost is recoverable from the chapter's own totals and is the number that actually answers 'what does $15,000 buy on-prem?' — a question the mini-case poses and leaves unanswered.
issue.evidence: Re-derivation from the chapter's own figures: 21 hosts x X + $10,000 staff = $155,816.93 -> X = $6,943.66/host/month; cross-check 32 x $6,943.66 + $10,000 = $232,197, matching the stated ~$232.2K. So $15,000/month buys about 2.2 on-prem 8xH100 hosts gross of staff, or about 0.7 hosts plus the $10K staff line — i.e. roughly one host, against a 21-host requirement. The chapter states the 10.4x overshoot but never the per-host on-premise cost, even though it is derivable from two numbers it prints.
issue.root_cause: The economics were framed as a cloud-versus-budget comparison because the cloud proxy was the number Ch 16 supplied, rather than being framed against the on-premise constraint the stakeholder actually imposed.
issue.correction: State the on-premise per-host monthly cost explicitly (~$6,944/host/month, derived from the two totals) and answer the stakeholder's question directly: '$15,000/month buys roughly two on-prem 8xH100 hosts (or one plus the $10K staff line) against a 21-host requirement — the gap is a factor of ~10, and it is a capital-and-staff gap, not a rental-rate gap.' Keep the cloud-equivalent as a secondary comparison, clearly labelled as a proxy for a deployment the stakeholder has excluded.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case states what $15,000/month buys in on-premise hosts and states the gap in those units; the cloud proxy is labelled as a non-actionable reference.

issue.quoted_clause: The architect generates three candidates using the method from §12.3. Candidate (a): a single 8×H100 host with 70B FP16 weights + 24 GB KV cache and prefix caching, which fits the memory budget (164 GB < 640 GB aggregate ...) — but as Chapter 8 shows, one 8×H100 host sustains only ~19,800 prefill-tokens/s at the idealized 35%-MFU TP=8 operating point (~19,780 tok/s per GPU; the host aggregate is the same rate, since each GPU carries 1/8 of the shared token stream — the ~2,472 figure is a full-model-equivalent FLOP rate, not a per-GPU capability), far short of the ~92K input tokens/s the 10 rps average demands, so the memory gate passes while the throughput gate already fails.
issue.observed: The mini-case's candidate-generation section re-narrates §3's arithmetic almost verbatim, including the parenthetical explanations of the TP=8 rate and the 2,472 figure. A mini-case should require the reader to perform the chapter's reasoning, not replay it. The genuinely new work in this mini-case (the budget analysis, the 32-host policy fleet, the operational constraint, the return-to-synthesis move) is squeezed into the last third, while the first two-thirds restate material the reader has just read.
issue.evidence: Structural comparison: §3 and §8 both state 140 + 24 = 164 GB < 640 GB, both state ~19,800 tok/s at 35% MFU with the same parenthetical, both state the 92K demand, and both state the ~15 GB / 14 + 1.2 GB residency for candidate (c). The mini-case adds no calculation the reader has not been handed.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case was written as a summary of the chapter rather than as an application of it; the chapter's own §8 title ('From Vague Ask to Candidate Architectures') promises the latter.
issue.correction: Compress the candidate-generation paragraphs to the inputs and the decisions (what the stakeholder's constraints are, what the architect computes, what the verdicts are) and move the arithmetic the reader can perform themselves into the exercise framing — e.g. give the per-host prefill rate and the demand and ask the reader to derive the host counts. Expand the budget and peak-fleet work, which is where the mini-case's unique contribution lies.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case contains at least one quantity the reader must compute rather than read, and its length is dominated by the new economic and peak-fleet analysis rather than by restating §3.

issue.page_hint: Ch 13 §3, opening paragraph of 'Placing the Canonical Workload'
issue.quoted_clause: The canonical enterprise-Q&A RAG workload's model residency is **server-class**, and at the 40 rps peak its deployment is a **cluster** of ~21 server-class hosts (Ch 16/17) — placed there by Table 13-1's *traffic > host goodput* trigger, not by weight-splitting.
issue.observed: The headline host count for the canonical workload is the full-utilization screen (21 hosts), which the same chapter later shows is 32 hosts under the Table 17-1 provisioning policy (70% x 95% + N-1). Leading with 21 understates the provisioned fleet by 52%, and a reader who cites '21 hosts' from this chapter will under-provision. Ch 12's mini-case gives both figures; Ch 13's headline gives only the smaller one.
issue.evidence: Re-derivation: 344/(17 x 0.665) = 30.43 -> 31 working + 1 spare = 32 total (the chapter's own arithmetic, stated later in the same section). 32/21 = 1.52, i.e. the policy fleet is 52% larger than the screen figure.
issue.root_cause: The section's opening sentence was written before the policy screen was introduced and was not updated when the policy numbers were added.
issue.correction: Lead with both: 'at the 40 rps peak its deployment is a **cluster** of ~21 server-class hosts at full utilization, or 32 under the Table 17-1 provisioning policy (70% x 95% + N-1)'. Add a one-line note that the screen figure is a capacity floor and the policy figure is the provisioned fleet.
issue.acceptance_test: The first host count a reader encounters for the canonical workload is accompanied by its policy counterpart, and no chapter quotes '21 hosts' without noting that it is the full-utilization screen.

issue.page_hint: Ch 13 §3, 'Memory' bullet; and the 17.5-slot figure throughout Ch 13
issue.quoted_clause: **Memory**: 70B FP16 weights = 140 GB; KV for the 9.5K max context at FP16 ≈ 24.9 GB; inference residency ≈ 165 GB [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]. An 8×H100 host (640 GB) fits this with ample headroom for concurrency (Ch11 showed ~24 GB per request × concurrent requests still fits).
issue.observed: Two issues. (1) The per-request KV is quoted as '~24 GB' here, but the 17.5-slot figure that drives every host count in the chapter is derived from 24.9 GB (the 9.5K basis), not 24 GB; a reader who divides 436 by 24 gets 18.2, not 17.5, and cannot reproduce the chapter's central capacity number. (2) The derivation of 17.5 is never shown — it appears as a bare figure. (3) 'ample headroom for concurrency' is in tension with the chapter's own conclusion that the KV budget is 68% of the host.
issue.evidence: Re-derivation: 436 GB KV budget / 24.9 GB per request = 17.51 slots (floor 17). 436 / 24.0 = 18.17. The 17.5 figure is therefore only reproducible from the 9.5K basis, which the chapter states for the 24.9 GB but not for the slot count.
issue.root_cause: The slot count was carried over from Ch 16/17 as a known constant rather than being re-derived where it is first used, and the two KV bases (9.2K and 9.5K) were not reconciled at the point of use.
issue.correction: Show the derivation inline: 'the canonical per-host KV budget is 640 - 140 (weights) - ~64 (runtime) = 436 GB; at the 9.5K max context each request holds 24.9 GB of KV, so a host holds 436/24.9 = 17.5 slots (17 whole slots after flooring)'. Replace '~24 GB per request' with '24.9 GB per request at the 9.5K max context' and replace 'ample headroom' with the actual figure ('the KV budget is 68% of the host, which is why the KV screen binds before the compute screen').
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can reproduce 17.5 and 17 from the text of Ch 13 §3 alone, and the per-request KV figure quoted in Ch 13 matches the basis used for the slot count.

issue.quoted_clause: Applying this chapter's ladder, the architect measures the three triggers. Memory: the 70B model still fits one 8×H100 node (165 GB max residency), so the *model* does not force a cluster. Traffic: host goodput is exceeded at ~100 rps — the binding trigger. Operational: the data privacy requirement still forbids a public hyperscale cloud.
issue.observed: The mini-case says it measures 'the three triggers', but the list it uses (Memory, Traffic, Operational) matches neither of the chapter's two lists: §2's ladder triggers are Memory, KV residency per GPU, Traffic, Contention/phase interference, Distance/geography; §4's three measurements are residency vs tier memory, host goodput ceiling vs demand, and communication fraction. The mini-case substitutes 'Operational' (which appears in §5's common mistakes, not in §2) and never exercises §4's third measurement, the communication fraction — even though the chapter's own escalation is to a multi-host cluster where that measurement is most relevant.
issue.evidence: Set comparison across §2, §4, and §8; the communication-fraction measurement (>~20% of step time on collectives) is stated in §4 and used nowhere in the chapter.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case was written from the chapter's conclusion (escalate to cluster, keep on-prem) rather than from the chapter's method, and the method's third measurement was dropped because it does not change the conclusion.
issue.correction: Either align the mini-case's list with §4's three measurements (and state the communication-fraction result for the chosen layout), or change the wording to 'the architect checks the ladder's binding triggers' and add the §2 triggers that were checked and found not to bind (KV residency per GPU, contention/phase interference, geography).
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case's checklist is traceable to a numbered list in §2 or §4, and every measurement the chapter defines is either exercised in the mini-case or explicitly marked as not applicable to the scenario.

issue.page_hint: Ch 12 §3, opening paragraph; vs §5 Common Mistakes
issue.quoted_clause: A single 8×H100 host provides 640 GB aggregate memory (8 ×80 GB), leaving ample headroom.
issue.observed: 'Ample headroom' is true for a single request and false for the host's actual operating point: the chapter's own canonical KV budget is 436 GB of 640 GB (~68%), and §5's common mistakes says 'at the canonical host concurrency the KV budget is 436 GB of 640 GB (~68%) — which is why KV is often the binding constraint'. The opening paragraph of the worked example therefore contradicts the chapter's own common-mistakes section.
issue.evidence: Re-derivation: 436/640 = 68.1% of host memory is KV budget at the canonical concurrency; 140/640 = 21.9% is weights; ~64/640 = 10% is runtime. The host is not 'ample headroom' in any operational sense.
issue.root_cause: The opening sentence was written for the single-request residency check and was not revisited when the chapter adopted the concurrent-host KV budget.
issue.correction: Replace with: 'A single 8×H100 host provides 640 GB aggregate memory (8 x 80 GB): 140 GB of weights plus a 436 GB KV budget at the canonical concurrency, leaving ~64 GB for runtime — ample for one request, but the KV budget is the host's dominant consumer.'
issue.acceptance_test: No statement in Ch 12 characterizes the 8xH100 host's memory as 'ample headroom' without qualifying it against the 68% KV budget.

issue.quoted_clause: **Candidate (b): P/D-disaggregated two-pool.** We keep the full 70B model in both pools and split by *phase* ... Crucially, P/D disaggregation does **not** raise the per-host prefill *ceiling* ... Economics: two hosts and added fabric as a baseline, more as each pool scales; it is the right architecture *at scale*, not a two-host answer to the canonical case.
issue.observed: Candidate (a) receives an explicit quality paragraph ('the 70B is the workload's quality reference ... the gate is satisfied relative to the reference') and an explicit SLO paragraph ('this is the SLO gate that Ch 14 must close'). Candidate (b) receives neither, even though it also runs the full 70B and has the same open SLO gate. The asymmetry makes (b) look better-scoped than it is and leaves the reader to infer (b)'s quality and SLO status.
issue.evidence: Structural comparison of the three candidate paragraphs: (a) has Memory / Throughput / SLO / Quality / Economics paragraphs; (b) has Residency / Win / Ceiling / Scaling / Economics; (c) has Residency / Quality / Throughput / Provisional.
issue.root_cause: The candidate paragraphs were written to emphasize each candidate's distinguishing feature rather than to score every candidate against the same three gates, so the common fields are unevenly populated.
issue.correction: Give each candidate the same five fields (Memory, Throughput, SLO, Quality, Economics) so the reader can compare like with like, and let the distinguishing feature be an additional paragraph rather than a replacement for a missing one.
issue.acceptance_test: Each of the three candidates in §3 has an explicit statement of its memory, throughput, SLO, quality, and economics status against the same three gates.

issue.quoted_clause: This candidate illustrates the extreme end of the KV-quantization space: the memory footprint is trivially small and its throughput is a genuine strength ... what keeps it from being competitive is quality, the still-open Ch 14 gate.
issue.observed: Candidate (c) is described as illustrating the KV-quantization space, but it changes two independent variables at once: the model class (70B -> 7B) and the KV precision (FP16 -> 4-bit). The chapter's own open-questions list is about 8-bit KV, not 4-bit, and the mini-case's evaluation plan ('we compare answer quality against the 70B baseline') cannot separate a model-class effect from a KV-quantization effect. The reader is invited to read a KV-quantization result out of a two-variable change.
issue.evidence: The chapter's §7 bullet is 'Whether 8-bit KV caching is sufficient for 9.2K context at FP16-equivalent quality' — a different precision from candidate (c)'s 4-bit, and a different model. §6's evaluation plan for (c) names only 'the quality-degradation trade-off' without specifying which change is being measured.
issue.root_cause: The candidate was constructed as a combined 'smaller model + quantized KV' option for economy, and the chapter then discussed it as though it were a KV-quantization experiment.
issue.correction: State explicitly that candidate (c) varies two factors and that its quality result is therefore an upper bound on the acceptable degradation, not an attribution to KV quantization. Add the missing single-variable candidate (70B with 8-bit KV, which the chapter already computes at 12.06 GB) as the isolating case, or state that the isolation is deferred to Ch 14's evaluation plan.
issue.acceptance_test: The chapter states which variables candidate (c) changes, and the evaluation plan names the comparison that isolates each variable.

issue.page_hint: Ch 12 §3, Candidate (b) and the memory summary
issue.quoted_clause: at the canonical per-host KV budget (640 − 140 weights − ~64 runtime ≈ 436 GB, Ch 7/17)
issue.observed: The '~64 GB runtime' allowance is load-bearing for the 436 GB KV budget, the 17.5-slot figure, and every host count in Ch 12 and Ch 13, but it is never explained in this chunk: the reader is not told what it covers (CUDA context, activation workspace, NCCL/collective buffers, allocator fragmentation, sampling/logit buffers) or how it was obtained. A reader cannot sanity-check it, and it is the difference between 17 and 18 slots per host.
issue.evidence: Sensitivity: 436/24.9 = 17.51 slots; if the runtime allowance were 32 GB instead of 64, the budget would be 468 GB and the slot count 18.8 (floor 18), changing the canonical peak fleet from 21 to 20 hosts and the 100 rps fleet from 51 to 49.
issue.root_cause: The runtime allowance was imported from Ch 7/17 as a constant and never surfaced with its composition, even though it is a first-order input to the book's capacity arithmetic.
issue.correction: Add a one-line breakdown of the ~64 GB (e.g. 'CUDA context and kernels ~8-10 GB, activation/workspace for the largest batched prefill, NCCL buffers for TP=8, and allocator headroom') with a pointer to Ch 7/17 for the derivation, and state that it is an estimate.
issue.acceptance_test: The runtime allowance is itemized or explicitly labelled as an estimate with a sensitivity note, and a reader can see why the KV budget is 436 GB rather than 500 GB.

issue.quoted_clause: Candidate (b), the P/D-disaggregated two-pool, is evaluated on the added complexity of inter-group communication and the pipeline overlap efficacy ... Candidate (c), the KV-quantized 7B model, is evaluated on the quality-degradation trade-off; we compare answer quality against the 70B baseline and compute the economic break-even point (number of hosts required) against the quality loss.
issue.observed: Two wording problems. (1) 'inter-group communication' is not the chapter's term; the pools are the groups, and the quantity of interest is the cross-pool KV transfer (which the chapter elsewhere calls the 'KV-transfer fabric'). (2) 'compute the economic break-even point (number of hosts required) against the quality loss' conflates two different quantities: a break-even point is the host count at which two alternatives cost the same, whereas 'number of hosts required' is a capacity result and 'quality loss' is not a cost. The sentence does not specify what is being compared with what.
issue.evidence: Terminology drift: the chapter uses 'pool', 'two-pool', 'prefill pool', 'decode pool', 'KV-transfer fabric', and 'inter-group' for the same two entities.
issue.root_cause: The evaluation-plan paragraph was written as a summary of the three candidates' evaluation needs and compressed the terminology and the comparison being requested.
issue.correction: Write 'the added complexity of cross-pool KV transfer and the pipeline overlap efficacy', and for (c): 'we compare answer quality against the 70B baseline and compute the host count at which the smaller model's lower infrastructure cost offsets its quality loss on the evaluation set'.
issue.acceptance_test: One term is used for the P/D pools throughout Ch 12, and the (c) evaluation plan names the two quantities being compared and the axis of comparison.

issue.page_hint: Ch 12 §7 (What We Still Don't Know), closing paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: These flags exist because home-lab measurements do not count as reference evidence per the evidence taxonomy; each is an open empirical question a team should validate against its own target workload, not a claim the handbook has settled.
issue.observed: The stated reason for the flags is an evidence-policy statement (home-lab measurements are not citable), which is not why these four questions are open. Three of them (4-bit KV quality, prefix-overlap effectiveness, KV-transfer overhead) are open because no systematic characterization exists in the literature or because they are workload-dependent; the fourth (8-bit KV quality) is open for the same reason. The sentence as written implies the questions would be closed if the author had run the measurements, which conflicts with the chapter's own [HYPOTHESIS] labelling and with the 'unknown because workload-dependent' category the taxonomy provides.
issue.evidence: The taxonomy referenced (Ch 4, Appendix A) distinguishes [HYPOTHESIS] from [UNRESOLVED] and from [ASSUMPTION]; the closing sentence collapses them into an evidence-provenance explanation.
issue.root_cause: A note about the author's own citation policy was placed where a note about the epistemic status of the four questions belonged.
issue.correction: Replace with a statement of the four questions' status: 'Each of these is open because the answer is workload-dependent or because no systematic characterization exists — not because the handbook lacks a measurement. A team should validate them against its own target workload before relying on them.'
issue.acceptance_test: The closing paragraph of §7 classifies each open question by why it is open, consistent with the book's evidence taxonomy, and does not imply that the author's own measurements would settle them.

issue.quoted_clause: The result, with the 74-host headroom fleet (78 hosts at the Table 17-1 policy): p95 TTFT back under 1.8 s at 100 rps [ILLUSTRATIVE SCENARIO RESULT], on site, without hyperscale
issue.observed: The sentence names two different fleet sizes (74 and 78) in a parenthetical without saying which one the stated result corresponds to, and the result itself is asserted rather than derived from the chapter's method. A reader cannot tell whether 'p95 TTFT back under 1.8 s' is the outcome at 74 hosts or at 78.
issue.evidence: The chapter's own arithmetic: 74 hosts x 1.977 rps = 146 rps capacity; 78 hosts x 1.977 = 154 rps; both are far above the 100 rps average, so both would give a similar TTFT — which is exactly why the ambiguity is harmless numerically but confusing rhetorically.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case reports two sizing policies because the chapter discusses both, and the closing sentence was written to carry both without selecting one.
issue.correction: Pick one fleet for the scenario result (the Table 17-1 policy fleet, 78 hosts, since that is the chapter's recommended policy) and state the other as the alternative: 'with the 78-host Table 17-1 policy fleet (74 hosts on the u-only screen), p95 TTFT returns under 1.8 s at 100 rps'. Add the one-line derivation of the TTFT outcome (per-host load 100/78 = 1.28 rps against a 1.98 rps ceiling -> negligible queueing; prefill of 9.2K tokens at 19,780 tok/s = ~0.47 s) so the result is derived rather than asserted.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case names one fleet for its result and shows the arithmetic that produces the stated TTFT.

issue.quoted_clause: | Local / edge | 1 | n/a (memory-bound) | 7-13B dense | low (on-device) | on-device/offline/connectivity (data residency → on-prem server or cluster tier) | ... | Cluster | tens-hundreds | InfiniBand/Eth | any that needs splitting | depends | model > node, or traffic > host goodput |
issue.observed: Two cell-level defects. (1) The Local/edge 'Model range' cell says '7-13B dense' with no precision qualifier, while §1 requires the qualifier ('up to ~7-13B at tight context, assuming 8-bit/4-bit weight quantization — 13B FP16 = 26 GB exceeds many edge GPUs'). A reader reading only the table will believe 13B FP16 fits an edge GPU. (2) The Cluster 'Model range' cell says 'any that needs splitting', which contradicts the chapter's own canonical placement: the canonical cluster is 21 hosts of *replicas* of a 70B that fits a node and needs no splitting. The 'When to use' cell ('model > node, or traffic > host goodput') is correct; the 'Model range' cell contradicts it.
issue.evidence: Internal comparison: §1's Server tier is described as 'the canonical enterprise-Q&A tier and the book's 8xH100 baseline', and §3 places the canonical workload's deployment in a cluster by traffic, not by splitting. 13B x 2 bytes = 26 GB, which §1 itself flags as exceeding many edge GPUs.
issue.root_cause: The table was drafted from the tier definitions rather than from the chapter's worked example, and the precision qualifier that §1 carries was not carried into the table.
issue.correction: Change the Local/edge model range to '7-13B dense (8/4-bit weights)' and the Cluster model range to 'any (split only if the model exceeds node memory)'. Add a footnote to the table pointing to §3 for the canonical placement.
issue.acceptance_test: Every model-range cell in Table 13-1 carries the precision assumption it depends on, and the Cluster row does not imply that a cluster requires weight splitting.

issue.page_hint: Ch 13 §3, closing paragraph of 'Placing the Canonical Workload'
issue.quoted_clause: So the **server** tier is the right *model-residency* archetype for the canonical workload — the model and its KV fit a single 8×H100 node and the per-request TTFT SLO is met on one host. It does **not** mean one host serves the whole arrival rate; a single host is latency-bound and the peak capacity is a fleet-computing question (Ch17).
issue.observed: The chapter's own headline says the canonical workload's deployment is a cluster, and its conclusion says the server tier is the right archetype. The distinction ('model-residency archetype' vs 'deployment tier') is real and carefully worded, but the reader is left without a single answer to the chapter's central question — 'which tier is the canonical workload in?' — and the two answers appear in the same section.
issue.evidence: §3 opening: 'at the 40 rps peak its deployment is a **cluster** of ~21 server-class hosts'. §3 closing: 'the **server** tier is the right *model-residency* archetype'. The chapter title and the ladder in Fig 13.1 are framed around placement, so the reader expects one placement.
issue.root_cause: The chapter needed to distinguish 'the tier whose memory budget the model fits' from 'the tier whose fleet the traffic requires', and the distinction was made by qualification rather than by naming two different questions.
issue.correction: Name the two questions explicitly and answer both in one place: 'Two questions, two answers: the canonical workload's *residency* is server-class (the model and its KV fit one 8xH100 node), and its *deployment* is cluster-class (the 40 rps peak requires ~21-32 hosts). The ladder rung is chosen by the deployment question; the server tier is the unit of replication.' Then make the same two-question distinction in the chapter's opening and in Fig 13.1's caption.
issue.acceptance_test: The chapter states one placement answer for the canonical workload, with the residency/deployment distinction made once and reused consistently.

issue.quoted_clause: On the *per-request latency* axis, Ch11's serving analysis indicates that continuous batching + prefix caching keeps p95 TTFT under the 2 s SLO on a single 8×H100 host *below capacity*
issue.observed: Ch 13 asserts as an established result what Ch 12's Table 12-1 records as unmeasured ('? TTFT SLO unmeasured (design target: median <=1.2 s, p95 <=2 s)'). Ch 13's bullet is labelled [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED], but the sentence attributes the claim to 'Ch11's serving analysis', which reads as a citation of an established finding rather than an analytical indication pending measurement.
issue.evidence: Cross-chapter comparison: Ch 12 Table 12-1 (a) SLO cell = '? TTFT SLO unmeasured (Ch 14)'; Ch 13 §3 = 'Ch11's serving analysis indicates that ... keeps p95 TTFT under the 2 s SLO'. Both are about a single 8xH100 host below capacity.
issue.root_cause: Ch 13 cites Ch 11's analysis as a settled result while Ch 12 has routed the same question to Ch 14's measurement gate; the two chapters were written at different times relative to the Ch 14 gate.
issue.correction: Harmonize the wording: 'Ch 11's analytical serving model indicates that continuous batching + prefix caching should keep p95 TTFT under the 2 s SLO on a single 8xH100 host below capacity; this remains an analytical indication until the Ch 14 measurement closes the SLO gate.'
issue.acceptance_test: Any statement in Ch 13 that a single host meets the TTFT SLO is labelled as analytical and cross-references the Ch 14 gate, matching Ch 12's table.

issue.page_hint: Ch 12 §3, Candidate (a) economics sentence; Table 12-2 cost row
issue.quoted_clause: Economics (recorded, not one of the three gates — §12.8): one host purchase, one software license tier.
issue.observed: The canonical economics live in Ch 16 (and are summarized in the §12.8 mini-case), but the pointer here sends the reader to the mini-case, which is a scenario rather than the canonical cost model. Table 12-2's cost row likewise cites '§12.8' for the cloud-equivalent figure. The reader looking for the canonical cost basis is sent to a worked scenario.
issue.evidence: Cross-reference check: §12.8 is the mini-case; the mini-case's cost figures are themselves attributed to 'Ch 16' and 'Ch 16 case (i)/KV-screen line'. The chain §3 -> §12.8 -> Ch 16 is one hop longer than necessary.
issue.root_cause: Section-level cross-references were written to the nearest available anchor rather than to the owning chapter.
issue.correction: Point to Ch 16 directly for the canonical cost basis ('Economics: recorded, not one of the three gates — the canonical cost model is Ch 16; the §12.8 mini-case applies it to this stakeholder'), and change Table 12-2's '§12.8' citation to 'Ch 16'.
issue.acceptance_test: Every cross-reference to the canonical economics points to the chapter that owns the cost model, and no reference routes the reader through a mini-case to reach it.

issue.page_hint: Ch 12 §3-§8 and Ch 13 §1-§8 (global within the chunk)
issue.quoted_clause: 'Ch. 11' / 'Ch 11' / 'Chs. 15–17' / 'Ch 12/8' / 'Ch 16/17' / 'Ch 13' / 'Ch 14' / 'Ch 4, Table 4-2'; '35%-MFU' / '35% MFU'; 'prefill-tokens/s' / 'prefill tokens/s' / 'prefill tok/s' / 'tokens/s'; 'conditional finalist' / 'conditional candidate'
issue.observed: Terminology and formatting drift within the two chapters: four different forms of the chapter reference ('Ch. 11', 'Ch 11', 'Chs. 15–17', 'Ch 12/8', 'Ch 16/17'); two forms of the MFU qualifier; four forms of the token-rate unit; and two near-synonyms for the candidate status ('conditional finalist' in §6 and Table 12-1, 'conditional candidate' in the Fig 12.1 caption and Table 12-2's closing note) where §6 defines 'finalist' precisely.
issue.evidence: Occurrences within the chunk: 'Ch. 11' (candidate (a) heading), 'Ch 11' (candidate (b), Ch 13 §2, §6), 'Chs. 15–17' and 'Chs. 14–16', 'Ch 12/8', 'Ch 16/17', 'Ch 13', 'Ch 14'; '35%-MFU' (candidate (a), §8) vs '35% MFU' (candidate (c)); 'prefill-tokens/s' (candidate (a)), 'prefill tokens/s' (candidate (c)), 'prefill tok/s' (Table 12-2), 'tokens/s' (§4).
issue.root_cause: The two chapters were drafted and edited separately, and no house style pass has been applied to cross-reference and unit formatting.
issue.correction: Adopt one form ('Ch 11', 'Chs. 15–17'), one MFU form ('35% MFU'), one rate form ('tok/s'), and one candidate-status term ('conditional finalist' for (a)/(b), 'gated candidate' for (c)), then apply it book-wide.
issue.acceptance_test: A grep for 'Ch\.' returns no hits in body text; 'MFU' appears in one form; the token-rate unit appears in one form; 'conditional candidate' and 'conditional finalist' are not used interchangeably.

issue.quoted_clause: In matched units, the fused kernel's HBM traffic is Θ(L²d²/M) against Θ(L²) for the materialized path — a reduction factor of M/d² (≈6× at d = 128, M ≈ 192 KB of fp16), not a lower order in L.
issue.observed: Two problems in one sentence. (a) The baseline is mis-stated: the FlashAttention I/O analysis (Dao et al.) gives the materialized path Θ(N² + Nd²), not Θ(N²). At the canonical shape (L = 9,200, d = 128) the omitted Nd² term (1.507e8) is larger than the L² term (8.46e7), so the stated baseline understates the naive path by ~1.8x. (b) The quoted reduction factor M/d² ≈ 6 is only the first of two terms: the full ratio (N² + Nd²) / (N²d²/M) = M/d² + M/N ≈ 6 + 10.7 ≈ 17x at L = 9,200. As written, a reader takes '≈6x' as the total-traffic reduction factor, which understates the paper's own result by ~3x at the canonical shape. (c) The two terms are also in different units: the Θ(L²) term counts fp32 score-matrix elements, the Θ(L²d²/M) term counts fp16 K/V elements.
issue.evidence: Recomputation: N² = 9,200² = 8.464e7; N d² = 9,200 x 128² = 1.507e8; N² + N d² = 2.354e8. FlashAttention: N²d²/M with M = 192 KiB = 98,304 fp16 elements gives 8.464e7 x 16,384 / 98,304 = 1.411e7. Ratio = 16.7x. M/d² alone = 6.0; M/N = 10.7. Separately, the caption's 'M/d²' is only reproducible if M (bytes) is divided by d² in bytes (32,768 B), not elements (16,384) — a reader dividing 196,608 by 16,384 gets 12.
issue.root_cause: The caption compresses a two-term I/O-complexity result into a single headline factor and drops the Nd² term from the baseline, without stating the element/byte convention.
issue.correction: Restate as: baseline Θ(L² + L d²) (score-matrix round-trip plus K/V re-reads) vs fused Θ(L²d²/M); reduction factor = M/d² + M/L ≈ 17x at L = 9,200, d = 128, M = 192 KiB; and state the unit convention explicitly ('M = 192 KiB = 98,304 fp16 elements; d² = 16,384 elements'). If the intent is to quote a conservative empirical figure instead, say so and label it [ILLUSTRATIVE].
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can reproduce the quoted reduction factor from the quantities printed in the caption, in one consistent unit, and obtains the same number; the baseline term includes the K/V re-read contribution.

issue.page_hint: Ch 15 §2, §3 (attention FLOP comparison heading), §4 (FlashAttention bandwidth illustration), §5 (Common Mistakes), Table 15-1 'kernel regime' column
issue.quoted_clause: making kernel choice (FlashAttention vs. SDPA) one of the first *kernel-level* optimizations to validate for long-context prefill ... *Attention FLOP comparison:* Scaled‑dot‑product attention (SDPA) for 9,200‑token prompts ... illustratively FlashAttention‑class ~400 GB/s achieved vs naive SDPA ~150 GB/s achieved for 9,200‑token contexts ... *Using scaled‑dot‑product attention without FlashAttention:* ... the naive kernel memory-traffic-bound ... | Light | ... | Compute (SDPA) |
issue.observed: 'SDPA' is used throughout Ch 15 as the name of the naive/materialized attention algorithm (explicit L x L score matrix). In PyTorch, `scaled_dot_product_attention` is an API that dispatches to FlashAttention, flash-decoding, or the memory-efficient backend — so 'naive SDPA' names something that does not exist under that name, and 'FlashAttention vs. SDPA' reads as 'FlashAttention vs. FlashAttention'. Table 15-1's 'kernel regime' cell 'Compute (SDPA)' additionally implies the canonical configuration runs the unfused kernel, contradicting §6's own recommendation of FlashAttention-2.
issue.evidence: Terminology audit across the chunk: 'SDPA' appears in §2, §3 (heading), §4, §5 and Table 15-1, always meaning the materialized/unfused path; 'FlashAttention' and 'FlashAttention-class' are used for the fused path. §6 recommends 'FlashAttention-2 for the attention computation'. The two names are used for two different kernels in the same chapter.
issue.root_cause: A library API name was adopted as an algorithm name, and the distinction was never made explicit for readers who know the PyTorch API.
issue.correction: Rename the unfused path throughout to 'materialized (unfused) attention' or 'naive attention (explicit L x L score matrix)', reserve 'SDPA' for the API, and change Table 15-1's kernel-regime cell to name the fused kernel the chapter actually recommends (e.g. 'Compute (FlashAttention-class)').
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in the book pairs 'SDPA' with 'FlashAttention' as if they were alternative implementations of the same operator; a reader who knows PyTorch's SDPA dispatcher does not conclude the book is recommending a non-existent kernel.

issue.page_hint: Ch 14 §3 Step 2 (TPOT bullet) and §8 mini-case, vs Ch 15 §1 (Concept)
issue.quoted_clause: Ch 14: '**TPOT** p50/p95 (SLO: p50 ≤ ~25 ms/token; record p95 for tail diagnosis, not SLO-bound).' and 'The SLO remains median TTFT ≤ 1.2 s, p95 TTFT ≤ 2 s and median TPOT about 25 ms.' | Ch 15: 'The canonical SLO this chapter measures against: TTFT median ≤ 1.2 s, p95 ≤ 2 s, TPOT median ≤ 25 ms, p95 ≤ 35 ms (Ch 4, Table 4-2).'
issue.observed: The canonical SLO is stated two different ways. Ch 15 quotes Ch 4 Table 4-2 as including a TPOT p95 ≤ 35 ms bound; Ch 14 twice states that the TPOT p95 is explicitly NOT SLO-bound and omits it from the SLO list. A reader who builds the deployment benchmark from Ch 14 would not enforce the TPOT p95 that Ch 15 treats as canonical.
issue.evidence: Cross-chapter comparison of the quoted SLO strings within the chunk; Ch 14's worksheet row 'TPOT | p50 / p95 | ~25 ms/token median' also carries only the median.
issue.root_cause: The canonical SLO was restated locally in Ch 14 rather than referenced, and the restatement dropped one of the four bounds.
issue.correction: Make Ch 14 quote the canonical SLO verbatim from Ch 4 Table 4-2 (all four bounds), or replace the local restatement with a pointer plus the two bounds Ch 14 actually uses. If the TPOT p95 is genuinely not part of the canonical SLO, fix Ch 15 §1 and its citation to Ch 4 Table 4-2 instead.
issue.acceptance_test: The SLO bound list is identical wherever it appears in Ch 14, Ch 15, Ch 16 and the mini-cases, and each instance either quotes Ch 4 Table 4-2 or is marked as a local subset.

issue.quoted_clause: for moderate lengths (2,000–4,000 tokens) the HBM bandwidth reduction can translate to a ~1.3–1.8× *attention-kernel* throughput gain on H100 (illustrative — bench the specific kernel on the target hardware) — attention-kernel throughput, not end-to-end request throughput: attention is only ~4–8% of forward FLOPs at 2–4K tokens, so the end-to-end gain is bounded near 4–8% even for a perfect attention kernel.
issue.observed: The stated upper bound on the end-to-end gain is derived from attention's share of FLOPs, but the end-to-end gain is bounded by attention's share of *runtime*. Attention is the memory-bound part of the forward pass while the parameter matmuls are compute-bound, so attention's runtime share exceeds its FLOP share; a perfect attention kernel can therefore yield more than 8% end-to-end. The sentence as written teaches an invalid inference and would cause an architect to under-value the kernel.
issue.evidence: Independent rederivation of the FLOP shares (which are correct): attention = 4 L² d x 80 layers; parameter matmul = 2 x 70e9 x L. At L = 2,000: 1.049e13 / (2.8e14 + 1.049e13) = 3.6%. At L = 4,000: 4.194e13 / (5.6e14 + 4.194e13) = 7.0%. Arithmetic-intensity check for the naive kernel at Br = 128, d = 128: ~4 B_r d / (2d + 3 B_r) = 102 FLOP/element vs the H100 ridge of ~147 FLOP/element (989 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s / 2 B), i.e. attention runs below the ridge while the matmuls run above it, so attention's runtime share exceeds its FLOP share.
issue.root_cause: A FLOP-share argument was used where a runtime-share argument is required; the chapter elsewhere makes exactly this distinction (kernel regime vs workload capacity deficit) but not here.
issue.correction: Replace the FLOP-share bound with the correct one: the end-to-end gain is bounded by attention's share of forward-pass runtime, which is at least its FLOP share and typically higher because attention is memory-bound; give the reader the measurement to make (attention kernel time / total step time from the profiler) rather than a FLOP-derived ceiling.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence no longer derives an end-to-end performance bound from a FLOP share; the reader is told which measured quantity bounds the gain, and the FLOP share is presented only as a FLOP share.

issue.page_hint: Ch 15 §3, 'Compute demand versus peak' paragraph and the following 'equivalent decode-side check' paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: On the bandwidth axis the same 12,000 tokens/s at a 17-request decode batch streams the 140 GB of weights once per step — 140 GB × (12,000/17) ≈ 98.8 TB/s of demand against the host's 8 × 3.35 = 26.8 TB/s HBM peak, a ~3.7× ratio — which is the axis on which decode actually binds. ... **The equivalent decode-side check, which the 19/21-host screen does not include:** ... bytes/token = 140 GB/B + 24.9 GB of KV per request ... ≈ 398 TB/s ... — ≈15× over.
issue.observed: Two decode-bandwidth computations are presented as if they were the same check, but they differ by 4x because the first omits KV traffic, which is the dominant term (24.9 of 33.1 GB/token). The first is introduced as the evidence for the conclusion ('which is the axis on which decode actually binds') and the second is then labelled 'equivalent'. A reader who stops at the first number concludes decode is ~3.7x over the bandwidth roofline; the complete figure is ~15x.
issue.evidence: Recomputation: weights-only 140 GB x (12,000/17) = 98,824 GB/s = 98.8 TB/s; 98.8/26.8 = 3.69x. Full: 140/17 + 24.9 = 33.14 GB/token; 12,000 x 33.14 = 397.6 TB/s; 397.6/26.8 = 14.8x. The KV term is 75% of total bytes/token.
issue.root_cause: The weights-only term was presented as a complete bandwidth check before the full bytes/token model was introduced, and the second computation was mislabelled 'equivalent' rather than 'complete'.
issue.correction: Present one computation: bytes/token = weights/B + KV per request, then the demand and the ratio. If the weights-only sub-term is worth keeping, label it explicitly as a partial term ('weights alone account for 98.8 TB/s of the 398 TB/s') and remove the word 'equivalent'.
issue.acceptance_test: Only one decode-bandwidth ratio is quoted as the answer, it includes KV traffic, and any partial term is labelled as partial.

issue.page_hint: Ch 15 §3 (decode-side screen) vs Ch 16 §3 Step 1 sizing-screen table
issue.quoted_clause: Ch 15: 'The 19/21-host prefill-and-KV screen above is therefore *not* a host count on its own: it is prefill-and-KV derived and must be combined with this decode-bandwidth screen (and both with measured SLO-goodput), because whichever axis binds sets the fleet.' | Ch 16: '| **N_hosts = max of the named screens** | **6 hosts** | **21 hosts under case (i) and case (iii); 22 under case (ii)** |'
issue.observed: Ch 15 states that the 21-host figure must be combined with a decode-bandwidth screen before it can be called a host count, but Ch 16's sizing-screen table — the table that produces the headline 21 hosts and every downstream TCO figure — contains only the KV-residency screen and the three prefill screens. The decode screen is never carried forward, never labelled non-binding, and never reconciled with the 21-host headline. A reader following Ch 15's instruction will look for the third screen in Ch 16 and not find it, and may suspect the fleet is under-sized.
issue.evidence: Ch 15's decode screen yields ceil(12,000/809) = 15 hosts, which is below both 19 (prefill case i) and 21 (KV), so the numeric outcome is unchanged; the defect is that the screen inventory is inconsistent between the two chapters and the non-binding result is never stated. Note also that Ch 15's screen uses B = 17 (the KV-slot ceiling) while the 21-host fleet actually runs ~16.4 in-flight requests per host at peak, so the screen is mildly optimistic as well.
issue.root_cause: Ch 16's screen inventory was fixed before Ch 15 added the decode-bandwidth screen, and no reconciliation note was added when Ch 15's screen was introduced.
