issue.acceptance_test: Parameter definitions are referenced to the subsection that defines them.

issue.page_hint: Ch 20 §3, paragraph beginning "The correct statement is: the fleet must satisfy every named screen"
issue.quoted_clause: The correct statement is: the fleet must satisfy every named screen, and the *larger* requirement wins — **19 hosts under case (i), 21 under case (iii), 22 under case (ii)**
issue.observed: The sentence labelled "The correct statement" gives 19 hosts as the governing requirement under case (i). Under case (i) the named screens are the KV/Little screen (21 hosts) and the case-(i) prefill screen (19 hosts); the larger requirement is 21, not 19. The same section's planning-bound caveat states "21 = the KV/Little screen under case (i)", and the §8 mini-case states "22 the raw-screen requirement" with the KV screen at 21 — so 19 is inconsistent with three other statements in the same chapter.
issue.evidence: Re-derivation: KV screen = ceil(40 x 8.6 / 17) = ceil(20.235) = 21 hosts (case-independent). Case-(i) prefill screen = ceil(368,000 / 19,780) = ceil(18.60) = 19 hosts. Max over screens under case (i) = 21. Under case (iii): KV 21, prefill ceil(368,000/18,210) = ceil(20.21) = 21 -> 21. Under case (ii): KV 21, prefill ceil(368,000/16,870) = ceil(21.81) = 22 -> 22. So the correct per-case maxima are 21 / 21 / 22, not 19 / 21 / 22. Benign reading tested: the list also happens to equal the three prefill-screen values (19/21/22), so it can be read as a prefill-screen list rather than a governing list — but under that reading the sentence still presents prefill-screen values under a "the larger requirement wins" frame, which is equally wrong. Either reading is defective.
issue.root_cause: A per-case screen enumeration was written where a per-case max was required; the KV screen (21) was dropped from the case-(i) row. The error is isolated to this sentence and does not propagate to the parenthetical caveat or the mini-case.
issue.correction: Rewrite the sentence to state the max explicitly, e.g.: "the fleet must satisfy every named screen and the larger requirement wins — 21 hosts under case (i) (KV 21 vs prefill 19), 21 under case (iii) (KV 21 vs prefill 21), 22 under case (ii) (KV 21 vs prefill 22); with the rho = 0.95 derate applied to the prefill screen, case (ii) rises to 23 hosts, which governs." If the intent was to list the prefill-screen values, label them as such ("the prefill screen alone gives 19 / 21 / 22") and keep the governing max separate.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader who takes the per-case governing requirement from this sentence and sizes the fleet obtains 21 / 21 / 22 hosts (and 23 with the rho derate), matching the §3 planning-bound caveat and the §8 mini-case table. No sentence in Ch 20 states 19 hosts as a fleet requirement.

issue.page_hint: Ch 20 §3 "Autoscaling economics"; dependent anchors in Ch 21 §3, Ch 22 §6, Ch 23 §3, Ch 25 §3 and §6
issue.quoted_clause: at the 40-rps peak the autoscaled fleet runs 21 hosts at (21 × $20 + $40) ÷ 144,000 requests/hr ≈ **$3.19 per 1K requests** ... The break-even against a statically provisioned 21-host fleet ($420/hr) sits at 19 hosts
issue.observed: The chapter's own governing sizing is 23 hosts (case-(ii) prefill screen with the rho = 0.95 derate), but the entire economics block — cost per 1K requests at peak, cost per 1K at average, the ~28% average-cost decline, and the static-fleet break-even — is computed on 21 hosts, the case-(i) KV screen that the chapter explicitly says is not the fleet size. The same 21-host figure is then carried into other chapters as the canonical fleet size and into the canonical cost rows.
issue.evidence: Governing screen (Ch 20 §3): case-(ii) prefill ceil(21.81/0.95) = 23 hosts. Cost on the governing fleet: (23 × $20 + $40) / 144,000 = $3.47 per 1K, not $3.19 — a 9% understatement of the peak cost per 1K. Break-even against a 23-host static fleet ($460/hr) moves from 19 hosts / ~37.6 rps to 21 hosts / ~41.5 rps. Dependent anchors: Ch 21 §3 ("216,000 × $24.97/1K ≈ $5,394" and "216,000 × ~$14.038/1K ≈ $3,032") inherit the 21-host self-host monthly cost (21 × ~$7.4K = ~$155.4K, the stated $155.8K); Ch 22 §6 ADR 0015 ("~$155.8K/mo (~$24.97/1K) self-host"); Ch 23 §3 ("a ~21–32-host fleet at the canonical peak"); Ch 25 §3 ADR 0016 Context ("the canonical fleet is 21 hosts at peak"); Ch 25 §6 ADR 0015 R1 and Consequences ("21-host KV-screen headline / 32-host N−1 policy").
issue.root_cause: The economics block was written against the KV-screen headline before the case-(ii) prefill screen was added as governing, and the stale host count was never propagated. This is one root cause with six dependent anchors, not seven independent errors.
issue.correction: Either (a) recompute the economics on the governing 23-host fleet and propagate 23 (and 34 under the full policy) to Ch 21 §3, Ch 22 §6, Ch 23 §3, Ch 25 §3 and Ch 25 §6, or (b) state explicitly in the economics block that the figures are computed on the 21-host KV-screen headline as a lower bound and that the governing 23-host fleet raises peak cost per 1K to ~$3.47 and moves the static break-even to ~41.5 rps. Whichever is chosen, add a one-line note in Ch 21 §3 and Ch 22 §6 that the $/1K rows inherit the host-count basis.
issue.acceptance_test: Every host count used to derive a cost figure in Ch 20, 21, 22, 23 and 25 is either the governing screen or is explicitly labelled as a lower bound; the peak cost per 1K in Ch 20 §3 equals (governing hosts × $20 + $40) / 144,000.

issue.page_hint: Ch 20 §4 note under Table 20-1; Ch 20 §8 "Aggregate-req/s note"
issue.quoted_clause: The aggregate-req/s 2× row is a **stress/soak** target, not the planning screen: sustaining 80 req/s needs ~41–43 hosts (see §8).
issue.observed: The soak-pool host count is computed from the KV screen only (41 hosts) and its rho-derated form (43 hosts), omitting the case-(ii) prefill screen that the chapter's own rule says governs. The chapter states twice that the larger requirement wins; the soak-pool figure does not apply that rule.
issue.evidence: At 80 rps: KV screen = ceil(80 x 8.6 / 17) = ceil(40.47) = 41; rho-derated KV = ceil(80 / (0.95 x 1.977)) = ceil(42.6) = 43. Case-(ii) prefill = ceil(736,000 / 16,870) = ceil(43.63) = 44 raw; with rho = 0.95, ceil(43.63/0.95) = ceil(45.93) = 46 hosts. So the governing soak-pool size is 46 hosts, not 41–43.
issue.root_cause: The soak-pool note was derived from the KV screen alone, contrary to the chapter's stated max-over-screens rule.
issue.correction: Restate as "~41–46 hosts (KV screen 41, rho-derated 43, case-(ii) prefill screen 44 raw / 46 with the rho derate — the governing figure)", or state explicitly that the note is KV-screen-only and therefore a floor.
issue.acceptance_test: The soak-pool host count in Ch 20 is >= the governing screen at 80 rps computed by the same max-over-screens rule used at 40 rps.

issue.quoted_clause: The break-even against a statically provisioned 21-host fleet ($420/hr) sits at 19 hosts, i.e. sustained demand ≤ ~37.6 rps: above that, autoscaling costs more than the peak-sized fleet it replaces.
issue.observed: The comparison is asymmetric: the autoscaled alternative is costed as (hosts x $20 + $40/hr) including the $40/hr fixed overhead, while the static alternative is costed as $420/hr with no overhead. The same infrastructure and staff overhead applies to a static fleet, so the static baseline is understated by $40/hr and the break-even is biased toward autoscaling.
issue.evidence: As printed: autoscaled break-even at N x 20 + 40 = 420 -> N = 19, demand 19 x 1.977 = 37.6 rps. With the overhead applied symmetrically: static 21-host fleet = 21 x 20 + 40 = $460/hr; autoscaled break-even at N x 20 + 40 = 460 -> N = 21, demand 21 x 1.977 = 41.5 rps. The printed conclusion ("above ~37.6 rps autoscaling costs more") is therefore wrong by ~4 rps, and it changes the sign of the recommendation in the 37.6–41.5 rps band.
issue.root_cause: The $40/hr overhead was added to one side of a two-sided comparison only.
issue.correction: Apply the $40/hr overhead to both alternatives (or state explicitly that the static baseline excludes it and why), and recompute the break-even. If the overhead is genuinely avoided by a static fleet, say so and justify it.
issue.acceptance_test: Both sides of the break-even comparison are costed on the same overhead basis, and the printed break-even demand can be reproduced from the printed inputs by a reader.

issue.quoted_clause: | **Scheduling overhead** | Fraction of per-query time spent in dispatcher, not compute | < 5% of the 2 s turn budget (= 100 ms) |
issue.observed: The metric's denominator (per-query time, i.e. the ~8.6 s service time) and the target's denominator (the 2 s TTFT turn budget) are different quantities. 5% of per-query time is ~430 ms, not 100 ms. As written, the row is internally inconsistent and cannot be measured as defined.
issue.evidence: 8.6 s x 5% = 430 ms; 2 s x 5% = 100 ms. The §3 scheduling-overhead paragraph uses the correct framing ("~1.2% of the canonical 8.6 s request and, equivalently, ≤ 5% of the 2 s TTFT SLO turn budget; the fraction is derived from the absolute number, not a second constraint"), so the table row contradicts the prose it summarizes.
issue.root_cause: The table row was written as a fraction-of-service-time metric but given a fraction-of-TTFT-budget target.
issue.correction: Redefine the row as "Scheduler-added latency as a fraction of the TTFT budget" with target "< 5% of the 2 s turn budget (= 100 ms)", or keep the per-query-time definition and change the target to "< 5% of the 8.6 s service time (= 430 ms)" — but the latter contradicts the §3 absolute target, so the first is preferable.
issue.acceptance_test: Every row of Table 20-1 has a definition and a target expressed over the same denominator, and the scheduling-overhead row agrees with the §3 paragraph.

issue.page_hint: Ch 20 §3, "Fleet aggregate throughput (illustrative form)", second bullet
issue.quoted_clause: **Token-throughput screen → 11 hosts (non-binding).** The token-throughput ceiling gives ⌈40 / 3.684⌉ = 11 hosts, which stays non-binding here.
issue.observed: One subsection earlier the chapter states that this exact division is invalid: "what makes the division wrong here is what its numerator mixes and its answer assumes, not its units" — the 35,000 tokens/s numerator is a phase-mixed prefill+decode total with no cost/phase-equivalence model. The chapter then performs the division and reports the result as a named screen, without repeating the caveat at the point of use.
issue.evidence: 35,000 / 9,500 = 3.684 req/s; ceil(40 / 3.684) = 11. The chapter's own §3 "Throughput bound" subsection states the division "is not achievable here" and that "aggregating the two phases into one 'total' rate requires an explicit cost/phase-equivalence model". A reader who skims the screen list will carry "11 hosts" forward as a legitimate capacity screen.
issue.root_cause: The caveat lives in a different subsection from the screen list, and the screen list was written as if the caveat did not apply.
issue.correction: Either drop the 11-host screen, or restate it as "an illustrative artifact of a phase-mixed rate, shown only to demonstrate that it is non-binding; it is not a valid screen without a phase-equivalence model". If retained, attach the caveat clause at the point of use.
issue.acceptance_test: No screen in Ch 20 is presented as a valid capacity screen while the chapter elsewhere declares the operation that produced it invalid.

issue.page_hint: Ch 20 §3, "Simultaneous feasibility check (prefill + decode coexistence)" and "Fleet aggregate throughput"
issue.quoted_clause: The ~93% leaves very little headroom before decode coexistence, interference, and the actual achieved MFU. ... with the standalone ρ = 0.95 derate applied to the prefill screen exactly as the policy arithmetic applies it, case (ii) rises to ⌈21.81 / 0.95⌉ = **23 hosts** — the largest requirement before the full policy
issue.observed: The chapter never states the prefill utilization implied by its own governing sizing, and it treats the decode-coexistence headroom inconsistently. The feasibility check says there is essentially no headroom for decode coexistence at the KV-bound rate, yet the sizing applies only a 5% rho derate and calls 23 hosts governing. The reader is never told that the governing fleet is prefill-saturated.
issue.evidence: At 23 hosts and 40 rps, per-host rate = 40/23 = 1.739 req/s; prefill demand = 1.739 x 9,200 = 16,000 tokens/s against the case-(ii) ceiling of 16,870 tokens/s = 94.8% prefill utilization. At 22 hosts (raw case-(ii) screen): 40/22 = 1.818 req/s -> 16,727 tokens/s = 99.2% of the ceiling. So the governing fleet leaves roughly 1–5% of host compute for decode, which is inconsistent with the §3 statement that the ~93% figure "leaves very little headroom before decode coexistence" and with the claim that the rho derate is a generic "throughput-efficiency derate" rather than a decode-coexistence allowance.
issue.root_cause: The feasibility check was performed at the KV-bound rate (2.0 req/s) rather than at the governing per-host rate implied by each screen, so the two analyses never meet.
issue.correction: Add the implied prefill utilization to the screen table (per-host rate, prefill tokens/s, % of the case-(ii) ceiling) and state the consequence explicitly: the governing case-(ii) sizing is prefill-saturated, so decode coexistence requires either more hosts, a lower planning MFU, or P/D disaggregation. State whether the rho = 0.95 derate is intended to represent decode-coexistence headroom; if it is, say so and stop treating the 93% figure as evidence of no headroom.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can state, from Ch 20 alone, the prefill utilization at the governing host count and what that implies for decode coexistence on the same host.

issue.quoted_clause: The **average** cost per query declines only along the canonical 10 → 40 rps ramp, where fixed overhead (model loading, infrastructure, staff) is spread across 4× the requests and across more SLO-compliant completions per observation window (Ch 14's goodput definition), cost per request may decline until additional capacity steps dominate; adding idle hosts at fixed demand increases unit cost.
issue.observed: The sentence is grammatically broken: a dangling clause ("cost per request may decline until additional capacity steps dominate") is spliced in after the parenthetical, leaving the subject of the main clause ambiguous and the semicolon clause orphaned. This is the chapter's opening Concept paragraph.
issue.evidence: Text inspection: the clause after the closing parenthesis has no grammatical attachment to the preceding subject ("The average cost per query declines...").
issue.root_cause: An edit inserted a clause without restructuring the sentence.
issue.correction: Rewrite as two sentences, e.g.: "The average cost per query declines along the canonical 10 → 40 rps ramp, because fixed overhead (model loading, infrastructure, staff) is spread across 4× the requests and across more SLO-compliant completions per observation window (Ch 14's goodput definition). It declines until additional capacity steps dominate; adding idle hosts at fixed demand increases unit cost."
issue.acceptance_test: The paragraph parses as complete sentences with one subject per clause; no orphaned clause remains after the parenthetical.

issue.page_hint: Ch 20 §2 Mental Model, second paragraph; §2 third paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: intelligent scheduling — such as consistent hashing for session affinity or predictive placement based on historical patterns — tends to keep utilization more uniform across the fleet and reduces tail latency. ... the fleet must sustain **~40 requests/s at peak**
issue.observed: Two small defects in the same section: (a) "tends to keep ... and reduces" mixes a modal construction with a finite verb; (b) the chapter opens §1 with an explicit unit convention ("rps denotes an arrival rate and req/s a capacity rate") but §2 then writes "~40 requests/s at peak" for an arrival rate, and §1 defines "Aggregate throughput" as "the total queries-per-second", introducing a third term ("queries") for the same quantity.
issue.evidence: Text inspection against the §1 convention sentence.
issue.root_cause: Unit convention was introduced but not applied consistently in later prose.
issue.correction: Fix the verb agreement ("tends to keep utilization more uniform across the fleet and to reduce tail latency"), and apply the convention: use "rps" for the arrival rate and "req/s" for capacity throughout, and use "requests" rather than "queries" for the counted object.
issue.acceptance_test: Every rate in Ch 20 is labelled rps (arrival) or req/s (capacity), and "queries" does not appear as a synonym for "requests".

issue.page_hint: Ch 20 §7 "What We Still Don't Know", bullet "Economic auto-scaling"
issue.quoted_clause: A fleet that runs at 20% utilization on average may be cheaper in the cloud; one at 80% utilization favors owned hardware.
issue.observed: The chapter's own §3 numbers imply a specific crossover (cloud $20/hr vs owned ~$8/hr amortized -> owned wins above ~40% duty cycle), but §7 substitutes a vaguer 20%/80% framing. The open-question bullet is therefore less precise than the chapter's own arithmetic allows, and the two are not reconciled.
issue.evidence: $8 / $20 = 0.40, so a fleet that is up more than ~40% of the time is cheaper owned. The 20%/80% pair is not derivable from any number in the chapter.
issue.root_cause: The open-questions bullet was written generically rather than from the chapter's own cost inputs.
issue.correction: Either state the crossover implied by the chapter's numbers (~40% duty cycle at $20/hr cloud vs $8/hr amortized owned) and note that the true threshold also depends on the amortization period, or remove the 20%/80% pair so the bullet does not appear to assert a threshold the chapter has not derived.
issue.acceptance_test: Any utilization threshold stated in Ch 20 is either derived from the chapter's printed cost inputs or explicitly labelled as an external rule of thumb.

issue.quoted_clause: the governing 23-host sizing (21 = the KV/Little screen under case (i); 22 = the ρ ≈ 0.95 derate of that screen — and, independently, the raw full-square case (ii) prefill compute screen, which also gives 22 and rises to 23 with the same ρ derate, the governing screen; 34 at the 70% × 95% + N−1 policy against 32 for KV-only — Ch 17 Table 17-1, u and ρ independent)
issue.observed: The KV/Little screen is labelled "under case (i)", but it is case-independent — it depends only on the KV ceiling and the residency time, not on the FLOP-counting convention. Ch 25's ADR 0015 R1 row states this correctly ("21 hosts (KV, case-independent)"), so the two chapters label the same screen differently.
issue.evidence: KV screen = ceil(lambda x W / C) with C = 17 slots and W = 8.6 s; no FLOP convention appears in the derivation. Ch 25 ADR 0015 R1: "21 hosts (KV, case-independent)".
issue.root_cause: Case labels were attached to the screen list positionally rather than by dependency.
issue.correction: Relabel as "21 = the KV/Little screen (case-independent)" and keep the case labels attached only to the prefill screens.
issue.acceptance_test: The case labels in Ch 20 and Ch 25 attach to the same screens with the same meaning.

issue.page_hint: Ch 20 §6, unnumbered subsection "The useful completion is an accepted output"
issue.quoted_clause: For a RAG fleet the useful completion is an *accepted* output — a response that passes the deadline, integrity, quality, and safety gates in the observation window — so hosts are sized against accepted outputs per observation window, not raw work ... a video-generation fleet is the clearest parallel beyond RAG
issue.observed: This subsection arrives without a heading number, without a transition, and pivots from RAG fleet sizing to a video-generation fleet in the middle of the Architecture Consequence section. It restates the Ch 14 goodput definition (accepted outputs per observation window) that Ch 20 has already invoked twice, and then adds a cross-domain analogy that is not used again. Its intellectual job (transfer the accepted-output accounting to another workload class) is real, but its placement inside §6 breaks the section's three-part structure (centralized scheduler / data colocation / graceful degradation).
issue.evidence: Structural inspection: §6 opens "Fleet-level optimization reshapes the serving architecture in three ways" and enumerates exactly three; the accepted-output subsection is neither numbered nor part of the three.
issue.root_cause: A cross-domain transfer note was appended to the section rather than integrated into it.
issue.correction: Either promote it to a numbered fourth consequence with a heading ("4. Accepted-output accounting") and connect it explicitly to the three preceding items, or move it to §7 as a transfer note, or cut it and keep the accepted-output definition to a single clause (the Ch 14 cross-reference already carries the concept).
issue.acceptance_test: §6's numbered list matches its introductory sentence, and every subsection in §6 has a heading and a stated job.

issue.page_hint: Ch 21 §3, "Reading the result"; also §3 "Cost of a good gated release"
issue.quoted_clause: Gating turns a risky 216K-request exposure (ungated) into a controlled ~3.6K-request canary — a ~60× reduction in blast radius for the cost of a 2-hour evaluation.
issue.observed: The 60× factor compares two different observation intervals: the ungated exposure is 6 hours of 100% of traffic (216,000 requests), the gated exposure is 2 hours of 5% of traffic (3,600 requests). Over a matched 6-hour window a 5% canary would expose 10,800 requests, i.e. a 20× reduction, not 60×. The chapter's headline economic claim therefore overstates the blast-radius benefit by 3×. Separately, the cost of gating is never quantified: a canary requires the candidate model to be resident alongside the incumbent, which for a 70B FP16 model on 8×H100 hosts means at least one additional host for the canary window (~$40 at $20/hr for 2 hours) — a small but real number that the chapter's own economics framing invites.
issue.evidence: 216,000 / 3,600 = 60 (as printed, mismatched intervals). Matched-interval: 216,000 x 0.05 = 10,800; 216,000 / 10,800 = 20. Canary capacity: 5% of 40 rps = 2 rps; at 1.977 req/s per host this needs 1 host; 1 x $20 x 2 h = $40.
issue.root_cause: The blast-radius comparison was made across two different exposure windows without normalizing the interval.
issue.correction: State the comparison on a matched basis: "over the same 6-hour window, a 5% canary exposes 10,800 requests — a 20× reduction; the 2-hour canary used here exposes 3,600". Add the canary's incremental cost (one additional resident model for the canary window) so the chapter's "cost of a good gated release" is actually costed.
issue.acceptance_test: Every blast-radius ratio in Ch 21 is computed over a stated, matched observation interval, and the gated path's incremental cost is quantified rather than described as "the cost of a 2-hour evaluation".

issue.quoted_clause: the incumbent's baseline failure rate on that subset is ~0.83% (3 in ≈360), and a one-sided binomial test at α = 0.05 returns p ≈ 6.4×10⁻⁵, so the gate fires
issue.observed: The binomial test is correct as computed, but the null rate it tests against is itself an estimate from 3 events in 360 trials, and the chapter does not acknowledge that the gate's firing is not robust to the null's own sampling uncertainty. At the upper end of a 95% interval for 3/360 (~2.3%), 12/360 is not significant (p ~ 0.13). The chapter presents the gate as a deterministic, reproducible decision rule; it is in fact sensitive to an estimated baseline.
issue.evidence: Recomputation of the printed p-value: exact binomial P(X >= 12 | n=360, p=1/120) = 6.36e-5, matching the printed 6.4e-5 — the arithmetic is correct. Wilson 95% interval for 3/360 is approximately [0.28%, 2.31%]. At p0 = 0.0231, P(X >= 12 | n=360) ~ 0.13 (Poisson lambda = 8.3), i.e. the gate would not fire.
issue.root_cause: The worked example treats an estimated baseline rate as a known null, and does not state the sensitivity.
issue.correction: Add one sentence: the null rate is estimated from 3 events, so the gate's power depends on the baseline's own confidence interval; either widen the baseline sample, use a one-sided test against the upper confidence bound, or state that the gate fires on the point estimate and that the false-promotion rate metric (§4) is what catches a mis-set baseline. The chapter's §4 false-promotion-rate metric is the natural place to make this connection.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case states the uncertainty in the null rate and either qualifies the gate's firing or explains how the false-promotion-rate metric covers the residual risk.

issue.quoted_clause: A year ago the architect might have, and watched p95 TTFT silently drift past the SLO for a week.
issue.observed: Broken sentence: the verb phrase after "might have" is missing, leaving a comma splice.
issue.evidence: Text inspection.
issue.root_cause: Dropped words during editing.
issue.correction: "A year ago the architect might have shipped it, and watched p95 TTFT silently drift past the SLO for a week."
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence parses; no orphaned auxiliary remains.

issue.quoted_clause: 1. **Gate pass rate** — the share of candidates the gate admits. A rising rate can mean better candidates *or* looser thresholds, so it is read only alongside the second number. **False-promotion rate** — how often a gated change later regresses in production; only this one directly indicates that the evaluation suite is losing fidelity.
issue.observed: The false-promotion rate is a second, separately named metric but is set as an unnumbered continuation of item 1, while the text refers to it as "the second number" — a reader looking for item 2 finds "Canary-to-production time" instead. The list therefore advertises four metrics but enumerates three numbered items.
issue.evidence: Text inspection of the numbered list in §4.
issue.root_cause: A metric was added to an existing item without renumbering.
issue.correction: Split into two numbered items (1. Gate pass rate, 2. False-promotion rate) and renumber the rest, or fold the false-promotion rate into item 1 explicitly as "read alongside the false-promotion rate" and remove the ordinal reference.
issue.acceptance_test: The number of metrics named in §4 equals the number of numbered items, and "the second number" resolves unambiguously.

issue.page_hint: Ch 21 §3, heading "Cost of a good gated release"
issue.quoted_clause: **Cost of a good gated release.** A canary at 5% traffic for 2 hours serves 5% × 288,000 ×2/8 ≈ **3,600 requests** through the candidate while it is measured against a full evaluation suite.
issue.observed: The heading promises a cost; the body gives a request count. The chapter's framing is "the economics of promotion gating", so the gated path's cost is the quantity the reader came for, and it is never stated.
issue.evidence: Text inspection; the canary's incremental cost is computable from the chapter's own inputs (see CH21-01).
issue.root_cause: Heading written for a cost argument; body delivered a volume argument.
issue.correction: Either add the cost (one additional resident model for the canary window, ~$40 at the chapter's $20/hr host rate, plus the evaluation-runner compute) or retitle the subsection to "Exposure of a good gated release".
issue.acceptance_test: Every subsection heading in Ch 21 §3 is matched by the quantity its body delivers.

issue.quoted_clause: the canary has served 3,600 requests with 12 legal-subset failures vs the incumbent's 3 expected at α = 0.05
issue.observed: The phrase "3 expected at α = 0.05" conflates two different quantities: 3 is the expected count under the incumbent's baseline rate (0.83%), while α = 0.05 is the significance level of the test. As written, the expected count appears to depend on the significance level.
issue.evidence: Text inspection; the following clause ("the incumbent's baseline failure rate on that subset is ~0.83% (3 in ≈360)") supplies the correct decomposition.
issue.root_cause: Compressed phrasing of two separate quantities.
issue.correction: "12 legal-subset failures against the 3 expected under the incumbent's ~0.83% baseline (one-sided binomial test, α = 0.05, p ≈ 6.4×10⁻⁵)".
issue.acceptance_test: The expected count and the significance level are never presented as a single quantity.

issue.page_hint: Ch 22 §8 mini-case, "The peak, not the average, sizes the fleet" and the following paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: The KV budget binds at a similar scale: Ch 17's 436 GB of KV per host (640 − 140 − 64) ÷ 24.1 GB/request ≈ 18 in-flight requests per host, and 40 rps × 8.58 s ≈ 343 in flight needs ~19 hosts. ... a homogeneous cluster sized at ~17–19 hosts clears both budgets (prefill- or KV-bound depending on the KV budget, with a 21-host build carrying the margin)
issue.observed: Ch 22 derives a KV screen of 18 slots / ~19 hosts, while Ch 20 and Ch 25 derive 17 slots / 21 hosts for the same constraint. The two differ in two ways at once — per-request KV (24.1 GB at 9.2K vs 24.9 GB at the 9.5K maximum) and the whole-slot floor (18 vs 17) — and neither chapter reconciles them. The consequence is a wrong conclusion: "~17–19 hosts clears both budgets" is false under Ch 20's screens (KV 21, case-(ii) prefill 22/23), and "~19 hosts" is itself a round-down of 19.06.
issue.evidence: Ch 22 basis: 436 / 24.1 = 18.09 slots; 343 / 18 = 19.06 -> 20 hosts on the whole-slot convention. Ch 20 basis: 436 / 24.9 = 17.51 -> floor 17; ceil(344/17) = 21 hosts. Ch 25 ADR 0015 R1 states "21 hosts (KV, case-independent)". Ch 22's own conclusion ("17–19 hosts clears both budgets") is contradicted by Ch 20's governing 23 hosts (case-(ii) with rho) and 34 under the full policy.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case recomputes the KV screen from a different per-request KV figure and without the whole-slot floor, and the resulting fleet conclusion is not reconciled with the chapter it cites.
issue.correction: Use the book's canonical screen in Ch 22 (17 whole slots at the 9.5K maximum, 21 hosts at 40 rps), state the per-request basis explicitly, and correct the conclusion to "a homogeneous cluster sized at ~21–23 hosts clears both budgets (KV 21, case-(ii) prefill 22 raw / 23 with the rho derate)". If the 9.2K-vs-9.5K distinction is deliberate, say so and show both.
issue.acceptance_test: The KV screen host count is identical wherever it appears (Ch 20, Ch 22, Ch 25), and Ch 22's fleet conclusion is >= the governing screen in Ch 20.

issue.page_hint: Ch 22 §6 Architecture Consequence, ADR 0015 excerpt; Ch 22 §8 mini-case
issue.quoted_clause: the single-region arithmetic gives ~$155.8K/mo (~$24.97/1K) self-host, ~$87.6K/mo (~$14.04/1K) on the cloud default paid-occupancy input, and ~$129.8K/mo (~$20.8/1K) managed API at the canonical 6.24M requests/mo
issue.observed: The three cost rows are arithmetically self-consistent (155.8/6.24 = 24.97; 87.6/6.24 = 14.04; 129.8/6.24 = 20.80 per 1K), but they inherit the 21-host fleet basis that Ch 20 identifies as non-governing (see CH20-02). The ADR excerpt does not state the host count behind the self-host row, so a reader cannot see the dependency.
issue.evidence: 21 hosts x ~$7.4K/mo = ~$155.4K, matching the stated $155.8K; at the governing 23 hosts the row becomes ~$170K/mo (~$27.3/1K).
issue.root_cause: Cost rows are quoted without their host-count basis, so a change to the governing screen does not propagate visibly.
issue.correction: Add the host count and the MFU/FLOP-case basis to the ADR 0015 Context in both Ch 22 §6 and Ch 25 §6, and re-derive the self-host row if the governing screen changes.
issue.acceptance_test: Each cost row in ADR 0015 states the fleet size and screen it assumes, and the row can be recomputed from that basis.

issue.page_hint: Ch 22 §7 "What We Still Don't Know", bullet "Cross-technology bandwidth numbers"
issue.quoted_clause: **Cross-technology bandwidth numbers** — Chapter 2 §7; HBM3e parts (e.g. H200) and the MI300X (HBM3, ~5.3 TB/s) publish higher peaks, which would move the GPU-count equation without changing the compute-bound vs bandwidth-bound classification. [HYPOTHESIS]
issue.observed: The bullet is tagged [HYPOTHESIS] as a whole, but its content is a published specification (H200 HBM3e and MI300X peak bandwidths are first-party FACT), with only the consequence ("would move the GPU-count equation") being derived. The immediately preceding sibling bullet in the same list correctly splits the two ("the 3.35 TB/s H100 figure is a theoretical peak (published spec — FACT), while real serving kernels may sustain less [HYPOTHESIS]"), so the list is internally inconsistent in how it applies the taxonomy.
issue.evidence: Text inspection of the two adjacent bullets; the house taxonomy separates provenance [1P] from status [FACT]/[DERIVED]/[HYPOTHESIS].
issue.root_cause: The label was applied to the bullet rather than to the clause it governs.
issue.correction: Split the label: "[1P][FACT] — H200 (HBM3e) and MI300X (HBM3, ~5.3 TB/s) publish higher peak bandwidths; [DERIVED] — substituting them moves the GPU-count equation without changing the compute-bound vs bandwidth-bound classification."
issue.acceptance_test: Each bullet in Ch 22 §7 labels its clauses individually, matching the practice of the adjacent bullet.

issue.page_hint: Ch 22 §6 Architecture Consequence; Ch 22 Table 22-1; Ch 20 §2; Ch 23 §3; Ch 24 §1
issue.quoted_clause: | decode weight-read per token | ~140 GB | full-weight-read model (70B FP16) [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] |
issue.observed: The canonical deployment's precision label is inconsistent across the book. Ch 20, Ch 22, Ch 23 and Ch 24 describe the canonical workload as "70B dense FP16", while Ch 25's ADR 0016 (Accepted) decides "Render the serving model in BF16" and states that this "sets the canonical deployment's precision label to BF16". Ch 25's opening acknowledges the drift ("a 70B dense FP16 deployment (FP16 label; see ADR 0016)") but no pointer exists in the chapters that use the FP16 label. The numbers are unaffected (both are 2 B/parameter), but the label is the book's canonical scenario identifier.
issue.evidence: Text inspection: "70B dense FP16" appears in Ch 20 §2, Ch 22 Table 22-1 and §6, Ch 23 §3, Ch 24 §1 and §3.3; ADR 0016 in Ch 25 §3 sets BF16 as the canonical label and states "every footprint, KV and cost figure in this handbook is unchanged".
issue.root_cause: ADR 0016 was added late and its effect on the canonical scenario's label was not propagated to the chapters that name it.
issue.correction: Add a one-clause pointer where the canonical model is first defined (Ch 4, Table 4-2) and at each later use, e.g. "70B dense FP16/BF16 (2 B/parameter either way; ADR 0016 sets the canonical label to BF16)", or change the canonical label once in Ch 4 and update the four downstream mentions.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader who reads Ch 20 and then Ch 25 does not encounter two different canonical precisions for the same deployment.

issue.quoted_clause: **→ Bound 2: long ~9,200-token inputs with retrieval, ~300-token outputs.** (A page of prose is roughly 500–700 tokens, so two to three pages plus retrieved sections lands in the low thousands; the exact 9,200/300 split is the canonical scenario imported from Ch 4, Table 4-2 rather than elicited here, and the pilot's tokenizer run replaces it.)
issue.observed: The parenthetical's own arithmetic does not reach the bound it justifies. Two to three pages at 500–700 tokens/page is 1,000–2,100 tokens; even with generous retrieved sections this "lands in the low thousands", not 9,200. The lead's own words ("a few pages") are also inconsistent with a 9.2K-token prompt (13–18 pages at the chapter's own page-to-token rate). The chapter flags that the split is imported rather than elicited, but the justification it offers actively undercuts the number.
issue.evidence: 2–3 pages x 500–700 tokens = 1,000–2,100 tokens; 9,200 tokens / 500–700 tokens per page = 13–18 pages. The chapter's own page-to-token figure is the source of the mismatch.
issue.root_cause: The parenthetical was written to explain the canonical import but was drafted with a page-count estimate that does not match the canonical context length.
issue.correction: Either change the parenthetical to state the arithmetic that reaches 9,200 (e.g. "two to three pages of pasted specs (~1,000–2,100 tokens) plus ~7,000 tokens of retrieved chunks") and note that the retrieved-context volume is the dominant term and was not elicited, or change the lead's dialogue to elicit a larger pasted context. The point the chapter wants to make — that the retrieved portion dominates and must be measured — is worth making explicitly.
issue.acceptance_test: The parenthetical's arithmetic, the lead's stated page count, and the 9,200-token bound are mutually consistent, or the mismatch is explicitly named as the thing the pilot must resolve.

issue.page_hint: Ch 23 §8 mini-case, mirror restatement and "The burst buffer, spelled out"
issue.quoted_clause: a 7B-class model on one on-prem GPU, resolving baseline tickets under 3 s, with a 200-rps burst buffer ... a decode-only ceiling of 100% MFU (≤141 rps — 7B FP16, ~500 output tokens/request, H100); with the ~500-token prefill included the *total* request rate is ~71 rps at 100% MFU (~21–28 rps at 30–40% MFU), so r = 50 in the worked example below is an optimistic decode-only illustration
issue.observed: The mini-case's own arithmetic shows that one H100 sustains at most ~71 req/s at a physically impossible 100% MFU (and ~21–28 req/s at the 30–40% MFU the book uses elsewhere), yet the mirror restatement commits the scope to "one on-prem GPU" with "a 200-rps burst buffer". The worked burst drain (r = 50) is itself above the realistic single-GPU rate, so the 3 s drain conclusion rests on a rate the chapter has already flagged as unattainable. The chapter's conclusion (bursts under a degraded SLO) is sound, but the committed scope statement is not.
issue.evidence: Recomputation: decode-only at 100% MFU = 989 TFLOPS / (2 x 7e9 FLOP/token) = 70,643 tokens/s / 500 output tokens = 141 req/s; with 500-token prefill, per-request FLOPs = 7 + 7 = 14 TFLOP -> 989/14 = 70.6 req/s; at 30–40% MFU = 21–28 req/s. r = 50 therefore requires ~71% MFU on one GPU. At r = 25 (40% MFU), a 200-rps 1-s burst queues 175 requests and drains in 7 s, not 3 s.
issue.root_cause: The burst arithmetic was carried out at an r the chapter had already declared unattainable, and the mirror restatement was written from the burst rate rather than from the capacity.
issue.correction: State the burst capacity the committed topology can actually absorb (one GPU at 21–28 req/s; N GPUs at N x that), and either size the burst buffer to the real drain rate or state the degraded-mode SLO in terms of the real r. The mirror restatement should say "one on-prem GPU serving ~5 rps average, with the 200-rps burst admitted under a queue-and-drain degraded mode at the measured single-GPU rate of ~25 req/s", and the burst arithmetic should be re-run at that r.
issue.acceptance_test: The r used in the burst arithmetic is at or below the rate the committed topology can sustain at the book's own planning MFU, and the mirror restatement's burst claim is consistent with it.

issue.quoted_clause: a ~21–32-host fleet at the canonical peak (Ch 17/20/24)
issue.observed: The fleet range quoted here omits Ch 20's governing figure (23 hosts, case-(ii) prefill with the rho derate) and the full-policy figure (34 hosts), both of which are stated in the chapter being cited. The range as printed (21–32) is not the range Ch 20 produces.
issue.evidence: Ch 20 §3 governing: 23 hosts (case-(ii) with rho = 0.95); full policy: 34 (case-(ii)) vs 32 (KV-only). Ch 25 ADR 0015 R1 lists 21 / 22 / 32 / 34.
issue.root_cause: The range was written from an earlier screen set and not updated when the case-(ii) prefill screen became governing.
issue.correction: Quote the range Ch 20 actually produces: "a ~21–23-host fleet at the canonical peak (32–34 under the 70% x 95% + N−1 policy)".
issue.acceptance_test: Any host-count range quoted outside Ch 20 matches the range Ch 20 derives.

issue.quoted_clause: Candidate A's 8-bit KV halves its own KV screen to ~2.5 hosts. At average load the two screens therefore converge near 5 hosts. Which one binds depends on the KV precision and the sustained MFU: prefill binds outright for Candidate A's 8-bit KV (KV screen ~2.5), while on the FP16 basis the binding screen flips near ~33% sustained MFU (prefill ~4.1 vs KV ~4.9 at 40%), inside the canonical 30–40% range.
issue.observed: The sentence "the two screens therefore converge near 5 hosts" follows directly from the statement that Candidate A's KV screen is 2.5 hosts, and is then contradicted by the very next sentence, which says Candidate A's KV screen is ~2.5 and that prefill binds outright for it. The convergence near 5 holds only on the FP16 basis (Candidate B), not for Candidate A.
issue.evidence: At 10 rps: prefill at 40% MFU = 12.88 / 3.164 = 4.07 hosts; KV FP16 = 86 x 24.9 / 436 = 4.91 hosts; KV 8-bit = 86 x 12.45 / 436 = 2.46 hosts. Crossover on the FP16 basis: 1.628/eta = 4.91 -> eta = 33.2%, matching the chapter's ~33% claim.
issue.root_cause: A summary sentence was written for the FP16 case and placed after the 8-bit case, so its antecedent is wrong.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: "On the FP16 basis (Candidate B) the two screens converge near 5 hosts at 40% MFU; on the 8-bit basis (Candidate A) the KV screen falls to ~2.5 hosts and prefill binds outright."
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 24 §3.3 asserts a convergence value that the following sentence contradicts.

issue.page_hint: Ch 24 §4.1 metrics table (row "Poisoned-hit rate"); §3.2 note; §8 mini-case
issue.quoted_clause: | **Poisoned-hit rate** | DERIVED | Fraction of retrievals that return at least one poisoned chunk | < 0.3% (0.003 per query) |
issue.observed: The metric's definition and its target use different denominators. The definition is per retrieval; the target's parenthetical is per query. With k = 5 retrievals per query, the per-query probability is roughly 5x the per-retrieval rate, so the target's meaning is ambiguous by a factor of five. §3.2's note reads the target on the per-retrieval basis ("the §4.1 target is a probability: the fraction of retrievals returning at least one poisoned chunk"), and §4.2's sampling plan (n = 1,000 retrievals) certifies it on that basis — but §8's mini-case again writes "≈0.003 per query".
issue.evidence: Per-retrieval probability under the null model = 1 - (1 - p)^5 = 0.005197 (0.52%); per-query probability with k = 5 is the same quantity only if a "query" is defined as one top-5 retrieval. The §4.2 certification arithmetic (0 observed -> 95% upper bound 0.299%; 1 observed -> 0.47% one-sided) is a per-retrieval calculation and is correct as such.
issue.root_cause: The metric was renamed from a per-query to a per-retrieval basis without updating the target's parenthetical and the mini-case's restatement.
issue.correction: Fix the target to "< 0.3% (0.003) of retrievals" and, if a per-query figure is wanted, state it separately as "< 1.5% of queries at k = 5". Update §8's mini-case to "≈0.003 of retrievals (≈3 poisoned-hit retrievals per 1,000 sampled retrievals)".
issue.acceptance_test: Every statement of the poisoned-hit rate in Ch 24 names its denominator, and the §4.2 certification arithmetic is expressed over the same denominator as the target.

issue.page_hint: Ch 24 §3.3, "The benchmark trap" and its [DERIVED] tag
issue.quoted_clause: its per-token cost is ~50% lower (half the host-hours: 4 hosts vs 8) ... [DERIVED] — the ~50% per-token cost delta = 1 − 4/8 host-hours at equal served volume (Candidate A 4 hosts vs Candidate B 8 hosts, same hardware and workload)
issue.observed: The [DERIVED] tag asserts "at equal served volume", but the two candidates are not compared at equal served volume and differ in two variables at once (host count and KV precision). At 10 rps, Candidate B's 8 hosts are roughly double what the screens require (KV FP16 4.9 hosts; prefill 4.1 at 40% MFU), so B is over-provisioned at the benchmark load; and Candidate A's 8-bit KV raises its own per-host capacity, so its host-hours at equal served volume would be fewer than 4. The 50% figure is therefore a ratio of provisioned host counts, not a cost-per-token delta at equal volume.
issue.evidence: At 10 rps the screens require ~4.1 hosts (prefill at 40% MFU) or ~4.9 hosts (KV FP16); Candidate B provisions 8. Candidate A's 8-bit KV raises its KV screen to ~2.5 hosts, so at equal served volume A would need fewer than 4 hosts, not exactly 4.
issue.root_cause: The narrative point (the initial recommendation was made on an average-load benchmark) is sound, but the quantitative tag overclaims what the comparison establishes.
issue.correction: Either re-tag the claim as "[ILLUSTRATIVE] — a 50% reduction in provisioned host-hours (4 vs 8) at the benchmarked load; this is not a cost-per-token comparison at equal served volume, because the two candidates differ in both host count and KV precision and B is over-provisioned at 10 rps", or add the equal-volume computation the tag claims.
issue.acceptance_test: The evidence tag for the 50% figure states the comparison actually performed, and the two candidates' differences (host count, KV precision) are enumerated before the comparison is drawn.

issue.quoted_clause: Each entry point accepts free-form text up to 4,096 tokens.
issue.observed: Read literally, this states a service limit of 4,096 tokens per entry point, which contradicts the canonical workload's ~9,200-token prompts (Ch 4 Table 4-2) served through the same web chat UI / API / Slack / terminal entry points. The intended meaning is almost certainly a probe-length cap for the red-team generator, but as written it reads as a product constraint.
issue.evidence: Canonical input = ~9,200 tokens (Ch 4 Table 4-2; Ch 22 Table 22-1). Ch 24 §1 assumes the canonical deployment.
issue.root_cause: A generator parameter was stated in the voice of a system constraint.
issue.correction: Rewrite as "Each entry point accepts free-form text; the red-team generator caps probe length at 4,096 tokens (the canonical workload's ~9,200-token prompts exceed this, so long-context injection paths are not covered by this probe set — see §7)" — and if the probe cap really does leave long-context injection untested, add that to the open-questions list.
issue.acceptance_test: No statement in Ch 24 can be read as imposing a 4,096-token limit on the canonical deployment's entry points.

issue.page_hint: Ch 24 §2 Mental Model, fenced code block
issue.quoted_clause:
```
Red Team → Probes →
Exposure Surface → Guardrails →
Metrics → Green Team →
Harden → Reduce → Loop
```
issue.observed: The chapter's mental model is rendered as an ASCII arrow diagram in a fenced code block, in monospace, with hard line breaks that split the loop across four lines. This is visually inconsistent with every other chapter in this part, which uses a typeset figure for the mental model or loop (Ch 21 Fig 21.1, Ch 24 Fig 24.1, Ch 25 Fig 25.1), and it is the one place in Ch 24 where the reader is asked to internalize the loop's shape. The line breaks also obscure that the loop is cyclic.
issue.evidence: Visual inspection of the source; the same chapter carries a proper figure (Fig 24.1) for the same loop.
issue.root_cause: The mental model was drafted as ASCII before the figure existed and never replaced.
issue.correction: Replace the code block with a typeset figure (or fold it into Fig 24.1 and reference it), so the mental model and the cycle figure are one visual object with consistent typography.
issue.acceptance_test: Ch 24's mental model is typeset, not monospace ASCII, and is visually consistent with the chapter's own Fig 24.1.

issue.quoted_clause: At this ADR's own operating point, C ≈ 17.5 concurrent 9,500-token requests, the KV read dominates instead: 17.5 × ~24.9 GB ≈ 435.6 GB (FP16) against 140 GB of weights. Halving the KV-read bytes then cuts decode memory traffic ≈38% (575.6 → 357.8 GB) and raises arithmetic intensity from ≈4.3 to ≈6.9 FLOP/byte.
issue.observed: The arithmetic-intensity figures omit decode attention FLOPs. At 9,500 tokens of context, decode attention costs 4 x d x L x n_layers = 4 x 8,192 x 9,500 x 80 = 24.9 GFLOP per token per sequence — the same order as the 140 GFLOP parameter term, and the book elsewhere treats the attention term as material (case (ii) adds 17.23% to prefill). Including it, the intensities are ~5.0 and ~8.1 FLOP/byte, not 4.3 and 6.9. The traffic-reduction figure (38%) is unaffected because it is a byte count.
issue.evidence: Decode FLOPs/token/sequence at L = 9,500 = 4 x 80 x 9,500 x 8,192 = 2.49e10 = 24.9 GFLOP. At C = 17.5: parameter term 17.5 x 140 = 2,450 GFLOP; attention term 17.5 x 24.9 = 435.8 GFLOP; total 2,885.8 GFLOP. Intensity = 2,885.8e9 / 575.75e9 = 5.01 FLOP/byte (FP16 KV); after halving KV bytes, 2,885.8e9 / 357.9e9 = 8.06 FLOP/byte. The printed 4.3 and 6.9 correspond to the parameter term alone (2,450/575.75 = 4.26; 2,450/357.9 = 6.85).
issue.root_cause: The intensity calculation counted only the weight-read FLOPs, omitting the attention FLOPs that the same chapter's context length makes material.
issue.correction: State the FLOP terms explicitly: "decode FLOPs per token per sequence = 140 GFLOP (parameters) + 24.9 GFLOP (attention over 9,500 tokens) = 164.9 GFLOP; at C = 17.5 that is 2,886 GFLOP per step against 575.8 GB (FP16 KV) or 357.9 GB (FP8 KV) — arithmetic intensity ≈5.0 rising to ≈8.1 FLOP/byte". If the parameter-only convention is retained deliberately, say so and note that it understates intensity by ~18% at this context length.
issue.acceptance_test: Every arithmetic-intensity figure in Ch 25 states which FLOP terms it includes, and the figure is reproducible from the printed FLOP and byte terms.

issue.quoted_clause: **Fleet-level effect:** the peak KV-residency screen moves from 21 hosts to ~11 (344 in-flight ÷ 35.0 concurrent per host = 9.8, +N−1); ADR 0015 R1 must be re-screened on adoption.
issue.observed: The bullet states the fleet effect as 21 -> ~11 hosts, but FP8 KV does not change the prefill screen, and the chapter's own governing screen is the case-(ii) prefill screen at 22 raw / 23 with the rho derate (34 under the full policy). The fleet therefore does not shrink to 11 hosts; the KV screen simply stops being the binding one. The ADR's own Context paragraph states this ("note FP8 KV does not shrink the case (ii) prefill screen"), but the Consequence bullet — the part a reader copies into a decision — does not, and the two are in tension.
issue.evidence: At FP8 KV: KV screen = ceil(344 / 35.0) = 10, +N−1 = 11. Case-(ii) prefill screen is unchanged at 22 raw / 23 with rho = 0.95 / 34 under the 70% x 95% + N−1 policy. Governing = max(11, 23) = 23.
issue.root_cause: The consequence bullet reports the movement of one screen without re-running the max-over-screens rule the chapter establishes elsewhere.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: "Fleet-level effect: the KV-residency screen moves from 21 hosts to ~11 (344 in-flight / 35.0 concurrent per host = 9.8, +N−1), but the case-(ii) prefill screen is unchanged at 22 raw / 23 with the rho derate, so the governing fleet size is unchanged at 23 hosts (34 under the full policy). FP8 KV removes the KV ceiling as a binding constraint; it does not shrink the fleet. ADR 0015 R1 must be re-screened on adoption."
issue.acceptance_test: The ADR's fleet-level effect is stated as the max over all screens, and matches the governing figure in Ch 20 and ADR 0015 R1.

issue.quoted_clause: **A worked HOLD record — ADR 0015, in this chapter's template** (the compact form appears at the Decision rung in Ch 22 §6; its decision body is kept, not rewritten — the status is updated to superseded, with a link to the successor).
issue.observed: The parenthetical contradicts the record it introduces on two counts: the record's Status field reads "HOLD — screened, not committed", not "superseded"; and the record's own falsification path says "ADR 0015 stays on file unchanged", with supersession described as a future event ("a successor record (ADR 0018 or later) lifts the HOLD and supersedes this one"). The parenthetical also states the opposite of the chapter's own supersession rule in Fig 25.1 ("the body is never rewritten, and only the Status line is updated when a successor supersedes it") — which is compatible with a future supersession but not with the present tense "is updated to superseded".

issue.quoted_clause: **Decision:** Render the KV cache in FP8 for the long-context decode path, keeping prefill and the retrieval/prompt phase in FP16.
issue.observed: The decision is ambiguous about the KV write path. KV tensors are produced during prefill and consumed during decode; a single cache cannot be "FP8 for decode" and "FP16 for prefill" without a conversion step. The intended reading is presumably that the KV cache is stored in FP8 (quantized at write time) while prefill activations remain FP16, but the sentence as written can be read as a per-phase cache format, which is not implementable.
issue.evidence: Text inspection; the ADR's own Consequences bullet ("KV residency per request falls from ~24.9 GB (FP16) to ~12.45 GB (FP8, raw byte-halving)") confirms a single stored format.
issue.root_cause: The decision was phrased by phase rather than by stored artifact.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: "Store the KV cache in FP8 (quantized at write time during prefill; prefill activations and the retrieval/prompt path remain FP16), so the resident KV per request halves."
issue.acceptance_test: The ADR's Decision names the stored artifact whose format changes, and is implementable as written.

issue.page_hint: Ch 26 §8 Step 1 (baseline inputs); §3 (Capstone Execution); §8 Step 2; Fig 26.2 takeaway
issue.quoted_clause: request rate ~2 rps (at the ~2.0 rps per-host analytical planning ceiling) ... at the offered ~2 rps against the ~2.0 rps analytical ceiling the assumed prefill-queue inflation already sits inside the 320 ms compute term
issue.observed: The baseline is placed at the host's analytical capacity ceiling: offered load ~2.0 rps against a per-host ceiling of ~2.0 rps, i.e. rho ~ 0.98-1.0. At that operating point a work-conserving queue has no finite steady-state wait, so no finite 'queue-inflated' compute term can be assigned to the baseline. The declared 320 ms compute term (and hence the 450 ms baseline p99) is not consistent with the declared offered load under any standard queueing model. The cached configuration, by contrast, runs at 1.3 rps (rho ~ 0.64) and does have a steady state, so the chapter's headline -44% compares a non-realizable baseline operating point against a stable one.
issue.evidence: Per-host ceiling = C / service time = 17.5 / 8.6 s = 2.03 rps (the chunk's own Ch 17/20 figures). Baseline offered load = 2.0 rps -> rho = 0.98. Cached engine load = 2.0 x 0.65 = 1.3 rps -> rho = 0.64. For scale, an M/M/1 at rho = 0.98 gives a mean wait of order rho/(mu(1-rho)) ~ 400 s, i.e. three orders of magnitude above the declared 320 ms total compute term. The chunk itself states the cached case is 'queue-light' and the baseline is 'queue-inflated'.
issue.root_cause: The scenario inputs were selected so that the component arithmetic closes (450 = 320+80+50; 250 = 120+80+50) without checking that the baseline's offered load is a stable operating point. The chapter's own caveat ('the utilisation that 320 ms embeds is a declared scenario input, not a queueing-model output') acknowledges the modelling gap but not the physical inconsistency.
issue.correction: Either (a) lower the baseline offered load to a stated fraction of the ceiling (e.g. 1.6-1.8 rps) and re-declare the queue-inflation term against that load, or (b) keep 2.0 rps and state explicitly that the baseline sits at the capacity ceiling where no finite steady-state queue exists, that the 450 ms is therefore a declared illustration rather than a realizable p99, and carry that statement into the -44% headline in §3 and the Fig 26.2 takeaway.
issue.acceptance_test: The §8 Step 1 baseline paragraph states the offered load's rho explicitly and either shows rho < 1 with a stated queueing assumption or states the rho ~ 1 non-stationarity caveat; the §3 and Fig 26.2 takeaway sentences carry the same caveat.

issue.quoted_clause: **-44% TTFT** against the ~450 ms uncached p99 baseline (queue-inflated baseline vs queue-light miss: 320 + 80 + 50 = 450 vs 120 + 80 + 50 = 250 - Step 1) - $(450-250)/450 \approx 44\%$.
issue.observed: The arithmetic is correct (200/450 = 44.4%) and the chapter discloses elsewhere that 'the -44% compares an overloaded operating point with a stable one rather than isolating a cache effect'. But the headline sentence itself, §3's 'yields an illustrative p99 TTFT ~ 250 ms versus the ~450 ms uncached single-node baseline', and the Fig 26.2 takeaway 'p99 TTFT ~250 ms (-44% vs the ~450 ms uncached baseline, not a blended average)' all present -44% as the pattern's effect. The takeaway's parenthetical addresses mean-vs-quantile, not the load mismatch, so a reader who reads only the takeaway gets a number the chapter itself says is not a cache effect.
issue.evidence: §8 Step 2: 'the -44% compares an overloaded operating point with a stable one rather than isolating a cache effect, and a matched-load run (2.0 rps with and without the cache) would isolate the smaller path-substitution effect this model does not claim.'
issue.root_cause: The caveat lives in the derivation paragraph but was not carried into the three places where the number is quoted as a result.
issue.correction: Add the load-mismatch qualifier to each headline statement, e.g. '-44% vs a queue-inflated baseline at 2.0 rps (not a matched-load cache effect; a matched-load run is required to isolate the cache effect)'.
issue.acceptance_test: Every occurrence of '-44%' in Ch 26 carries the qualifier, or the number is explicitly demoted to a labelled scenario comparison rather than a pattern benefit.

issue.quoted_clause: a circuit breaker trips after 5 consecutive timeouts - a timeout being a request that misses the p99 <= 800 ms TTFT deadline above
issue.observed: A p99 is a quantile of a latency distribution, not a per-request deadline. Defining the breaker's per-request timeout as 'misses the p99 <= 800 ms target' makes the breaker shed requests that are inside the SLO, since the SLO explicitly permits up to 1% of requests to exceed 800 ms. An implementer following this literally would trip on compliant traffic and would shed exactly the tail the SLO is designed to tolerate.
issue.evidence: §3 states the SLO as 'a stricter p99 <= 800 ms TTFT target'; Table 26-2's verification target is a p99; Table 26-3's breaker FACT is 'timeout count / 30 s'. No separate per-request deadline is defined anywhere in the chapter.
issue.root_cause: A distributional SLO target and a per-request timeout threshold were collapsed into a single number.
issue.correction: Separate the two concepts: keep 'p99 TTFT <= 800 ms' as the SLO, and define the breaker's per-request timeout as a distinct named threshold (e.g. 'a request exceeding the 800 ms per-request deadline, set at or above the SLO target'), stating the relationship between the two and why the breaker threshold is chosen relative to the SLO.
issue.acceptance_test: Ch 26 §3 Pattern C and Table 26-3 define the timeout threshold as a per-request deadline distinct from the p99 SLO, with the relationship stated in words.

issue.root_cause: The scaling basis was left implicit, so the number's sensitivity to the queue-inflation assumption is invisible.
issue.correction: State the scaling basis explicitly ('scaled with resident-request occupancy, which at unchanged service time is proportional to arrival rate') and note the unchanged-service-time assumption it depends on.
issue.acceptance_test: The provenance note names the quantity the 45% -> 29% scaling is proportional to and states the assumption it depends on.

issue.figure: FIGURE 2.2 (Prefill and decode split by the roofline ridge)
issue.issue: The caption's capacity conclusion is stated with a broken unit and magnitude: 'the stated TTFT deadline implies ~1.9 FLOPS/second, exceeding the compared single-H100 theoretical peak (989 TFLOPS)'. As printed, 1.9 does not exceed 989, and 'FLOPS/second' is not a valid rate unit (FLOPS already denotes a per-second rate). The intended value is evidently ~1.9e15 FLOP/s (~1.9 PFLOPS), which does exceed 989 TFLOPS and does support the stated conclusion - but the printed form makes the conclusion self-contradictory and would be quoted verbatim by a reader or a downstream document. The caption also never states the TTFT deadline value it depends on, so the derivation cannot be checked from the page.

issue.acceptance_test: Re-derive the required prefill throughput from the book's own canonical inputs (prefill tokens x FLOPs/token, divided by the stated TTFT deadline) and print it with correct units, e.g. '~1.9e15 FLOP/s (~1.9 PFLOPS)'. The caption must also state the deadline value and the one-line derivation (tokens x FLOPs/token / deadline) so the comparison with 989 TFLOPS is checkable. issue.figure: FIGURE 2.2 (Prefill and decode split by the roofline ridge)
issue.issue: The caption's arithmetic-intensity value for the canonical prefill, '~2K FLOP/byte', is inconsistent with the book's own canonical workload and with the caption's own decode value. For a weight-traffic-dominated prefill, AI = (2 x P x n) / (2 x P) = n FLOP/byte, i.e. the arithmetic intensity of a prefill pass is approximately the number of tokens processed. The canonical workload's prefill is 9,200 input tokens (Table 1-1, printed 10: '1,200 prompt + 8K context'), which gives AI ~ 9.2K FLOP/byte, not ~2K. The caption's own decode figure of '~1 FLOP/byte' is exactly the n=1 case of the same relation, so the two numbers in the same sentence are mutually inconsistent under one model. The value is also inconsistent with the caption's capacity number: 1.9e15 FLOPs at 2K FLOP/byte implies ~950 GB of traffic, whereas the canonical 70B BF16 weight footprint is ~140 GB (implying AI ~13.6K). The regime conclusion (prefill compute-bound) survives any of these values, but the number, the marker position, and the word 'canonical' cannot all be right.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 44 (printed 24), caption: '(1) Regime: arithmetic intensity places the canonical prefill point ~2K FLOP/byte, well to the right of the ~295 ridge - so prefill sits in the compute-bound regime; decode at ~1 FLOP/byte sits in the memory-bound regime.' Canonical input length from Table 1-1 (printed 10): 'input tokens / request ~9,200 ... (1,200 prompt + 8K context)'. Figure annotation: 'H100 SXM, BF16 dense: 989 TFLOPS peak, 3.35 TB/s HBM3 -> ridge at 295 FLOP/byte'.
issue.acceptance_test: Reconcile against Ch 7/Ch 8: (a) if the canonical prefill is 9,200 tokens, the caption must read ~9.2K FLOP/byte (or the book must show the derivation that yields 2K, e.g. a different prefill length or a different traffic denominator); (b) the figure's prefill marker must sit at the same x-value as the caption states; (c) the caption's capacity number must be consistent with the same AI value. Confirm all three agree before release.
