issue.issue: Three small defects in one table. (a) The derivation column is inconsistent: the two token-rate rows show their arithmetic ('9,200 x 10', '9,200 x 40') but the ratio row shows only '[canonical scenario] [DERIVED]' with no division, so the reader must supply 9,200 / 300 themselves. (b) The 'value' column is far wider than its contents require, leaving a large empty gap between the values and the derivation column and making the table read as two disconnected blocks. (c) The prose immediately above the table reports output throughput ('Output tokens/s: 300 x 10 = 3,000 tokens/s output'), which has no row in the table, even though the table's own title promises 'Token throughput'.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 30 (printed 10): table rows read 'input tokens / request | ~9,200', 'output tokens / request | ~300', 'input / output ratio | ~30x | [canonical scenario] [DERIVED]', 'input tokens/s @ 10 rps | ~92,000 | 9,200 x 10', 'input tokens/s @ peak 40 rps | ~368,000 | 9,200 x 40'; prose above: 'Output tokens/s: 300 x 10 = 3,000 tokens/s output.'
issue.acceptance_test: Add the missing division to the ratio row ('9,200 / 300 ~ 30x'), add a row 'output tokens/s @ 10 rps | ~3,000 | 300 x 10', and rebalance the column widths so the value column is sized to its content. Confirm on the rendered page that no derivation cell wraps to more than two lines and that the table's vertical extent does not grow.

issue.issue: All four figure pages in this batch place the figure and its caption at the top of the page and then leave roughly a quarter to a third of the text block empty, with no body text following on the page. The result is four pages that read as half-pages and that break the reading rhythm between the figure and the prose that interprets it. This is a composition issue rather than a content issue, but it is visible on every figure page in the batch.
issue.evidence: Rendered pages 28, 29, 36 and 44 (printed 8, 9, 16, 24): in each case the figure occupies the upper portion, the caption follows, and the lower portion of the text block is blank down to the bottom margin.
issue.acceptance_test: Reflow so that each figure is followed on the same page by at least one paragraph of body text (or so that the figure is placed to share a page with the section that interprets it). Confirm on the rendered pages that no page in this batch ends with more than roughly one line of trailing whitespace above the bottom margin.

issue.figure: FIGURE 3.4 (Dense vs MoE parameter allocation and KV cache behavior)
issue.issue: The figure's per-token weight-traffic line and the caption state the same quantity with different units and different values, and the caption's decomposition understates the expert traffic by 2x. Figure reads: 'per token: top-2 = 11.4 GB (2 x 5.78) / + 1.4 GB always-on = 12.8 GB / ~ 25.6 GB'. Caption reads: 'only ~12.8 GB is active per token: the always-on attention/shared weights (~1.4 GB) plus the two routed experts (11.4 GB)'. Three mutually inconsistent readings are available to the reader: 12.8 GB (caption), 24.2 GB (if 11.4 GB/expert and 1.4 GB always-on are literal), or 25.6 GB (figure's last line). The figure's own chain only closes if the first two numbers are billions of PARAMETERS (11.56 + 1.4 = 12.96 B params, x2 bytes = 25.9 GB) rather than GB; the 'GB' labels on those two lines are therefore wrong. Separately, the caption's 'two routed experts (11.4 GB)' is the size of ONE expert (5.78B params x 2 B = 11.56 GB); two experts are 22.8-23.1 GB, as the figure's own legend states ('active experts = 23 GB resident (2 x 11.4)').
issue.evidence: Re-derivation from the figure's own stated inputs: 1 expert = 5.78B params x 2 B/param = 11.56 GB (figure prints 11.4 GB). Top-2 = 23.1 GB. Always-on per token = 1.4 GB (figure) or 1.4B params = 2.8 GB (if the '12.8' chain is in B params). Per-token active weight traffic is therefore 24.2 GB or 25.9 GB, never 12.8 GB. The figure's '~ 25.6 GB' is the only value consistent with a B-params reading of the chain, but it is unlabeled and unreconciled with the caption. The caption's '~12.8 GB' is a unit slip (12.8 B params) that directly contradicts the figure's '~ 25.6 GB' on the same page. This is the figure whose entire purpose is a quantitative dense-vs-MoE contrast, and the number an architect would carry away (per-token weight traffic, which sets decode bandwidth demand) is ambiguous by a factor of two.
issue.acceptance_test: Pick one unit convention and apply it to every line of the figure and the caption. Recommended: state per-token active weight traffic in GB only, e.g. 'per token: top-2 experts 23.1 GB (2 x 11.56) + always-on 1.4 GB = 24.5 GB' (or whatever the always-on figure resolves to), and delete the '~ 25.6 GB' line or label it explicitly with what it represents. The caption must then quote the same number as the figure. If '~ 25.6 GB' was intended as a comparison to a different model (e.g. the ~12.8B-active challenger at FP16), label it with that model's name. A reviewer recomputing 2 x 5.78B x 2 B/param + always-on from the figure's own printed inputs must land on the same number the caption prints.

issue.issue: The expert size is stated two mutually inconsistent ways: '1 expert = 5.78B params = 11.4 GB (FP16)'. 5.78B params x 2 bytes/param = 11.56 GB, not 11.4 GB. The legend's 'inactive experts = 68 GB (6 x 11.4)' and 'active experts = 23 GB resident (2 x 11.4)' are consistent with 11.4 GB/expert (= 5.7B params), while the '5.78B' figure is not. The 1.4% discrepancy propagates into the per-token line ('2 x 5.78') and into the caption's '11.4 GB'.
issue.evidence: 8 x 11.4 GB = 91.2 GB ~ '91 GB experts' (consistent). 8 x 5.78B x 2 B = 92.5 GB, which does not equal the printed 91 GB. 8 x 5.7B x 2 B = 91.2 GB, which does. The internally consistent parameter set is 5.7B/expert, not 5.78B.
issue.acceptance_test: Either change '5.78B params' to '5.7B params' (or print 11.56 GB), or change '11.4 GB' to '11.56 GB' and re-derive the legend's 68/23/91/94 GB figures. All four of '1 expert = ...', 'inactive = 68 GB', 'active = 23 GB', 'experts = 91 GB' must be mutually consistent to within the printed rounding.

issue.issue: The MoE grid contains nine cells but only eight are labeled (E1-E8); the ninth cell (bottom-right) is blank white and is not represented in the legend. The legend defines exactly three swatches (blue = all 140 GB resident & active; gray = inactive experts; orange = active experts). A reader cannot tell whether the blank cell is the always-on/shared-weight block (3 GB), an empty slot, or a rendering artifact. Since the figure's headline claim is 'MoE total resident = 94 GB = 91 GB experts + 3 GB always-on', the always-on block is exactly the quantity the blank cell appears to stand for, and it is the one element left undecoded.
issue.evidence: Visual inspection of the rendered page: the MoE grid is 3 rows x 3 columns; cells E1-E8 are filled (E1 and E4 orange, E2/E3/E5/E6/E7/E8 gray); the ninth cell is empty with no border fill and no label. No legend entry corresponds to it.
issue.acceptance_test: Either label the ninth cell (e.g. 'shared/always-on 3 GB') and add a legend swatch for it, or remove it so the grid is 3x2 + a separate labeled always-on block. A reader must be able to account for all 94 GB from the drawn elements without doing arithmetic the figure does not show.

issue.issue: The two grids encode different things and are not proportional, so the visual comparison the figure invites is wrong. The dense panel draws 20 identical unlabeled squares; the MoE panel draws 8 named expert cells plus one blank. Area ratio 20:9 = 2.2x, while the parameter/residency ratio the figure states is 140 GB : 94 GB = 1.49x. The caption's caveat 'not shown to scale' is attached only to the MoE, leaving the dense grid apparently to scale. A reader glancing at the picture will conclude the dense model is roughly twice the MoE, which is not what the numbers say. The dense squares are also unlabeled, so the reader cannot tell what a square represents (layers? blocks? parameter groups?), while the MoE cells are explicitly experts.
issue.evidence: Visual inspection: dense grid = 4 rows x 5 columns of blue squares; MoE grid = 3 rows x 3 columns of expert cells. Caption: 'An 8-expert MoE keeps full expert set as resident weights - ~94 GB, not shown to scale'. The 'not shown to scale' qualifier does not cover the dense grid, and the two grids use different cell semantics (generic chunk vs named expert).
issue.acceptance_test: Make the encoding explicit and consistent: either (a) state in the figure that cells are schematic and non-proportional, applying the caveat to BOTH panels, or (b) make the cell areas proportional to bytes (e.g. 140 GB vs 94 GB drawn to scale) and label what one cell represents in each panel. A reader should not be able to infer a parameter ratio from the drawn areas that contradicts the printed 140 GB / 94 GB.

issue.issue: The caption parenthetical appears to read '(~10^7)' in the clause 'the active-expert fraction (~10^7) vs ~27B'. The exponent is not legible at 150 dpi and, more importantly, no quantity in the figure or caption corresponds to 10^7. The sentence is a list of three differences (weight residency, active-expert fraction, attention shape) between the dense/MoE pair and the challenger; the active-parameter fraction of the MoE is 12.8B of ~47B = ~0.27, and of the challenger ~14B of ~27B = ~0.52. Neither is 10^7. As printed, the clause is uninterpretable and appears to be a corrupted number.
issue.evidence: Rendered-page inspection: the parenthetical is a base-10 numeral with a superscript that cannot be resolved at print size; no quantity in FIG 3.4 has that magnitude (the smallest printed quantity is 1.4 GB). The caption's own later paragraph gives the active quantities (12.8 B params for the MoE; ~14B active of ~27B for the challenger), neither of which matches.
issue.acceptance_test: Replace the parenthetical with an explicit, legible quantity and value, e.g. 'the active-parameter fraction (~0.27 of the MoE's ~47B vs ~0.52 of the challenger's ~27B)'. The value must be recomputable from the numbers printed elsewhere in the same caption.

issue.issue: The term 'always-on' is used for two different quantities on the same figure without distinction: 'MoE total resident = 94 GB = 91 GB experts + 3 GB always-on' and 'per token: ... + 1.4 GB always-on'. The caption explains the 1.4 GB as 'the always-on attention/shared weights', i.e. a subset of the 3 GB, but the figure gives no hint that the per-token figure is a subset rather than the same quantity. A reader may reasonably ask why the always-on block shrinks from 3 GB to 1.4 GB per token, and the figure gives no answer (the likely answer - embeddings and lm_head are resident but not fully read per token - is exactly the kind of distinction the book should make explicit).
issue.evidence: Figure text: 'MoE total resident = 94 GB = 91 GB experts + 3 GB always-on' vs 'per token: top-2 = ... + 1.4 GB always-on = ...'. Caption: 'the always-on attention/shared weights (~1.4 GB)'.
issue.acceptance_test: Rename the two quantities distinctly in the figure (e.g. 'always-on resident 3 GB (incl. embeddings + lm_head)' vs 'always-on read per token 1.4 GB (attention + shared)'), or add a one-line note stating why the per-token read is smaller than the resident footprint.

issue.issue: The caption sentence 'A dense 70B activates all 70B parameters per token (resident weights + 140 GB, KV grows linearly with context)' is garbled: 'resident weights + 140 GB' reads as a sum of two things when 140 GB IS the resident weight footprint. Separately, the figure never states the dense per-token weight traffic (140 GB/token) as a number, so the headline contrast of the figure - dense reads 140 GB of weights per token while the MoE reads roughly 25 GB - is left for the reader to assemble, and the caption's '12.8 GB' (see FIG-3.4-01) actively misleads in that assembly.
issue.evidence: Caption text as rendered; figure legend states 'all 140 GB resident & active' but no per-token dense figure is printed.
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite as 'A dense 70B reads all 140 GB of weights per token (all 70B parameters resident and active)'. Add the dense per-token traffic as an explicit number in the figure so the dense-vs-MoE ratio is visible without arithmetic.

issue.issue: The caption claims a property the drawing does not show. Caption: 'a full-canvas masked sampler that accepts positions out of order while recomputing bidirectional prefixes'. Panel B's middle canvas shows positions 1, 2 and 3 accepted in order (A, B, C) with position 4 still '?', i.e. strictly in-order acceptance. The distinguishing feature of full-canvas masked sampling - that a later position may be committed before an earlier one - is never depicted, so the figure cannot support the caption's claim. A reader who takes the picture as evidence would conclude that masked diffusion accepts tokens left to right, which is the autoregressive behavior the figure is contrasting against.
issue.evidence: Rendered panel B: canvas 1 = [?][?][?][?]; canvas 2 = [A][B][C][?] with a dashed orange bracket over A,B,C; canvas 3 = [A][B][C][D]. No canvas shows a gap in the accepted prefix.
issue.acceptance_test: Either change the middle canvas to show out-of-order acceptance (e.g. [?][B][?][?] -> [A][B][C][?]) or amend the caption to describe what is drawn ('accepts selected positions, recomputing the bidirectional prefix each evaluation'). The caption's claim must be visible in the drawing.

issue.issue: Panel B's final canvas marks A, B, C, D with the same solid-blue brackets that the caption defines as 'finalized prefix state' - the marking the book elsewhere uses to signal reusable, cacheable prefix state. The caption's own point for this panel is the opposite: 'Full bidirectional forwards: fixed IDs can still acquire new KV.' As drawn, the reader can conclude that a full-canvas masked sampler ends with a stable, reusable prefix, which is precisely the misconception the caption is trying to prevent. The figure and the caption are in tension on the single most consequential property of the panel.
issue.evidence: Caption key: 'Solid brackets mark finalized prefix state, not just accepted IDs' and 'accepted token IDs alone do not establish reusable KV'. Panel B's final canvas uses solid blue brackets on all four cells, identical to panel A's finalized prefix. The caption's warning that fixed IDs can still acquire new KV applies to the sampling process, which the figure's terminal canvas does not distinguish from panel A's terminal canvas.
issue.acceptance_test: Make the distinction visible: either use a distinct marking for panel B's terminal canvas (e.g. a note 'KV not reusable: full-canvas recompute') or add a caption clause stating explicitly that the terminal canvas in panel B is a completed sample, not a reusable prefix, and that the reusable-prefix marking is deliberately absent. A reader must not be able to carry away 'masked diffusion yields a reusable prefix' from the drawing.

issue.issue: The figure uses three cell states (solid-blue finalized cell, '?' undetermined cell, '-' not-yet cell) and two bracket styles (solid blue, dashed orange), but the caption's key defines only the solid blue ('Solid brackets mark finalized prefix state'). The dashed orange bracket - which carries the panel's main point about recomputation and repeated evaluations - is never defined; the reader must infer it from the 'repeat evaluations' annotation. The '-' glyph is also used with two slightly different senses (panel A: not yet generated; panel C: position not yet in scope because it belongs to a future block), and neither sense is stated.
issue.evidence: Caption text: 'Solid brackets mark finalized prefix state, not just accepted IDs' and 'Loops represent repeated evaluations, not fixed counts or proportional time.' No clause defines the dashed orange bracket or the '-' cell.
issue.acceptance_test: Extend the caption's key to three lines: solid blue bracket = finalized prefix state (reusable); dashed orange bracket = accepted but not finalized / recomputed region; '?' = undetermined position in scope; '-' = position not yet in scope. Each glyph must be decodable from the caption alone.

issue.issue: Panel C is titled 'Block-causal diffusion: refine, commit, advance' and the caption says it 'finalizes an active block before advancing' and that 'A valid block-causal boundary prevents later blocks changing it', but the drawing contains no visible block boundary. The canvas is a single row of four cells with no separator, bracket, or shading distinguishing the active block from future blocks, so the defining property of block-causal sampling - that a committed block is immutable and later blocks cannot revise it - is not readable from the picture. The reader sees a four-cell canvas that differs from panel B only in the placement of '?' and '-'.
issue.evidence: Rendered panel C: 'causal prefix' -> [?][?][-][-] -> [A][B][?][?] (dashed orange over A,B) -> [A][B][C][D]. No block delimiter is drawn between cells 2 and 3 or elsewhere.
issue.acceptance_test: Draw the block boundary explicitly (a vertical rule or a bracketed group between the committed block and the pending block) and show the pending block being refined while the committed block is drawn as immutable. A reader must be able to state what the block boundary is from the drawing alone.

issue.issue: Panel A is headed 'Continuous diffusion (schematic state values; bars = token probabilities)'. Labeling the bars as token probabilities inside the continuous-diffusion lane invites the reader to conclude that continuous diffusion operates over a categorical token distribution - i.e. that the continuous lane is just a differently-drawn discrete diffusion. The caption draws exactly the opposite distinction ('a continuous-noise lane and a categorical-MASK lane'), and the prose above the figure says 'Forward: q, add corruption', which is a continuous-state operation. The figure's own label undercuts the distinction the figure exists to make.
issue.evidence: Panel A header text as rendered: 'A Continuous diffusion (schematic state values; bars = token probabilities)'. Panel B header: 'B Masked discrete diffusion (one categorical choice)'. Caption: '...in a continuous-noise lane and a categorical-MASK lane.'
issue.acceptance_test: Relabel panel A's bars so the state type is unambiguous, e.g. 'schematic continuous state (shown as a categorical readout for illustration)' or 'schematic state values (not a token distribution)'. The reader must not be able to conclude that continuous diffusion is defined over token probabilities.

issue.issue: The 'noise prior' canvas does not read as noise. Its bars are of roughly the same varying heights as the 'clean continuous data' canvas, so the visual progression clean -> partly corrupted -> noise prior is carried entirely by the captions under the boxes rather than by the drawing. In a continuous diffusion the forward process drives the marginal toward a broad, near-uniform distribution; showing that flattening would make the corruption direction self-evident and would let the picture do the work the labels currently do.
issue.evidence: Rendered panel A: the third canvas's bar heights are comparable in spread to the first canvas's; no flattening toward uniform is visible.
issue.acceptance_test: Make the third canvas visibly flatter (near-uniform bars) and, if desired, the second intermediate, so that a reader who ignores the labels still reads 'progressive corruption toward a prior'. Verify at print size that the flattening is visible.

issue.issue: Printed page 44 is a figure-only page whose figure begins roughly a quarter of the way down the page, leaving a large empty band at the top and a comparable band at the bottom. The page reads as an accidental float placement rather than a designed figure page. This is the same pattern visible on printed page 97 (FIG 6.1), suggesting a systematic float-placement issue rather than a one-off.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 64: blank from the top margin to approximately 28% of the page height before the figure title 'Wan2.2 A14B: active != resident parameters'; the caption ends at roughly 72% of the page height.
issue.acceptance_test: Adjust float placement (or add a short lead-in paragraph) so the figure sits at the top of the page or the page is filled; no printed page should carry an unexplained blank band exceeding roughly 20% of the page height.

issue.issue: The two-line annotation 'Denoising schedule progresses / Not two experts within one forward' is placed in the gap between the two dashed checkpoint-to-stage arrows, where it reads as a label on those arrows rather than as a statement about the stage-to-stage transition. The black arrow from 'High-noise stage' to 'Low-noise stage' already carries the schedule-progression meaning, so the annotation is both ambiguously placed and partly redundant.
issue.evidence: Rendered figure: the annotation sits between the two vertical dashed blue arrows, above the horizontal black arrow.
issue.acceptance_test: Move the annotation so it unambiguously annotates the horizontal stage-to-stage arrow (or place it as a caption-side note), and confirm at print size that no reader can take it as an arrow label for the dashed arrows.

issue.issue: The figure's disclosure of its own main caveat is typographically weak. The caption's central claim is that the mapping is 'non-exclusive: in practice a dimension often influences several decisions at once', but the figure draws a strict one-to-one bipartite mapping with no cross-links, and the only in-figure disclosure is the small light-gray italic line 'primary mapping shown; cross-influences omitted (see caption)' at the bottom. At print size that line is the least visually prominent element on the page, so a reader who skims the figure (the normal case) receives the one-to-one message the caption explicitly disclaims.
issue.evidence: Rendered figure: the caveat line is set in small italic gray type, centered below the last row, with no rule, box, or color to distinguish it from a source note.
issue.acceptance_test: Give the caveat line at least the weight of the figure's other annotations (e.g. non-italic, darker, or set in a tinted band), or draw one representative cross-link (e.g. Latency SLO -> model size/type, which the caption itself names) so the non-exclusivity is visible in the geometry.

issue.issue: The two arrows from 'Five selection surfaces' are both labeled 'split', which asserts that the five surfaces are partitioned between the retrieval leg and the generation leg. That is not what the caption describes: the five surfaces (quality, latency, KV cache, cost per token, retrieve-vs-generate) are the criteria applied to model selection, and each leg is evaluated against all of them - latency and cost-per-token matter for the embedding model as much as for the generator. As drawn, the figure teaches a partitioning model that the caption's own framing ('the five surfaces are the model-selection dimensions') contradicts, and a reader could conclude that, for example, KV cache is only a generation-leg concern.
issue.evidence: Rendered figure: 'Five selection surfaces' -> two arrows, both labeled 'split' -> 'Retrieval leg' and 'Generation leg'. Caption: 'The five surfaces are the model-selection dimensions; they are deliberately distinct from the end-to-end evaluation gates...'.
issue.acceptance_test: Relabel the two arrows so they do not assert partition (e.g. 'applies to', 'evaluated for'), or draw the five surfaces feeding both legs with a shared bracket. The figure must not imply that any surface applies to only one leg.

issue.issue: The abbreviation 'S/tok' in the 'Five selection surfaces' box is ambiguous and undefined on the page: 'S' can plausibly mean seconds (a latency measure, which would duplicate the adjacent 'latency' surface) or dollars (a cost measure, which would duplicate the workload box's 'cost'). The reader cannot resolve it from the figure or the caption, and the two readings point to different architectural decisions.
issue.evidence: Rendered box text: 'quality . latency . KV cache . S/tok . retrieve-vs-generate'. The caption lists the surfaces only by name ('the five surfaces are the model-selection dimensions') without expanding 'S/tok'.
issue.acceptance_test: Spell the surface out in the figure (e.g. '$/token' or 's/token'), or define it in the caption's first sentence. If it is a cost surface, the caption should say so, since 'cost' appears separately in the workload box.

issue.issue: The terminal box reads 'base + RAG + quadrals'. 'Quadrals' is not a standard term and is not defined on the inspected pages. If it denotes the four evaluation gates the caption enumerates (retrieval quality, embedding recall, grounding, final answer quality), then the figure contradicts the caption's explicit statement that those gates 'are not shown here because this figure is a selection map, not an evaluation pipeline'. If it denotes something else, the reader has no way to know what.
issue.evidence: Rendered box text: 'RAG system decision / base + RAG + quadrals'. Caption: '...those gates are measured on the target corpus and are not shown here because this figure is a selection map, not an evaluation pipeline.'
issue.acceptance_test: Either replace 'quadrals' with the term the chapter actually uses for that comparison, or define it in one clause in the caption. If it denotes the four gates, remove it from the figure or amend the caption's 'not shown here' clause so the two do not conflict.

issue.issue: Printed page 97 carries FIG 6.1 alone, with roughly 25% blank space above the figure and roughly 30% below the caption. The figure is small relative to the page and the surrounding white space makes the page look unfinished rather than composed. The same top-band artifact appears on printed page 44 (see FIG-3.3-01), so this is a systematic float-placement issue.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 97: blank from the top margin to approximately 25% of page height before the first box; the caption ends at approximately 68% of page height.
issue.acceptance_test: Either enlarge the figure to use the available measure and pull it to the top of the page, or place it on a page with running text so the white space is not a full-page band. No printed page should carry an unexplained blank band exceeding roughly 20% of the page height.

issue.figure: FIG 26.1 — Workload fingerprints on the six axes
issue.issue: The chat series drawn in the figure does not match the chat series stated in the prose on the facing page. The prose asserts exact values ('the long-context RAG Q&A scores 0.95 / 0.20 / 0.70 / 0.55 / 0.40 / 0.45, chat 0.35 / 0.95 / 0.50 / 0.90 / 0.35 / 0.90, batch 0.55 / 0.60 / 0.30 / 0.85 / 0.35 / 0.90'), but the orange 'High-throughput chat' bars read approximately 0.75 on 'Cost sensitive' and approximately 0.55 on 'Output tokens'. The RAG and batch series agree with the prose on all six axes; only the chat series diverges, on exactly two axes.
issue.evidence: Axis calibration from the rendered plot: y=0.0 at the baseline and y=1.0 at the top gridline, 0.2 per tick. 'Cost sensitive' group: blue ~0.55, orange ~0.75, green ~0.85 (prose: chat 0.90). 'Output tokens' group: blue ~0.45, orange ~0.55, green ~0.90 (prose: chat 0.90). The prose also asserts 'the same table is carried in the archetypes' and 'the bar values are [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]', so the figure and the table are claimed to be the same dataset. A reader comparing the figure with the sentence on the next page will find two contradicting numbers on the same spread.
issue.acceptance_test: Open the source data for FIG 26.1 and the archetypes table (Table 26.1) and confirm they are the same six-value vector per family. Either (a) correct the two chat values in the prose/table to the drawn values, or (b) correct the two drawn bars to 0.90 / 0.90. Re-render and verify that all eighteen bars equal the eighteen stated values to within the axis-reading tolerance, and that the prose sentence and the figure agree on the facing-page spread.

issue.figure: FIG 26.1 — Workload fingerprints on the six axes
issue.issue: The bars carry no value labels, so the exact numbers the prose claims for this figure cannot be read off the figure at all. The reader must estimate each of eighteen values from a 0.2-spaced axis, and the prose then asserts them to two decimal places. This is precisely the condition under which FIG26-01 could go unnoticed, and it makes the figure non-authoritative for the 'authored intensity' dataset it is the sole visualization of.
issue.evidence: The rendered chart shows only the axis ticks (0.0–1.0 by 0.2) and the legend; no bar is annotated with its value. The caption's only quantitative statement is 'per-axis 0–1 scale; compare within an axis, not across axes.' The prose on PDF 447 supplies the numbers instead.
issue.acceptance_test: Add a value label to each of the eighteen bars (or replace the chart with the table that the prose says carries the same data). Verify at print size that the labels are legible and do not collide with the legend or the axis, and that every label equals the corresponding value in the prose and in Table 26.1.

issue.figure: FIG A.1 — 2026 frontier MoE extreme sparsity
issue.issue: The Kimi K3 row's parameter annotation is inconsistent with its own bar by a factor of ten. The bar is labelled 3.7% and the row annotation reads '280B/104B active', but 104/280 = 37.1%, not 3.7%. The other three rows are internally consistent (13/284 = 4.58% -> 4.6%; 18/320 = 5.63% -> 5.6%; 6/125 = 4.80% -> 4.8%), so the Kimi row is the outlier and the annotation almost certainly omits a decimal point ('10.4B' would give 10.4/280 = 3.71% -> 3.7%).
issue.evidence: Rendered annotation text: '280B/104B active'. Recomputation: 104 / 280 = 0.3714 -> 37.1%, which would not fit on the plotted axis (0–10%) and is not what is drawn. With '10.4B': 10.4 / 280 = 0.03714 -> 3.7%, matching the drawn bar and the label. The figure's own footnote states 'the displayed fractions are [DERIVED] by division', so the annotation and the bar are contractually bound to each other.
issue.acceptance_test: Check the source annotation string for the Kimi K3 row. If it is '10.4B', correct the string and re-render, then verify at print size that the decimal point is visible (see FIGA1-04). If it is genuinely '104B', the bar value and the label must change to 37.1% and the axis must be rescaled. Acceptance: for every row, active/total recomputed from the printed annotation equals the printed percentage to within the rounding bound.

issue.figure: FIG A.1 — footnote (asterisk note) and caption
issue.issue: The footnote states the Qwen bar's derivation with the division inverted: '* Own bar = backbone ratio (125B ÷ 6B open-activation)'. 125 ÷ 6 = 20.8, which is not the 4.8% plotted. The bar is 6 ÷ 125 = 4.8%. As written, the footnote's formula does not produce the number the figure displays, and 'backbone ratio' is not defined anywhere on the page.
issue.evidence: Footnote text as rendered: 'Own bar = backbone ratio (125B ÷ 6B open-activation), excluding the 51B re-gram and 4B MTP; VENDOR-REPORTED total/active counts; the displayed fractions are [DERIVED] by division; parameter definitions vary across vendors.' Bar label: '4.8%'. 6/125 = 0.048; 125/6 = 20.83.
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite the footnote so the arithmetic reproduces the plotted value, e.g. 'Own bar = active fraction of the backbone only (6B ÷ 125B = 4.8%), excluding the 51B re-gram and 4B MTP'. Acceptance: a reader can substitute the two printed numbers into the printed formula and obtain the printed percentage.

issue.figure: FIG A.1 — chart subtitle vs caption/footnote
issue.issue: The chart's own subtitle states a denominator rule that the figure then breaks for one of its four bars: 'denominator: each model's own vendor-reported total, varies by vendor'. The Qwen bar's denominator is explicitly NOT the vendor-reported total — it is the 125B backbone only, excluding the 51B re-gram and 4B MTP. The caption and footnote acknowledge this, but the subtitle, which is the first thing the reader reads inside the figure, asserts the opposite.
issue.evidence: Subtitle as rendered: 'denominator: each model's own vendor-reported total, varies by vendor'. Footnote: 'Own bar = backbone ratio ..., excluding the 51B re-gram and 4B MTP'. Caption: 'the Qwen bar is its 125B backbone only, so the four bars are not one-for-like series'. The subtitle is the only one of the three that claims a uniform denominator.
issue.acceptance_test: Change the subtitle to state the actual rule, e.g. 'denominator: vendor-reported total except the Qwen bar (backbone only); denominators differ by vendor'. Acceptance: subtitle, footnote and caption all describe the same denominator for every one of the four bars, and no reader can infer from the subtitle alone that all four share one denominator.

issue.issue: Box 2's drawn diagnosis contradicts the caption's description of the same box and the mini-case's diagnosis. Box 2 reads 'decode bandwidth-bound (low-batch regime)'; the caption says the DERIVED stage 'for this TTFT budget is prefill- and queue-dominated'; and §26.8 (PDF 453) builds the baseline on 'prefill compute inflated by queueing' and 'the baseline is queue-inflated'. A reader who trusts the figure concludes the capstone's bottleneck is decode bandwidth; a reader who trusts the caption concludes it is prefill and queueing. These are different diagnoses and they imply different patterns.
issue.evidence: Box 2 text as rendered: '2 · DERIVED / decode bandwidth-bound / (low-batch regime)'. Caption: 'the DERIVED stage (box 2), which for this TTFT budget is prefill- and queue-dominated'. PDF 453: 'the 450 ms is a service-time sum with a queue-inflated compute term ... so the baseline is queue-inflated, not queue-free' and 'the baseline p99 came from a measured latency distribution'.
issue.acceptance_test: Decide which diagnosis the capstone actually supports and make box 2, the caption, and §26.8 state the same one. If the intended diagnosis is prefill/queue-dominated, box 2 must say so (e.g. 'prefill- and queue-dominated at the offered load'); if decode bandwidth-bound is intended, the caption and §26.8 must be rewritten. Acceptance: a reader who reads only the figure, only the caption, or only §26.8 reaches the same bottleneck conclusion.

issue.issue: Box 1's operating point is not reconcilable with the per-host ceiling the caption and §26.8 use. Box 1 states 'request rate ~2 rps' together with 'utilization ~45%', while the caption calls '~2.0 rps' the 'per-host ceiling' and §26.8 states 'the rps is the ~2.0 rps the host can actually sustain, not a multiple of it'. If the offered request rate equals the host's sustained capacity, utilization is 100%, not 45%. If 2 rps is the capacity and the offered load is ~0.9 rps, then 'request rate ~2 rps' is mislabelled. Either way one of the two numbers in box 1 is wrong, and 'utilization' has no stated denominator (request-rate utilization? GPU/SM utilization?).
issue.evidence: Box 1 as rendered: 'request rate ~2 rps / utilization ~45% / baseline TTFT p99 ~450 ms'. Caption: 'as the offered load presses on the host's ~2.0 rps per-host ceiling (box 1's assumed inputs)'. PDF 453: 'the host serves ~2.0 rps (Ch 17:20) ... the rps is the ~2.0 rps the host can actually sustain, not a multiple of it'.
issue.acceptance_test: State the denominator explicitly in box 1 (e.g. 'offered load ~0.9 rps = 45% of the ~2.0 rps per-host ceiling' or 'request rate ~2 rps (per-host ceiling); GPU utilization ~45%'). Acceptance: the offered load, the utilization fraction, and the per-host ceiling are mutually consistent under one stated reading, and the same reading is used in the caption and in §26.8.

issue.issue: The caption's stated chain does not match the chain drawn. The caption gives 'Chain: ASSUMPTION (box 1 holds assumed scenario inputs, not instrumented FACTs) -> DERIVED (box 2) -> ASSUMPTION', which omits the PATTERN stage entirely and ends on a stage the figure places last. The figure draws four stages: 1 ASSUMPTION -> 2 DERIVED -> 3 PATTERN -> (feedback) 1 ASSUMPTION.
issue.evidence: Caption as rendered: 'Chain: ASSUMPTION (box 1 holds assumed scenario inputs, not instrumented FACTs) -> DERIVED (box 2) -> ASSUMPTION; the validation step compares the load test's measured TTFT p99 against the hypothesis criterion ...'. Figure: boxes labelled '1 · ASSUMPTION', '2 · DERIVED', '3 · PATTERN', with a red feedback arrow returning to box 1.
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite the caption's chain to enumerate all four stages in the drawn order, including the PATTERN stage and the feedback return. Acceptance: the caption's chain, read as a sequence of stage names, is exactly the sequence of box headers in the figure.

issue.issue: The caption's central claim — 'an assumption that fails validation returns to box 1 for adjustment' — cannot be represented by the drawn topology. The only return path is the red arrow, and it originates at box 3 (PATTERN), which is reached only after the validation arrow has passed. A failed validation therefore has no drawn path back to box 1; the diagram instead shows 'adjust + pick pattern' as the feedback action, conflating 'the assumption was wrong, revise it' with 'a pattern was selected, measure it'.
issue.evidence: Caption: 'The loop closes by measurement — an assumption that fails validation returns to box 1 for adjustment, and only measured FACTs enter the decision.' Figure: green arrow 'validate p99 < 300 ms (target <= 800 ms)' runs from box 2 down to box 3; the red arrow labelled 'feedback' / 'adjust + pick pattern' runs from box 3 left and up to box 1. There is no arrow from the validation step back to box 1.
issue.acceptance_test: Either add a distinct 'validation failed' return path from the validation step to box 1 (visually distinguishable from the 'pattern selected' feedback path), or rewrite the caption so it describes the path the figure actually draws. Acceptance: every transition the caption asserts is drawable in the figure, and the figure contains no transition the caption contradicts.

issue.issue: The validation criterion is labelled with a bare 'p99' ('validate p99 < 300 ms (target <= 800 ms)'). The metric is not named. Elsewhere the book is careful to distinguish TTFT p99 from TPOT/ITL p99, and the caption itself writes 'TTFT p99 < 300 ms' and 'p99 <= 800 ms TTFT target'. A reader who sees only the figure cannot tell which latency distribution is being gated.
issue.evidence: Arrow label as rendered: 'validate / p99 < 300 ms / (target <= 800 ms)'. Caption: 'compares the load test's measured TTFT p99 against the hypothesis criterion (TTFT p99 < 300 ms ...) under the capstone's p99 <= 800 ms TTFT target'.
issue.acceptance_test: Change the arrow label to 'validate TTFT p99 < 300 ms (target <= 800 ms)'. Acceptance: the metric named in the figure matches the metric named in the caption and in §26.8, and no bare 'p99' remains in the figure.

issue.issue: The caption's closing sentence is not parseable as written: 'the p99 tail is a validation step measure, where p99 is the miss value, not a blend.' The intended point (p99 is a pass/fail criterion, not an average of the distribution) is defensible, but the sentence as printed does not state it, and it is the sentence that closes the figure's argument.
issue.evidence: Caption as rendered: '... -> the p99 tail is a validation step measure, where p99 is the miss value, not a blend.'
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite as a single unambiguous sentence, e.g. 'the p99 tail is measured at the validation step, where p99 is the pass/fail criterion rather than an average of the distribution.' Acceptance: the sentence parses on one reading and states the intended distinction.

issue.figure: FIG 25.1 — The Anatomy of an Architecture Decision Record
issue.issue: The annotation 'kept, not edited' beside ADR-001 contradicts the caption's own rule. The caption states 'The body's never rewritten, and only the Status line is updated when a successor supersedes it', and the figure's own header reads 'ADR-001 (superseded)' — so the status line was in fact edited. As drawn, the annotation denies any edit to a record whose status line demonstrably changed.
issue.evidence: Figure annotation as rendered: 'kept, not edited' (italic, upper right of the ADR-001 card). Figure header: 'ADR-001 (superseded)'. Caption: 'The body's never rewritten, and only the Status line is updated when a successor supersedes it.'
issue.acceptance_test: Change the annotation to 'body kept; status line updated' or 'kept on file; body not edited'. Acceptance: the annotation and the caption describe the same mutation rule, and the annotation does not deny the status change the figure itself displays.

issue.issue: Red carries two unrelated meanings in one figure: it marks ADR-002's identity (its border and title) and it marks the inheritance link (the dashed bracket and its label). A reader scanning the page can reasonably read the red dashed bracket as 'part of ADR-002' rather than 'a relationship between the two records'. Blue is used both for ADR-001's border and for the field labels inside both cards, so blue likewise does not encode card identity consistently.
issue.evidence: Rendered: ADR-001 card has a blue border with blue field labels; ADR-002 card has a red border with blue field labels; the bracket, its hooks, and the label 'consequences of ADR-001 may become the context of ADR-002' are red.
issue.acceptance_test: Reserve one hue for record identity (both cards) and a second, visually distinct treatment (e.g. a dashed grey or a distinct arrowhead) for the inheritance link, or label the link explicitly as a relationship. Acceptance: no hue in the figure denotes two different things, and the link is identifiable as a link in grayscale.

issue.issue: The italic annotations ('kept, not edited', 'the record', 'the situation', 'the choice', 'the effects', 'rejected options') are set noticeably smaller than the field labels and appear to fall at or below the 8 pt floor for figure in-text annotations. At print size the right-hand descriptors are the least legible elements on the page, and they carry the field definitions that the caption then repeats.
issue.evidence: Rendered at 150 dpi: the right-column italic descriptors are visibly smaller than the bold left-column field labels; 'kept, not edited' is smaller still. No measurement was possible from the render alone.
issue.acceptance_test: Measure the rendered annotation type sizes in the source and confirm every in-text annotation is >= 8 pt at final trim size; enlarge if not. Acceptance: the smallest glyph in the figure is >= 8 pt and the right-hand descriptors are readable at 100% on a printed copy.

issue.figure: Archetypes table (Table 26.1) — continuation on this page
issue.issue: The table occupying the lower half of this page carries a repeated header row but no visible caption and no '(continued)' marker on the page; only two data rows ('Training', 'Real-time multimodal') are visible here, while the table's caption and earlier rows must be on PDF 445. A reader arriving at this page sees a headerless fragment of a table whose caption is two pages back, and the visible rows do not include the three scored families that FIG 26.1 visualizes.
issue.evidence: Rendered page shows a top rule, a header row ('Workload | Input | Output | Dominant constraint | First strategy to evaluate', with 'Dominant constraint' wrapping onto two lines), two rows, and a bottom rule — with no caption above or below. PDF 447 refers to 'the archetypes' and to 'the §26.2.1 matrix' as the source of the three scored families.

If so, add a '(Table 26.1 continued)' marker above the repeated header on this page; if the split is not required, keep the table whole. issue.page: PDF 457 / printed 437 (caption); table body on PDF 459

issue.issue: The caption 'Table 26.3 — Pattern templates in the library.' is the last line of PDF 457, while the table body does not appear until PDF 459 (PDF 458 is occupied by FIG 26.2). A caption separated from its table by a full page and an intervening figure is a visible production defect: on PDF 457 the reader sees a table title with no table, and on PDF 458 the figure interrupts the reference.

issue.issue: The provenance of FIG 26.1's dataset is cited to a section that cannot contain it. The prose says 'The three scored workload families from the §26.2.1 matrix — long-context RAG Q&A, high-throughput chat, and batch inference', but §26.2 on this same page is titled 'Quantization decision record' and has no visible subsections; the workload archetypes and the matrix belong to §26.1. issue.acceptance_test: Correct the reference to the section that actually contains the matrix (verify against the source; §26.1 is the candidate). Acceptance: the cited section exists, is titled consistently with the content it is cited for, and contains the matrix that FIG 26.1 visualizes.

issue.issue: Two reference problems in the same sentence. (a) 'applies the §6.2.1 model' points into Chapter 6, while the method being applied — 'locate the dominant constraint' — is the §26.1 archetypes method used on the facing pages; this looks like a dropped '2'. (b) 'the matrix's Short-prompt RAG Q&A row' names a row that appears nowhere else in the chapter; the three scored families are named on PDF 447 as 'long-context RAG Q&A, high-throughput chat, and batch inference', and the two rows visible on PDF 446 are 'Training' and 'Real-time multimodal'. 'Short-prompt RAG Q&A' may be a legitimate row on PDF 445, but the name conflicts with 'long-context RAG Q&A' and the reader has no way to resolve it.
issue.evidence: PDF 453: 'the matrix's Short-prompt RAG Q&A row (short input, tail latency/queueing dominant constraint), and applies the §6.2.1 model (locate the dominant constraint: tail latency/queueing under the p99 ~ 800 ms TTFT target)'. PDF 447: 'The three scored workload families from the §26.2.1 matrix — long-context RAG Q&A, high-throughput chat, and batch inference'. PDF 446 visible rows: 'Training', 'Real-time multimodal'. NOT VERIFIED against PDF 445.
issue.acceptance_test: Check PDF 445 for the archetypes table's full row set and for the existence of a §6.2.1. Correct the section number to the section that defines the dominant-constraint method, and confirm that the row name used on PDF 453 matches the row label printed in the table. issue.issue: The figure carries no evidence label, and its in-figure title ('Each family peaks on a different axis') states a claim that appears nowhere in the caption. The [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] label for these bar values exists only in the prose on the next page, so the figure is not self-describing: a reader who lifts the figure (or reads it on a screen where the facing page is not visible) sees authored numbers presented without their status.
issue.evidence: Caption as rendered: 'FIGURE 26.1: Workload fingerprints on the six axes.' In-figure title: 'Each family peaks on a different axis'. PDF 447: 'Because each bar is an author-chosen input, the bar values are [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]; only a value computed from them (e.g. a ratio of two bars) would be [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED].'
issue.acceptance_test: Add '[ILLUSTRATIVE]' to the figure subtitle or to the caption, and either carry the 'each family peaks on a different axis' claim into the caption or remove it from the figure. Acceptance: the figure states its own evidence status, and every claim asserted inside the figure is also stated in the caption.

issue.figure: FIG A.1 — right-hand annotations and footnote
issue.issue: The right-hand parameter-count annotations ('284B/13B active', '280B/104B active', '125B backbone/6B active (+51B re-gram, 4B MTP)', '320B/18B active') and the four-line asterisk footnote are set in the smallest type on the page and appear to sit at or below the 8 pt floor. This is where the figure's arithmetic lives, and it is also where the FIGA1-01 decimal-point ambiguity would be resolved — a reader who cannot resolve '104B' from '10.4B' cannot check the bar at all.
issue.evidence: Rendered at 150 dpi: the annotations and the footnote are visibly smaller than the bar value labels ('4.6%', '3.7%', '4.8%', '5.6%') and than the y-axis category labels. The Kimi annotation's decimal point is not resolvable in the render.
issue.acceptance_test: Measure the annotation and footnote type sizes in the source and confirm >= 8 pt at final trim size; enlarge if not, and re-check that the Kimi annotation's decimal point is unambiguous at 100% print size. Acceptance: every in-text annotation in the figure is >= 8 pt and each parameter count can be read without ambiguity.

issue.figure: FIGURE A.5 — Shared weights do not remove executed work (lower panel, "Actual stop" row)
issue.issue: A solid flow arrow runs from the dashed "pass 3 (not executed)" box to the orange "exit" box. The figure's own key defines solid arrows as flow and dashed boxes as not executed, so the drawing simultaneously asserts that pass 3 is not executed and that flow passes through it. The caption's claim "A true exit omits later work" is contradicted by the drawn path, which a reader scanning left-to-right reads as pass 1 -> pass 2 -> pass 3 -> exit.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 462, lower panel: boxes "pass 1", "pass 2", "pass 3" (dashed border, italic "(not executed)"), "exit" (orange). The connector pass 2 -> pass 3 is dashed; the connector pass 3 -> exit is solid with a solid arrowhead. Key text below the figure: "Dashed arrows = weight reuse; dashed box = not executed" and "Solid arrows = flow; labelled boxes mark exit / selection".
issue.acceptance_test: Redraw so the solid flow path is pass 1 -> pass 2 -> exit, with the "pass 3 (not executed)" ghost placed off the main path (e.g., offset above the row) and reached only by a dashed arrow from pass 2; or, if the linear layout is retained, replace the pass 3 -> exit connector with a dashed/annotated "skipped" connector and add an explicit flow-terminus marker at pass 2. Acceptance: on visual inspection of the rendered page, no solid arrow originates from any box labelled "(not executed)", and the Actual-stop path can be read as two executed passes.

issue.figure: FIGURE A.5 — top panel (shared weight set / passes / iteration caches) and its arrow key
issue.issue: The key "Dashed arrows = weight reuse" is false for one of the two classes of dashed arrows in the top panel. The dashed arrows that connect each pass box to its "iteration N / history cache" box represent a cache write (data flow), not weight reuse. As drawn, the figure's own key tells the reader that the history caches are reached by weight reuse — the exact inverse of the point the figure exists to make (weights are shared; history state is not).
issue.evidence: Rendered page 462, top panel: "one shared core weight set" -> three dashed arrows -> pass 1 / pass 2 / pass 3 (weight reuse, correctly keyed); pass 1 / pass 2 / pass 3 -> "iteration 1 / history cache", "iteration 2 / history cache", "iteration 3 / history cache" via dashed arrows (cache write, mis-keyed). Key line: "Dashed arrows = weight reuse; dashed box = not executed". In-figure note: "Separate iteration caches shown; sharing is not automatic".
issue.acceptance_test: Use two distinct arrow styles and label both in the key, e.g. "dashed = shared weight set applied to each pass" and "solid thin = history cache written by that pass (not shared)". Acceptance: no arrow style in the figure carries two different meanings, and the key line for the pass->cache arrows names a cache write.

issue.issue: The caption describes only the lower panel ("Distinct iteration caches for the separate-case") and never states what the upper panel shows, even though the upper panel carries the figure's title claim ("Shared weights do not remove executed work"). The upper panel's structure is described only by the in-figure note "Separate iteration caches shown; sharing is not automatic". Separately, the caption names the mechanism "shared-depth execution" while the figure title names it "Shared weights" — two names for one thing in one figure.
issue.evidence: Caption as printed: "FIGURE A.5: Shared-depth execution reuses weights, not necessarily history state. Distinct iteration caches for the separate-case. A true exit omits later work; ..." Figure title as printed: "Shared weights do not remove executed work".
issue.acceptance_test: Caption names both panels explicitly (e.g. "upper panel: one weight set applied across three passes, each pass writing its own history cache; lower panel: two exit paths from the same passes") and uses one term for the mechanism throughout the figure and caption. Acceptance: a reader who sees only the caption can state what the upper panel depicts.

issue.issue: The first legend entry ends with a dangling "— 2022": "Model architecture (dashed) — foundation, efficiency, MoE; darker shade = MoE — 2022". Read literally the date attaches to the legend entry as a whole rather than to the MoE shade cue, and it duplicates the "2022" already printed beside the MoE Transformer bar. A reader may reasonably take the legend to be dated 2022.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 454, legend line 1 reads "Model architecture (dashed) — foundation, efficiency, MoE; darker shade = MoE — 2022". The MoE Transformer bar carries its own right-hand marker "2022".
issue.acceptance_test: Remove the trailing "— 2022" from the legend (the bar already carries the year), or rewrite as "darker shade = MoE (2022)". Acceptance: no date appears in the legend except as an explicit era-marker key, and no legend entry can be read as carrying a date.

issue.issue: The legend asserts a shade cue ("darker shade = MoE") but demonstrates only one brown swatch, so the cue is not shown. The reader must compare the three architecture bars to discover which is the darker one, and in grayscale the cue depends entirely on that comparison rather than on the legend.

issue.acceptance_test: Add a second, darker brown swatch to the legend (or split the entry into "architecture" and "MoE architecture" with two swatches) so the shade cue is legible without comparing bars. Acceptance: the two browns remain distinguishable in a grayscale proof and the legend alone identifies which bar is the MoE one.

issue.figure: FIGURE A.3 — in-figure annotation vs. drawn year markers
issue.issue: The figure's own annotation claims a precision convention it does not apply: "approximate era markers (≈), not release dates", yet no bar carries an "≈" glyph — the years are printed bare (2017, 2020, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2024, 2025, 2025, 2026). The caption's "The dates are approximate era markers, not release dates" is therefore carried by prose alone, and the "(≈)" in the annotation points at a convention that is absent from the drawing.

Bar markers as printed: 2017, 2020, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2024, 2025, 2025, 2026 — no approximation glyph on any of them.
issue.acceptance_test: Either prefix each year marker with "≈" (e.g. "≈2017") or change the annotation to "approximate era markers, not release dates" and delete the unused "(≈)". issue.figure: FIGURE A.4 — right-hand chapter cross-reference column
issue.issue: Seven of the eight bands carry a chapter cross-reference; the band "Inside post-training (build-time)" carries none. The asymmetry reads as an omission rather than as a deliberate statement that no chapter covers build-time post-training. Notation is also inconsistent within the column: "Ch17-20" is a range while every other entry is a comma list ("Ch18, Ch20", "Ch19, Ch24", "Ch7, Ch8", "Ch3, Ch8").
issue.evidence: Rendered page 456, right column top to bottom: "Ch18, Ch20"; "Ch17-20, Ch24"; "Ch19, Ch24"; "Ch22"; [blank, aligned with "Inside post-training (build-time)"]; "Ch10"; "Ch7, Ch8"; "Ch3, Ch8".
issue.acceptance_test: Give the post-training band a chapter reference, or an explicit note such as "no dedicated chapter", and normalize the range notation to the comma-list form used elsewhere. Acceptance: every band carries either a reference or a stated reason for having none, and all references use one notation; each chapter number is checked against the book's chapter list.

issue.issue: The system-side / model-side distinction is encoded by hue alone in the legend ("blue = system-side · green = model-side"). In grayscale the two families collapse to similar mid-tones; the only non-hue cues are the rotated SYSTEM / MODEL labels at the left and an unexplained lightness jump at the blue/green boundary. The legend does not tell the reader that the left-hand labels carry the family distinction, so a grayscale reader is left to infer it.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 456: legend line "blue = system-side · green = model-side · within each family, shade = further from the weights is darker". Five system-side bands are blue (navy at top through pale blue at bottom); three model-side bands are green (dark green at top through pale green at bottom). The only non-color family markers are the rotated "SYSTEM" and "MODEL" labels beside the vertical arrow.
issue.acceptance_test: Add a non-hue cue for family membership — e.g. a bracket or group label per family, or a hatch on the model-side bands — and state in the legend that family membership is also marked by the SYSTEM / MODEL brackets. issue.issue: The footnote states "x% remaining = (100 − x)% reduction, for every row" with an exact equality while every input in the table is approximate ("~7%", "~10%", "~23%", "~33%"). The derived reduction inherits the input's approximation, so the exact "=" is inconsistent with the operator discipline the table itself uses. This is the one place in the figure where a derived quantity is stated more precisely than its inputs.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 451, table cells: "100%→~7%", "100%→~10%", "100%→~23%", "100%→~33%". Footnote: "*Metric scopes differ. x% remaining = (100 − x)% reduction, for every row."
issue.acceptance_test: Change to "x% remaining ≈ (100 − x)% reduction", or add "(exact only if x is exact)". Acceptance: the operator used on the derived reduction matches the precision of the value it is derived from, and no derived quantity in the figure is stated more precisely than its inputs.

GLM-5.3-Flash row: KV cell "reported 2026-08 per-layer KV (BF16)"; Compute cell "attention only per head / layer" (no date). Source line: "DeepSeek V4: arXiv 2606.19348."
issue.acceptance_test: Move the reporting date to the row level (e.g. under the model name) or repeat it in the compute scope cell, so both metrics in a row carry the same date. issue.issue: The caption directs the reader to "the paragraph above beginning 'Same message as Fig 7.1's GQA line'". Because FIGURE A.2 sits at the top of printed p. 451, that paragraph is on the preceding page, so "above" is not resolvable from the figure's own page and the reader must hunt for it.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 451 shows the figure occupying the top of the page with the caption below it; no paragraph beginning "Same message as Fig 7.1's GQA line" appears on this page.
issue.acceptance_test: Replace "the paragraph above" with an explicit pointer (e.g. "the paragraph on p. 450 beginning ..."). Acceptance: the quoted opening words are verified to occur at the referenced location, and the pointer resolves without a page-flip guess.

issue.issue: The box warns only that the rows are not a cross-model performance ranking. It does not warn that a FLOP ratio is not a latency ratio, which is the most likely misreading of the compute column ("100%→~10%", "100%→~27%", "100%→~33%") — a reader may infer a proportional speedup. The book's own argument elsewhere separates FLOPs from latency, so the figure should carry the same guard rather than relying on the reader to remember it.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 451, box text: "NOT A CROSS-MODEL PERFORMANCE RANKING / Each row is relative to that model's OWN stated baseline — no shared scale". Compute column values: "100%→~10%" (DeepSeek V4-Flash), "100%→~27%" (DeepSeek V4-Pro), "100%→~33%" (GLM-5.3-Flash), with scope "single-token inference FLOPS" and "attention only per head / layer".
issue.acceptance_test: Extend the box or the footnote with one clause (e.g. "a FLOP ratio is not a latency ratio") and confirm the caption repeats the guard. Acceptance: the figure contains no wording from which a reader can derive a latency or throughput claim from the compute column.

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.5 — 'KV cache size vs context, by attention geometry (full-MHA vs GQA)'
issue.issue: The plotted GQA FP16 curve is computed with a 16x KV reduction (~0.16 MB/token) while the caption and the figure's own parenthetical state an 8x reduction (64:8 query-to-KV head ratio, 2.62 -> 0.33 MB/token). The legend, the plotted curve, and the in-plot value 'GQA FP16 at 128K = 21 GB' are mutually inconsistent with the caption and with the figure's own '(2.62 -> 0.33 MB/tok)' annotation.
issue.evidence: Recomputation from the book's own canonical geometry (80 layers, 64 query heads, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, FP16 = 2 B): full-MHA KV/token = 2 (K,V) x 64 x 128 x 2 B x 80 = 2,621,440 B = 2.62 MB (matches legend and caption). GQA at 64:8 = 2 x 8 x 128 x 2 B x 80 = 327,680 B = 0.32768 MB/token = 0.33 MB (matches caption '8x smaller' and the in-plot '(2.62 -> 0.33 MB/tok)'). The figure's legend reads 'GQA FP16 (~0.16 MB/tok)' and the plotted green curve passes ~16 GB at 100K and ~21 GB at 128K, which corresponds to 0.16 MB/token = 163,840 B/token, i.e. 4 KV heads (64:16, a 16x reduction). At 128K the caption-consistent value is 0.32768 x 128,000 = 41.9 GB, not 21 GB. Corroboration that 0.33 is the intended value: the caption's 'the GQA FP16 line reaches that budget only at ~1.32M tokens' is 436,000 MB / 0.33 MB = 1.32M (and 436,000 / 0.32768 = 1.33M); the plotted 0.16 curve would reach 436 GB only at 2.73M tokens. So the caption's headline conclusion is derived from 0.33 while the drawn curve encodes 0.16.
issue.acceptance_test: Regenerate the figure from the canonical geometry and assert: (a) the GQA FP16 series equals 0.32768 MB/token and passes through (128K, 41.9 GB) and (1.33M, 436 GB); (b) the legend reads 'GQA FP16 (~0.33 MB/tok)'; (c) the in-plot annotation reads 'GQA FP16 at 128K = 42 GB (2.62 -> 0.33 MB/tok)'; (d) the caption's '8x smaller' and '~1.32M tokens' are unchanged. If the 16x figure is intentional, the caption's '64:8' and '8x smaller' must be corrected instead and the head ratio stated in the legend.

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.6 — 'Memory floor: inference vs fine-tuning (canonical 70B, FP16 unless noted)'
issue.issue: The note enumerating the full-fine-tune components does not sum to the plotted bar. The note says 'Full fine-tune: FP16 weights + FP16 grads + Adam m/v (~ 16 B/param)' but those components total 12 B/param, not 16. The bar (~1120 GB) and the caption (~1,120 GB) both correspond to 16 B/param, which is the mixed-precision AdamW figure (FP32 master weights + FP32 grads + m + v), not the FP16 breakdown the note gives.
issue.evidence: 2 B (FP16 weights) + 2 B (FP16 grads) + 4 B (FP32 Adam m) + 4 B (FP32 Adam v) = 12 B/param -> 70e9 x 12 = 840 GB, which is 280 GB below the drawn bar. 16 B/param -> 70e9 x 16 = 1,120 GB, matching the bar and the caption. The note's parenthetical '(~ 16 B/param)' is therefore inconsistent with its own enumerated components; the reader cannot tell whether the missing 4 B/param is an FP32 master-weight copy (the standard explanation) or an arithmetic error.
issue.acceptance_test: Make the note's enumerated components sum to the plotted total and state the precision of each: either 'FP32 master weights + FP32 grads + Adam m/v (16 B/param)' or 'FP16 weights + FP16 grads + Adam m/v (12 B/param)' with the bar relabelled ~840 GB. Add a build-time assertion that (bytes/param) x 70e9 equals the plotted bar height for every bar.

issue.figure: FIGURE 6.2 — 'Latency distribution: the mean hides the tail'
issue.issue: The red dashed vertical line labelled 'sample p99' is drawn at ~5.0 s (coincident with the straggler cluster), but the figure's own annotation box states 'sample p99 (interpolation) = 1.33s' and the prose on printed p. 98 states 'this sample's p99 (= 3.33 s)'. Three mutually inconsistent values are given for one quantity, and the drawn line position contradicts both the box and the prose. The box separately lists 'population p99 = 5.0 s', which is what the drawn line at 5.0 s actually represents.
issue.evidence: Within the figure alone: the red dashed line sits at x = 5.0 s (the straggler cluster) while the annotation box gives the sample p99 as 1.33 s. Cross-page: printed p. 98 reads 'The population p99 is 5.0 s, even this sample's p99 (= 3.33 s) still looks healthy'. The figure's box reads 'sample p99 (interpolation) = 1.33s'. A reader who trusts the drawn line concludes the sample p99 is 5.0 s; a reader who trusts the box concludes 1.33 s; a reader who trusts the prose concludes 3.33 s. The figure's own construction (N = 10,000; 9,900 log-normal draws with median 0.8 s; 100 stragglers at 5.0 s; linear interpolation on the sorted sample) implies the interpolated p99 sits between the largest log-normal draw (~1.3 s) and the first straggler (5.0 s), i.e. ~1.3-1.4 s, which matches the box and not the prose or the line.
issue.acceptance_test: Relabel the red dashed line 'population p99 = 5.0 s' (the value the box already assigns to it), and reconcile the sample p99 to a single number across the figure box and printed p. 98. Add a build-time check that every percentile printed in the figure equals the value computed from the same sorted sample used to draw the histogram, and that the drawn line's x position equals the printed value within one pixel.

issue.figure: FIGURE 6.2 — 'Latency distribution: the mean hides the tail'
issue.issue: The red hatched region is labelled '1% stragglers (> 5 s cross the SLO)'. The straggler cluster is AT 5.0 s, not above 5 s, per the prose ('a 1% straggler cluster at 5.0 s') and the figure's own box ('population p99 = 5.0 s'). The parenthetical reads as a claim that the stragglers exceed 5 s, which is false and also inconsistent with the drawn region, which is centred on 5.0 s and straddles it.

The hatched band in the figure spans roughly 4.5-5.5 s, i.e. centred on 5.0 s. The label's '> 5 s' is therefore both wrong and inconsistent with the geometry it labels.
issue.acceptance_test: Change the label to '1% stragglers (cluster at 5.0 s, past the 2 s SLO)' or equivalent; assert that no annotation in the figure states a strict inequality that the drawn geometry contradicts.

issue.figure: FIGURE 6.2 — 'Latency distribution: the mean hides the tail'
issue.issue: The 2 s line is labelled in the figure as 'SLO 2 s (TTFT budget)' but the caption calls the same line the '2 s request-latency line' and explains that request-latency violations are a superset of TTFT violations. Labelling the line '(TTFT budget)' invites exactly the conflation the caption is written to prevent, and the caption's phrase 'the p95 SLO is met' adds a third characterisation of the same line.

Caption: 'while 1% of requests exceed the 2 s request-latency line - a superset of TTFT violations, and a tail a p99 SLO does not surface' and 'the light band shades the full SLO-violating region (> 2 s)'. issue.figure: FIGURE 6.2 — 'Latency distribution: the mean hides the tail'
issue.issue: The p90 (0.94 s) and p95 (0.99 s) reference lines are 0.05 s apart on an axis spanning 0-6 s. At print size this is roughly 2-3 pt of separation, so the two dashed lines are effectively coincident and only the offset text labels distinguish them. issue.figure: FIGURE 7.5 — 'KV cache size vs context, by attention geometry (full-MHA vs GQA)'
issue.issue: Three bare ratio annotations ('8x' near 10K, '3.5x' near 100K, '16x' near 1000K) are placed inside the plot with no stated referent. The reader cannot tell what is being divided by what, and the three different values at three different context lengths cannot be reconciled with the caption's single stated 8x GQA reduction (which would be a constant, not three values).

The in-plot labels '8x', '3.5x', '16x' appear at three x positions with no accompanying text naming the two quantities compared. issue.figure: FIGURE 7.5 — 'KV cache size vs context, by attention geometry (full-MHA vs GQA)'
issue.issue: The annotation '9.5K max context (32K in ~500 GB)' contains a quantity (~500 GB) that is not derivable from any curve, reference line, or legend entry in the figure, and the parenthetical's referent is never stated. The reader is left to guess whether 500 GB is a KV pool, a total residency, or a hardware capacity.

None yields ~500 GB. The caption explains the 9.5K figure ('~24.9 GB at 9.5K (total weights+KV residency then ~165 GB, 7.1)') but says nothing about 500 GB. The vertical 9.5K guide also appears to run the full plot height rather than terminating at the constraint it marks, so it reads as a generic x-position rather than a limit.

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.5 — 'KV cache size vs context, by attention geometry (full-MHA vs GQA)'
issue.issue: The right-hand annotation block ('FP16 full-MHA at 128K = 335 GB / FP8 full-MHA at 128K = 168 GB / GQA FP16 at 128K = 21 GB ...') is set in small type directly over the plotted region, where it sits on top of gridlines and the flat '8xH100 raw (640 GB)' line, and it is the only place the reader can find the 128K values. The 335 GB and 168 GB values are correct (2.62 x 128,000 = 335 GB; 1.31 x 128,000 = 168 GB), so the block is worth keeping but must be legible and correct.

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.2 — 'History recurrence and attention history have different lifetimes'
issue.issue: The caption states 'the KV row is cumulative (snapshot 3 retains KV1+KV3)', but the figure's third snapshot shows KV1, KV2 and KV3. The caption's parenthetical contradicts the drawn content and would, if read literally, assert that KV2 is discarded.
issue.evidence: Figure, bottom row: the third group contains three boxes labelled KV1, KV2, KV3, captioned '3 cached tokens'. Caption: 'the KV row is cumulative (snapshot 3 retains KV1+KV3)'. The figure's own sub-label '3 cached tokens' and the caption's word 'cumulative' both indicate KV1+KV2+KV3.
issue.acceptance_test: Change the caption to '(snapshot 3 retains KV1+KV2+KV3)'. Add a caption/figure cross-check that every token identifier named in a caption appears in the corresponding drawn group.

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.2 — 'History recurrence and attention history have different lifetimes'
issue.issue: The figure draws three equal-weight state boxes ('state after t1', 'state after t2', 'state after t3') side by side, which visually implies that three recurrent states are held simultaneously. The caption and the figure's own note both assert the opposite ('recurrent snapshots are successive, not jointly retained'). The drawn geometry therefore permits exactly the wrong inference, and the correction is carried only by a small note.
issue.evidence: Top row: three identically styled pink boxes labelled 'state after t1 / fixed-size state', 'state after t2 / ...', 'state after t3 / ...'. Bottom row: the KV boxes are cumulative and grow (1, 2, 3 boxes), so the two rows are visually parallel in weight even though their lifetimes differ. The figure's note 'Arrows = token input / state flow; snapshots are schematic' and the caption's 'successive, not jointly retained' are the only signals that the earlier states are overwritten.
issue.acceptance_test: Make the visual encoding carry the claim: fade or outline the superseded state boxes (t1, t2) and keep only the latest filled, or stack the snapshots with an explicit 'overwritten' marker on the earlier ones. Assert that the number of visually solid state boxes equals the number of retained states (one).

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.3 — 'Quantization choices are not execution guarantees'
issue.issue: Two of the three dispatch branches are visually and verbally near-identical and the figure never states what distinguishes them. 'Fused dequant / Weight dequantization e.g., W4A16 GEMM' and 'Reconstruct / Higher-precision weights + GEMM' both end in a GEMM against higher-precision weights; the reader cannot tell whether the distinction is kernel fusion versus materialisation, memory residency, or simply which kernel the vendor ships.
issue.evidence: Bottom row of the figure: 'Native FP4 math / Compact low-bit operand arithmetic'; 'Fused dequant / Weight dequantization e.g., W4A16 GEMM'; 'Reconstruct / Higher-precision weights + GEMM'. The caption likewise does not disambiguate them ('loading still requires a kernel-required runtime layout with compatible dispatch').
issue.acceptance_test: Give each branch a one-line discriminator that names the resource it changes (e.g. 'dequantise inside the GEMM prologue - no FP16 weight copy in HBM' versus 'materialise FP16 weights once - costs 2 B/param of extra HBM but uses ordinary GEMM kernels'), and state the memory consequence of each in the caption.

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.3 — 'Quantization choices are not execution guarantees'
issue.issue: The note 'Repacking does not imply numerical conversion' is attached to the load/repack step but reads as a general statement about the whole path, which the 'Reconstruct' branch contradicts (reconstructing higher-precision weights is a numerical up-conversion). Symmetrically, the bottom note 'No compatible kernel: reject; fallback is not guaranteed' sits directly beneath a branch ('Reconstruct') that a reader will naturally read as the fallback.
issue.evidence: Figure: 'Runtime tensors in the kernel-required layout / Repacking does not imply numerical conversion' -> 'compatible dispatch' -> 'Reconstruct / Higher-precision weights + GEMM'; bottom notes 'Only supported combinations can load and execute.' and 'No compatible kernel: reject; fallback is not guaranteed.' Caption: 'Unsupported combinations may be rejected; fallback is not guaranteed.' The figure therefore simultaneously shows a fallback-looking branch and states that fallback is not guaranteed, without distinguishing a deliberate load-time choice from an automatic runtime fallback.
issue.acceptance_test: Scope the repacking note explicitly to the arrow ('repacking changes layout only; values are unchanged') and label the 'Reconstruct' branch as a deliberate load-time decision ('explicit up-conversion at load time - a choice, not an automatic fallback'), so that the two statements no longer appear to conflict.

issue.issue: The caption and the figure subtitle both assert that bar widths are proportional to bytes ('Payload and local-scale bar widths are proportional to bytes'; 'Bar widths are proportional to bytes and local-scale bytes only'), but the scale segments - the entire point of the figure - appear to be drawn wider than their byte share, and the two bars appear to be drawn to equal total width despite representing 17 B and 18 B. If a minimum-width rule was used to keep the scale segments visible, the proportionality claim is false exactly where it matters.
issue.evidence: MXFP4 bar: light payload segment (16 B) spans roughly 335 px and the dark scale segment (1 B) roughly 25 px, i.e. about 21 px/B. NVFP4 bar: two light segments (8 B each) span roughly 145 px each (about 18 px/B) and the dark '2 B scales' segment spans roughly 70 px, i.e. about 35 px/B - roughly twice the byte-proportional width. Both bars appear to span the same total x-range although they represent 17 B and 18 B (a 5.9% difference that should be visible on a common scale).
issue.acceptance_test: Measure the rendered segment widths and assert the ratios 16:1 (MXFP4) and 8:8:2 (NVFP4) within 5%, and that the NVFP4 bar is 5.9% longer than the MXFP4 bar. If a minimum-width rule is required for legibility, replace the proportionality claim with an explicit scale break or a note that the scale segments are drawn at minimum width, and move the byte counts into the labels (which already carry them).

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.6 — 'Memory floor: inference vs fine-tuning (canonical 70B, FP16 unless noted)'
issue.issue: The figure asserts '~5 GB over 2xH100' for the inference bar, but the y-axis spans 0-1400 GB, so a 5 GB difference between the bar top (165 GB) and the 160 GB reference line is about 0.36% of the axis height - roughly one pixel at print size. The claim is therefore not verifiable from the chart, and the bar top and the 2xH100 line are visually indistinguishable.
issue.evidence: Y-axis ticks run 0, 200, 400 ... 1400 GB. Inference bar labelled '~165 GB'; legend line '2xH100 (160 GB)'. 165 - 160 = 5 GB = 0.36% of the 1400 GB axis. The annotation '~5 GB over 2xH100' is the only carrier of this fact.
issue.acceptance_test: Add a zoomed inset or a broken axis for the inference bar region so that the 160 GB and 165 GB levels are visually separable, or replace the annotation with an explicit statement that the overshoot is below the chart's resolution and give the numbers in the caption.

issue.issue: The boxed note '8 query heads : 1 KV head (x 8 groups)' is inconsistent with the drawing, which shows three groups (three K/V boxes) with an ellipsis. The parenthetical '(x 8 groups)' is ambiguous: it reads either as 'the canonical model has 8 KV-head groups' (64 query heads total) or as 'the ratio is multiplied by 8', and neither reading is what the picture shows.
issue.evidence: Figure: three groups of eight blue query-head glyphs, each fanning into one orange 'K/V' box, followed by an ellipsis on both rows. Boxed note: '8 query heads : 1 KV head (x 8 groups)'. Caption: 'the load-bearing number is the n_q : n_kv ratio (8 : 1 here) - 8 query heads share one KV head, so the per-token KV falls x8'.
issue.acceptance_test: Make the count explicit and consistent with the drawing, e.g. '8 query heads : 1 KV head (3 of 8 groups shown)' or '64 query heads : 8 KV heads (8 groups of 8)'. Assert that the group count named in the note matches the number of groups drawn or is explicitly marked as elided.

issue.issue: Grayscale distinguishability of the percentile markers is weak: p50 is a green dashed line and p90/p95 are blue dashed lines, which in grayscale differ mainly in a small luminance step, and the p90/p95 pair is already nearly coincident (see FIG-6.2-04). issue.issue: Unit wording: both local lines read '= 4.25 bit/value' and '= 4.5 bit/value'. The unit is a count of bits per value and should be plural ('bits/value'), consistent with the book's other per-token units.
issue.evidence: Figure text: 'Local: 17 B / 32 = 0.53125 B/value = 4.25 bit/value' and 'Local: 18 B / 32 = 0.5625 B/value = 4.5 bit/value'. The arithmetic is correct (17/32 = 0.53125 B = 4.25 bits; 18/32 = 0.5625 B = 4.5 bits).
issue.acceptance_test: Change 'bit/value' to 'bits/value' in both lines; grep the manuscript for 'bit/value' and normalise.

issue.issue: Label placement is inconsistent between the two bars: payload labels ('32 E2M1 values = 16 B', '16 values = 8 B') sit inside the bar, while the scale labels ('1 B scale', '2 B scales') sit below and outside it. The reader must move the eye between two different label positions to compare the two rows, and the scale labels are the ones that carry the figure's actual message.

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.2 — 'History recurrence and attention history have different lifetimes'
issue.issue: Caption grammar: 'a recurrent layer group updates hidden state, fixed-shape state' is a comma splice and is missing an article; the intended meaning is that the recurrent group updates a hidden state which is fixed-shape.
